Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Barnes ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  condition 

of  affairs  at  New  Berne. 

U.  S.  Tug  Poppy, 

Hampton  Roads ,  February  4, 1864 — 10  p.  m. 

My  Dear  Admiral:  I  have  just  left  the  general,  and  have  explained, 
as  you  desired,  our  situation.  The  following  additional  particulars  have 
just  been  received: 

The  enemy  are  mostly  on  the  south  side  of  the  Trent,  in  number  not 
more  than  8,000.  Their  efforts  are  principally  against  Fort  Gaston, 
which  holds  out  manfully  and  is  likely  to  do  so.  There  is  a  small  force 
on  the  north  side,  but  inactive.  There  is  plenty  of  ammunition  and 
ninety  days’ provisions  at  New  Berne.  Citizens  (white  and  black)  to 
the  number  of  five  full  companies,  have  volunteered  for  the  defense  of 
the  place,  and  are  under  arms  in  the  intrenchments.  Palmer  is  reason¬ 
ably  confident,  and  General  Butler  thinks  he  can  make  a  long  siege  of 
it.  He  does  not  entertain  the  idea  of  going  there  himself.  He  says 
that  everything  has  been  done  that  can  be,  and  if  the  fortifications  are 
worth  a  cent,  the  place  can  stand  the  attack. 

The  Underwriter  was  lying  aground  off  Foster’s  Wharf  at  3  o’clock 
on  the  morning  of  the  2d  instant.  Several  of  her  boats  were  away  on 
some  sort  of  an  expedition,  object  unknown.  The  enemy  approached 
in  boats  and  answered  their  hail  properly;  mistaking  them  for  her  own 
boats,  they  were  permitted  to  come  alongside  and  get  on  board  without 
hindrance.  The  rebels  then  set  tire  to  her  and  she  soon  blew  up,  all 
this  within  a  few  hundred  yards  from  the  general’s  headquarters.  Most 
of  the  officers  and  crew  were  then  captured,  and  the  enemy  were  pro¬ 
ceeding  to  carry  their  prisoners  off  in  their  boats  when  our  people, 
headed,  as  it  is  understood,  by  Engineer  Allen,  rose  upon  their  captors 
in  the  boats,  seized  the  officers  and  men,  and  brought  them  safely  into 
New  Berne,  where  they  now  are.  So  there  is  a  little  leaven  to  the  loaf. 
The  enemy  is  reported  as  moving  on  Plymouth  and  Washington. 

At  8  o’clock  on  the  morning  of  the  2d,  Flusser,  with  the  Miami  and 
three  other  gunboats,  was  at  Northwest  Point,  mouth  of  the  Neuse,  on 
his  way  up  to  New  Berne.  The  enemy  have  possession  of  Newport  and 
communication  with  Beaufort  is  cut  off.  General  Butler  is  going  to 
send  the  Brewster  to  New  Berne  to-morrow  forenoon,  and  if  you  have 
any  dispatches,  he  will  delay  her  for  you.  If  you  have  nothing  to  send, 
please  telegraph  him  in  the  morning.  He  has  just  received  a  dispatch 
from  Mr.  Fox,  saying  that  he  (Mr.  Fox)  will  be  here  Saturday,  wind  and 
weather  permitting.  I  have  sent  the  telegrams  and  have  delivered  the 
order  in  regard  to  ammunition  to  Commander  Lynch. 

Very  truly  and  respectfully, 

Acting  Kear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee,  IT.  S.  Navy. 


J.  S.  Barnes.

Report  of  Fleet  Paymaster  Upham ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  referring  to  the  investment 
by  the  enemy  of  New  Berne ,  N.  C. 


Naval  Store  House, 
Bogue  Island,  February  4,  1864. 


Sir  :  This  part  of  the  country  is  in  a  terrible  state  of  excitement. 
The  rebels  are  in  full  force  in  this  district,  estimated  at  from  6,000  to 
25,000.  New  Berne  is  strongly  invested  and  surrounded,  it  is  said. 
Newport  taken  after  a  very  severe  fight,  in  which  the  Ninth  Vermont 
lost  160  men.  Rebels’  loss  said  to  be  500,  camp  and  stores  of  all  kinds 
burned  before  leaving.  Beaufort  and  Morehead  threatened,  but  it  is 
believed  that  the  gunboats  and  fort  can  hold  both  places.  Women  and 
children  in  fort  or  on  board  ships.  A  large  quantity  of  naval  stores 
already  destroyed.  It  will  be  impossible  to  get  at  the  amount  at  pres¬ 
ent.  The  railroad  and  telegraph  in  possession  of  the  enemy. 

I  shipped  yesterday  and  the  day  before  most  of  the  stores  in  this 
vicinity,  say  about  $20,000  worth.  It  was  very  fortunate  I  was  on  the 
ground,  as  in  the  excitement  no  one  else  would  have  attended  to  naval 
stores.  I  do  not  think  it  would  be  proper  or  prudent  for  me  to  leave 
the  ground  until  I  see  how  matters  are  to  terminate.  My  main  agent, 
Mr.  McChesney,  was  taken  prisoner  on  Monday  while  attending  to  his 
business  near  Batch  elder’s  Creek,  which  fact  makes  it  much  more  neces¬ 
sary  that  I  should  be  here  at  least  for  a  short  time. 

1  received  a  telegram  from  Paymaster  Mellach  on  Monday  in  which 
he  said,  “My  money  is  safe.'’ 

I  hope  the  naval  stores  at  New  Berne  are  safe.  I  trust  the  gunboats 
will  protect  them.  Mr.  Wood’s  clerk  was  at  New  Berne  on  Saturday; 
says  he  left  there  the  Commodore  Hull,  Underwriter,  Lockwood ,  Hetzel, 
and  he  thinks  one  other.  The  Underwriter  was  a  total  loss.  It  is 
understood  here  that  about  one  half  ot  officers  and  crew  ot  the  ship 
were  away  on  duty,  the  balance  taken  prisoners. 

It  is  believed  here  that  the  rebels  have  been  repulsed  at  Fort  Totten, 
and  that  New  Berne  may  hold  out  until  reinforcements  arrive. 

Two  thousand  Union  troops  only  at  New  Berne  and  600  at  the  fort, 
Morehead,  and  Beaufort,  a  very  small  force  to  cope  with  a  large  desper¬ 
ate  force  of  from  10,000  to  20,000  men.  You  will  receive  an  official 
statement  of  facts  from  Captain  Dove,  and  please  receive  this  as  a  sim¬ 


ple  memorandum. 

Very  respectfully,  your 


obedient  servant, 

Charles  C.  Upham,  U.  S.  Navy. 


[Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee.] 


Pursuit  and  destruction  of  the  blockade  runner  Nut  field,  February  4-5, 

1864. 


Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Roe,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Sassacus. 

U.  S.  S.  Sassacus, 

Off  New  River  Inlet,  North  Carolina ,  February  4,  1864. 

(Received  February  13.) 

Sir:  Having  destroyed  the  steam  paddle-wheel  blockade  runnei 
Wild  Dayrell,  of  about  440  tons,  I  stood  out  to  sea  last  night  and 
regained  my  position  on  the  Bermuda  line  at  daylight  this  morning. 
About  7  o’clock  a.  m.  I  discovered  a  blockade  runner  to  the  northward 


460  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

and  westward,  when  I  fired  up,  and  at  about  8  o’clock  was  in  full  pur¬ 
suit.  The  chase  was  about  12  miles  distant;  she  changed  course  and 
headed  in  for  the  land.  I  steadily  gained  upon  her,  logging  about  12 J 
to  13  knots  per  hour,  when  I  perceived  she  was  throwing  overboard 
her  cargo. 

A  little  after  12  o’clock  I  got  her  within  long  range  of  my  100-pounder 
rifle  and  opened  fire,  planting  my  shell  all  about  her. 

Being  to  the  southward  of  her,  I  cut  her  off,  when,  at  about  quarter 
before  1  o’clock,  she  headed  in  for  this  inlet  and  ran  ashore.  Her  crew 
fired  her,  left  her  engine  running,  and  fled  precipitately  in  their  boats. 
I  boarded  her  about  1  o’clock  p.  in.,  and  found  her  to  be  the  paddle- 
wheel  steamer  Nuffield,  of  750  tons,  from  Bermuda,  inward  bound. 
One  of  her  boats  had  capsized,  and  1  rescued  from  drowning  her  purser. 
The  rest  of  the  boat’s  crew  were  supposed  to  be  drowned.  We  com¬ 
menced  putting  out  the  fire  in  her  hold  and  made  arrangements  for 
hauling  her  off,  if  possible. 

From  the  purser,  whom  we  rescued  from  drowning,  I  learn  that  she 
is  a  perfectly  new  iron  steamer,  having  an  assorted  cargo  of  merchan¬ 
dise,  munitions  of  war,  Enfield  rifles,  and  a  battery  of  eight  Whitworth 
rifled  guns,  and  a  quantity  of  pig  lead.  This  battery  and  the  lead  she 
threw  overboard  during  the  chase. 

She  had  been  among  the  blockading  fleet  below  last  night,  but  made 
her  escape  and  fell  into  our  hands  to-day.  The  chase  of  the  Sassacus 
was  very  beautiful,  for  the  Nuffield  is  one  of  the  last  and  best  steamers 
out  of  the  Thames,  and  we  overhauled  her  handsomely. 

February  5,  1864. — I  continue  the  above  report.  During  the  preced¬ 
ing  night  1  found  the  Nuffield  so  far  thrown  up  by  the  action  of  the 
sea,  that  it  was  utterly  impossible  to  get  her  off.  I  therefore  removed 
from  her  the  Enfield  rifles,  a  quantity  of  quinine,  and  several  compasses, 
and  set  her  on  fire.  About  this  time  the  U.  S.  S.  Florida  came  up,  and 
both  vessels  riddled  her  with  shot.  I  saw  the  vessel  thoroughly  de¬ 
stroyed,  and  put  to  sea  about  7  o’clock  this  p.  m. 

I  transmit  herewith  the  appraisement  of  the  value  of  the  Nuffield , 
and  also  a  list  of  arms,  etc.,  taken  from  her,  and  await  your  orders  as 
to  the  disposition  to  be  made  of  them.  I  allowed  the  officers  and  crew 
to  take  some  provisions,  blankets,  and  some  small  articles  for  their 
own  use. 

While  I  profoundly  regret  my  inability  to  preserve  these  valuable 
prizes,  I  am  consoled  by  the  thought  that  the  enemy  is  deprived  of 
resources  of  immense  value. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

F.  A.  Boe, 

Lieutenant-  Commander . 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads 


Report  of  Commander  Crosby,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Florida. 


U.  S.  S.  Florida, 

Off  New  Inlet,  North  Carolina ,  February  5,  1864. 
Sir:  This  morning  at  7  a.  m.  I  ran  up  to  the  wreck  of  the  Wild 
Dayrell  to  see  that  she  was  thoroughly  destroyed,  and  found  that  she 
was  well  burned.  I  then  opened  fire  upon  her  with  the  starboard  bat¬ 
tery  and  put  a  number  of  shot  through  her  hull,  which  made  the 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


461 


destruction  complete.  After  we  had  ceased  firing  and  were  standing 
offshore,  a  battery  of  Whitworths  opened  from  the  mainland  upon  us. 
The  first  shot  passed  through  our  smokestack  and  wounded  Lewis 
Owens,  seaman,  slightly,  by  a  piece  of  iron  rivet  driven  from  the  smoke¬ 
stack;  the  other  shots  fell  short.  We  returned  the  fire,  but  our  guns 
could  not  reach  the  enemy,  whose  position  we  could  only  discover  by 
the  smoke  of  his  guns. 

We  then  stood  on  up  the  coast  toward  New  Inlet,  and  discovered  the 
Sassacus  at  anchor  with  a  blockade  runner  on  shore.  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Eoe  reported  that  he  tried  to  get  her  off,  but  could  not 
succeed,  as  she  was  too  hard  aground.  Her  name  was  the  Nutfield,  of 
London,  from  Bermuda,  about  ten  days  out,  loaded  with  munitions  of 
war  and  merchandise. 

The  Sassacus  chased  her  about  60  miles  and  gained  on  her;  got 
within  long  range  10  miles  from  here.  She  had  her  under  fire  one  hour, 
and  chased  her  ashore  yesterday  at  12:45  p.  m.  She  threw  overboard 
eight  rifled  cannon  and  a  quantity  of  lead  during  the  chase.  The 
Sassacus  got  about  600  stand  of  rifles  and  a  quantity  of  sabers,  after 
which  she  set  fire  to  her.  We  then  opened  fire  upon  her  and  riddled 
her  well.  She  is  a  complete  wreck  and  lies  at  the  mouth  of  New  River 
Inlet.  She  was  a  beautiful  new  steamer,  side- wheel  and  420  [?]  tons, 
English  measurement,  had  one  smokestack  and  foremast,  and  hull  of 
iron. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Roe  got  her  log,  papers,  etc.,  chronometer 
and  charts,  in  fact,  everything  pretty  much  that  belonged  to  her.  Her 
log  shows  12  knots,  the  most  that  is  recorded.  She  was  a  valuable 
steamer.  Captain  Waller  commanded  her.  All  of  her  crew  escaped 
except  one  man,  who  was  captured. 

I  have  a  case  of  musket  caps,  percussion,  taken  from  the  Wild  Day- 
rell ,  containing  270,000  caps,  which  I  will  turn  over  to  the  ordnance 
department  at  Beaufort,  to  be  held  subject  to  your  orders.  I  suppose 
they  are  quite  valuable  and  that  I  ought  to  have  turned  them  over  to 
Lieutenant-Commander  Roe,  as  the  vessel  would  probably  be  consid¬ 
ered  as  his  prize  only,  and  not  ours. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Peirce  Crosby, 

Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Beport  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Flusser,  U.  S.  Navy,  advising  an 
increased  force  in  the  sounds  of  North  Carolina  in  view  of  the  critical 
condition  of  affairs. 

IT.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Pamlico  Sound,  February  5,  1864 — 7:30  p.  m. 
Sir:  I  am  returning  to  Plymouth  from  Washington,  [H.  C.|.  I  have 
also  been  to  Hew  Berne.  I  left  Plymouth  on  the  morning  of  the  3d 
instant,  having  heard  from  General  Wessells  that  Hew  Berne  and 
Washington,  [H.  C.],  were  besieged  by  the  enemy.  At  Hew  Berne  I 
obtained  some  information  which,  being  confirmed  at  Washington,  I 
deem  worthy  of  your  notice. 

Our  late  papers  place  Longstreet  in  the  neighborhood  of  Knoxville, 
Tenn.,  with  a  large  force.  Prisoners  and  refugees  here  say  that  he  is 
now  in  this  State  with  his  own  and  a  portion  of  Ewell’s  corps.  Who¬ 
ever  commands  the  rebel  force  in  Horth  Carolina,  all  persons  agree  in 
making  the  force  very  large.  I  have  on  board  now  a  man  who  was 
formerly  engaged  on^the  blockade  runners  from  Wilmington.  I  am 
carrying  him  to  General  Wessells  at  Plymouth.  He  left  Wilmington 
on  last  Monday.  At  Kinston  he  saw  some  5,000  troops.  The  men  said 
there  were  to  be  00,000  in  the  State  before  long.  He  also  saw  some 
pontoons  and  six  large  launches,  each  with  a  gun  mounted.  This  non¬ 
descript  force  is  said  to  have  as  many  as  seventy  boats  with  them. 
Some  of  these  boats  were  used  in  the  capture  of  the  Undencriter. 

The  boats  may  have  been  prepared  for  an  attack  on  Roanoke  Island. 
With  half  the  above  number,  capable  of  carrying  40  men  each,  the 
execution  of  such  a  scheme  would  be  quite  easy. 

The  men  of  this  flotilla  are  said  to  have  boasted  that  they  would 
destroy  all  the  gunboats  in  the  sounds. 


464 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  rebels  will,  I  think  (and  I  believe  it  is  the  general  opinion),  again 
attack  New  Berne  at  an  early  clay.  Some  think  they  are  waiting  for 
reinforcements,  and  others  that  they  were  frightened  off  by  hearing 
that  we  were  heavily  reinforced.  There  was  such  a  report  in  New 
Berne,  arising  from  the  running  about  of  and  blowing  of  whistles  by 
steamers  and  locomotives  during  the  night. 

At  Washington  it  was  reported  to  day  that  20,000  men  were  advanc¬ 
ing  in  two  columns  on  that  place.  The  report  was  deemed  reliable  by 
the  officers. 

Of  course  there  will  be  many  wild  rumors,  but  there  is  no  doubt  of 
the  presence  of  a  large  force  of  rebels  in  the  State,  and  if  we  desire  to 
hold  it  we  must  also  have  a  large  force  here  and  soon.  We  have  not  in 
the  sounds  a  sufficient  number  of  gunboats  to  be  of  any  great  service 
if  New  Berne,  Washington,  and  Plymouth  were  attacked  simulta¬ 
neously.  The  army  relies  on  our  boats  to  play  a  very  important  part 
in  the  defense  of  these  places.  Plymouth  is  the  most  easily  defended 
place  of  the  three.  It  has  the  advantage  of  having  no  dry  land  between 
it  and  the  mouth  of  the  Roauoke  on  which  to  erect  batteries.  Its  water 
communications  can  not,  therefore,  be  interrupted  by  a  land  force. 
Gunboats  would  be  able  to  cooperate  there  with  greater  chance  of 
being  useful  than  at  either  of  the  two  other  places.  AtNew  Berne  and 
at  Washington  boats  would  be  apt  to  be  opposed  by  batteries  on  bluffs, 
and  would  prove  no  match  for  them.  Then  the  communication  by  water 
would  be  closed  and  the  garrisons  starved  out.  The  rebels  destroyed 
the  railroad  between  New  Berne  and  Beaufort.  The  blockade  runner 
mentioned  above  says  he  saw  the  ironclad  building  at  Kinston.  She 
was  still  on  the  stocks;  had  part  of  her  iron  on.  He  saw  no  iron  near 
her  to  finish  her  with.  I  wish  to  send  this  letter  by  Roanoke  Island. 
I  will  examine  the  man  again  to  morrow,  and  if  I  elicit  anything  more 
will  send  it  on. 

Pardon  this  very  long  letter. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

0.  W.  Flusser, 
Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Loads. 


Report  of  Fleet  Paymaster  JJpham,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  quiet  condition 

of  affairs  at  Beaufort ,  N.  C. 

Beaufort  Harbor, 
Saturday  Evening,  February  6,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  pleasure  of  advising  you  that  there  is  comparative 
quiet  in  this  vicinity.  This  morning  Captain  [William]  Holden,  U.  S. 
Army,  and  a  telegraph  operator  arrived  from  New  Berne;  they  came 
by  hand  car  most  of  the  way,  ferrying  over  the  streams  where  the 
bridges  had  been  burned.  They  report  the  road  free  from  rebels. 

It  is  said  the  telegraph  will  be  in  operation  to-morrow,  and  the  cars 
will  run  on  Monday. 

I  went  up  the  road  to-day  as  far  as  Newport  Barracks.  I  find  some 
turpentine  remaining  there,  and  I  learn  that  some  considerable  quan¬ 
tity  is  on  the  road  uninjured.  I  am  encouraged  in  the  belief  that  the 
loss  in  naval  stores  is  not  as  severe  as  I  first  supposed.  Yet,  no  doubt 
quite  a  large  quantity  is  destroyed;  enough,  no  doubt,  to  cause  much 
trouble  and  confusion.  I  shall  leave  for  New  Berne  as  soon  as  possible, 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


4G5 


and  return  to  the  Minnesota ,,  without  delay,  the  moment  I  can  he  spared 
from  this  part  ot  my  duty.  I  hear  that  very  little  damage  was  sus¬ 
tained  at  New  Berne  or  vicinity.  The  only  bad  loss  was  the  destruction 
of  the  Underwriter. 

No  vessels  from  the  blockade  have  arrived  since  the  Emma  on  Tues¬ 
day  last. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

ClIAS.  0.  Ul’HAM, 

Fleet  Paymaster. 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  S.  P.  Bee, 

Commanding  Forth  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

P.  S. — Sunday  morning:  The  wires  are  again  cut,  and  a  fight  was 
going  on  last  night  between  our  troops,  under  Colonel  Jourdan,  and 
the  rebs,  some  6  miles  from  Newport.  Colonel  Jourdan  overtook  the 
rebs  some  6  or  8  miles  from  Newport  Barracks,  and  they  turned  and 
gave  him  fight.  We  here  have  not  heard  the  result  of  the  action.  I 
hear  from  Captain  Bowen  that  the  hands  are  steadily  at  work  repair¬ 
ing  the  bridges  on  the  road.  I  think  the  raid  has  nearly  expended 
itself  and  has  proved  a  sad  failure  to  the  raiders. 

Yery  respectfully, 

C.  C.  IT.

Report  of  Commander  Dove ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  condition  of  affairs 

near  Beaufort ,  N.  C. 


Naval  Station, 
Beaufort ,  N.  C .,  February  6 ,  1864. 

Sir:  The  arrival  of  the  [#.  JS.j  Spaulding  yesterday  with  the  Twenty- 
first  Connecticut  Kegiment  and  the  Neiv  Berne  from  the  blockade 
caused  me  so  much  business  that  I  had  no  time  to  make  a  report  in 
writing.  I  went  off,  however,  in  the  face  of  a  southeaster  and 
explained  to  Captain  Harris  verbally  the  situation  of  affairs.  In  the 
evening  the  officer  commanding  the  launch  reported  the  rebel  force,  as 
ascertained  from  persons  who  had  conversed  with  them,  to  be  about 
2,100  and  about  200  of  them  cavalry.  They  destroyed  everything  in 
Newport,  [N.  C.],  and  evacuated  it  at  11  a.  m.  on  the  4th  instant.  They 
do  not  appear  to  have  crossed  the  river  toward  Beaufort,  but  stated  on 
leaving  that  they  were  going  up  to  New  Berne  to  capture  it  and  return. 
The  reinforcements  were  pushed  on  to  the  front,  and  an  advance  was 
made  by  Colonels  Jourdan  and  Dutton.  When  I  left  them,  about  noon 
yesterday,  their  plan  was  to  go  as  far  as  they  could  by  rail,  and  then 
follow  the  rebels  up  on  foot.  As  they  did  not  seem  to  have  more  than 
i,000  or  1,200  men,  they  may  meet  with  a  reverse.  The  Nansemond  is 
in  the  sound  to  cover  them,  assisted  by  one  schooner-rigged  fiat,  with 
a  24  pounder  howitzer  and  men  from  the  Mercedita. 

The  loss  of  the  ten  days’ rations  by  tho  Ninth  Vermont  .Regiment  was 
not  only  a  great  loss  to  us,  but  a  great  assistance  to  the  enemy,  as 
they  seem  to  be  living  mostly  on  corn,  peanuts,  and  sweet  potatoes.  If 
supplies  to  our  army  do  not  arrive  soon  we  will  also  be  in  a  very  bad 
condition. 

February  7,p.  m. — I  went  to  Newport  yesterday  forenoon  in  company 
with  Colonels  Jourdan  and  Stone  to  examine  the  works  and  see  what 
was  going  on.  The  magazine  in  the  fort  there  had  been  blown  up,  the 
three  guns  disabled,  spiked,  and  carriages  destroyed,  the  flagstaff  cut 
down  and  the  flag  carried  off  by  the  rebels,  and  the  railroad  culvert  and 
bridge  burned. 

When  I  left,  about  noon.  Colonel  Jourdan  had  started  off  on  a 
reconnoissance  with  a  battalion  of  the  Ninth  Vermont  and  some  40  or 
50  cavalry. 

About  4  p.  m.  I  received  a  telegram  from  one  of  his  staff,  informing 
me  that  the  colonel  had  discovered  the  enemy  in  force,  infantry,  cavalry, 
and  artillery,  and  had  been  obliged  to  fall  back.  Late  in  the  evening 
I  learned  that  he  had  gone  on  to  New  Berne  in  a  hand  car  with  an  aid 
of  General  Palmer’s.  His  object,  no  doubt,  is  to  obtain  reinforcements 
from  there,  and  return.  In  the  evening  I  visited  the  Mercedita  and 
Emma ,  and  gave  cautions  for  the  night. 

As  the  army  quartermaster  could  only  furnish  one  flat  on  which  to 
mount  a  howitzer,  the  launch,  which  was  no  longer  required  in  New¬ 
port  Biver,  was  withdrawn,  and  they  were  both  sent  up  to  the  Nanse¬ 
mond  in  the  sound. 

The  rebels  are  prepared  with  boats  and  sailors  for  a  night  attack  of 
boat  and  for  crossing  to  Bogue  Island. 

There  was  another  alarm  this  forenoon  of  the  approach  of  the  rebel 
force.  Went  up  to  the  lines  to  see  their  direction  and  give  the  vessels 
abetter  position.  Sent  an  officer  with  the  signal  book  and  flags  to 
headquarters,  Morehead  City,  so  as  to  give  the  proper  information  from 
the  flagstaff  to  the  harbor. 

The  Mercedita  was  moved  a  little  lower  down. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


467 


Colonel  Ripley  made  a  reeonnoissance  toward  Newport  and  found 
that  the  rebels  had  fallen  back  again.  Their  movements  are  very 
unaccountable  to  me.  I  think,  however,  that  we  can  now  give  them  a 
warm  reception  if  they  approach  within  our  range. 

The  Spaulding  left  very  unexpectedly  at  6  p.  m.  without  my  getting 
this  dispatch  on  board. 

There  are  still  no  arrivals  from  the  blockade. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benjamin  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  lb  Lee,

Report  of  Captain  Sands,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  the  report  of  the  com¬ 
manding  officer  of  the  B.  S.  S.  Cambridge  regarding  the  destruction  of 
the  steamer  Dee,  February  6,  1864. 

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Jackson, 

Off  New  Inlet,  Cape  Fear  River,  N.  C.,  February  7,  1864. 
Sir:  I  have  the  pleasure  to  inform  you  of  the  destruction  of  another 
blockade  runner,  the  twin  propeller  steamer  Dee,  run  on  shore  near 
Masonboro  Inlet  on  the  night  of  the  5th  instant,  and  destroyed  next 
morning  by  the  Cambridge. 

I  enclose  herewith  Commander  Spicer’s  report  of  the  circumstance. 
The  seven  prisoners  captured  I  send  to  you  by  the  Howquah. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

B.  F.  Sands, 

Captain,  U.  S.  Navy,  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  off  Newport  News. 

P.  S. — February  8. — Yesterday  the  Niplion  went  up  and  hove  over¬ 
board  170  pigs  of  lead  from  the  Dee ,  it  being  too  rough  to  bring  it  away. 
Nearly  all  the  bacon  was  burned  up;  much  of  the  lead  was  melted 
and  melting.  From  prisoners  we  learn  there  were  about  200  pigs  of 
lead  in  the  cargo,  the  rest  of  the  cargo  being  bacon  and  spirits.  Bacon 
still  burning  and  vessel  broken  and  completelv  destroyed. 

B.  F.  S. 


[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Cambridge, 

Off  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  February  6,  1864. 

Sir:  I  would  respectfully  inform  you  that  at  8  a.  m.  this  day  1  dis¬ 
covered  a  steamer  ashore  and  on  fire  about  1  mile  to  the  southward  of 
Masonboro,  which  proved  to  he  the  blockade  runner  Dee,  from  Hamil¬ 
ton,  Bermuda,  for  Wilmington,  N.  C.  Having  boarded  and  found  it 
impossible  either  to  extinguish  the  flames  or  to  get  her  off,  I  opened  Are 
upon  and  completely  destroyed  her.  We  succeeded  in  capturing  seven 
of  her  crew,  a  list  of  whose  names  I  herewith  enclose,  and  wait  further 
orders  with  regard  to  the  disposition  of  the  pi  isoners.  We  also  secured 
a  life  boat,  which  was  found  beached  near  the  steamer,  and  have  it  with 
us;  also  three  log  books  of  a  previous  trip  belonging  to  the  engineer’s 
department  of  the  vessel,  a  small  telegraph  flag  of  Marryatt’s  Code, 


468 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


and  a  package  containing  a  number  of  copies  of  a  work*  entitled  uTlie 
Cotton  Trade,’7  by  McHenry.  Several  of  these  books  are  addressed  to 
the  leading  members  of  the  so-called  Southern  Confederacy,  Jefferson 
Davis,  and  others.  In  this  package,  which  is  directed  to  E.  M.  Maury, 
Richmond,  are  also  files  of  English  newspapers  and  other  reading 
matter. 

Soon  after  the  boats  landed  several  shots  were  fired  at  the  men  from 
the  woods,  but  without  effect.  By  information  received  from  the  pris¬ 
oners  it  seems  that  the  Dee  was  commanded  by  Captain  George  H.  Bier, 
formerly  a  lieutenant  in  the  U.  S.  Navy,  and  that  she  had  already  made 
three  successful  trips.  Her  cargo  consisted  of  bacon,  a  proportion  of 
lead,  and  a  small  quantity  of  coffee.  She  ran  ashore  at  3:30  a.  m., 
either  by  design  or  through  the  ignorance  of  the  pilot,  was  then  fired, 
her  captain  and  others  escaping  by  means  of  boats  up  the  inlet. 

Very  respectfully,  yours, 

Wm.  F.  Spicer, 

Commander.

Report  of  Commander  Davenport ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  referring  to  condition  of 
affairs  at  Neiv  Berne  and  Washington ,  N.  C. 

U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  Neiv  Berne ,  N.  C .,  February  7,  1864. 

Admiral  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  let¬ 
ters  of  the  28th  and  29th  January  and  3d  of  February. 

I  write  in  haste  now;  will  send  a  detailed  report  as  soon  as  I  have 
time. 

At  present  I  have  enough  ordnance;  will  give  you  notice  as  early  as 
pracficable  of  my  wants. 

Just  now  all  is  quiet  here,  but  the  enemy  have  possession  of  New¬ 
port,  [N.  C.],  drove  us  back  to  Morehead  [City]  this  morning.  I  think 
Beaufort  ought  to  be  protected  by  gunboats. 

The  Miami ,  Southfield,  and  Whitehead  arrived  here  promptly  on  the 
4th,  when,  receiving  information  that  Washington  was  threatened  and 
assistance  called  for,  I  sent  the  Miami  and  Whitehead  there  immedi¬ 
ately.  I  learned  this  morning  that  both  these  vessels  have  returned  to 
Plymouth,  in  consequence  of  the  state  of  affairs  there. 

The  enemy  must  be  in  force  in  this  State,  and  will  doubtless  annoy 
us  at  all  points.  I  have  recovered  a  12-pounder  howitzer  from  the 
Underwriter,  anchor,  and  chain.  I  have  just  learned  that  a  steamer 
leaves  for  Beaufort  via  Core  Sound,  and  I  write  in  great  haste. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  K.  Davenport, 

Commander  and  Senior  Naval  Officer  in  Sounds  of  North  Carolina. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  8.  Navy,  to  the  Secretary  of  the 
Navy  regarding  the  restoration  of  the  light  vessel  off  Frying  Pan 
Shoals. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va .,  February  8,  1864. 
Sir:  The  Department  has  been  heretofore  informed  that  the  light- 
boat  off  Frying  Pan  Shoals  has  gone  adrift,  and  Commander  Almy 
reports  that,  having  found  its  way  to  Port  Royal,  it  has  there  been 
appropriated  for  service  off  Martin’s  Industry  Shoals. 

Commander  Almy  further  represents  the  necessity  of  restoring  this 
vessel  to  her  original  position  or  sending  another  light  vessel  to  supply 
her  place  off  the  Frying  Pan.  At  the  point  of  the  shoals  laud  can  not 
be  seen,  and  the  want  of  a  mark  to  guide  our  boats  safely  around  this 
dangerous  point  is  much  felt  by  the  blockaders,  to  whom  the  light  was 
of  great  service,  as  well  as  to  the  mercantile  marine  generally,  to  whom 
a  light  vessel  is,  perhaps,  more  necessary  off  Frying  Pan  Shoals  than 
at  Martin’s  Industry. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Off  IF ashington,  N.  C.,  February  .5,  1864. 

From  all  I  can  understand,  we  are  to  have  very  active  times  in  this 
department.  The  attack  on  your  outposts  at  New  Berne  is  only  the 
beginning  of  large  operations  in  eastern  North  Carolina.  The  South¬ 
ern  newspapers,  supposing  that  we  were  done  for,  have  let  the  cat  out 
the  bag.

[Pamlico].

Renshaw.

Letter  from  Com  mander  Davenport ,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Commander  Renshaw,

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  February  9,  1864. 

Sir:  I  had  a  confidential  dispatch  from  General  Butler  last  evening 
asking  for  aid,  and  informing  me  that  General  Wessells, _  under  date  ot 
the  7th  instant,  at  noon,  reports  that  the  enemy,  gathering  at  Halifax, 
threaten  him  with  flatboats,  having  guns  mounted.  They  come  from 
Lee’s  army.  General  Wessells  asks  for  help,  especially  for  gunboats,  as 
his  are  absent,  meaning,  I  suppose,  the  navy  gunboats  which  went  from 
Plymouth  to  the  defense  of  New  Berne. 

I  send  the  Eutaw  to  join  you,  and  will  send  orders  to  the  blockade 
for  the  Sassacus  to  do  so  also,  and  when  the  Wyalusing  arrives  she  will 
be  added  to  the  force  in  the  sounds,  all  for  present  purposes. 

Meanwhile  send  the  Miami ,  Lieutenant-Commander  Flusser,  the 
Southfield,  and  any  other  available  gunboats  to  Plymouth  and  make 
such  disposition  of  the  gunboats  as  will  meet  the  exigencies  of  the  serv¬ 
ice  in  the  sounds,  placing  the  most  and  best  gunboats  at  the  points 
most  requiring  them,  taking  care  to  keep  them  all  in  sufficient  watei  to 
enable  them  to  float  and  move. 

All  the  gunboats  must  exercise  the  utmost  vigilance  ami  guard 
against  surprise.

in  the  Neuse  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne,  N.  C.,  Februarg  9,  1864 — 3  p.  m. 

Admiral:  All  is  just  now  quiet  here.  I  sent  a  boat  (improvised 
into  a  gunboat)  up  the  river  this  morning  to  reconnoiter.  She  was 
tired  on  about  8  miles  above  this,  but  drove  the  enemy  away  by  the 
judicious  use  of  shells.

Reports  of  Commander  Frailey ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  discovery  of 
the  beached  steamer  Spunkie,  February  9,1864. 

U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City, 

Off  Western  Bar ,  Wilmington ,  N.  G.,  February  13,  1864. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  report  that  at  daylight  on  the  morning  of  the  9th 
instant  a  long  and  low  side- wheel  steamer,  painted  white,  with  one 
white  smokestack  and  schooner-rigged,  was  discovered  ashore  on  the 
beach  a  short  distance  west  of  Caswell,  presenting  a  broadside  view  to 
us,  with  her  head  to  the  westward,  rendering  it  difficult,  however,  to 
add  if  beached  on  running  in  or  coming  out. 

Two  tugs  have  been  daily  employed  since  then  in  endeavors  to  extri¬ 
cate  her  from  her  position,  but  without  avail,  notwithstanding  the  very 
favorable  weather  we  have  had  for  several  days  past,  but  as  the  wind 
has  veered  to  an  opposite  point  S.  W.,  with  a  low  barometer  and 
threatening  appearances,  it  is  to  be  hoped  she  has  made  her  last  trip. 
I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jas.  Madison  Frailey, 
Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads.

Off  Western  Bar,  Wilmington ,  N.  C.,  February  17,  1864. 
Sir:  I  beg  leave  to  report  that  I  have  to-day  received  on  board  this 
steamer  from  the  U.  S.  S.  Montgomery  6  Confederate  prisoners  belong¬ 
ing  to  the  Tenth  Regiment  North  Carolina  Troops,  who  came  off  to  that

steamer  tlie  niglit  previous  in  a  boat  belonging  to  the  prize  steamer  Pet , 
and  in  which  boat  the  pilot  and  12  of  the  Pet's  crew  escaped  to  the 
shore  a  few  minutes  previous  to  the  Montgomery's  taking  possession  of

They  had  not  seen  the  President’s  proclamation,  nor  heard  of  it,  but 
are  ready  and  willing  to  take  the  oath  of  allegiance. 

In  addition  to  other  information  gained  from  them,  I  learn  that  the 
steamer  reported  in  my  communication  of  the  13th  as  having  been  seen 
on  the  beach  near  Fort  Caswell  on  the  morning  of  the  9th  had  been 
beached  while  attempting  to  get  in;  that  the  principal  portion  of  her 
cargo,  consisting  of  blankets,  shoes,  and  provisions,  had  been  removed 
from  her,  but  that  the  vessel  was  a  wreck,  having  broken  in  two.  She 
proved  to  be  the  Spunkie.  A  list  of  clothing  furnished  them  herewith 
accompanies  this  communication,  marked  “B,”  and  which  act  I  trust 
will  meet  with  your  approval.

Destruction  of  the  steamers  Emily  and  Fanny  and  Jenny,  February  10, 
,  '  1864. 

Report  of  Commander  Crosby,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Florida. 

U.  S.  S.  Florida, 

Off  New  Inlet,  February  10,  1864. 

Sir  :  At  5 : 50  a.  m.,  discovered  a  steamer  inshore  and  to  the  northward 
of  us ;  fired  the  12-pounder  howitzer  at  her  and  stood  inshore  to  head  her 
off;  drove  her  ashore  above  Masonboro  Inlet.  Discovered  about  the 
same  time  another,  ashore  about  half  a  mile  to  the  northward  of  her. 


474 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Sent  boats  and  took  possession  of  them.  They  proved  to  be  the 
side- wheel  steamer  Fanny  and  Jenny ,  from  Nassau,  live  days  out.  Cap¬ 
tain  Coxetter  commanded  her.  He  and  the  paymaster  were  drowned 
while  trying  to  land  on  the  beach;  the  remainder  of  the  crew,  25  in 
number,  were  captured  and  are  on  board  this  vessel.  She  was  loaded 
with  a  few  small  articles  of  merchandise;  had  a  good  deal  of  coal. 

The  other  was  the  screw  steamer  Emily ;  left  Bermuda  February  4; 
cargo  of  salt  and  a  few  barrels;  her  crew  and  captain  escaped. 

Anchored  and  sent  a  hawser  to  the  Fanny  and  Jenny ,  but  before  we 
got  our  heavy  hawser  to  her  the  enemy  opened  on  us  with  a  Whit¬ 
worth  battery  at  long  range,  the  first  four  shots  striking  the  hull,  doing 
some  damage  to  the  wheel,  which  can  be  easily  repaired.  As  the  enemy 
had  our  exact  range,  and  hitting  us  each  time,  I  slipped  the  cable  and 
pulled  in  the  hawser  and  fastened  it.  The  enemy  continued  firing  at 
us,  but  shot  fell  short  about  from  200  to  400  yards;  fired  our  Dahl- 
greu  50-pounder  at  them,  but  could  not  reach  them.  As  their  fire  from 
the  guns  and  musketry  increased,  I  ordered  the  steamers  to  be  set  on 
fire  and  destroyed,  which  was  done,  my  men  being  on  the  wrecks,  pre¬ 
venting  our  firing  near  them. 

Our  paymaster  received  a  severe  flesh  wound,  but  not  dangerous. 

We  were  in  4J  fathoms  when  these  vessels  were  discovered  and 
anchored  in  3  fathoms  water  to  send  our  hawsers. 

We  lett  them  both  in  flames,  aground.  I  send  the  log  books-  taken 
from  the  Emily ,  which  give  all  the  information  we  have  of  her. 

I  have  a  Confederate  flag,  taken  from  the  Fanny  and  Jenny ,  a  spy¬ 
glass,  the  chronometer,  one  sextant,  and  her  charts. 

A.s  the  opportunity  otters  I  send  the  flags  taken  from  the  Emily , 
Wild  Day  veil,  and  Fanny  and  Jenny. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Peirce  Crosby, 

Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

The  boat  destroyed  the  steamers  while  under  the  fire  of  the  enemy. 
The  officers  and  men  in  them  performed  their  duty  well. 

Peirce  Crosby, 

Commander. 


Additional  report  of  Commander  Crosby,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Florida. 


U.  8.  S.  Florida, 

Off  Alasonboro  Inlet,  February  11,  1864. 

Sir:  Enclosed  1  send  a  list  of  prisoners  taken  from  the  steamer 
Fanny  and  Jenny.  The  engineers  of  that  vessel,  when  she  was  boarded 
by  our  boats,  ottered  every  assistance  in  their  power  in  their  depart¬ 
ment. 

Hie  steamers  which  we  set  on  fire  yesterday  burned  all  last  night, 
and  this  morning  I  found  them  completely  destroyed  by  fire  and  the 
sea  washing  over  them.  The  Emily  had  two  lower  masts  and  had 
apparently  been  dismantled  to  run  the  blockade.  I  saw  by  the  papers 
taken  from  her  that  she  had  been  brig-rigged.  She  was  perfectly  new 
and  a  very  handsome  steamer,  expensively  fitted  out.  After  she  had 
burned  some  time,  an  explosion  took  place  on  board  of  her,  and  her  stern 
has  settled,  apparently  blown  open.  I  am  informed  by  the  second 
engineer  of  the  Fanny  and  Jenny  that  ten  vessels  sailed  for  Wilmington 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  475 

during  this  dark  of  the  moon.  Three  have  been  destroyed,  and  one 
put  back,  broken  down,  leaving  six  others  to  be  heard  from.  The  City 
of  Petersburg  was  one  of  the  six,  and  she,  I  think,  ran  in  safe.  She 
started  in  company  with  the  Fanny  and  Jenny  from  Nassau,  but  soon 
left  her,  being  a  faster  vessel.  I  send  a  list  and  description  of  some  of 
the  vessels  running  from  Nassau  to  Wilmington,  given  me  by  the  second 
engineer  of  the  Fanny  and  Jenny.  The  pilot  of  the  Fanny  and  Jenny 
was  named  Burrows  [Burroughs],  and  from  the  description  I  imagined 
him  the  same  man  we  took  on  a  previous  occasion;  was  appointed  a 
pilot  and  deserted  from  the  Shobolon ;  he  escaped  and  got  on  shore 
safe.  Captain  Coxetter  was  drowned  with  a  number  of  others.  He  is 
said  to  be  a  nephew  of  the  Coxetter  who  has  been  so  successful  in 
running  the  blockade. 

The  Emily  had  a  cargo  of  salt— possibly  something  under  it — all,  how¬ 
ever,  was  destroyed. 

The  shot  which  struck  this  vessel  yesterday  cut  off  one  paddle-wheel 
arm  and  broke  a  second  and  cut  one  rim  of  the  wheel  in  two.  A  shell 
exploded  under  the  guard,  but  did  little  damage;  fortunately  our  boil¬ 
ers  and  steam  drum  were  not  touched.  They  are  much  exposed,  and 
were  evidently  the  point  aimed  at.  The  precision  of  the  enemy’s  fire 
with  those  guns  is  very  remarkable. 

At  the  time  we  discovered  the  Fanny  and  Jenny,  the  Florida  was 
lying  in  a  quarter  less  4  fathoms,  and  in  endeavoring  to  keep  close 
inshore  the  Fanny  and  Jenny  accidentally  ran  aground,  when  a  shot  from 
our  rifie  howitzer  passed  over  them,  causing  the  captain  to  leave  pre¬ 
cipitately,  followed  by  a  portion  of  his  crew.  The  second  engineer  tells 
me  that  there  was  a  handsome  sword,  gold  mounted,  for  General  It.  E. 
Lee  on  board.  It  was  destroyed  with  the  vessel ;  it  was  a  presentation 
sword. 

The  engineers  and  crew  tell  me  that  the  steamer  stopped  two  or  three 
times  during  the  night  of  the  capture,  when  running  down  the  coast, 
and  sent  a  boat  ashore  to  ascertain  their  position,  and  during  the  time 
anchored,  and  that  they  were  not  aware  of  their  position  when  they 
ran  aground. 

It  was  their  captain’s  intention  to  make  the  land  about  2  miles  north 
of  Fort  Fisher.  They  were  running  13  knots  at  the  time,  and  passed 
over  one  shoal  to  another. 

Had  we  been  unmolested  two  hours  longer,  I  think  both  vessels  might 
have  been  gotten  off;  but  under  the  circumstances  I  considered  it  the 
surest  plan  to  destroy  them  effectually,  which  was  done  in  one  hour  and 
a  half  after  they  were  discovered.  Sharpshooters  were  collecting  rap¬ 
idly  behind  the  sand  hills,  and  in  positions  not  easily  to  be  dislodged 
by  our  fire,  except  by  endangering  our  own  men. 

After  the  vessels  were  on  fire,  the  Cambridge  came  in  sight  and  sent 
her  boat  in  to  look  at  the  vessels.  Some  of  her  men  were  severely 
wounded  by  the  rebel  sharpshooters. 

The  City  of  Petersburg  has  two  strike  masts  and  telescopic  funnels. 

From  all  I  can  learn  from  the  engineers  of  the  Fanny  and  Jenny ,  a 
13-knot  vessel  would  outrun  the  greater  part  ot  the  blockade  runners. 

The  Pet ,  I  am  told,  is  one  of  the  most  successful  runners,  and  is  not 
capable  of  making  more  than  8  or  9  knots. 

In  my  hasty  letter  of  yesterday  reporting  the  destruction  of  these 
steamers,  I  mentioned  the  good  conduct  of  the  officers  and  crew  on  the 
occasion.  I  would  now  particularly  mention  the  zealous  and  efficient 
conduct  of  Acting  Master  John  McGowan,  jr.;  also  of  our  pilot,  J.  W. 
Taylor,  whose  services  were,  on  this  occasion  as  well  as  heretofore, 


476 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


invaluable  to  me  on  the  blockade.  I  would  respectfully  recommend 
him  for  promotion  to  be  master  pilot. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Peirce  Crosby. 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  requesting  the  consideration  of  the  Depart¬ 
ment  for  the  engineers  of  the  steamer  Fanny  and  Jenny. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  February  26,  1864. 

Sir:  Commander  Crosby,  commanding  the  U.  S.  S.  Florida,  reports 
to  me  that  the  engineers  of  the  blockade  runner  Fanny  and  Jenny, 
destroyed  by  the  Florida  on  the  10th  instant,  cheerfully  rendered  him 
all  the  assistance  in  their  power  in  his  energetic,  though  unsuccessful, 
efforts  to  secure  his  prize  by  getting  her  afloat.  In  consequence  of 
these  representations,  I  am  induced  to  present  them  for  the  considera¬ 
tion  of  the  Department.  These  engineers  are  now  prisoners  on  board 
the  Brandywine ,  and  will  be  sent  to  New  York  by  the  New  Berne,  if 
not  let  off'  for  their  good  services. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P,  Lee

Report  of  Acting  Master  Studley ,  U.  S.  Nam/,  requesting  instructions 
regarding  the  detention  of  naval  vessels  by  a  shot  across  the  bote. 

U.  S.  S.  Young  Rover, 

Guard  Ship ,  off  Fort  Monroe ,  Va .,  February  11,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  a  small  side-wheel  steamer, 
painted  lead  color,  aud  having  guns  on  board,  to  all  appearances  one 
of  our  naval  vessels,  passed  out  this  evening  at  5:  30. 

The  officer  of  the  deck  hailed  her,  but  received  no  answer.  He 
reported  the  fact  to  me,  and  asked  if  he  should  tire  across  her  bow. 

As  she  was  so  far  away  and  so  far  out,  I  told  him  not  to  tire  across 
her  bow.  Shall  I  in  future  tire  across  the  bows  of  our  naval  vessels? 

Our  vessels  generally,  I  think,  go  very  much  farther  away  than  is 
necessary,  and  we  frequently  have  to  send  a  boat  to  them,  as  they  are 
out  of  hailing  distance. 

1  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  B.  Studley, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  Young  Rover. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  off  Newport  News.

of  United  States  vessels. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  February  11,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  the  Department  the  arrival  of  the 
Fequot  on  the  8th  instant  from  Yew  York;  the  Valley  City  on  the  9th 
instant  from  Baltimore,  and  the  1  icJcsburg  on  the  10th  instant  from 
Yew  York;  and  the  departure  on  the  9th  instant  of  the  Monticello  for 
the  Wilmington  blockade,  aud  the  Eutaw  for  temporary  duty  in  the

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Blake,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Eutaw,  of  the  grounding  of  that  vessel  at  Eatteras  Inlet. 

U.  S.  S.  Eutaw, 

Hatter  as  Inlet ,  February  11,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  arrived  here  on  the  10th 
instant  at  1:30  p.  m.,  and  in  obedience  to  instructions  immediately 
called  upon  the  commandant  of  the  post,  in  order  to  gain  information 
in  regard  to  the  military  situation,  also  to  procure  a  sound  pilot.  He 
informed  me  that  no  change  has  occurred  in  the  military  status  other 
than  that  you  are  already  in  possession  of.  The  commandant  also 
informed  me  that  he  had  received  information  that  the  rebels  had 
a  number  of  barges  and  flatboats  in  the  sound  capable  of  carrying 


478 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


a  large  number  of  troops,  with  which  they  intended  baking  demon¬ 
strations  against  isolated  places,  our  transports,  and  small  gunboats. 
On  receiving  this  information  he  dispatched  the  only  armed  vessel  at 
his  command  for  the  purpose  of  a  recounoissance.  Not  being  able  to 
cross  the  bulkhead  at  night,  I  remained  at  anchor  until  8  o’clock 
instant.  I  procured  the  services  of  a  sound  and  swash  pilot,  also  of  a 
tug  to  assist  me  through  the  Swash  channel.  As  the  marks  fore  and 
aft  indicated,  her  draft  was  7  feet  6  inches,  and  finding  8  feet  3  inches 
on  the  bulkhead,  I  apprehended  no  great  difficulty  in  being  able  to 
work  the  vessel  over.  The  ship  reached  the  shoal  at  the  top  of  high 
water  in  the  center  of  the  channel,  when  she  took  the  ground  heavily, 
and  in  spite  of  every  exertion  of  the  tug  and  our  own  steam  power  was 
unable  to  get  her  over  or  back  again  into  deep  water.  Independent  of 
the  injury  she  might  receive  lying  aground,  she  completely  blocked  the 
channel,  preventing  the  passage  of  other  vessels.  I  had,  therefore,  no 
other  alternative  than  to  lighten  the  vessel,  for  which  purpose  I  have 
employed  the  schooner  Nellie  Potter  at  an  expense  of  $20  per  day.  I 
hope  by  discharging  a  portion  of  my  shot,  provisions,  and  some  coal, 
to  be  able  to  get  over  by  9  o’clock  in  the  morning,  and  proceed  accord¬ 
ing  to  my  instructions.  From  the  above  statement  you  will  perceive 
that  I  shall  not  be  able  to  recross  the  bar  with  the  usual  supply  of 
coal  and  provisions,  except  at  the  full  spring  tides.  As  the  ship  sits 
square  on  the  bottom,  I  do  not  apprehend  any  injury  resulting  to  her 
from  her  position. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Homer  0.  Blake, 
Lieutenant- Commander ,  77.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear  Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Commander  Dove ,  77.  S.  Navy,  regarding  general  matters  at 

Beaufort ,  N.  C. 

U.  S.  Ordnance  Schooner  Arletta, 

Naval  Station,  Beaufort ,  N.  C.,  February  11,  1864. 

Sir:  Since  my  letter  No.  27,  February  0  and  7,  affairs  on  this  station 
have  resumed  their  usual  quiet  as  far  as  the  rebels  are  concerned. 

The  arrival  of  a  large  quantity  of  army  supplies  makes  a  correspond¬ 
ing  increase  of  business  on  shore.  Most  of  these  are  being  sent  up  to 
New  Berne.  One  bridge  on  the  railroad  is  still  unrepaired;  they  have 
therefore  to  be  transported  across  to  the  train  from  New  Berne. 

At  present  the  cars  leave  Morehead  City  at  3:30  p.  m.,  and  return 
at  5  p.  m.  with  the  mail  and  passengers  from  New  Berne. 

The  Nansemond  will  leave  this  afternoon  for  her  station.  Her  com¬ 
mander  has  rendered  good  service  here  in  getting  into  Bogue  Sound  so 
promptly  last  Monday  week,  February  1.  His  presence  there  con¬ 
tributed,  no  doubt  to  check  approach  of  the  rebels  in  that  direction. 

The  Dacotah  arrived  this  forenoon  having  one  case  of  decided  small¬ 
pox  on  board  and  another  suspicious.  The  usual  precautions  have  been 
taken  and  the  man  sent  to  the  hospital  appropriated  to  that  disease. 
She  is  anchored  outside  of  all  the  other  vessels. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benjamin  M.  Hove, 

Commander.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  submitting  to  the 

Department  the  case  of  permit  granted  by  Major-General  Butler ,  TJ.  S. 

Army  to  the  steamer  Princeton,  to  carry  supplies  through  blockade. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  February  12,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  beg  leave  to  enclose  to  the  Department  a  copy  of  a  permit 
sent  to  me  this  morning  by  the  hands  of  Mr.  Sanborn,  deputy  provost- 
marshal  and  agent  of  Adams  Express  Company,  by  Major-General 
Butler. 

By  the  terms  of  this  letter  it  will  be  seen  that  the  steamer  Princeton 
is  to  be  permitted  to  pass  through  the  blockading  squadron  in  the 
Chowan  and  Roanoke  rivers,  provided  I  will  give  orders  to  that  effect. 
The  inference  is  that  family  supplies  are  to  go  beyond  our  lines,  as  the 
products  of  the  country  are  to  be  brought  by  her  within  our  lines  in 
exchange. 

The  LII,  LIII,  and  LTY  paragraphs  of  Treasury  regulations  are  quoted 
as  being  in  accordance  with  the  terms  of  the  permit.  I  have  no  copy 
of  Treasury  regulations  containing  paragraphs  with  such  numbers,  and 
supposing  that  other  regulations  may  have  been  issued,  not  in  my  pos¬ 
session,  or  that  there  may  have  been  some  clerical  error  I  returned  the 
permit,  taking  a  copy,  without  action  on  my  part,  in  order  that  I  might 
more  fully  understand  the  matter. 

Under  the  VII  and  VIII  paragraphs  of  Treasury  instructions,  Septem¬ 
ber  11,  1863,  such  traffic  would  seem  to  be  prohibited,  and  as  General 
Butler’s  permit  is  with  the  proviso  of  my  sanction,  and  as  I  conceive  I 
have  no  authority  under  the  order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  of 
March  31,  1863,  to  authorize  the  transportation  of  any  goods,  wares,  or 
merchandise  into  any  State  declared  to  be  in  insurrection  by  the  Presi¬ 
dent,  I  have  deemed  it  proper  to  submit  the  case  to  the  Department 
for  its  decision  and  instructions. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Gomdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Horn  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  G.

Letter  from  Major-General  Peck,  U.  S.  Army ,  to  Mojo?- General  Butler , 

U.  8.  Army ,  regarding  the  expected  attack  upon  New  Berne  and  the 

sounds. 

Hdqrs.  Army  and  District  of  North  Carolina, 

New  Berne ,  N.  C.,  February  13,  1864. 

General:  My  information  is  of  sucli  a  nature  as  to  induce  the 
belief  that  Jeff.  Davis  has  decided  upon  recovering  New  Berne  and 
the  sounds,  probably  as  a  preliminary  step  to  Lee’s  retrograde  move¬ 
ment  in  the  spring.  Both  rams  are  expected  down  the  Neuse  and 
Boanoke  in  conjunction  with  laud  troops.  It  seems  certain  that  the 
one  at  Kinston  is  intended  to  come  down  on  the  next  high  water. 

I  have  just  ordered  some  old  hulks  to  be  placed  in  the  Neuse,  above 
the  city,  and  shail  leave  to-morrow  evening  for  Washington  and  Ply¬ 
mouth. 

All  are  at  work  strengthening  our  lines  where  most  needed.  The 
railway  is  in  order  again. 

Good  cavalry  is  of  the  highest  moment  to  us  in  North  Carolina. 

General  Pickett  has  arrested  General  Barton  for  his  part  in  the  late 
affair. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  J.  Peck, 

Major-  General.

Report  of  Commander  Davenport,  U.  8.  Navy,  regarding  affairs  off  New 

Berne,  N.  C. 

TJ.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne ,  N.  C.,  February  12,  1864. 

Admiral:  The  enemy  attempted  to  reconnoiter  our  position  last 
night  by  the  river;  were  tired  on  by  our  picket  boats. 

They  are  doubtless  about,  but  I  have  no  fears  if  they  attack  while  I 
am  here. 

I  want  more  gunboats.  Washington  should  not  be  left  with  only  the 
Louisiana. 

We  have  the  railroad  now  (on  sufferance),  and  I  trust  we  will  be  able 
to  control  it. 

I  will  keep  you  advised  of  things  here. 

In  haste. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  K.  Davenport,

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy,  giving  a  resume  regard¬ 
ing  capture  and  destruction  of  blockade  runners  off  Wilmington. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  February  15, 1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  the  Department  the  circumstances 
attending  the  capture  and  destruction  by  the  blockading  forces  oft 

N  w  R— vol  9 - 31 


482 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Wilmington  of  the  following  blockade  runners,  of  whibh  I  have  pre¬ 
viously  informed  you  by  telegraph:  The  Wild  Dayrell,  Nutfield ,  Dee, 
Emily,  and  the  Danny  and  Jenny. 

Upon  the  reporting  of  the  Sassacus,  Lieutenant  Commander  Roe,  she 
was  assigned  by  me  to  duty  as  an  outside  cruiser,  to  cruise  upon  the 
line  of  bearing  between  New  Inlet  and  Bermuda,  not  farther  to  the 
eastward  than  the  meridian  of  75°  west  longitude,  a  station  where  her 
reputation  for  speed  would  be  severely  tested,  one  in  which  a  very  fast 
cruiser  w  uld  prove  a  great  stumbling  block  to  the  blockade  runners. 
The  result  has  equaled  my  expectations,  and  the  destruction  of  the 
steamers  Wild  Dayrell  and  Nutfield  by  the  Sassacus,  both  new  and  fast 
steamers,  the  latter  on  her  first  voyage,  are  added  to  the  long  list  of 
disasters  to  the  blockade  runners. 

Upon  the  morning  of  the  1st  instant  Lieutenant-Commander  Roe 
discovered  black  smoke  inshore  of  him,  and,  pursuing  it,  discovered 
the  Wild  Dayrell  on  shore,  near  Stump  Inlet.  He  boarded,  and  found 
her  to  be  partially  filled  with  an  assorted  cargo.  Her  crew  had  aban¬ 
doned  her  and  fled  to  the  shore.  After  great  exertions  to  get  her  afloat, 
in  which  he  was  assisted  by  the  Florida ,  it  was  found  impracticable, 
and  she  was  completely  destroyed.  Lieutenant  Commander  Roe  esti¬ 
mates  her  value,  with  her  cargo,  at  about  $200,000.  After  completing 
the  destruction  of  the  Wild  Dayrell ,  the  Sassacus  proceeded  to  take  up 
her  assigned  station,  and  at  7  o’clock  on  the  morning  of  the  4th  instant 
a  blockade  runner  was  discovered  to  the  northward  and  westward  of 
him,  distant  12  miles.  Chase  was  immediately  given  and  after  a  five 
hours’ chase  the  steamer  was  brought  under  fire,  and  finding  escape 
impossible  she  ran  on  shore  at  1  o’clock  p.  m.,  near  New  River  Inlet. 

Her  officers  and  crew  escaped  to  the  land  in  their  boats;  one  boat 
load,  however,  was  capsized  and  the  crew  drowned,  with  the  exception 
of  a  Mr.  Mell,  the  purser  of  the  steamer,  who  was  rescued  from  drown¬ 
ing  by  the  boats  of  the  Sassacus,  which  were  immediately  sent  in  to 
take  possession  of  the  prize.  She  proved  to  be  the  English  steamer 
Nutfield,  from  Bermuda,  bound  to  Wilmington,  previously  mentioned  in 
consular  dispatches.  From  Mr.  Mell,  who  was  rescued,  I  learn  that  her 
cargo  was  munitions  of  war,  arms,  a  battery  of  eight  Whitworth  guns, 
and  pig  lead.  The  guns  and  lead  were  thrown  overboard  during  the 
chase.  Finding  it  impossible  to  get  the  Nutfield  afloat,  after  great 
exertions  to  that  end,  she  was  fired  and  destroyed.  Some  700  rifles  and 
a  quantity  of  cavalry  sabers,  together  with  other  articles,  were  rescued 
from  her,  and  will  be  sent  in  for  adjudication  at  an  early  date. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Roe  reports  that  the  Sassacus  attained  a 
speed  of  13£  knots  and  gained  rapidly  upon  his  chase,  reported  one  of 
the  fastest  steamers  yet  sent  to  run  the  blockade. 

Upon  the  6th  instant  the  Cambridge  discovered  a  steamer  ashore  and 
on  fire,  about  1  mile  south  of  Masonboro  Inlet,  which  proved  to  be  the 
blockade  running  steamer  Dee,  from  Bermuda  to  Wilmington.  Finding 
it  impossible  to  extinguish  the  flames  or  to  get  her  off,  Commander 
Spicer,  of  the  Cambridge,  abandoned  the  attempt,  and  still  further  de¬ 
stroyed  her  by  firing  into  her.  Seven  of  her  crew  were  captured,  and 
are  now  held  as  prisoners  on  the  Cambridge.  From  these  prisoners  I 
learn  that  the  Dee  was  commanded  by  G.  H.  Bier,  formerly  a  lieutenant 
in  the  United  States  naval  service.  She  was  loaded  with  lead,  coffee, 
and  bacon,  all  of  which,  with  the  vessel,  were  completely  destroyed. 

At  5: 50  a.  m.  on  the  10th  instant  a  steamer  was  discovered  from  the 
Florida ,  standing  along  the  shore  toward  New  Inlet.  After  pursuing 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


483 


and  tiring  at  tier,  she  ran  on  sliore  near  Masonboro  Inlet.  Commander 
Crosby  sent  bis  boats  and  took  possession  of  her.  Slie  proved  to  be 
the  side-wheel  steamer  Fanny  and  Jenny ,  commanded  by  the  notorious 
Captain  Coxetter,  who,  with  the  purser,  was  drowned  in  endeavoring 
to  reach  the  shore.  The  remainder  of  her  crew,  25  in  number,  were 
captured,  and  are  now  prisoners  on  board  the  Florida.  The  steamer 
was  loaded  with  merchandise  and  coal.  The  enemy  opened  tire  upon 
the  wreck  and  upon  the  Florida  with  musketry  and  Whitworth  guns, 
by  which  tire  Acting  Assistant  Paymaster  W.  F.  Keeler  received  a 
severe  but  not  dangerous  wound.  Finding  it  impossible  to  get  the 
steamer  afloat  after  great  exertions,  Commander  Crosby  ordered  the 
steamer  to  be  tired,  which  was  done  under  a  severe  tire  of  the  enemy. 
The  Florida •  received  some  damage  from  the  fire  of  the  enemy,  which 
can  readily  be  repaired.  At  the  same  time  that  the  Fanny  and  Jenny 
ran  on  shore  another  steamer  was  seen  from  the  Florida  ashore  about 
one-half  mile  to  the  northward  of  the  Fanny  and  Jenny ,  which  was  also 
boarded  by  the  Florida's  boats.  This  proved  to  be  the  Emily ,  from 
Nassau,  with  a  cargo  of  merchandise  and  salt.  She  was  also  fired  and 
destroyed,  as  it  was  impossible  to  get  her  afloat. 

The  Fanny  and  Jenny ,  Emily ,  and  Nut  field  are  new  vessels,  and  this 
is  supposed  to  be  the  first  attempt  to  run  the  blockade. 

The  Wild  Dayrell  has  made  one  successful  voyage,  and  the  Dee  is  an 
old  offender. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Fear  Admiral,  Comely.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Commander  Davenport,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  general  matters 

pertaining  to  his  command. 

U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne,  N.  C.,  February  15, 186  L 

Admiral  :  I  sent  the  Ceres  yesterday  with  two  tugs  to  work  at  the 
Entail',  aground  on  the  Swash. 

The  water  is  very  low  just  now  everywhere  in  the  sounds,  but  I  hope 
the  assistance  I  send  her  will  suffice  to  get  her  afloat.  I  shall  dispatch 
the  Southfield  to  Plymouth  as  soon  as  the  Eut.aw  arrives. 

General  Palmer  is  of  opinion  (in  which  I  concur)  that  a  gunboat  with 
a  battery  like  the  Southfield  should  be  here  just  now. 

We  are  trying  to  obstruct  the  river  above. 

Everything  shall  be  done  in  my  power  to  carry  out  your  wishes  and 
to  assist  the  Army. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  K.  Davenport,

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Gillis ,  U.  SfiNavy ,  regarding  expedition 
up  the  James  River  in  search  of  escaped  Union  prisoners. 

IT.  S.  Gunboat  Commodore  Morris, 

Newport  News ,  February  16 ,  1864. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  this  date  I  got  underway,  and, 
with  the  Shokokon  in  company,  proceeded  up  the  James  River  as  far  as 
the  Chickahomiuy,  keeping  a  bright  lookout  along  the  bank  for  the 
Union  prisoners  that  you  informed  me  were  reported  to  have  made 
their  escape  from  Richmond;  saw  nothing  of  them,  either  going  up  or 
on  our  arrival  at  the  mouth  of  the  Cliickahominy.  We  arrived  at  the 
mouth  of  the  Chickahomiuy  at  12  m.,  remaining  there  until  2  p.  m., 
when,  not  seeing  anything  of  the  party  that  we  were  in  search  of,  I 
returned  according  to  your  instructions. 

On  the  way  down  I  saw,  near  the  upper  end  of  the  battery  at  the 
north  end  of  Burwell’s  Bay,  a  signal  station,  from  which  the  enemy 
were  then  signalizing.  Saw  nothing  else,  either  going  or  returning, 
worthy  of  note. 

V ery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  H.  Gillis, 

Lieutenant- Commander,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  chase  by 
the  U.  S.  S.  Connecticut  of  a  steamer  answering  the  description  of  the 
Fergus  or  Presto. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  February  16,  1864. 
Sir:  Commander  Almy,  under  date  the  11th  instant,  reports  having 
chased  a  blockade  runner  for  fifteen  hours,  between  noon  January  31 
and  3  a.  m.  February  1,  whose  description  answered  to  the  Fergus  or 
Presto.  As  the  latter-named  vessel  is  reported  to  have  run  on  shore 
while  attempting  to  enter  Charleston  on  February  2,  having  left  Nassau 
January  29,  it  would  seem  to  point  to  the  Presto  as  the  vessel  chased 
by  the  Connecticut  and  by  her  run  off  from  Wilmington.  The  chase 
commenced  100  miles  south  of  Wilmington,  the  lately  increased  force 
of  this  squadron  having  enabled  me  to  station  the  Connecticut,  with 
other  vessels,  for  outside  cruising  on  the  highways  between  Wilmington 
and  Bermuda  and  Nassau,  a  disposition  which  very  greatly  increases 
the  hazards  of  blockade  running  and  consequently  the  efficiency  of  the 
blockade,  as  the  recent  accumulated  disasters  to  the  blockade  runners 
very  clearly  show. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Off  Western  Bar,  Wilmington ,  N.  G.,  February  16,  1864. 
Str:  It  affords  me  great  satisfaction  and  pleasure  to  inform  you  of

486  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

tlie  U.  S.  S.  Montgomery ,  Acting  Yolunteer  LieuteiivaAt  Commanding 
Faucon,  of  the  English  steamer  Pet ,  of  and  from  Nassau,  master,  Boss 
Davis,  while  attempting  to  run  into  Wilmington.  Her  master  acknowl 
edges  having  destroyed  all  her  papers,  except  the  register,  by  burning

vessel  when  his  services  in  Boston  shall  no  longer  be  required.  Acting

officers  and  crew  made  up  from  the  other  vessels  of  the  squadron,  a 
list  of  which  is  herewith  forwarded,  marked  “A”. 

The  Pet  had  on  deck  several  barrels  of  liquor  and  a  quantity  of  fruits 
and  vegetables.  The  latter  two  articles,  being  of  a  perishable  nature 
and  already  partially  decayed,  I  directed  to  be  distributed  among  the 
officers  and  crews  of  the  vessels  attached  to  the  blockade,  which  I 
trust  may  meet  with  your  approval.  The  liquor  was  struck  below  In 
main  hold  and  hatches  battened  down. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jas.  Madison  Frailey, 
Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Faucon,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IJ.  S.  S.  Montgomery. 

U.  S.  S.  Montgomery, 

Off  Western  Bar ,  Wilmington ,  N.  (7.,  February  16,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  11 :  55  p.  m.  on  the  15th  instant, 
Lockwood’s  Folly  Inlet  bearing  about  N.,  2  miles  distant,  5£  fathoms 
water,  wind  fresh  from  N.  W.,  sky  overcast,  saw  a  vessel  to  W.  N.  W.  of  us. 
At  once  gave  chase,  steering  N.  W.  by  W.  Finding  her  moving  inshore, 
I  steered  into  4£  fathoms,  hugging  the  shore.  The  chase  discovering 
this  stood  at  once  off  to  the  southward.  At  12 : 30  on  the  10th,  near¬ 
ing  the  chase,  challenged  her  twice  with  the  night  signals.  Not  receiv¬ 
ing  an  answer,  fired  the  30  pounder  rifled  gun  on  the  forecastle  directly 
at  her.  At  12:45  fired  a  second  shot,  when  the  chase  hove  to,  let  off 
steam,  and  lowered  two  boats,  which  at  once  left  her  with  some  of  her 
people. 

At  this  moment,  the  ship  being  under  strong  headway,  we  rapidly 
passed  the  chase,  merely  seeing  the  boats  alter  they  had  left  her. 
Wore  round  and  sent  Acting  Ensign  W.  O.  Putnam  on  board  with 
Acting  Second  Assistant  Engineer  James  Pollard  and  a  boat’s  crew  to 
take  charge  of  the  prize. 

As  soon  as  they  were  in  possession  I  stood  to  the  N.  W.  some  3 
miles  in  hopes  of  picking  up  the  boats  that  had  left,  but  without  success. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


487 


The  vessel  proved  to  be  the  steamer  Pet ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence, 
which  names  are  painted  on  her  stern;  and  also  ascertained  by  her 
certificate  of  British  registry,  the  only  paper,  with  some  boat  notes, 
found  on  board. 

The  captain  of  the  Pet  admitted  that  he  had  burned  his  mails,  log 
book,  and  all  his  papers  before  capture,  and  that  he  was  a  fair  prize. 

At  the  time  of  capture  no  other  vessel  was  in  sight;  nor  was  any 
vessel  seen  until  daylight,  when  we  made  the  ships  of  the  squadron  to 
the  S.  E.  At  once  transferred  such  of  the  Pet’s  officers,  passengers, 
and  crew,  17  in  all,  as  were  found  on  board.  We  afterward  ascertained 
that  13  persons  had  left  in  the  boats,  including  the  pilot. 

Stood  in  again  to  our  station,  the  prize  following,  at  5  a.  m.,  off  Locn.- 
wood’s  Folly.  At  daylight,  seeing  nothing  of  the  boats  which  had  left 
the  Pet  during  the  night,  moved  out  with  the  prize  and  anchored  near 
the  Quaker  City. 

The  Pet  is  an  iron  vessel,  2  years  old ;  14  feet  long,  20  wide,  and  11 
depth  of  hold;  tonnage,  233;  register  tonnage,  171;  there  being  a 
reduction  of  02  tons  for  space  for  propelling  power.  She  has  two 
24-inch  cylinders,  24-inch  stroke,  direct-action  condensing  engines. 
She  carries  450  bales  of  cotton.  Hull  and  engines  in  good  order. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  H.  Faucon, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Bear  Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne ,  N.  C.,  February  16,  1864. 

Admiral  :  One  schooner  has  been  sunk  at  a  proper  place  up  the  river 
to  obstruct  the  channel,  and  others  will  be  as  soon  as  possible. 

The  ram  is  without  doubt  a  fixed  fact;  deserters  and  refugees  confirm

I  learn  this  morning  that  the  Eutaw  has  gotten  over  the  Swash  and 
I  hope  to  see  her  this  evening  or  to-morrow. 

The  Valley  City  had  arrived  at  Hatteras. 

The  water  is  extremely  low. 

I  shall  send  the  Southfield  to  Plymouth  immediately  on  the  arrival  of 
the  Eutaw ,  and  the  Valley  City ,  or  some  other,  to  Washington.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Quackenbusli ,  77.  S.  Navy ,  commanding 
U.  S.  S.  Pequot ,  of  putting  into  Beaufort ,  N.  0.,  on  account  of  sickness 
and  injuries  sustained  in  gale. 


U.  S.  S.  Pequot, 

Beaufort,  N.  C.,  February  17,  1864. 

Sir  :  In  consequence  of  the  smallpox  and  measles  having  broken  out 
among  the  crew  of  this  vessel,  and  also  having  the  davits  of  the  sec¬ 
ond  launch  carried  away  during  the  gale  of  the  15th  instant,  I  deemed 
it  necessary  to  put  into  Beaufort  in  order  to  have  the  sick  removed  to 
the  hospital,  to  prevent,  if  possible,  the  further  spreading  of  the  disease 
on  board.  I  trust  there  Avill  be  no  other  cases,  but  I  greatly  fear  there 

During  the  gale  of  the  15th  instant  this  vessel  behaved  remarkably 
well  until  the  wind  shifted  from  the  S.  E.  to  the  S.  W.,  which  created  a 
heavy  cross  sea.  I  was  then  obliged  to  batten  down  the  hatches,  as 
the  vessel  rolled  so  deep  as  to  completely  submerge  the  hammock  rails, 
and  the  waist  boats  which  were  raised  several  feet  above  them.  In  a 
word,  I  never  witnessed  such  rolling  in  my  life,  and  hope  never  to  again. 
I  am  happy  to  say  I  had  the  good  fortune  to  save  the  second  launch 
after  the  davits  had  been  carried  away.  Since  my  arrival  on  the  sta¬ 
tion  assigned  me,  I  have  endeavored  to  carry  out  your  instructions 
fully.  Accompanying  this,  I  send  you  my  abstract  log,  and  my  reply 

to  Surgeon  Sharp’s  report. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

’  S.  P.  Quackenbush, 

Lieu  tenant-  Commander. 


Acting  Bear- Admiral  S.  P.  Lee,

Report  of  Lieutenant-  Commander  Gillis,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  expedition 
up  the  James  River  in  search  of  escaped  Union  prisoners. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Commodore  Morris, 

Newport  News,  February  18,  1864. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  instructions  of  the  17th  instant,  I  went  on 
board  the  Commodore  Jones,  and,  with  the  U.  S.  S.  Shokokon,  proceeded 
up  the  James  River  for  the  purpose  of  affording  aid  to  any  of  the  Union 
prisoners  who  had  escaped  from  Richmond.  It  being  late  in  the  after¬ 
noon  when  we  started,  we  were  unable  to  reach  the  Chickahominy  until 
late  in  the  evening.  I  therefore  bad  the  vessels  anchor  off  Jamestown 
Island  until  this  morning  at  daylight,  when  we  got  underway  and 
stood  up  the  river  as  far  as  Claremont,  about  5  miles  above  the  mouth 
of  the  Chickahominy;  fired  several  guns  and  showed  our  largest 
ensign;  saw  no  signals  that  would  indicate  the  presence  of  anyone 
wishing  to  communicate  with  the  vessel,  but  discovered  that  the  rebels 
had  a  picket  and  signal  station  on  the  upper  side  of  the  mouth  of  the 
Chickahominy,  and  I  am  of  the  opinion  that  none  of  those  we  were  in 
search  of  could  possibly  avoid  being  retaken  should  they  make  their 
appearance  in  that  vicinity.  I  left  the  mouth  of  the  Chickahominy  at 
12  m.  and  returned  to  my  station,  leaving  the  Commodore  Jones  on 
picket. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  H.  Gillis, 

Lieutenant- Commander,  U.  S.  Navy . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

U.  S.  S.  Morse, 

Off  Yorktown ,  Va.,  February  2,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  respectfully  report  that  having  received  information  that  some 
torpedoes  had  been  placed  in  York  Eiver,  near  Purtan  Bay,  some  18 
miles  above  Yorktown,  I  received  permission  to  proceed  up  the  river, 
from  Acting  Master  Wright,  and  if  possible,  find  where  these  torpedoes 
were  laid.  Yesterday  morning  proceeded  up  the  river,  and  when  abreast 
of  the  ferry  saw  some  oyster  boats  close  inshore;  lowered  boats  from 
this  vessel  and  succeeded  in  capturing  four  of  them.  When  off  Pinka- 
tink  Creek,  came  to  anchor;  saw  several  more  in  the  creek;  sent  in 
boats  and  captured  eight  of  them,  one  being  a  scow  lately  built  for  the 
purpose  of  transporting  grain  up  the  river. 

Several  of  these  boats  have  been  carrying  on  a  steady  trade  between 
this  place  and  the  White  House.  Three  of  these  boats  had  cargoes  in 
them,  consisting  of  11  plows,  a  quantity  of  plowshares,  4  boxes  of 
tobacco,  and  9  sacks  of  salt,  also  2  anchors  and  cables.  There  being 
some  more  plows  (new)  housed  in  a  storehouse  close  to  the  river  bank, 
and  not  having  room  to  bring  them  on  board,  the  officer  in  charge 
destroyed  them.  These  goods  had  all  just  arrived  direct  from  Richmond. 

Swept  the  river  around  and  across  by  Purtan  Bay,  but  could  not  find 
any  torpedoes;  returned  again  to  Yorktown  this  afternoon. 

i  respectfully  await  your  orders  as  to  what  may  be  done  with  these 
boats,  goods,  etc. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Adolphus  Dennett, 

Acting  Ensign  and  Executive  Officer. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Oomdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  off  Newport  News. 


U.  S.  S.  Morse, 

Off  Yorktown ,  Va.,  February  14,  1864. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  report  that,  having  been  informed  by  General 
Wistar  (commanding  army  forces  at  Yorktown)  on  the  night  ot  the  12th 
instant  that  he  was  about  to  send  two  companies  of  cavalry  on  a  scout 
up  York  River  as  far  as  Potopotank  Creek,  and  having  heard  that  there 
were  one  or  more  small  vessels  engaged  in  a  regular  trade  between 
Potopotank  Creek  and  White  House,  1  concluded  to  proceed  up  the 
river  and,  if  possible,  capture  these  vessels.  Got  underway  on  the 
morning  of  the  13th  instant  and  proceeded  up  York  River.  When 
abreast  of  Pinkatink  Creek  saw  a  boat  hauled  up  on  the  beach ;  brought 
her  alongside,  and  found  on  board  one  plow,  one  box  tobacco,  a  few 
books,  and  a  small  amount  of  calico.  Hearing  that  torpedoes  were 
placed  50  feet  apart  across  the  river  from  Moody’s  Wharf  to  Purtan 
Island  Point,  lowered  boats  and  swept  the  river  with  small  chains,  the 
vessel  following  in  the  track  of  the  boats;  found  no  impediment  what¬ 
ever.  I  do  not  believe  there  are  any  torpedoes  below  Goff’s  Point,  but 
across  from  Goff’s  Point  to  Terrapin  Point  and  in  the  forks  of  the  river 
at  West  Point  I  believe,  from  information  received,  that  there  are  cer¬ 
tainly  torpedoes  placed  there.  On  arriving  off  the  mouth  of  Potopo¬ 
tank  Creek  came  to  anchor;  saw  our  cavalry  on  shore  and,  having  two 
of  the  Signal  Corps  on  board  this  vessel,  signalized  with  the  cavalry 
and  found  everything  quiet  around  the  creek.  Lowered  all  boats  with 
armed  crews  and  proceeded  up  Potopotank  Creek  about  3  miles;  found

a  small  sloop  of  about  5  tons,  laden  with  nearly  200  busjhfels  of  corn,  also
