Sir:  I  regret  to  report  that  early  yesterday  morning  a  two-masted, 
schooner- rigged  steamer,  with  single  smokestack,  was  found  to  have 
entered  during  the  night,  but  not  without  grounding  near  or  on  the 
bar  between  Bald  Head  and  Port  Caswell,  remaining  there  until  the 
following  high  water,  when  she  was  taken  off  by  tugs  and  up  the  river. 

She  doubtless  evaded  the  squadron  shortly  after  the  moon  set,  as  at 
that  time  she  was  plainly  seeu  and  chased  by  the  Aries,  but,  unfor¬ 
tunately,  Captain  Devens  soon  lost  sight  of  her  after  turning  her 
offshore,  but  was  doubtless  soon  afterwards  doubled  upon. 

The  State  of  Georgia  must  leave  here  to-morrow  or  next  day  for  Beau¬ 
fort,  and  I  shall  be  compelled  to  follow  with  this  ship  by  Tuesday,  the 
23d,  which  will  weaken  the  force  considerably  until  our  return. 

I  have  to  report  the  arrival  on  the  16th  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Vicksburg ,  and 
on  the  17th  of  U.  S.  S.  Monticello,  which,  with  the  Montgomery,  Merce- 
dita,  and  Aries,  will  compose  the  squadron  after  my  departure,  unless 
the  Maratanza  and  Emma  should  return. 

The  latter  vessel,  much  to  my  surprise,  has  been  abseut  seventeen 
days. 

The  prize  steamer  Pet ,  captured  on  the  night  of  the  16th  instant  by 
Lieutenant  Commanding  Paucon  in  the  Montgomery ,  started  for  Boston 
yesterday  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  Edmund  Kemble,  lately  attached 
to  this  ship. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Acting  Master  Studley , 
U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  means  to  be  employed  to  bring  vessels  to. 

Strictly  confidential.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

February  19,  1864. 

Sir:  Referring  to  my  instructions  of  January  29,  1863,  on  your  file, 
you  are  hereby  ordered  always  to  fire  blank  cartridges  to  bring  vessels 
to  which  are  attempting  to  cross  the  blockade,  and  not  to  fire  a  shotted 
gun  of  any  sort  until  you  find  that  no  attention  is  paid  to  the  blank 
cartridges  already  fired,  when,  under  your  personal  supervision  always, 
you  may,  if  it  be  absolutely  necessary,  fire  a  ball  or  shot,  but  never 
into  any  vessel  or  in  such  direction  that  the  bullet  or  shot  will  reach 
the  shore  either  direct  or  by  ricochet.  You  must  not  make  this  order 
public,  but  notify  your  executive  officer  and  officers  of  the  deck  that 
balls  or  shots  are  not  to  be  fired  except  under  your  personal  supervi¬ 
sion.  You  will  occupy  such  a  position  outside  of  the  line  of  Fortress 
Monroe  light  house  and  the  Rip  Raps  as  will  obviate  all  chance  of 
striking  any  person,  especially  a  sentry  on  shore.  You  may  arrest, 
detain,  and  report  vessels  arriving  winch  intentionally  violate  the 
blockade,  and  those  going  out  may  be  so  fil  ed  at  as  to  bring  them  to 
without  doing  any  injury.  Besides,  you  can  generally  ascertain  the 
names  of  outward-bound  offenders,  and  detain  and  report  them  on  their 
return. 

See  that  your  boarding  officer  has  a  correct  copy,  certified  by  you,  of 
my  order  of  January  29,  1863,  to  show  to  every  vessel  that  you  board 
other  than  a  man-of-war. 

Respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  etc. 

Acting  Master  I.  B.  Studley, 

Commanding  Ouardsliip  Young  Rover ,  Hampton  Roads. 


Unofficial  letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  the 
Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  regarding  the  blockade  and  blockade 
runners. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  February  20, 1864. 
Sir:  Yours  of  the  17th  came  to  hand  last  evening.  Thank  you  for 
your  agreeable  congratulations  on  the  last  hit  off  Wilmington,  which 


496 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


makes  tlie  number  of  blockade  runners  captured  or  destroyed  since 
July  12,  26,  and  since  the  blockade  was  strengthened  last  fall  the 
number  is  23  steamers  lost  to  the  trade. 

Can  the  history  of  the  blockade  beat  this  ? 

1  don’t  believe  that  many  prizes  will  be  made  hereafter;  the  runners 
now  take  to  the  beach  too  readily  when  they  see  a  bloekader  by  day  or 
night.  1  pride  myself  on  the  conduct  of  the  blockade,  which  has  given 
me  mneli  care,  thought,  and  writing,  My  instructions  will  show  this 
when  I  send  them  to  you;  they  certainly  cover  the  whole  ground,  and 
work  well,  though  several  runners  have  got  in  lately.  I  think  the 
additions  to  the  runners  are  less  than  the  numbers  destroyed,  etc.  Did 
you  not  disclose  too  much  to  the  runners  in  publishing  that  part  of  my 
dispatch  about  the  Sassacus  which  exposed  her  cruising  ground?  She 
and  the  Eutaw  were  ordered  to  the  sounds.  The  Eutaw  got  aground 
on  the  Swash.  They  were  both  ordered  to  the  outside  blockade  several 
days  ago — the  Sassacus  to  intercept  the  Bermuda  and  the  Eutaw  the 
Nassau  runners.  The  Sassacus  has  done  well  and  the  Eutaw  will  do 
well,  and  may  be  better  as  to  speed  than  the  Sassacus.  I  congratulate 
you  on  the  success  of  this  class.  With  a  little  improvement  in  the 
steering  in  some  of  them,  they’ll  beat  the  Clyders. 

Trade,  I  suspect,  is  the  demon  which  instigates  all  attacks  on  the 
blockade  and  blockaders.  Its  profitable  monopoly  requires  strict  exclu¬ 
sion  of  foreign  competition,  and  scarcely  tolerates  the  form  of  blockade 
against  inland  trade. 

You  reminded  me  the  other  day  that  General  Dix  objected  to  the 
boarding  vessel  blockading  off  Hampton  Roads.  As  boarding  returns 
are  required  of  cruisers  in  time  of  peace,  how  can  they  be  dispensed 
with  in  time  of  war  and  blockade,  which  the  Navy  is  required  to  keep 
in  good  faith  ? 

I  hear  nothing  more  about  the  surrender  of  our  naval  magazine, 
building,  and  grounds.  They  are  much  needed,  and  the  (Jarstairs  con¬ 
tinues  on  demurrage.  Chief  Engineer  Long’s  force  and  knowledge  are 
much  needed  at  the  Gosport  navy  yard.  The  Atlanta ,  a  horrid  thing 
to  live  in,  left  here  before  the  Tacony  took  the  place  of  the  Wyalusing; 
she  experienced  bad  weather,  and  did  well.  I  trust  you  mean  to  give 
me  the  swift  dispatch  and  mail  steamer  which  I  have  applied  for — the 
B.  E.  Lee,  Merrimac ,  or  Banshee  would  do  well.  I  need  something  to 
take  the  mail  and  special  orders  in  an  emergency.  When  I  leave  here 
squadron  papers  pile  up  and  office  work  gets  behindhand.  The  New 
Berne  passes  semioccasion  ally  instead  of  semimonthly,  and  the  FahTcee 
blockades  and  feeds  the  bar  tenders,  wTho  carry  but  little  coal.  Only 
consider  the  superfluity  of  army  transportation  and  our  absolute  want. 

The  blockade  off  Wilmington  is  the  blockade  of  two  widely  separated 
entrances,  each  requiring  as  much  force  as  Charleston  did,  if  not  more. 
Experience  teaches  that  a  mere  inner  line  will  not  answer  for  blockad¬ 
ing  in  this  steam  era.  Now  the  blockaders  are  from  1  to  2  miles,  and 
more,  apart.  This  is  only  thick  when  it  is  so  dark  that  all  is  thickness. 
In  estimating  the  sea  strength  of  this  blockading  squadron,  one  must 
only  count  the  steamers  off  Wilmington.  The  rest  are  keels,  not  pen¬ 
nants.  Winter  blockading  is  very  trying  to  machinery,  and  nearly 
a  third  of  the  vessels,  sometimes  more,  are  absent  for  repairs  and  coal, 
going,  returning,  or  at  Beaufort,  not  to  speak  of  those  (like  the  Monti- 
cello,  away  three  months)  at  Northern  ports. 

I  thank  you  for  the  Peterhoff.  I  hope  she  is  suited  to  the  service. 
Captain  Eorbes  said  I  was  to  have  the  Cherolcee.  I  hope  so.  Where  is 
Lam  son?  I  have  a  special  want  for  him,  and  trust  he  is  not  to  be 
detached  from  this  squadron.  Can’t  you  give  me  Clitz?  He,  too, 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


407 


knows  the  requirements  of  this  blockade.  It  is  a  grave  mistake  to 
make  changes  on  blockade  services.  An  officer  acquainted  with  the 
situation  is  of  more  account  than  one  of  equal  merit  who  is  not. 
Where  are  all  the  regular  navy  officers?  Except  the  few  on  this  ship 
and  the  Roanoke  there  are  but  two  this  side  of  Cape  Henry,  three  in 
the  sounds,  and,  say,  two  or  three  dozen,  old  and  young,  off  Wilmington. 
Will  you  not  give  this  blockading  squadron  its  proportion  of  the  fast 
navy  vessels?  As  far  as  blockade  running  is  concerned,  this  squadron 
has  more  to  do  than  all  the  others.  Wilmington  and  its  entrances  and 
adjacent  inlets  require  more  attention  than  all  the  rest  of  the  coast. 
The  depots  at  Bermuda  and  Nassau  are  tributary  to  it.  A  modern 
blockading  squadron  has  much  more  to  do  than  merely  threatening  an 
entrance.  It  should  intercept  runners  where  daylight  shows  them 
after  a  long  night’s  run  from  either  end  of  their  lines.  In  no  other 
way  can  a  wooden  blockade  be  made  effective.  Out-runners  can  not 
be  stopped  just  off  an  entrance  which  they  can  pass  any  dark  night. 

You  will  be  surprised,  on  examination,  to  find  how  few  steamers  of 
the  number  and  kind  assigned  can  be  kept  immediately  off  each  bar  to 
Wilmington  at  one  time.  It  is  the  severest  service  imaginable,  and 
strangely  well  do  the  steamers  stand  it;  but  more  and  new  and  swift 
ones  are  absolutely  needed  for  the  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 
Since  last  summer  only  has  this  blockading  force  been  much  more  than 
nominal  for  want  of  strength. 

How  many  of  the  new  monitors  are  to  come  to  me,  and  when  may 
they  be  expected?  I  long  to  cooperate  with  an  army  capable  of  invest¬ 
ing  Bichmond  or  Wilmington,  a  la  Vicksburg.  What  chance  of  it, 
and  when? 

Very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee. 


Hon.  G.  V.  Fox, 

Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy,  advising  that  the 

military  authorities  direct  the  placing  of  obstructions  in  the  Roanoke 

River. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  February  20,  1864. 

Sir  :  General  Peck  desires  the  senior  naval  officer  at  Plymouth  to 
sink  the  two  light-boats  now  there  in  the  opening  in  piling  obstruction 
just  above  the  town. 

I  think  it  best  that  the  defense  of  obstructions  should  be  left  to  the 
military  authorities,  and,  if  thought  necessary  by  them,  conducted  by 
their  engineers,  and  I  propose  to  suggest  this  course  to  General  Butler. 

If  General  Butler  or  General  Peck  desires  it,  may  these  old  light 
vessels  be  applied  to  this  purpose?  They  were  once  sunk  by  the  rebels 
and  raised  by  the  Light-House  Board,  and  are  not  of  much  value  now. 

I  enclose  a  copy  of  a  report*  from  Lieutenant-Commander  Flusser, 
dated  February  16,  and  received  to  day. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Letter  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  to  the  Secretary  of  the 
Navy,  requesting  instr  uctions  regarding  the  limits  seaward  of  the  North 
Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

IT.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  February  23,  1864. 
Sir  :  I  am  not  aware  that  the  limits  seaward  of  the  North  Atlantic 
Blockading  Squadron  under  my  command  have  been  defined  by  the 
Department. 

The  necessities  of  an  effective  modern  blockade  require  a  consider¬ 
able  extent  for  cruising,  to  intercept  and  chase  steam  blockade  runners; 
and  I  have  always  considered  my  limits  as  extending  seaward  as  far  as 
this  object  required,  and  that  wherever  a  man-of-war  of  my  squadron, 
acting  under  my  orders,  was  cruising  was  necessarily  embraced  in  my 
limits.  It  will  be  difficult  to  define  exact  limits,  except  of  harbors  and 
inlets  on  the  coast,  between  the  cruisers  of  this  and  the  adjoining 
squadron;  but  no  inconvenience  to  the  public  service  need  be  experi¬ 
enced  from  not  drawing  a  dividing  line  seaward  between  this  and  the 
next  squadron, 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


499 


I  respectfully  request  to  know  tlie  Department’s  construction  of 
its  orders  establishing  the  limits  of  the  North  Atlantic  Blockading 
Squadron. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  r.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Roe ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  rqghrding  condition  of 

TJ.  S.  S.  Sassacus. 


IT.  S.  S.  Sassacus, 
Uatteras  Inlet ,  February  22,  1864. 

Sir  :  Having  received  information  to  the  effect  that  the  canal  com¬ 
munication  from  New  Berne  to  Fort  Monroe  was  closed  by  ice,  and 
consequently  I  may  be  unduly  detained  here,  and  as  the  Sassacus  can 
not  proceed  upon  her  cruise  on  account  of  derangements  to  her  machin¬ 
ery,  I  have  thought  it  better  for  me  to  proceed  at  once  to  Norfolk  and 
report  in  person  to  the  admiral  without  unnecessary  delay.  I  shall 
therefore  proceed  to  Fort  Monroe  to-morrow. 

I  beg  you  will  be  pleased  to  forward  all  mails  that  may  arrive  at  New 
Berne  for  this  vessel  to  Norfolk. 

Trusting  that  my  course  will  be  approved  by  the  admiral, 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  etc., 

F.  A.  Roe, 

Lieutenant- Commander.

Letter  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  to  Commander  Daven¬ 
port,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  relative  to  Confederate  vessels  on  the  Neuse  and

Confidential.]  IT.  s.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Newport  News,  February  23,  1864. 

Sir:  Your  number  203  of  16th  instant  is  received.  I  have  asked 
General  Butler  for  the  information  lie  had  or  might  be  able  to  obtain 
concerning  the  rams  said  to  be  building  in  the  Roanoke  and  Neuse 
rivers.  General  Butler  sent  me,  in  a  confidential  communication  on  the 
Kith,  a  copy  of  a  letter  from  General  Peck  of  13th,  stating  that  both 
rams  aie  expected  down  the  Neuse  and  Roanoke  in  conjunction  with 
land  troops.  It  seems  certain  that  the  one  at  Kinston  is  intended  to 
come  down  on  the  next  high  water.  General  Butler  remarks,  however 
that  he  does  not  much  believe  in  either  ram. 

Respectfully,  yours, 


S.  P.  Lee,

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  reauest 
for  a  guard  of  marines  for  the  U.  S.  8.  Sassacus. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Of  Newport  News,  Va.,  February  25,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  transmit  enclosed  to  the  Department  a  communication  from 
Lieutenant-Commander  Boe,  IT.  S.  S.  Sassacus,  of  the  24th  instant, 
requesting  that  a  marine  guard  may  be  allowed  his  vessel. 

If  any  vessels  in  the  service  require  marines  more  than  others  they 
are  those  engaged  in  blockade  service,  who  have  frequently  to  deal 
with  blockade  runners  full  of  liquor.  It  is  my  belief,  from  verbal 
reports  that  I  have  received,  that  several  blockade  runners  which  have 
been  destroyed  might  have  been  captured  but  for  these  causes — the 
want  of  marines  as  sentries  and  the  large  quantities  of  liquor  on  board 
of  them. 

The  desire  to  have  marine  guards  is  very  generally  expressed  by 
commanding  officers  on  the  blockade,  whose  professional  experience 
has  shown  the  necessity  for  them  on  this  service. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

'  S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gtdeon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy,  Washington ,  1).  C.

U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Barney,

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  I  got  underway  off  Hol¬ 
loway’s  [Halliday’s]  Point  on  the  morning  of  24th  instant  to  send  a

505 


rebel  deserter  to  the  flagship  (that  I  took  on  board  the  evening 
previous). 

1  left  the  schooner  Lion,  of  Philadelphia,  at  anchor  near  the  above- 
mentioned  place,  giving  the  captain  instructions  that  in  case  he  sees 
the  enemy  to  set  his  ensign  at  the  main  masthead.  About  two  hours 
after  my  leaving,  the  officer  of  the  deck  reported  that  the  ensign  was 
flying  from  the  schooner’s  masthead;  upon  nearing  the  vessel,  I  saw 
some  (supposed  to  be  armed)  men  on  shore.  The  captain  of  the 
schooner  told  me  that  they  fired  a  volley  of  musketry  at  him,  their  shot 
falling  short  of  the  vessel.  I  fired  two  IX-inch  and  one  100  pounder 
Parrott  rifle  5-second  shell  into  the  woods  where  they  were,  and  I  saw 
nothing  of  them  afterward. 

1  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jambs  M.  Williams,

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Flusser ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  affairs 

in  the  Roanoke  River. 


U.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Plymouth ,  N.  C.,  February  25,  1864. 

Sir:  On  the  22d  instant  I  sent  Acting  Master  Welles  in  the  White- 
head  with  25  men  from  this  vessel  up  the  Roanoke  to  destroy  a  mill  at 
which  the  rebel  garrison  of  Rainbow  Bluff  were  having  corn  ground. 
The  mill  was  found  about  21  miles  above  this  place;  it  was  the  property 
of  one  Jordan,  who  is  in  the  rebel  Army.  Mr.  Welles  burned  it  to  the 
ground.  No  enemy  was  seen. 


Some  torpedoes  were  reported  in  the  river  a  mile  above  Jordan’s 
place  by  the  people  thereabouts.  People  residing  on  or  near  the  river 
have  been  warned  by  the  rebels  from  fishing  in  certain  parts  of  the 
river  where  they  profess  to  have  sunk  torpedoes.  I  do  not  know 
whether  there  are  any  in  the  river  or  not,  but  if  there  are  they  can 
easily  be  removed  by  dragging  with  two  small  boats  and  a  line,  if  we 
should  ever  desire  to  ascend  beyond  their  reported  position.  Whether 
the  report  is  correct  or  incorrect,  it  comes  from  the  rebels,  and  would 
argue  rather  fear  of  our  advance  than  an  intention  on  their  part  to  attack. 
A  hen  the  ironclad  is  completed,  if  a  large  rebel  land  force  is  in  the 
State,  she  might  be  brought  to  make  a  combined  attack  on  this  place. 
She  will  never  venture  down  without  such  support. 

A  lather  respectable  man  came  into  our  lines  from  Raleigh  some 
days  since.  He  says  the  ironclad  is  to  have  two  thicknesses  of  1^-inch 
iron,  the  layers  at  right  angles  to  each  other.  He  says  further  that  she 
is  spoken  of  as  intended  for  auxiliary  defense  at  Rainbow  Bluff:  that 
the  people  say  we  have  mounted  here  several  Parrott  300  pounders- 
that  she  could  not  endure  their  fire,  and  will  not  be  risked  under  it.  ’ 

I  wrote  you  some  days  siuce  that  General  Peck,  when  he  was  here 
stated  that  the  rebels  had  received  reinforcements  in  this  State  to  the 
number  of  5,000  men.  My  own  opinion  is,  although  I  have  no  infor¬ 
mation  on  which  to  ground  it,  that  the  force  which  appeared  before 
New  Berne  was  en  route  to  Mobile,  and  that  for  that  reason  New  Berne 
was  not  attacked;  they  had  not,  or  thought  they  had  not,  time  to 
delay.  1  did  expect  an  attack  on  New  Berne  for  the  first  few  days 
after  the  disappearance  of  the  rebels  before  the  city,  but  after  that 
concluded  they  had  gone  farther  south.  If  my  supposition  is  cor 
reef,  I  tear  General  Sherman  may  meet  a  larger  force  on  his  wav  than 
he  anticipated.  J 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  W.  Flusser, 

...  ,,  .  ,  .  ,  „  Lieutenant- Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy,  giving  information 
regarding  the  ironclad  under  construction  in  the  Roanoke  River. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  February  26,  1864. 

Sir  :  Lieutenant-Commander  Flusser,  IT.  S.  S.  Miami,  reports  as  fol¬ 
lows,  under  date  of  20tli  instant: 

Brigadier-General  Wessells  informed  me  yesterday  that  he  had  heard  that  25,000 
pouncts  of  iron  had  been  sent  from  Wilmington  about  two  weeks  since  to  be  put  on 
the  ironclad  building  at  Halifax,  on  the  Roanoke  River.  The  story  came  indirectly 
from  two  men  who  visited  Atlanta,  Ga.,  some  time  since  to  carry  negroes  from 
this  State,  and,  returning,  passed  through  Wilmington.  They  and  the  iron  came  in 
the  same  train.  Although  one  of  these  men  is  wealthy,  of  good  standing,  and  was 
formerly  an  officer  of  the  rebel  Army,  he  was  not  permitted  to  visit  the  boat  at 
Halifax,  but  was  told  none  but  navy  officers  could  see  her. 

The  engine  is  reported  in  her  and  is  said  to  be  good,  but  not  new. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  thi  chairman  of  the 
Light- House  Board ,  regarding  channel  buoys  in  Beaufort  Harbor ,  and 
the  use  of  old  light-boats  as  obstructions. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  February  27,  1864. 
Admiral:  The  Coast  Survey  has  issued  a  new  chart  of  Beaufort 
Harbor  and  recalled  those  previously  in  use,  as  the  channel  has  been 
found  to  have  changed  materially. 

The  channel  buoys,  as  now  placed  and  marked  upon  the  old  chart,  do 
not  mark  the  deepest  water,  and  lately  vessels  entering  strike  fre¬ 
quently.  I  would  respectfully  suggest  that  the  buoys  be  replaced  and 
their  positions  marked  upon  the  new  chart  at  the  earliest  moment,  as 
the  increasing  number  of  blockaders  going  to  Beaufort  for  coal  calls  for 
prompt  action  to  prevent  accidents. 

Major-General  Peck,  commanding  the  army  forces  in  North  Carolina, 
has  applied  to  me,  through  Major-General  Butler,  for  the  old  light-boats 
now  at  Plymouth,  to  obstruct  the  Neuse  and  Roanoke  rivers,  in  order 
to  prevent  the  rebel  ironclads  said  to  be  building  up  those  rivers  com¬ 
ing  down  to  assist  in  an  attack  on  New  Berne  or  Plymouth. 

I  have  answered  General  Butler  that  the  light-boats  were  under  the 
control  of  the  Light-House  Board,  and  suggested  his  making  applica¬ 
tion  there  for  them;  at  the  same  time,  if  he  considered  there  was  any 
pressing  military  necessity  for  such  a  conversion  of  them,  I  should  not 
object  or  interfere  with  his  taking  them. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  admiral,  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 
Rear-Admiral  Siiubrick, 

Chairman  Light-House  Board,  Washington,  I).  C.

Hdqrs.  Army  and  District  of  North  Carolina, 

New  Berne ,  N.  G.,  February  28,  1864. 

Commodore  :  A  concurrence  of  testimony  indicates  that  this  posi¬ 
tion  is  about  to  incur  a  formidable  attack. 

Dispatches  from  the  military  commander  at  Washington  are  to  the 
effect  that  he  has  information  of  a  meditated  attack  upon  that  place 
within  a  few  days,  which  will  probably  be  preliminary  to  that  upon 
New  Berne. 

Major-General  Peck  directs  me  to  request  you,  if  there  are  not  already 
two  gunboats  in  the  vicinity  of  Washington,  and  if  the  demands  else¬ 
where  are  not  such  as  to  prevent,  that  another  boat  may  be  sent  to  a 
position  off  Washington  for  a  short  time. 

It  is  the  geueral’s  impression  that  there  are  already  two  there.

Report  of  Commander  Davenport ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  disposition 

of  vessels  of  his  command. 

U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne,  N.  G.,  February  28,  1864. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  semimonthly 
statement  of  the  disposition  of  vessels  in  the  sounds  for  term  ending 
at  date : 

February  16. — The  Granite  sailed  for  Hatteras.  The  Ceres  arrived 
from  Hatteras. 

February  17. — The  Seymour  sailed  for  Croatan  Sound  with  surveying 
party.  The  Eutaw  arrived  from  Hampton  Roads. 

February  18.— The  Lockwood  sailed  for  Hatteras  with  dispatches  from 
Admiral  Lee  for  the  Sassacus.  The  Southfield  sailed  for  Plymouth. 

February  19. — The  Valley  City  arrived  from  Hampton  Roads. 

February  20. — The  Lockwood  arrived  from  Hatteras. 

February  22. — The  Valley  City  sailed  for  Washington. 

February  25. — The  Eutaw  sailed  for  Beaufort. 

February  26. — The  Lockivood  sailed  to  accompany  and  protect  the 
U.  S.  Coast  Survey  schooner  Hall ,  surveying  in  the  Neuse  River.

Boat  expedition  to  Smithville,  N.  C.,  for  the  purpose  of  capturing  the 
commanding  general ,  February  29,  1864. 

Report  of  Lieutenant  Cushing,  U.  S.  Navy. 

IL  S.  S.  Monticello, 

Off  Wilmington ,  N.  C .,  March  5,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  passed  the  forts  at  the  entrance 
to  this  harbor  with  two  boats  and  20  men  on  the  night  of  the  29th  of 
February,  and  proceeded  np  the  river  to  Smith ville.  My  object  was  to 
land  at  that  town  and  capture  the  commanding  general,  and  to  board 
any  vessels  that  might  be  found  at  anchor. 

I  succeeded  in  landing  directly  in  front  of  the  hotel,  hid  my  men 
under  the  bank,  captured  some  negroes  at  work  in  a  salt  works,  and  thus 
gained  such  information  as  desired.  Then,  leaving  most  of  the  men  to 
guard  the  boats,  1  proceeded  with  Acting  Ensign  J.  E.  Jones  and  Act¬ 
ing  Master’s  Mate  W.  L.  Howorth  and  one  seaman  to  General  Hebert’s 
headquarters  (situated  across  the  street  from  the  barracks,  containing 
about  1,000  men).  I  effected  an  entry  and  captured  the  chief  engineer 
of  these  defenses,  but  found  that  the  general  had  gone  to  Wilmington 
the  same  day.  The  adjutant-general  escaped  from  the  door  after 
severely  wounding  his  hand,  but  thinking  that  a  mutiny  was  in  prog¬ 
ress,  took  to  the  woods  with  a  great  scarcity  of  clothing,  and  neglected 
to  turn  out  the  garrison.  My  boat  was  about  50  yards  from  the  Smith  - 
ville  fort,  and  not  so  far  from  the  sentinel  on  the  wharf,  but  I  succeeded 
in  bringing  my  prisoner  oft'  so  quietly  that  they  did  not  discover  me. 
The  signal  lights  were  made  so  tardily  that  I  was  abreast  of  Fort  Gas- 
well  before  they  knew  that  boats  were  in  the  harbor,  and  they  did  not 
get  a  shot  at  us.  The  papers  captured  were  unimportant.  The  Scotia 
ran  out  just  before  I  reached  the  anchorage,  so  I  did  not  have  the 
pleasure  of  calling  on  her  captain.  I  send  Captain  Kelly,  G.  S.  Army, 
to  you,  deeply  regretting  that  the  general  was  not  in  when  I  called. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  B.  Cushing, 
Lieutenant,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads. 

1  brought  off  the  negroes  captured.

Letter  of  Major-General  Whiting,  C.  S.  Army,  to  Flag-Officer  Lynch,  C.  S.  Navy. 

Headquarters  Department  of  the  Cape  Fear, 

Wilmington ,  March  2 ,  1864. 

Flag-Officer  :  Night  before  last  a  party  of  the  enemy  in  two  small 
boats  with  muffled  oars  rowed  in  between  Fort  Caswell  and  Bald  Head 
and  landed  at  the  upper  part  of  Smithville,  conducted  evidently  by 
some  one  perfectly  familiar  with  the  localities.  They  went  to  the  house 
occupied  by  General  Hebert  for  his  residence  and  succeeded  in  captur¬ 
ing  Captain  Kelly,  of  his  staff.  A  flag-of-truce  boat  appeared  yester¬ 
day  from  the  enemy,  with  which  I  permitted  communication.  It  was 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


513 


learned  that  the  party  was  commanded  by  a  Lieutenant  Jones,*  of  the 
U.  S.  Navy,  and  that  their  object  was  the  capture  of  General  Hebert. 
A  few  days  since  a  party  of  6  men,  belonging  to  the  Tenth  North  Caro¬ 
lina  Battalion,  was  ordered  about  sundown  to  take  a  boat  in  which 
some  of  the  crew  of  the  steamer  Pet  had  lauded  along  the  beach  to  Fort 
Caswell.  They  took  the  opportunity  to  desert.  No  doubt  on  their 
information,  and  perhaps  also  a  knowledge  of  localities  formed  by  men 
formerly  on  the  coast  survey,  the  attempt  was  made.  It  was  certainly 
very  daring,  and  the  actors  deserve  great  credit. 

You  are  aware  of  the  impossibility  of  discovering,  small  boats  from 
the  shore  at  night  in  a  wide  entrance.  To  avoid  a  repetition  of  any 
such  attempt  I  now  respectfully  call  your  attention  to  the  suggestion, 
that  if  you  have  the  means  at  command  guard  vessels  or  boats  be  estab¬ 
lished  by  the  Navy  at  such  points  as  maybe  regarded  most  suitable.  I 
will  be  able  to  supply  a  number  of  boats  for  the  use  of  the  Navy,  though 
I  hope  you  will  be  able  to  station  armed  vessels  as  a  relief  or  reserve 
for  outpost  guard  boats.  These  boats  should  be  required  to  bring-to  all 
boats  or  vessels  moving  in  their  vicinity  at  night  and  thoroughly  ascer¬ 
tain  their  character,  and  to  that  end,  should  this  or  any  similar  sugges¬ 
tion  be  adopted,  instructions  will  be  given  to  the  military  authorities, 
that  no  difficulty  may  occur  in  complete  cooperation. 

This  matter  is  now  presented  for  your  consideration,  and  I  shall  be 
glad  to  hear  from  you  on  the  subject. 

Yery  respectfully, 

W.  H.  C.  Whiting, 

Major-  General ,  Commanding. 

Flag-Officer  W.  F.  Lynch, 

Commanding  C.  >8.  Naval  Forces ,  North  Carolina. 


Letter  of  Flag-Officer  Lynch,  C.  S.  Navy,  to  Major-General  Whiting,  C.  S.  Army. 

Headquarters  Naval  Defenses, 

Wilmington ,  N.  C.:  March  2 ,  1864. 

General  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  com¬ 
munication  of  this  date,  and  am  disposed  to  do  all  in  my  power  to 
prevent  a  recurrence  of  the  transaction  to  which  you  allude.  Unfortu¬ 
nately  the  men  under  my  command  consist  mostly  of  conscripts,  whose 
loyalty  is  not  unquestionable,  and  if  sent  in  boats  they  might,  as  twice 
elsewhere  and  once  here  (in  the  case  of  the  Tenth  North  Carolina  Bat¬ 
talion),  desert  to  the  enemy. 

The  North  Carolina  is  having  a  new  smokestack  and  some  repairs  to 
her  battery,  preparatory  to  taking  a  position  lower  down,  and  the  other 
ironclad  is  being  pushed  forward  toward  completion  with  all  expedition. 
The  small  new  steamer  Yadkin  and  the  tug  Equator  are  fitting  for  the 
same  locality,  and  their  cruising  about  occasionally  will  be  far  more 
effective  than  rowing  guard  with  boats  manned  with  unreliable  crews.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Off  Plymouth,  N.  C.,  March  8,  1864. 

Sir:  On  the  morning  of  the  1st  instant  I  received  a  note  from  Gen¬ 
eral  Wessells,  a  copy  of  which  1  enclose.  Half  an  hour  after  its  recep¬ 
tion  1  was  underway  in  the  Southfield,  with  the  Whitehead  in  company, 
bound  up  the  Chowan  Kiver. 

In  the  mouth  of  the  Chowan  I  met  the  steamer  Massasoit,  and  was 
informed  that  the  Bombshell  was  above  Petty  Shore  and  cut  off  by 
artillery  and  infantry  stationed  at  that  point. 

The  Massasoit  had  been  prevented  from  running  into  the  trap  by 
receiving  warning,  when  a  mile  below  the  battery,  from  one  of  the 
Bombshell’s  men,  sent  through  the  swamp  to  give  notice  of  her  situation. 

I  had  received  information  some  weeks  previously  from  the  man 
whom  the  rebels  forced  to  show  them  the  place,  an  old  steamboat  cap¬ 
tain  on  the  Cbowau  and  lately  a  master  in  the  rebel  Navy,  that  ten 
torpedoes  had  been  placed  in  the  channel  (which  is  there  little  more 
than  100  yards  wide)  at  Petty  Shore,  so  I  dared  not  attempt,  with  boats 
of  such  great  draft  (the  TV  hitehead  was  drawing  7V  feet,  the  Southfield 
9^),  to  run  by. 

Just  before  dark  we  came  near  the  supposed  position  of  the  battery. 

I  went  on  board  the  Whitehead ,  moved  up  slowly,  and,  the  wind 
being  across  the  river,  was  about  to  anchor  so  that  the  rifled  100- 
pounder  might  be  brought  to  bear  upstream,  when  the  rebels  opened 
tire  on  us  with  a  fieldpiece  about  GOO  yards  off'. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


515 


The  anchor  was  kept  fast,  the  port  guns  brought  to  bear,  and  the 
fire  of  the  enemy  returned  briskly. 

In  a  few  minutes  it  became  too  dark  to  fire  with  any  accuracy,  or  to 
maneuver  the  boat  without  danger  of  grounding,  so  we  dropped  back 
a  mile  and  anchored  between  swamps  for  the  night. 

I  intended  sending  a  small  boat  up  that  night  with  an  order  to  the 
Bombshell  to  run  down  nest  morning,  but  the  enemy  had  possession  of 
both  sides  of  the  narrow  river,  with  fires  on  both  banks,  which  so  lit 
up  the  stream  that  no  boat  could  pass  unseen.  At  2  o’clock  next 
morning  I  sent  two  soldiers  on  shore  to  make  their  way  through  the 
swamp  to  the  Bombshell ,  carrying  a  letter  to  her  captain,  saying  that 
if  he  would  come  down  during  the  day  I  would  silence  the  battery. 

He  was  to  fire  a  gun  when  he  was  ready. 

At  11  a.  m.  the  soldiers  returned,  saying  the  enemy  were  on  all  the 
paths  through  the  swamp,  and  that  they  had  been  unable  to  reach  the 
Bombshell.  They  further  reported  a  large  force  on  the  north  bank  of 
the  river  (10,000  men  with  artillery) ;  that  more  artillery  had  been  sent 
for,  and  that  on  the  Sunday  preceding  (this  was  Wednesday)  an  order 
had  been  sent  to  Murfreesboro  for  a  32-pounder.  As  soon  as  the  sol¬ 
diers  returned  we  moved  up  and  opened  fire  on  the  place  from  which 
we  had  received  a  fire  the  evening  before. 

Shortly  after  we  opened  the  Bombshell  commenced  firing,  and,  from 
the  sound  of  her  guns,  I  knew  she  was  approaching.  Receiving  no 
return  from  the  fieldpiece,  we  fired  at  the  supposed  position  of  the  bat¬ 
tery,  about  1  mile  above  us. 

The  battery  was  so  posted  in  a  bend  as  to  command  the  approach 
from  above,  while  it  could  not  bring  a  gun  to  bear  downstream,  conse¬ 
quently  we  had  an  enfilading  fire  on  it. 

At ‘S  o’clock  in  the  afternoon  I  dropped  down  in  the  Southfield  to  give 
the  men  dinner,  leaving  the  Whitehead  to  fire  slowly  with  her  rifled  gun. 

The  Bombshell  had  then  been  for  an  hour  within  sound  of  our 
steam  whistle,  and  I  had  repeatedly  signaled  her  by  three  long  blasts 
to  come  down.  She  answered  the  signal  but  did  not  obey. 

The  position  of  the  battery  was  hidden  from,  us  at  all  times  by  an 
intervening  point,  over  which  we  fired,  while  the  Bombshell  had  it  in 
plain  view.  So,  although  there  was  no  response  from  it,  as  she  kept 
firing  I  supposed  the  rebels  were  still  there,  and  reserving  their  fire 
till  she  should  pass  immediately  under  their  guns. 

I  learned  from  the  Massasoit,  when  I  met  her  at  the  mouth  of  the 
Chowan,  that  the  Bombshell  had  been  firing  at  9  o’clock  the  previous 
evening,  so  I  feared  she  might  have  been  carried  by  boarders.  I  there¬ 
fore  sent  a  note  to  General  Wessells,  saying  that  if  he  would  send  me  a 
hundred  soldiers  in  her,  putting  up  some  bales  of  hay  or  cotton  to  pro¬ 
tect  tnem  from  musketry,  I  would  take  charge  of  her,  run  the  battery, 
and  retake  the  Bombshell. 

The  Massasoit  came  up  with  90  men,  but  with  orders  not  to  go  under 
the  guns  of  the  battery,  so  if  I  had  needed  her  she  would  have  been 
useless. 

There  was  another  bluff  3  miles  below,  which  I  thought  the  rebels 
might  fortify  and  make  it  very  difficult  to  pass. 

I  determined,  therefore,  to  fire  briskly  for  half  an  hour  after  dinner, 
and  if  the  Bombshell  had  not  appeared  at  the  expiration  of  that  time, 
to  convoy  the  Massasoit  below  the  lower  bluff  with  the  Southfield,  leav¬ 
ing  the  Whitehead  to  bring  off  such  of  the  crew  of  the  Bombshell  as 
could  reach  her,  provided  the  captain  should  determine  to  destroy  her 
and  take  to  the  swamp.  He  had  expressed  an  intention  to  do  so,  rather 
than  run  the  battery. 


516 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


As  we  got  underway  after  dinner  the  Whitehead  signaled  a  boat  com¬ 
ing.  The  captain  of  the  Bombshell ,  afraid  to  run  tlie  battery  in  the 
steamer,  had  risked  four  men  in  an  open  boat,  in  broad  daylight,  where 
they  must  surely  have  been  captured  if  any  enemy  was  there.  He  sent 
me  word  that  he  had  a  large  number  of  people  on  board  in  addition  to 
his  crew;  that  he  was  out  of  provisions  and  short  of  coal,  and  that  he 
feared  to  come  down  as  he  thought  the  enemy  had  masked  batteries. 
I  sent  the  boat  immediately  back  with  a  message  that  the  enemy  had 
gone,  or  his  boat  would  have  been  intercepted,  but  that  if  there  were 
any  batteries,  I  would  silence  them,  and,  finally,  if  he  were  not  down  in 
an  hour  I  would  leave  him.  Shortly  afterwards  he  rounded  the  point 
and  came  down  unmolested. 

We  then  moved  down  together,  firing  briskly  from  the  Southfield  at 
the  lower  bluff,  till  we  ascertained  there  was  nothing  there. 

I  have  been  thus  lengthy  in  this  report,  as  I  desired  you  to  under¬ 
stand  the  reason  of  the  expenditure  of  so  much  ammunition,  about 
which  I  feel  somewhat  mortified. 

The  enemy,  no  doubt,  moved  off  at  daylight  of  the  2d  instant.  All 
the  ammunition  of  the  second  day  was  wasted  through  the  cowardice 
of  the  captain  of  the  Bombshell ;  his  boat  was  scarcely  worth  it. 

I  mentioned  the  report  of  the  presence  of  a  large  rebel  force  on  the 
north  bank  of  the  Chowan.  To-day  I  learn  from  Edenton  that  Pickett’s 
division  is  over  there  after  provisions.  Eumor  says  there  are  10,000  to 
15,000  men,  no  doubt  a  great  exaggeration. 

If  it  is  necessary  to  have  these  army  gunboats  (and  I  have  thought 
from  the  meager  shipments  of  seamen,  and  the  large  number  of  sea¬ 
faring  men  enlisting  in  the  Army,  it  would  be  well  to  give  the  military 
control  of  the  inuer  waters,  and  to  put  us  on  the  deep),  they  should  at 
least  be  commanded  by  people  holding  commissions  from  the  Govern¬ 
ment  of  the  United  States,  and  not  by  irresponsible  persons  appointed 
by  quartermasters.  I  enclose  reports  of  Captains  French  and  Barrett, 
with  a  sketch  by  W.  B.  Newman  of  the  Southfield’s  100-pounder,  burst 
I  regret  to  say,  at  the  first  fire  on  the  evening  of  the  1st  instant. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  W.  Flusser, 

,  .  Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads. 

P.  S. — I  have  just  learned  that  the  enemy  had  at  Petty  Shore  500 
men  and  four  pieces  ot  artillery;  that  they  left  shortly  after  we  opened 
fire  on  the  morning  of  the  2d  instant,  stating  as  a  reason  for  moving 
that  our  guns  were  of  such  long  range  that  we  could  reach  them  while 
lying  beyond  their  range.  They  were  at  Petty  Shore  to  cover  the 
transportation  of  provisions  across  the  river  from  the  northern  bank 

We  have  a  rumor  here  of  a  great  Union  victory  at  Suffolk. 

The  draft  of  the  Bombshell  was  3£  feet,  and  of  the  Massasoit  5A,  so 
they  might  have  passed  over  obstructions  on  which  our  boats  would 
strike.

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Barrett,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Whitehead. 

U.  S.  S.  Whitehead, 

Off  Plymouth ,  N.  C.,  March  4,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  compliance  with  your  order 
I  started  fiom  this  place  at  1 1 :  30  a.  m.  of  the  1st  instant  and  proceeded 
in  company  with  the  U.  S.  S.  Southfield ,  up  the  Chowan  River,  for  the 
purpose  of  dislodging  the  enemy,  who  had  cut  off  the  retreat  of  the 
army  steamer  Bombshell  by  planting  artillery  on  the  bluffs  at  Petty 
Shore.  Nothing  of  importance  transpired  until  we  arived  in  the 
vicinity  of  the  bluff  where  we  supposed  the  enemy  to  be  posted.  I 
proceeded  cautiously  up  the  river  in  advance  to  reconnoiter  and  ascer¬ 
tain,  if  possible,  the  enemy’s  position. 

At  6  p.m.  the  enemy  opened  fire  on  us  with  two  fieldpieces,  at  the 
distance  of  600  yards,  their  guns  being  masked  behind  the  dense  foli¬ 
age  on  the  slope  and  crest  of  the  river  bank.  We  promptly  returned 
the  fire  with  shell  and  shrapnel  from  our  100-pounder  ride  and  24- 
pounder  howitzers,  silencing  the  enemy’s  guns  in  about  fifteen  minutes. 
As  it  was  now  getting  quite  dark,  we  dropped  down  the  river  about  a 
mile  and  came  to  anchor  near  the  steamer  Southfield  for  the  night  con¬ 
cealing  lights  and  using  every  precaution  to  guard  against  surprise. 

At  11  a.  m.  of  the  3d  [2d J,  [  weighed  anchor  and  proceeded  up  the 
river  in  obedience  to  your  orders,  in  company  with  the  U.  S  S  South- 
field  At  12  o’clock  opened  fire  with  our  100-pounder  rifle,  shelling  the 
woods  and  bluffs,  but  the  enemy  did  not  reply.  At  4  p.  m  the  army 
steamer  Bombshell  steamed  down  the  river  past  the  bluffs  unmolested 
and  reported  that  the  enemy  had  left.  I  started  for  this  place  at  5 
p.  in.,  and  arrived  here  at  10  p.  m.  of  the  same  day. 

It  gives  me  pleasure  to  state  that  the  officers  and  crew  under  mv 
command  performed  their  duties  in  a  cool  and  efficient  manner.  I  have 
no  casualties  to  report,  with  one  exception,  that  of  Thomas  H.  John¬ 
stone,  who  had  his  arm  severely  injured  by  the  recoil  of  rifle  gun  of 
which  he  was  second  captain.  ’

was  from  Wilmington,  bound  to  Nassau,  loaded  with  cotton  Puttimr 
a  prize  master  and  prize  crew  on  board,  I  ordered  her  to  Boston  touclf

521 


The  name  of  the  Scotia  will  be  found  to  be  mentioned  in  two  places 
in  extracts  received  by  you  December  4,  1S63. 

I  have  now  on  board  of  the  Connecticut  36  prisoners  from  her,  com¬ 
prising  crew  and  passengers;  several  of  the  latter  are  men  who  have 
been  wrecked  in  some  of  the  blockade  runners  which  have  been  driven 
ashore,  and  were  returning  to  their  homes  at  Nassau. 

One  of  them  is  from  the  Presto ,  run  ashore  and  destroyed  on  Sulli¬ 
van’s  Island  in  attempting  to  get  into  Charleston  on  the  morning  of 
February  2. 

It  seems  that  I  was  right  in  the  conjecture  expressed  in  my  let¬ 
ter  to  you  of  February  11  that  the  steamer  chased  by  the  Connecticut 
January  31  and  February  1  for  fifteen  hours  was  the  Presto.  This 
prisoner  confirms  the  fact  in  every  particular. 

A  description  of  the  Presto  will  be  found  in  the  extract  received  by 
you  November  23,  1863. 

I  desire  information  and  instructions  from  you  in  regard  to  money 
found  on  the  persons  and  among  the  baggage  of  prisoners  from  block¬ 
ade  runners.  Should  it  be  taken  from  them  at  all  times,  or  taken  from 
them  when  it  exceeds  a  certain  amount,  or  should  it  all  be  left  with 
them? 

Of  course  they  all  lay  claim  to  it  as  private  property,  yet  much  of 
this  money  is  used,  no  doubt,  in  trade  for  buying  and  selling — in  one 
word,  for  carrying  on  the  blockade  running  business. 

On  board  of  the  Scotia  when  she  was  captured  was  a  man,  wife, 
three  children,  and  nurse,  as  passengers,  going  from  Wilmington  to 
Nassau,  whom  I  left  on  board  of  her  to  go  north.  This  man  was  a  Jew, 
and  had  paid,  or  was  to  pay  a  thousand  dollars  to  have  himself  and 
family  conveyed  to  Nassau.  They  had  several  trunks,  and  since  the 
prize  started  off  the  prisoners  on  board  here  have  stated  that  he  had  a 
large  sum  of  money  with  him.  I  didn’t  have  their  baggage  searched. 
The  question  is,  whether  this  money,  if  found,  should  be  put  with  the 
vessel  and  cargo  to  go  before  the  court.  I  respectfully  submit  it  for 
your  consideration. 

Since  the  foregoing  was  written  the  fact  has  been  divulged  by  these 
prisoners  that  the  Jew  passenger  is  the  principal  owner  of  the  Scotia. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  J.  Almy, 

Commander.

Report  of  Commander  Dove,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  expected  attach  of  the 

enemy  upon  Newport ,  N.  C. 

U.  S.  Naval  Station, 
Beaufort,  N.  C..,  March  1,  1864. 

Sir:  Information  received  by  General  Peck  at  New  Berne  and  com¬ 
municated  to  Colonel  Jourdan,  commanding  this  subdistrict,  lias  caused 
them  to  make  preparations  to  meet  the  rebels  in  another  attack  which 
they  meditate.  It  is  part  of  the  plan  to  strike  at  Newport.  Colonel 
Jourdan  has  consequently  thrown  all  his  disposable  force  at  that  point 
and  organized  the  local  force,  composed  of  residents  of  Beaufort,  white 
and  black,  for  its  defense.  He  has  informed  Captain  Ridgely  and  myself 
of  his  plans,  which  include  support  by  the  gunboats.  As  the  rebels 
are  evidently  coming  in  greater  force  than  before,  greater  force  from  us 
will  be  required. 

It  is  not  likely  that  any  small  vessels  can  be  withdrawn  from  the 
sounds,  as  directed  in  your  instructions  of  the  16th  of  February.  They 
will  be  needed  in  the  Neuse.  There  are  now  in  port  the  Shenandoah , 
Pequot,  New  Berne,  State  of  Georgia ,  Quaker  City,  and  Florida.  Only 
the  Shenandoah  and  Pequot  have  boats  which  can  carry  a  howitzer. 

If  it  is  true  that  the  rebels  have  twenty  launches,  with  naval  officers 
and  sailors  to  man  them,  they  can  give  us  some  trouble. 

The  Shenandoah  and  Mount  Vernon  have  been  detained  for  the  last 
two  days  by  the  swell  on  the  bar.  The  Connecticut  got  out  on  Sunday 
before  it  commenced.  It  is  hoped  the  Mount  Vernon  will  get  out  this 
forenoon.  If  so,  she  has  orders  to  send  the  Nansemond  up  here,  as  she 
is  the  only  vessel  which  can  get  into  Bogue  Sound.  At  present  the 
Pequot  is  stationed  near  the  Morehead  depot.  The  Quaker  City  .and 
Florida  will  be  placed  so  as  to  command  Bogue  Sound  as  far  as  their 
rilled  guns  will  reach.  If  there  are  any  light-draft  gunboats  available, 
it  is  much  to  be  desired  that  they  be  sent  down  here  to  assist. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benjamin  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy,  giving  information 
received  from  Commander  Davenport ,  regarding  affairs  in  the  Neuse 
River ,  and  the  force  in  the  sounds. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  March  4,  1864. 
Sir:  Commander  Davenport,  under  date  of  February  29,  sends  me 
the  following  information,  which  he  says  was  communicated  to  him 
officially  by  General  Peck,  viz:  ‘‘There  are  thirteen  pontoon  bridges 
now  ready  for  use  at  Goldsboro,  and  they  are  taking  up  the  blockade 
between  this  and  Kinston.  Two  regiments  of  cavalry  are  at  Cove 
Creek,  10  or  12  miles  this  side  of  Kinston.” 

Commander  Davenport  considers  the  position  of  affairs  critical,  and 
urges  the  sending  of  reinforcements. 

The  force  at  present  in  the  sounds  consists  of  the  following  vessels: 
Hetzel ,  Miami ,  Seymour,  Louisiana,  Granite,  Valley  City,  Southfield, 
Whitehead,  Commodore  Hull,  Lockwood,  Ceres,  Tacony. 

The  Wyalusing  will  also  be  dispatched  in  a  few  days,  when  her 
repairs  are  completed  at  the  Norfolk  navy  yard.  I  have  written  to 
the  commandant  at  Baltimore  to  hasten  as  much  as  possible  the  repairs 
on  the  double-enders  Hunchback  and  Commodore  Perry , 

The  most  important  positions  in  the  sounds  are  strongly  defended 
by  earthworks.  The  number  of  wooden  vessels  already  "there  will 
perhaps  be  as  sufficient  as  a  larger  number  of  the  same  sort  of  vessels. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

lion.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Capture  of  the  British  steamer  Don,  March  4,  1864. 

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Quackenbush,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pequot. 

U.  S.  S.  Pequot, 

Off  Beaufort ,  N.  C.,  March  4,  1864. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  I  have  this  day  succeeded 
in  capturing  the  British  double-screw,  iron  steamer  Don,  Captain  Cory, 
c  days  out  from  Nassau^  bound  to  \Vilming’ton?  witli  a  cargo  of  army 
blankets,  shoes,  clothing,  etc. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


525 


At  9:40  a.  m.,  a  black  smoke  bearing  west  was  reported  from  aloft. 
I  immediately  changed  my  course  and  steered  for  it.  Jn  the  course  of 
half  an  hour  the  steamer  making  the  smoke  was  plainly  visible,  show¬ 
ing  English  colors  and  standing  in  a  southerly  direction. 

When  within  about  a  mile  of  [her],  I  ordered  a  shot  to  be  thrown 
across  her  bows,  and  as  she  paid  no  attention  to  it,  I  ordered  another 
shot  to  be  thrown  ahead  of  her,  and  one  over  her. 

As  she  still  continued  on  her  course,  I  commenced  firing  at  her,  when, 
after  a  few  rounds,  she  hauled  down  her  colors  and  stood  toward  this 
vessel.  When  sfie  had  approached  within  a  short  distance,  I  dispatched 
two  armed  boats  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensigns  W.  F.  Chase  and  George 
Lamb  and  Acting  Master’s  Mate  John  Shaw  to  take  possession,  if  she 
proved  to  be  a  lawful  prize.  It  was  found  that  the  vessel’s  papers  had 
been  thrown  overboard,  and  possession  was  taken  forthwith.  The  Don 
is  a  new  vessel  of  from  250  to  3t)0  tons,  and  can  steam  14  knots.  The 
capture  was  effected  at  11  a.  m.,  no  other  vessels  being  in  sight,  and 
the  weather  fine  and  clear,  in  latitude  34°  Off  N.,  longitude  76°  31/  W. 

The  above  is  a  copy  of  my  report  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  sent 
in  the  prize,  and  to  be  forwarded  from  Boston. 

In  addition  to  the  foregoing,  I  send  you  a  brief  statement  made  by 
Captain  Cory,  of  the  Don:  During  the  forty-eight  hours  previous  to  his 
capture,  on  "his  first  attempt  to  run  into  Wilmington,  and  before  he 
could  make  Masonboro  light,  he  found  so  many  blockaders  obstructing 
his  course  that  he  was  obliged  to  run  out  again. 

At  6  p.  m.  on  Wednesday,  2d  instant,  he  ran  across  the  bow  of  a 
large  three-masted  blockader  and  again  at  9  a.  m.,  on  the  3d  instant, 
he  ran  close  under  her  stern,  but  escaped  unharmed  each  time,  although 
fired  at  repeatedly.  He  assigns  as  a  reason  for  our  capturing  him  that 
his  tires  were  dirty  and  his  flues  clogged,  and  his  men  worn  out  with 
constant  hard  labor;  that  at  the  time  of  his  capture,  he  was  only  carry¬ 
ing  about  10  pounds  of  steam.  He  also  states  that  his  vessel  had  sailed 
for  Wilmington  nine  times,  but  succeeded  in  getting  in  only  four  times; 
that  during  one  of  his  trips  he  had  been  chased  by  the  Quaker  City , 
but  had  outrun  her,  the  Don  being  then  new  and  in  perfect  running 
order. 

He  says  that  Masonboro  light  is  the  guide  for  blockade  runners 
entering  Wilmington.  1  think  the  Pequot,  was  running  lli  or  12  knots 
when  she  overhauled  the  Don.  The  Don  was  built  expressly  for  run¬ 
ning  the  blockade,  and  cost  £23,000.  Captain  Cory  thinks  the  vessel 
and  cargo  to  be  worth  about  £40,000.  The  crew  and  officers  of  the  Don 
amounted  to  43  officers  and  men  all  told,  besides  one  passenger. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  P.  Quackenbush, 
Lieutenant-  Commander ,  U.  IS.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear  Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Newport ,  News,  Ya. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  March  19,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  would  call  the  attention  of  the  Department  to  the  statement 
made  by  the  captain  of  the  captured  blockade  runner  Don ,  that  he  had 
sailed  nine  times  for  Wilmington,  but  had  only  succeeded  iu  entering 


526 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


four  times;  and  that  for  forty-eight  hours  previous  to  his  capture  he 
had  encountered  so  many  blockaders  that  lie  had  been  obliged  to  run 
out,  having  been  chased  twice  on  the  2d  instant  by  a  large  three- 
masted  blockader — tbe  Dacotah. 

I  transmit  herewith  some  extracts  from  letters  taken  from  prisoners 
on  the  Don ,  which  go  to  show  the  difficulties  experienced  in  attempt¬ 
ing  to  violate  the  blockade  of  Wilmington;  one  writer  stating  that 
“not  one  vessel  out  of  ten  gets  in;”  another  “expects  no  more  letters; 
shall  not  get  them;  *  *  *  so  many  blockaders  about.” 

These  evidences  from  such  sources  of  the  efficiency  of  the  blockade 
are  very  gratifying.  The  original  letters  were  sent  to  the  district  judge, 
Boston. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Hays,  V.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
seizure  of  twelve  canoes  in  York  River. 


U.  S.  S.  Crusader, 
Yorktown,  Va.,  March  5,  1864. 

Sir  :  In  two  instances  I  observed  boats,  canoes  from  Yorktown  that 
had  permission  to  oyster  in  York  River,  clandestinely  making  their  way 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


527 


up  Severn  River.  I  gave  chase  in  the  first  instance,  but  they  avoided 
me  by  running  up  small  creeks  and  hiding  their  boats.  I  warned  them 
all  around  there  and  told  the  people  to  discountenance  those  acts. 
Yesterday  I  discovered  another  boat  running  the  blockade,  and  as  I  do 
not  know  what  cargoes  they  run  in  them,  I  determined  to  break  up  the 
entire  business,  and  thought  the  best  way  to  do  so  was  to  remove  all 
the  canoes  around  there  that  I  could  find,  which  I  did,  amounting  to 
twelve,  which  number  I  brought  around  and  turned  over  to  Captain 
Babcock. 

Hoping  my  conduct  will  meet  your  approbation,  I  am,  very  respect¬ 
fully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Peter  Hays, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding.

[Enclosure  1.] 

IT.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  Va.,  March  7,  1864. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order,  I  submit  the  following  information 
concerning  the  capture  of  the  army  tug  Titan,  gained  from  William  H. 
Dunn,  the  telegraph  operator  at  Cherrystone,  at  the  time  of  the 
occurrence. 

On  Saturday  morning,  March  5,  a  party  of  guerrillas  surprised  and 
captured  the  guard  and  telegraph  operator  and  cut  the  telegraph  wires. 
The  Titan  and  steamer  TEolus  were  lying  at  anchor  about  2  miles  from 
the  wharf  at  the  time.  The  JEolus  got  underway  and  came  into  the 
wharf  (unsuspectingly),  and  was  immediately  boarded  and  captured  by 
the  guerrillas,  who  put  on  the  clothing  taken  from  their  prisoners,  and 
on  the  Titan  coming  in,  captured  her  also. 

In  the  meantime,  a  part  of  them  (the  guerrillas)  were  destroying  the 
Government  property  and  killing  all  horses,  in  order  to  facilitate  their 
escape. 


*  See  also  Series  I,  Vol.  5,  pp.  398-402. 


528 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


After  the  capture  of  the  Titan ,  they  took  $3,000  from  the  captain  of 
the  JEolus ,  and  bonded  and  disabled  that  vessel. 

My  informant  further  says  that  guerrillas  spoke  of  taking  the  Titan 
up  the  Piankatank.  They  came  across  from  that  river  in  open  boats  to 
St.  George’s,  landed,  and  came  to  Cherrystone,  where  they  secreted 
themselves  two  or  three  days  before  they  attacked  the  guard  at  day¬ 
break.  In  the  eagerness  and  excitement  of  the  guerrillas  to  get  off  with 
their  prize,  the  operator  secreted  himself  on  the  JEolus ,  thus  escaping. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  M.  Skardon, 

Acting  Master’s  Mate. 

Acting  Rear- Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

[Enclosure  2.] 

II.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va. ,  March  7 ,  1864. 

General  :  You  merely  informed  me  on  the  evening  of  the  5th  instant 
that  you  had  news  of  a  meditated  attack  upon  our  forces  at  Suffolk, 
that  your  telegraph  tug  was  captured,  and  the  line  of  the  eastern  shore 
broken  up. 

I  immediately  sent  two  gunboats,  one  on  the  sea  and  the  other  on  the 
bay  side  of  the  eastern  shore  counties,  to  find  and  capture  these  rebels, 
and  recapture  the  vessel  or  vessels  taken  by  them. 

Yesterday  I  sent  another  gunboat  to  enquire  after  and  follow  up  the 
pirates. 

I  sent  Ensign  Miller  this  morning  to  ask  you  for  full  information  as 
to  the  occurrence,  and  how  the  matter  now  stands,  but  you  were  absent. 

I  desire  to  have  such  information  as  you  now  have,  or  may  hereafter 
obtain,  concerning  the  captures  made  by  and  subsequent  movements 
of  these  pirates. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral. 

Major-General  Benj.  F.  Butler, 

Commanding  Department  Virginia  and  North  Carolina.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Sheldon,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Shokokon. 

U.  S.  S.  Shokokon, 

Off  Newport  Neics ,  March  7,  1864. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  orders,  March  5,  9:30  p.  m.,  I  immediately 
proceeded  to  Old  Point  Comfort,  communicated  with  the  U.  S.  S.  Baron, 
Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Simmons,  and  delivered  to  him  the  orders 
received  from  the  flagship.  At  5:30  a.  m.,  March  0,  obtained  a  pilot 
and  proceeded  to  Cherrystone  Inlet  in  search  of  the  army  tug  Titan , 
captured  by  the  rebels.  It  blowing  heavy  from  N.  R.  E.,  and  a  high  sea 
running,  was  not  able  to  communicate  with  the  shore.  Proceeded  up 
along  the  eastern  shore  of  Virginia,  carefully  examining  the  coast  as 
far  as  Tangier  Island;  could  not  learn  anything  of  her  there.  I  pro¬ 
ceeded  across  the  bay  to  the  mouth  of  the  Rappahannock  ;  communi¬ 
cated  with  the  senior  officer  on  that  station,  Acting  V  olunteer  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Hooker,  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  Yankee;  learned  that  the  Titan 
had  run  in  and  gone  up  Piankatank  River  on  the  afternoon  of  the  5th 
instant.  He  also  informed  me  that  Commodore  Parker,  with  a  force 
of  five  gunboats,  left  this  morning  (7th  instant);  had  gone  up  the  river 
to  recapture  her,  if  possible.  I  asked  permission  to  follow  the  gun¬ 
boats  up  the  river,  but  Lieutenant  Hooker  deemed  the  force  sufficient 
which  had  already  gone,  and  would  not  give  consent  for  me  to  go  up. 
I  then  proceeded  down  the  bay  to  this  anchorage. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  B.  Sheldon, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  off  Newport  News. 


Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Hays,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Crusader. 


U.  S.  S.  Crusader, 

»  Yorktown ,  March  8,  1864. 

Sir  :  On  Friday  night  I  arrived  here  with  some  twelve  canoes,  cap¬ 
tured  in  Severn  River  that  day,  and  being  in  want  of  wood  I  remained 
here,  but  didn’t  get  off,  owing  to  the  lowness  of  the  tide,  until  late 
Saturday  night.  Early  Sunday  morning,  6th,  I  learned  from  Captain 
Babcock  that  some  rebels  had  captured  the  Government  tug  Titan  in 
Cherrystone  Inlet,  and  I  was  ordered  by  him  to  go  in  pursuit  of  her, 
which  I  did  at  once.  I  met  in  the  bay  the  Shokokon  and  was  informed 
by  her  captain  that  he  was  going  over  to  Tangier  Sound.  I  laid  Sun¬ 
day  night  in  Mobjack  Bay  to  blockade  the  rivers  there,  and  Monday 
morning  early  I  went  up  to  communicate  with  the  Potomac  Flotilla  and 
learned  she  had  run  in  the  Piankatank  at  1*1  in.,  Saturday,  and  that

some  of  the  flotilla  had  gone  in  pursuit  of  her.  1  laid  ^t’the  mouth  of

Report  of  Acting  Volunteei  Lieutenant  Simmons,  IT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Dawn. 

U.  S.  S.  Dawn, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  March  9,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  very  respectfully  report  that  your  order,  dated  March  5,  9  p.  m., 
ordering  me  to  proceed  with  the  Dawn  under  my  command  to  cruise 
on  the  Atlantic  coast  of  the  eastern  shore  counties  of  Virginia,  between 
Cape  Charles  and  Hog  Island,  for  the  purpose  of  capturing  if  possible 
the  army  tug  Titan,  which  was  reported  to  have  been  captured  by  the 
enemy  at  or  near  Cherrystone  Inlet,  eastern  shore  of  Virginia,  was 
received  by  me  at  11:30  p.  m.  same  night.  Having  but  18  tons  of  coal 
in  this  ship,  I  immediately  took  on  board  60  tons  of  coal  from  the  armv 
wharf  at  Fort  Monroe,  by  permission  of  Captain  James,  army  quarter¬ 
master  at  that  post.  After  obtaining  a  pilot,  at  8  a.  m.  I  proceeded  to 
sea  in  search  ot  the  Titan.  I  steamed  as  close  as  possible  to  the  land, 
the  wind  blowing  fresh  at  the  time,  until  Hog  Island  light  bore  W.  by 
S.  Finding  the  sea  too  rough  to  communicate  with  the  shore,  I 
returned  with  this  vessel,  under  canvas  only,  for  the  purpose  of  exam¬ 
ining  the  several  inlets,  until  night  coming  on,  I  steamed  in  under  Cape 
Charles  and  anchored,  thinking  the  Titan  might  attempt  to  get  to  sea 
under  cover  of  night. 

On  the  morning  of  the  7tli  I  again  proceeded  north  as  far  as  Hog- 
Island,  and  seeing  nothing  of  the  tug  returned  to  Myrtle  Island,  and, 
the  sea  having  gone  down,  communicated  with  the  shore,  but  could 
learn  nothing  of  the  Titan.  Feeling  satisfied  in  my  own  mind  that  she 
was  not  in  that  vicinity,  and  the  weather  looking  bad,  I  returned  to 
Hampton  Roads,  and  there  learned  the  Titan  had  gone  up  the  Pianka- 
tank.  I  at  once  started  for  Newport  News  to  report. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  W.  Simmons, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Dawn. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  assistance 
extended  to  Major-General  Butler ,  at  Suffolk,  Va. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  March  6,  1864. 

Sir:  Last  evening  I  received  a  communication  from  Major-General 
Butler,  stating  that  there  was  an  attack  meditated  upon  our  force  at 
Suffolk,  and  that  the  rebels  had  captured  the  telegraph  boat  and 
broken  up  the  telegraph  line  to  the  eastern  shore,  and  asking  with 
what  force  I  could  aid  them  on  the  Nansemond. 

I  immediately  dispatched  the  light-draft  steamer  Stepping  Stones  to 
Suffolk  to  communicate  with  the  army  there,  and  learn  the  situation, 
and  also  directed  the  Commodore  Barney,  already  in  the  Nansemond,  to 
give  such  assistance  as  might  be  necessary. 

The  Sliokokon  was  also  sent  to  cruise  along  the  bay  shore  of  the 
eastern  counties  of  Virginia,  pursue  and  recapture  the  telegraph  boat 
if  possible;  at  the  same  time  the  Dawn  was  dispatched  to  cruise  along 
the  Atlantic  coast  of  those  counties  for  the  same  purpose  and  to  gather 
any  information  relating  to  the  capture. 

I  have  not  been  informed  of  the  particnlars  of  this  raid  by  the  enemy. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Williams ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  an  expedition 

in  the  Nansemond  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Barney, 
Nansemond  River ,  Virginia ,  March  6,  1864. 

Sir  :  At  9:30  p.  m.  of  the  5tli  instant,  Acting  Master  Campbell,  of 
the  Stepping  Stones ,  came  on  board  and  reported  that  his  vessel  was 
aground.  He  gave  me  a  copy  of  his  orders.  I  tried  several  times  to 
tow  him  off  the  bank,  but  found  it  impossible  to  do  so.  I  then  took  the 
responsibility  of  proceeding  up  the  river  as  near  as  possible  to  the 
orders  given  to  me  by  Acting  Master  Campbell. 

On  my  way  up  the  river  I  saw  a  number  of  flash  lights  on  the  star¬ 
board  side.  I  shelled  the  point  of  the  river  where  the  lights  were  seen. 
At  2  a.  m.  of  the  6th,  came  to  an  anchor  2  miles  above  Sleepy  Hole, 
finding  it  impossible  to  proceed  farther  on  account  of  the  density  of  the 
night. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  M.  Williams, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee,

Capture  of  the  British  steamer  Mary  Ann ,  March  6',  1864. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  additional  information. 

H.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Fa.,  March  17 ,  1864. 

Sir:  I  transmit  enclosed  two  reports,  Nos.  1#  and  2#,  from  Com¬ 
mander  G.  M.  Bansom,  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  Grand  Guff  attached  to  this 
squadron,  of  the  capture  on  the  6th  of  March  of  the  British  steamer 
Mary  Ann  of  235  tons  (gross),  English. 

Commander  Bansom  reports  that  the  prize  was  just  out  of  Wilming¬ 
ton,  bound  for  Nassau,  and  that  her  cargo  consisted  principally  of  354 
bales  of  cotton  and  about  65  boxes  and  2  drums  of  tobacco:  that  in  the 
chase  she  threw  overboard  about  100  bales  of  the  cotton,  as  nearly  as 
could  be  estimated. 

Her  parchment  register,  which  had  been  thrown  overboard  and 
picked  up,  I  forwarded  to  the  district  judge  at  Boston,  where  the  prize 
has  been  sent. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Gomdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C.

U.  S.  S.  Grand  Gulf, 

At  Sea ,  Long.  78°  12'  IF.,  Lat.  32°  21'  N .,  March  6,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  vessel,  after  a  chase  of 
three  hours  and  thirty  minutes,  this  morning  overhauled  and  captured 


Substantially  duplicates. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


533 


the  English  steamer  Mary  Ann  (blockade  runner),  fourteen  hours  from 
Wilmington,  N.  C.,  bound  to  Nassau,  New  Providence. 

The  steamer  was  reported  in  sight  from  the  masthead  at  6:40  a.  in., 
bearing  W.  S.  W.,  and  immediately  we  stood  in  chase.  At  10:10  a.  m., 
after  the  third  shot  from  our  100-pounder  Parrott  gun,  the  stranger 
turned  around  and  surrendered,  in  longitude  78°  11/  45"  W.,  latitude 
32°  2P  N.  There  was  no  other  vessel  in  sight  at  any  time  during  the 
chase,  nor  at  any  time  to  day. 

The  Mary  Ann  is  an  iron  side- wheel  steamer  of  235  tons  (gross),  Eng¬ 
lish,  and  superior  in  some  respects,  1  think,  to  the  Banshee.  Her  cargo 
consisted  principally  of  354  bales  of  cotton  and  about  65  boxes  and  2 
drums  of  tobacco  ;  but  in  the  chase  she  hove  overboard  about  100  bales 
of  the  cotton,  as  nearly  as  could  be  estimated.  She  did  not  show  any 
colors  at  any  time,  from  the  commencement  of  the  chase  to  the  time 
she  was  surrendered  as  a  prize. 

I  enclose  herewith  a  certificate  of  her  registry,  which  was  picked  up 
from  the  sea. 

I  have  sent  the  Mary  Ann  to  Boston,  Mass.,  in  charge  of  Lieutenant 
Frederick  Rodgers,  with  an  acting  third  assistant  engineer,  an  acting 
master’s  mate,  and  a  prize  crew,  consisting  of  14  men ;  leaving  on  board 
of  her  also  her  captain,  first  mate,  and  chief  engineer.  But  I  instructed 
Lieutenant  Rodgers  to  touch  at  Beaufort,  N.  O.,  and  obtain  there  a 
sufficient  supply  of  coal. 

She  had  on  board  a  large  number  of  passengers,  of  whom,  together 
with  her  crew,  I  have  received,  on  board  of  this  vessel,  64.  I  respect¬ 
fully  ask  your  instruction  regarding  the  disposition  to  be  made  of  them. 

The  highest  speed  attaiued  by  this  vessel  in  the  chase  was  Ilf  knots, 
against  a  fresh  breeze  and  a  moderate  head.sea,  and  her  average  speed 
was  10 £  knots. 

I  enclose  herewith,  also,  lists,  in  duplicate,  of  the  officers  and  crew 
of  this  vessel  who  are  entitled  to  share  in  whatever  may  accrue  of  prize 
money  from  this  capture. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  M.  Ransom, 

Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Samuel  Phillips  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads. 


Additional  report  of  Commander  Ransom,  II.  S.  Navy,  regarding  property  and  prisoners. 

U.  S.  S.  Grand  Gulf, 
Beaufort ,  N.  C .,  March  9 ,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  7 th  instant  I  succeeded 
in  picking  up  from  the  sea  16  bales  and  a  quantity  of  loose  cotton 
which  had  been  thrown  overboard  by  the  prize  steamer  Mary  Ann  in 
the  chase  of  the  6th  instant. 

I  have  to  state  also  that  eight  table  forks  and  a  fish  knife  (supposed 
to  be  silver)  were  found  in  the  possession  of  one  of  the  prisoners,  which 
he  acknowledged  to  have  taken  from  the  cabin  of  the  Mary  Ann;  also 
a  marine  opera  glass,  belonging  to  the  prize,  was  found  in  the  posses¬ 
sion  of  another  prisoner.  1  have  taken  possession  of  these  articles, 
awaiting  your  decision  regarding  the  disposition  to  be  made  of  them. 

The  weather  being  exceedingly  rough  yesterday,  I  deemed  it  advisa¬ 
ble  to  put  into  this  port,  with  a  view  to  get  rid  of  the  64  prisoners  men¬ 
tioned  in  my  report  of  the  6th  instant,  and  the  cotton,  amounting  in 
all  to  about  18  bales. 


534 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


I  regret  these  circumstances,  sir,  which  have  occasioned  my  coming 
thus  soon  into  port,  because  it  takes  from  me  a  large  portion  of  the 
time  that  otherwise,  by  your  order,  I  might  have  remained  outside. 

I  respectfully  ask  your  indulgence,  after  having  received  a  full  sup¬ 
ply  of  coal,  for  another  term  of  outside  cruising.  If  another  such 
opportunity  might  be  afforded  to  me,  I  believe  I  would  avail  much  by 
the  experience  just  acquired. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  M.  Ransom, 

Commander.

longitude  77°  51'  W.,  latitude  32°  39'  N.  Explain  all  the  circumstances 
which  led  to  its  being  found,  and  ask  whether  the  Government  has  any 
claim  upon  the  same,  or  whether  it  belongs  wholly  to  the  officers  and 
crew  of  this  vessel. 

In  any  event,  you  will  be  guided  by  his  counsel  regarding  the  proper 
disposition  to  be  made  of  it,  and  inform  me,  by  his  advice,  also,  whether 
it  is  necessary  or  proper  that  1  should  furnish  the  Department  with  a 
separate  prize  list  for  the  cotton  thus  picked  up  from  the  sea. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  yours,  etc., 

George  M.  Ransom, 

Commander. 

Acting  Ensign  Oiias.  H.  Cadieu, 

In  charge  of  prize  steamer  Mary  Ann,  Boston,  Mass.

of  Georgia,  regarding  the  striking  of  that  vessel  in  coming  out  of  Beau¬ 
fort  Harbor. 

U.  S.  S.  State  of  Georgia, 

Off  Western  Bar,  March  6, 1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  again  to  report  that  I  was  detained  at  Beaufort  some  six 
days  for  want  of  water  on  the  bar,  and  that  the  vessel  struck  twice  in 
coining  out  on  Friday  last. 

I  really  do  not  think  it  safe  to  trust  this  vessel  in  going  in  or  out  of 
that  harbor.  She  is  very  old  and  would  not,  in  my  opinion,  stand  much 
thumping. 

The  magazine  has  commenced  leaking  within  the  last  three  weeks, 
and  I  attribute  it  to  my  striking  when  I  came  out  of  Beaufort  the  first 
time. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  Nicholson, 

Commander.

Letter  from  Commander  Davenport,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Lieutenant- Commander 
Flusser,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  Confederate  ram  in  the  Roanoke 
River. 


U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne ,  N.  0.,  March  6,  1864. 

My  Dear  Flusser:  I  have  received  your  two  letter's.  I  have  just 
been  examining  a  deserter— a  cavalry  sergeant  in  the  rebel  Army— that 
Renshaw  sent  down. 

He  states  that  the  ram  up  the  Roanoke  is  about  ready ;  that  the  inten¬ 
tion  is  to  attack  Plymouth.  They  will  send  a  small  force  to  New  Berne 
and  Washington  to  prevent  reinforcements  being  sent  to  Plymouth,  and 


then  attack  you  in  force. 

In  regard  to  the  newspaper  article  referred  to,  I  suppose  it  was  writ¬ 
ten  by  some  poor  fellow  who  is  working  for  his  bread. 

Yours,  faithfully, 

H.  K.  Davenport. 


Lieutenant-Commander  C.  W.  Flusser,  U.  S.  Navy.
