Sinking  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Peterhoff  in  collision  with  the  U.  S.  S.  Monticello, 
March  6,  and  her  destruction  March  7,  1864. 

Report  of  Captain  Sands,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  off  New  Inlet,  Cape  Fear  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Jackson, 

Off  New  Inlet,  Cape  Fear  River,  March  6,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  the  loss  ot  the  U.  S.  S.  /  etcrhof) ,  commanded 
by  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  T.  Pickering,  having  been  run  into  and 
immediately  sunk  by  the  Monticello  at  5:10  a.  m.  this  morning,  and  now 


536 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


lies  in  5  fathoms  water  about  1  mile  south  of  Sheep  Hegd  Rock,  south  of 
New  Inlet  Bar;  officers  and  crew  saved,  but  the  vessel  a  total  loss. 

Upon  approaching  the  day  anchorage  this  morning  soon  after  day¬ 
light  and  examining  the  inner  line  of  blockaders,  I  discovered  the  Peter- 
hoff,  apparently  hull  down,  near  her  station  (No.  3),  but  farther  in  than 
she  should  have  been  at  this  time  of  the  morning.  Not  seeing  her 
move  and  fearing  she  was  disabled,  I  dispatched  the  Nansemond  to 
ascertain  the  fact,  which  vessel  returned,  in  company  with  the  Monti- 
cello ,  with  the  boat’s  crew  and  officers  of  the  Peterlioff, ,  saving  part  of 
their  effects. 

The  Monticello  was  from  the  Western  Bar  on  her  way  to  Beaufort  for 
coal,  with  orders  to  communicate  with  me  here,  and  had  gotten  within 
our  inner  line,  where  she  should  not  have  been  at  that  time. 

To  prevent  such  disasters,  and  to  guard  against  embarrassment  of 
vessels  at  their  night  station,  I  have  endeavored  to  impress  upon  the 
commanding  officers  off  Wilmington  returning  to  the  blockade  after 
dark  the  necessity  of  keeping  outside  the  lines  till  daylight. 

I  enclose  herewith  the  reports*  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Pick¬ 
ering  and  Lieutenant  Cushing. 

I  have  directed  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Pickering  to  distribute 
among  the  vessels  here  as  many  of  his  crew  as  may  be  required,  the 
residue  to  be  delivered  on  board  the  Badger  at  Beaufort  for  any  of  the 
vessels  among  those  that  may  need  them. 

I  would  take  them  all  on  board  this  vessel,  but  having  a  case  of 
smallpox  on  board  of  us,  I  deem  it  prudent  to  keep  newcomers  out  of 
the  ship  until  it  is  seen  whether  it  spreads.  Acting  Volunteer  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Pickering  will  report  to  you  in  person. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

B.  F.  Sands, 

Captain ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  off  Newport  News.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Trathen,  IT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Mount  Vernon. 

U.  S.  S.  Mount  Vernon, 

Off  New  Inlet ,  North  Carolina,  March  8,  1864. 

Sir:  In  pursuance  of  instructions  received  from  you  on  the  7th 
instant  to  destroy  as  much  as  possible  of  the  wreck  of  the  U.  S.  S. 
Peterhoff  to  prevent  its  falling  into  the  hands  of  the  enemy,  at  6:15 
p.  in.  yesterday  we  got  underway  in  company  with  IT.  S.  S .Niphon  and 
steamed  into  within  200  yards  of  the  wreck  and  anchored  with  kedge 
in  44  fathoms  water,  Fort  Fisher  bearing  N.  £  E.,  Bald  Head  S.  W.  by 
W.  |  W.  At  7 : 40  p.  m.  dispatched  two  boats  and  20  men  from  this 
ship,  well  armed,  and  two  boats  and  20  men  from  U.  S.  S.  Niphon,  all 
under  command  of  Acting  Master  Edward  W.  White,  of  this  vessel, 
who  proceeded  to  the  wreck.  The  enemy  appeared  to  be  very  active, 
telegraphing  from  Fort  Caswell  to  Fort  Fisher  with  night  signals;  at 
10 : 55  p.  m.  the  fore  and  main  masts  fell  from  the  wreck  of  the  Peterhoff 
with  a  great  crash.  At  12: 15  this  morning  the  boats  returned,  and 
Acting  Master  White  reported  that  on  reaching  the  wreck  he  found  5 
feet  of  water  over  her  spar  deck,  and  that,  in  addition  to  cutting  away 
all  her  masts,  he  had  unbent  or  cut  away  all  her  sails,  also  all  of  her 
standing  and  running  rigging,  leaving  nothing  above  her  spar  deck, 
and  spiked  and  thrown  overboard  the  30-pounder  Parrott  rifle  gun  on 
the  forecastle  and  the  howitzer  from  the  quarter  deck.  The  main-deck 
guns  could  not  be  got  at.  He  reports  that  nothing  now  remains  of  the 
wreck  above  water  except  the  smokestack,  which  could  not  be  removed 
in  consequence  of  there  being  too  much  sea  for  the  boats  to  remain  any 
longer  near  the  vessel.  During  the  whole  night  the  weather  was  very 
dark  and  considerable  sea  rolling  over  the  wreck,  which  placed  the 
boats  at  times  in  considerable  danger. 

Having  carried  out  your  orders  as  fully  as  possible,  we  hove  up  the 
kedge  and  steamed  to  our  night  station  No.  5;  the  U.  S.  S.  Niphon  also 
proceeded  to  her  station. 

Sir,  I  remain,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant. 

James  Trathen. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Commander  W.  A.  Parker,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Comdg.  77.  8.  S.  Tuscarora,  Senior  Officer  Present  off  New  Inlet.

be  liable  to  fall  into  the  hands  of  the  rebels,  making  a  complete  wreck 
of  her  by  cutting  away  her  masts  and  throwing  overboard  such  guns 
as  could  be  got  at,  namely,  one  12-pounder  howitzer  and  one  30-pounder

Parrott.  Articles  saved  and  brought  on  board,  viz,  Qiih  foresail,  taken 
off  the  yard  whole;  greater  part  of  main  spencer,  main  topgallant  sail 
and  fore  spencer;  about  twenty  blocks,  mostly  small,  and  part  of  main 
rigging.  Foresail  not  required  on  board  this  ship.  Most  of  the  other 
articles  required  for  immediate  use.  The  vessel  is  sunk  in  about  4J 
fathoms  of  water,  the  poop  and  forecastle  being  about  1  foot  under

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  retirement 

of  the  enemy  from  Suffolk ,  Va. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  March  7 ,  1864. 

Sir:  Acting  Master  Campbell,  commanding  the  Stepping  Stones, 
returned  from  the  Nansemond  River  yesterday  afternoon,  reporting  the 
enemy,  which  had  been  reported  as  menacing  Suffolk,  had  retired  and 
that  the  officer  commanding  our  forces  at  that  place  had  reported  that 
they  were  not  to  be  found  in  that  vicinity. 

At  a  later  hour  last,  evening  I  received  a  telegram  from  Major- 
General  Butler,  stating  that  the  enemy  had  retired  from  Suffolk  and 
that  the  gunboats  were  no  longer  required  in  the  Nansemond.  The 
Stepping  Stones  has  accordingly  been  withdrawn,  but  the  Commodore 
Barney  remains  as  a  guard  boat  in  the  lower  Nansemond. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Extracts  from  consular  reports  received  by  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee , 

U.  S.  Navy,  March  7,  1864. 

From  IT.  S.  consul  at  Cardiff,  dated  February  11,  1864 : 

A  large,  or  rather  long,  iron  steamer  has  just  come  in  here  to  load 
with  coal  for  Nassau.  Her  name  is  the  North  Heath,  of  London.  She 
is  about  260  feet  long,  with  large  paddle  wheels,  and  very,  very  sharp. 
She  doubtless  intends  to  engage  in  the  business  of  blockade  running, 
and  will  be  hard  to  catch,  but  when  caught  will  be  a  good  vessel  for 
us,  for  a  faster  vessel  I  have  never  seen.  Hoping  she  will  soon  grace 
wur  own  Navy  under  some  other  name,  1  am,  etc.  (This  is  Begbie’s 
steamer  Gertrude.)

From  U.  S.  consul  at  Teneriffe,  dated  February  2,  1864: 

Blockade  runner  Annie,  under  the  English  flag,  arrived  at  this  port

From  IT.  S.  consul  at  Liverpool,  dated  February  3,  1864: 

The  steamer  Mary ,  late  Prince  Albert,  cleared  from  here  on  Saturday 
evening  last,  January  30,  for  Havana,  in  command  of  Captain  J.  Peat.

From  U.  S.  consul  at  London,  dated  February  12,  1864: 

The  North  Heath,  late  Gertrude ,  left  last  Saturday  for  Cardiff’,  no 
doubt  to  take  in  coal  for  Bermuda  or  Nassau.  One  report  is  that 
Bigbie  will  send  this  and  the  other  boat,  A.  10,  now  here,  either  to  sell  or 
bring  out  cotton.  What  army  supplies  are  now  going  forward,  I  am 
confident,  are  sent  on  speculation  by  citizens  from  the  insurgent  States 
and  by  Europeans,  not  by  the  agents  of  the  rebel  Government.  I  have 
information  from  two  separate  sources,  unknown  to  each  other,  that 
the  Government  as  a  government  has  no  funds  in  Europe.  Its  agents 
here  say  their  cotton  loan  is  all  gone,  and  that  they  now  have  nothing 
to  raise  funds  on  except  such  Government  cotton  as  can  be  got  out.  So 
that,  according  to  the  admission  of  those  who  control  their  affairs  in 
Europe,  made  in  confidence  to  each  other,  the  success  of  their  opera¬ 
tions  on  this  side  of  the  Atlantic  just  now  depends  on  the  amount  of 
Government  cotton  they  are  able  to  run  through  the  blockade. 

A  correspondent  at  London,  under  date  of  February  8,  1864,  says 
that  some  large  boilers  intended  for  powerful  steam  vessels  are  being 
shipped  in  the  Thames,  with  the  intention  of  running  the  blockade 
either  at  Charleston  or  Wilmington.  He  thinks  the  boilers  are  being 
loaded  into  barges  above  bridge  in  the  Thames  for  their  conveyance  to 
some  ship  lying  off  Greenwich,  which  he  understands  only  awaits  their 
embarkment  to  sail  at  once  to  the  destination  before  intimated.

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Txtscarora, 

At  Beaufort ,  N.  C.,  March  16,  1864. 
***#### 

At  daylight  on  the  7th  instant  we  saw  a  rebel  propeller  ashore  near 
Fort  Fisher,  which  had  run  the  blockade  during  the  night,  and  appeared 
like  a  man-of-war  having  a  heavy  pivot  gun. 

With  the  assistance  of  several  steam  tugs  she  got  into  deeper  water 
and  proceeded  up  the  river. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wi.  A.  Parker,

[Telegram.]  ' 

Yorktown,  March  8, 1864. 

The  gunboat  Morse ,  Lieutenant-Commander  Babcock,  left  here  Sun¬ 
day,  6th  instant,  at  noon,  to  afford  relief  to  Colonel  Dahlgren’s  party. 
Monday,  ith  instant,  at  7  a.  in.,  near  West  Point,  the  Morse  picked  up 
5  men  who  had  been  attracted  by  the  Morse's  signal  guns  and  were 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


541 


guided  to  tlie  river  by  a  friendly  negro,  who  provided  them  with  a  boat. 
Four  of  these  were  Colonel  Dahlgren’s  white  soldiers  and  one  was  his 
colored  servant.  They  represent  that  Colonel  Dahlgren’s  party  was 
surrounded  by  cavalry  and  infantry,  and  that  he  was  killed,  and  that 
they  saw  more  than  one-half  of  his  men  afterwards  give  themselves  up 
as  prisoners.  Colonel  Dahlgren’s  servant  says  that  he  saw  the  colonel’s 
naked  body,  which  had  been  stripped,  with  the  ring  finger  cut  off. 
The  Crusader ,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Hays,  commanding  one  of 
the  several  gunboats  sent  after  the  Titan ,  came  in  here  this  morning 
and  reports  that  Commander  Parker  left  the  Piankatank  last  evening, 
where  he  had  seen  the  Titan  burned  to  the  water’s  edge,  and  had  cap¬ 
tured  seven  of  Wood’s  canoes.  One  of  the  gunboats  had  fired  into  the 
wreck  of  the  Titan  to  destroy  the  machinery. 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Babcock,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding 

U.  S.  S.  Morse,  of  an  attempt  to  render  assistance  to  a  detachment  of 

cavalry  near  Mattapony  River. 

U.  8.  S.  Morse, 

Off  Yorktown,  Va. ,  March  8,  1864. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  report  that  on  the  morning  of  the  6th  instant 
Colonel  Ryan,  having  received  information  that  a  detachment  of  cav¬ 
alry  under  command  of  Colonel  Ulric  Dahlgren  was  surrounded  by  a 
large  force  of  rebels  near  the  Mattapony  River  and  was  in  a  precarious 
situation,  he  requested  me  to  proceed  up  the  river  and,  if  possible  to 
do  so,  afford  them,  assistance.  Got  underway  and  proceeded  up  the 
[York]  river;  when  abreast  of  Purtan  Island  Point  swept  the  river 
with  telegraph  wire  from  the  boats  for  torpedoes,  and  followed  with  the 
vessel  in  their  wake.  At  dark  came  to  anchor  off  Terrapin  Point. 
Fired  at  intervals  during  the  day  and  night  signal  guns  to  attract 
the  attention  of  the  cavalry.  In  the  morning  got  underway  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  slowly  up  the  river,  keeping  a  vigilant  lookout  on  both  banks 
of  the  river  for  any  cavalry.  When  off  Brick  House  Farm,  saw  a  boat 
inshore  with  some  men  in  it  coming  for  the  vessel;  they  proved  to  be  5 
cavalrymen  belonging  to  Colonel  Dahlgren’s  command.  It  appears  by 
the  statement  of  these  men  that  their  colonel  having  been  shot,  and 
the  whole  command,  numbering  about  100  men,  under  command  of  a 
major,  were  so  closely  surrounded  and  pressed  by  a  large  force  of  both 
rebel  cavalry  and  infantry,  and  deeming  it  impossible  to  cut  their  way 
through,  the  major  ordered  them  to  disband,  leaving  their  horses, 
equipments,  etc.  '  These  men  saw  fully  one-half  the  command  surrender 
themselves  as  prisoners.  The  colonel’s  body  servant  (colored)  being 
one  of  the  5  received  on  board,  states  that  after  Colonel  Dahlgren  had 
been  shot  the  citizens  in  the  vicinity  stripped  him  and  actually  cut  off 
his  fingers  for  the  purpose  of  taking  some  rings  which  he  had  on  them. 
These  men  were  piloted  to  the  bank  of  the  Mattapony  River  by  a 
colored  man,  who  procured  a  small  skiff  for  them,  and  they  proceeded 
down  the  river,  having  heard  our  signal  guns,  and  at  daylight  came 
within  sight  of  this  vessel.  Proceeded  up  the  river  to  West  Point; 
went  into  the  Mattapony  River  and  came  to  anchor;  found  one  pon¬ 
toon  and  two  skiff's  on  the  beach  at  West  Point,  brought  them  on 


542 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


board.  At  noon  again  got  underway  and  proceeded  tip  the  Mattapony 
River  about  3  miles  to  a  rebel  storehouse  (in  which  last  May  we  made 
a  capture  of  corn  and  rye)  and  found  in  it  25  sacks  of  corn,  2  bags  of 
wheat,  and  G  sacks  of  salt,  all  consigned  to  a  commission  merchant  in 
Richmond,  Ya.  From  information  received  a  week  since,  there  were 
in  this  storehouse,  but  since  carried  to  White  House,  2,000  barrels  of 
flour.  Returned  down  the  Mattapony  and  went  up  the  Pamunkey 
River  about  3  miles.  Kept  a  strict  lookout  continuously  on  both 
banks  and,  not  seeing  any  more  cavalry,  concluded  that  the  remainder 
had  been  captured. 

I  had  the  forks  of  both  rivers  swept  for  torpedoes  with  telegraph  wire 
before  proceeding  up  with  the  vessel,  but  found  no  obstructions  what¬ 
ever.  Arrived  at  this  place  and  came  to  anchor  last  evening  at  7  p.  m. 
Turned  over  the  five  men  to  the  military  authorities  at  this  place. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  A.  Babcock, 

Lieutenant  Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  off  Newport  News.

Cooperation  with  army  forces  in  an  expedition  to  King  and  Queen  Court- 
House  and  Middlesex  County,  March  8-13,  1864. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  reports. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  March  19,  1864. 

Sir:  On  the  8th  instant  I  accompanied  Generals  Butler  and  Meigs 
to  Yorktown  to  arrange  a  joint  army  and  navy  expedition  to  operate, 
first,  up  the  Pamunkey  against  the  rebel  forces  in  the  neighborhood  of 
King  and  Queen  Court-House  which  had  attacked  Colonel  Dahlgren’s 
party,  and  then  against  a  party  of  the  enemy  who  were  reported  to  be 
fitting  out  an  expedition  from  Middlesex  County,  in  the  peninsula 
formed  by  the  Rappahannock  and  the  Piankatank.

Confidential.]  XJ.  S.  S.  Morse, 

Yorktown ,  Tuesday ,  March  8 ,  1864 — ip.  m. 

Sir  :  General  Kilpatrick  will  leave  here  at  daylight  to-morrow,  9th 
instant,  with,  say,  2,000  cavalry  to  attack  the  rebels  at  King  and  Queen 
Court-House,  who  captured  Colonel  Dahlgren’s  party  and  killed  him. 
General  Butler  will  dispatch  2,000  infantry  from  Nortolk  at  9  a.  m. 
to  morrow,  to  be  here  by  2  p.  m.,  when,  joined  by  1,000  infantry  and 
commanded  by  General  Wistar,  they  will  proceed  and  land  at  Shep¬ 
pard’s  Lauding,  near  the  mouth  of  the  Mattapony.  You  will  accom¬ 
pany  these  troops  from  Yorktown  to  Sheppard’s  Landing  witli  the 
gunboats  named  in  the  margin,  protect  them,  and  give  them  all  the  aid 
in  your  power.  When  the  movement  against  King  and  Queen  Court- 
House  is  over,  or  when  the  above  landing  is  made,  General  Wistar  will 
inform  you  how  long  he  shall  need  the  presence  of  the  gunboats  at 
Sheppard’s  Landing.  General  Wistar  does  not  expect  to  reembark 
there,  but  to  march  back,  and  he  does  expect  to  march  across  to  Mid¬ 
dlesex  County  to  the  point  of  the  peninsula  between  the  Piankatank 
and  the  Rappahannock,  where  the  rebels  are  said  to  be  fitting  out  a 
boat  expedition.  General  Wistar  desires  that  you  should  be  with  the 
gunboats  between  tlie  mouth  of  the  Rappahannock  and  a  point  10  miles 
below  Urbaua  from  Friday  evening  next  to  Saturday  evening,  to  pre¬ 
vent  the  rebels  from  escaping  across  the  river.  General  Wistar  does 
not  expect  to  communicate  with  you  there.  General  Butler  will  notify 
Commander  Parker  of  this  expedition,  and  if  the  latter  should  be  there, 
you  will  be  subject  to  his  orders  while  operating  with  him.  Make  your 
report  to  me,  however,  as  soon  as  practicable.  Put  yourself  in  com¬ 
munication  with  General  Wistar  and  strive,  as  you  have  always  done, 
to  advance  the  public  interests. 

Respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

On  the  morning  of  the  9th  instant  at  11  a.  m.  NGfeneral  Kilpatrick 
and  staff  arrived  on  board  this  vessel;  four  transports  arrived  off  York- 
town  at  noon  with  troops.  At  1  p.  m.  General  Wistar  arrived  on  board 
this  vessel  with  his  staff.  At  1 :  30  p.  m.  got  underway;  signaled  IT.  S. 
gunboats  Shokokon  and  General  Putnam  to  get  underway  and  follow  with 
the  transports.  Proceeded  up  the  river  with  this  vessel,  fleet  following- 
in  our  wake.  At  7 : 20  p.  in.  entered  the  Mattapony  River,  and  at  7  : 45, 
being  abreast  of  Sheppard’s  Landing,  and  the  night  being  very  dark, 
placed  men  with  lanterns  on  the  dock  as  a  guide  to  the  transports, 
ordering  the  Shokokon  to  anchor  below  the  transports  and  the  Putnam 
again  below  her,  while  I  remained  above  them  with  this  vessel.  The 
transports  went  at  once  alongside  the  dock  and  began  disembarking 
the  troops.  At  10 :  30  General  Putnam  came  alongside  with  two  army 
gunboats  and  some  launches  which  had  come  up  the  river  with  orders 
for  General  Wistar,  but  after  communicating  with  him  returned  again 
down  the  river;  about  midnight  there  arrived  two  more  transports 
with  troops.  General  Kilpatrick  and  staff  then  went  ashore  from  this 
vessel.  At  8  a.  m.  on  the  morning  of  the  10th  instant  General  Wistar 
and  staff  went  on  shore  from  this  vessel,  all  troops  being  disembarked, 
and  the  transports  at  anchor  in  the  stream.  Troops  marched  away, 
leaving  a  picket  guard  around  the  wharf.  General  Wistar  on  leaving 
this  vessel  requested  me  to  wait  until  the  evening  and  if  possible  he 
would  commuuicate  with  me,  but  if  he  did  not  that  I  should  return  to 
Yorktown  that  evening  with  the  fleet.  At  10:50  a.  m.  got  underway 
and  went  alongside  the  wharf  at  Sheppard’s  Landing,  having  the  Gen¬ 
eral  Putnam  above  the  transports  and  the  Shokokon  below  them.  At 
12:30  army  tug  Seth  Low  arrived  with  a  dispatch  for  General  Wistar 
or  Kilpatrick,  but  having  no  means  of  communicating  with  them,  I 
took  charge  of  it,  and  when  I  returned  to-day  delivered  it  to  General 
Wistar.  At  5  p.  m.  ordered  General  Putnam  to  get  underway  and  pro¬ 
ceed  down  the  river  with  two  transports.  At  5:30  received  on  board 
from  the  Shokokon  a  refugee  from  Richmond,  whom  I  turned  over  to 
the  military  authorities  on  my  arrival  at  Yorktown.  At  6  ordered  the 
Shokokon  to  proceed  down  the  river  with  three  transports  in  com¬ 
pany.  Took  on  board  the  picket  guard,  and  having  received  no 
communication  from  General  Wistar,  at  7:30  proceeded  down  the 
river  with  one  transport  in  company.  At  9:30  p.  m.  weather  set¬ 
ting  in  very  thick,  and  not  being  able  to  see  the  land  on  either  side  of 
the  river,  came  to  anchor  and  burned  a  blue  light  as  a  signal  to  the 
other  vessels  which  were  close  to  me.  At  5 : 30  a.  m.  on  the  morning  of 
the  11th  instant,  got  underway  and  proceeded  for  Yorktown,  where 
we  came  to  anchor  at  8 :  30.  Fog  again  set  in  very  thick,  but  at  12 : 30 
p.  m.  partially  cleared  up.  At  1:30  p.  m.  got  underway  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  down  the  river,  but  the  fog  again  setting  in  very  thick,  came  to 
anchor  at  2 : 40;  weather  again  clearing  up,  at  3 : 30  p.  in.  signalized  the 
Shokokon  and  General  Putnam  to  get  underway  and  follow  this  vessel. 
After  dark  the  weather  again  set  in  very  thick  on  the  horizon,  but 
clear  overhead;  burned  two  rockets  as  a  signal  to  General  Putnam , 
which  she  answered.  Came  to  anchor  at  9  p.  m.  At  5: 30  a.  m.  on  the 
morning  of  the  12th  instant  again  got  underway,  and  when  off  the 
mouth  of  Piaukatank  River  exchanged  signals  with  theU.  8.  S.  Curri¬ 
tuck,  of  the  Potomac  Flotilla,  and  when  off  the  mouth  of  the  Rappa¬ 
hannock  saw  the  gunboats  Yankee ,  Freeborn,  Tulip,  and  Fuchsia; 
communicated  with  the  senior  officer  present,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Ldward  Hooker,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Yankee ,  and  was  informed 
by  him  that  on  Wednesday  morning  at  9  a.  m.  (five  hours  before  the

U.  S.  S.  Shokokon, 

Off  Yorktown ,  March  13 ,  1864. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  orders  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee,  I 
reported  to  you  the  8th  instant,  4 : 30  p.  m.,  for  any  duty  you  might 
assign.  At  6:30  received  orders  to  get  underway  and  to  proceed  to 
the  mouth  of  the  Poquosin  River;  communicate  with  the  U.  S.  S.  Gen¬ 
eral  Putnam ,  with  orders  to  Acting  Master  Savage  to  proceed  to  York¬ 
town  without  delay,  which  orders  I  obeyed,  arriving  back  at  10:30 
p.  m.  At  7  a.  m.,  9th  instant,  repaired  on  board  the  Morse  and  learned 
that  the  gunboats  Morse ,  Shokokon ,  and  General  Putnam  were  to 
accompany  the  army  transports  up  York  River  on  an  expedition  as  far 
as  West  Point.  At  2  p.  m.  got  underway,  the  Morse  leading  the  way, 
the  Shokokon  and  Putnam  following  with  the  transports;  proceeded  up 
the  river.  At  7 : 30  p.  m.  arrived  at  a  wharf  about  1  mile  above  West 
Point,  on  the  west  bank  of  the  Mattapony  River,  where  the  troops 
were  landed.  The  gunboats  were  ordered  to  remain  there  for  the 
night.  I  received  an  order  to  drop  down  the  river  a  quarter  of  a  mile 
below  the  transports,  the  Putnam  about  the  same  distance  below  the 
Shokokon ;  we  anchored.  At  9  p.  m.  boats  were  discovered  passing  up 
the  river;  were  stopped  by  the  Putnam.

Immediately  got  underway,  proceeded  down  to  thfe  Putnam ,  and 
learned  that  they  were  launches  sent  by  General  Graham.  I  reported 
them  to  you  and  received  permission  for  them  to  pass  up,  as  they 
wished  to  communicate  with  General  Wistar.  At  8:30  a.  in.,  11th 
instant,  the  troops  moved  away;  received  orders  to  remain  at  anchor. 

At  4  p.  m.  was  ordered  to  move  farther  down  the  river,  near  a  bluff 
a  short  distance  above  West  Point,  to  prevent  the  enemy  from  placing 
a-  battery  on  a  deserted  work.  At  5 : 30  p.  m.  picked  up  a  refugee  from 
Richmond,  whom  I  sent  you.  At  6  p.  m.  received  orders  to  proceed  to 
Yorktown  with  three  transports,  but  on  account  of  a  dense  fog  did  not 
get  down  until  6  a.  m.  11th  instant.  At  11  a.  m.  received  orders  to 
proceed  to  the  Rappahannock;  the  fog  being  so  thick,  did  not  leave 
until  3:40  p.  m.,  when,  in  company  with  the  Morse  and  Putnam ,  pro¬ 
ceeded  up  to  near  the  mouth  of  the  Rappahannock,  the  fog  being  so 
thick  that  it  was  not  safe  to  go  farther,  and  came  to  an  anchor.  At  5 
a.  m.,  12th  instant,  got  underway  and  steamed  into  the  mouth  of  the 
Rappahannock;  communicated  with  the  fleet  there;  then  steamed  up 
the  river  to  a  point  about  5  miles  below  IJrbana;  came  to  an  anchor, 
and  kept  a  bright  lookout  for  any  troops  that  might  be  in  the  neigh¬ 
borhood;  6:30  p.  m.,  not  seeing  any  of  our  troops,  got  underway, 
and  keeping  as  near  the  position  as  possible  that  we  had  through 
the  day,  kept  underway  all  night,  keeping  a  strict  lookout  for  any  sig¬ 
nals  that  might  be  made,  and  to  prevent  the  enemy  from  crossing.  At 
6 : 30  a.  m.  the  Morse  came  within  hail;  was  ordered  to  follow  her  down, 
after  communicating  with  the  fleet  at  the  mouth  of  the  river;  steamed 
away  for  this  anchorage,  arriving  here  at  2  p.  m.  of  this  day. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  B.  Sheldon, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Lieutenant-Gommander  Charles  A.  Babcock,

U.  S.  S.  General  Putnam, 

Off  Yorktown ,  Va.,  March  13,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  fo  you  my  proceedings  in  the  late 
expedition  under  your  command. 

March  8. — At  anchor  in  Poquosin  River.  At  7  p.  m.  was  signalized 
by  the  U.  S.  S.  Shokokon,  Acting  Master  Sheldon,  commanding.  I 
immediately  got  underway  and  proceeded  within  hail.  Received 
orders  to  proceed  to  Yorktown  and  there  report  to  the  senior  officer. 
At  10:30  p.  m.  came  to  anchor  off  Yorktown  and  reported  to  you. 

March  9. — At  1 :30  p.  in.  received  orders  from  you  to  proceed  up  the 
York  River  in  company  with  the  U.  S.  S.  Morse  and  U.  S.  S.  Shokokon, 
to  convoy  four  army  transports  loaded  with  troops,  under  command  of 
Generals  Wistar  and  Kilpatrick.  At  7:30  p.  m.  covered  the  landing  of 
the  troops  from  the  transports  at  Sheppard’s  Landing,  on  the  Matta- 
pony  River,  about  2  miles  above  West  Point.  At  9  p.  in.  received 
orders  from  you  to  proceed  to  the  rear  of  the  fleet  and  protect  them 
from  any  approach  of  the  enemy  in  that  direction.  At  10  p.  m.  dis¬ 
covered  several  launches  filled  with  men  approaching  the  fleet  in  a 
suspicious  manner.  I  immediately  beat  to  quarters  and  slipped  the 
cable,  hailed  them,  and  after  examination  found  them  to  be  army 
launches  with  reinforcements  from  General  Graham  for  the  expedition 
of  Generals  Wistar  and  Kilpatrick;  convoyed  them  to  you,  and 
returned  to  my  station.  At  12  midnight  several  more  steam  trans- 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  547 

ports  arrived;  examined  them  and  found  they  were  attached  to  the 
expedition. 

March  10. — At  10  a.  m.  received  orders  to  proceed  above  the  fleet  to 
protect  the  transports  and  look  out  for  the  approach  of  the  enemy. 
At  5  p.  in.  received  orders  to  convoy  two  army  transports  to  York- 
town.  At  10  p.  m.  came  to  anchor,  being  thick  fog. 

March  11. — At  5:30  a.  m.  weighed  anchor  and  proceeded  to  York- 
town.  At  9  a.  m.  arrived  at  Yorktown;  received  orders  to  proceed 
alongside  the  U.  S.  S.  Mystic  for  a  supply  of  coal.  At  11  a.  m.  came  to 
anchor.  At  1  p.  m.  received  orders  to  proceed  to  the  Rappahannock 
River  to  cooperate  with  Generals  Wistar  and  Kilpatrick’s  forces,  in 
company  with  U.  S.  steamers  Morse  and  Shokokon.  At  9  p.  m.  came  to 
anchor  off  the  Rappahannock  River  in  a  thick  fog. 

March  12. — At  5 : 30  a.  m.  weighed  anchor  and  proceeded  into  the  Rap¬ 
pahannock  River.  At  10  a.  m.,  in  obedience  to  orders,  took  my  station 
oft'  Lockley’s  Point  to  look  out  for  the  enemy  and  the  arrival  of  our 
forces.  At  5  p.  m.  received  orders  to  weigh  anchor  and  keep  under¬ 
way  on  that  station  during  the  night,  and  look  out  for  the  enemy  or 
signals  from  our  forces. 

March  13. — At  5  a.  in.,  having  received  no  signal,  and  no  appearance 
of  the  enemy,  received  orders  to  follow  you  to  Yorktown.  At  3  p.  m. 
arrived  at  Yorktown  and  came  to  anchor. 

Sir,  I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

.  H.  H.  Savage, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  TJ.  S.  8.  General  Putnam.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  robbing 
and  firing  of  schooner  Julia  Baker,  March  11, 1864. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  March  19,  1864. . 

Sir:  Acting  Master  Williams,  commanding  Commodore  Barney, 
reports  on  12th  instant  that  the  schooner  Julia  Baker,  of  Georgetown, 
[Me.],  Fras.  Lowe,  master,  was  robbed  and  set  on  fire  on  the  night  of 
the  11th  instant. 

About  $2,500  were  taken  from  her,  and  her  captain  and  5  men  are 
missing.  Two  boats  filled  with  men  were  seen  going  in  the  direction 
of  Chuckatuck  Creek  at  3  a.  m.  on  the  12th,  who  were  probably  the 
perpetrators  of  the  act. 

The  Commodore  Barney  was  anchored  about  2  miles  from  where  the 
schooner  lay,  and  received  no  notice  of*  the  attack  before  daylight. 

The  guerrillas  in  this  vicinity  are  becoming  quite  bold,  and  have 
recently  on  different  occasions  fi-ed  with  musketry  on  oyster  schooners 
and  on  our  picket  boats. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Baton,  V.  S.  Navy,  commanding 
U.  S.  S.  Admiral,  regarding  the  chase  of  a  large  steamer ,  March  12, 
1864. 

U.  S.  S.  Admiral, 

Hampton  Roads,  Virginia ,  March  14,  1864. 
Sir  :  I  have  to  report  that  while  on  the  passage  of  this  vessel  from 
Port  Poyal,  in  latitude  32°  50',  longitude  77°  33',  a  steamer  was  sighted 
from  this  ship’s  masthead;  gave  chase;  gained  on  her;  made  her  out  a 
large  English-built  steamer,  side- wheel,  about  900  tons  burden,  broad 
beam,  low  hull,  two  smokestacks,  stripped  to  her  lower  masts,  painted 
a  very  light  lead  color,  clean,  and  apparently  new.  Chased  twelve 
hours;  pushed  her  so  hard  that  she  threw  overboard  between  400  and 
500  bales  of  cotton.  We  gained  on  her  while  running  14  and  14.4  knots. 
Her  speed  must  have  been  about  13£  knots.  I  discontinued  the  chase 
when  night  came  on,  in  latitude  31°  10',  longitude  75°  50';  this  was  on 
the  12th  instant. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  B.  Eaton, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  additional 
gunboats  necessary  for  the  protection  of  the  eastern  shore  counties  of 
Virginia. 

Navy  Department, 
Washington ,  T>.  C.,  March  14,  1864. 
Sir:  The  necessities  of  the  service  require  at  least  six  light-draft, 
side-wheel,  swift  steam  tugs,  not  to  draw  over  or  5  feet  when  loaded, 
and  carrying  a  light  gun  on  a  center  pivot  at  each  end. 

These  light-draft  steam  gunboats  are  required  to  protect  the  eastern 
shore  counties  of  Virginia  and  to  operate  in  the  narrow  waters  which 
the  enemy  have  recently  threatened  and  which  constitute  a  part  of  the 
army  lines  of  defense  for  Norfolk. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear.  Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 
Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

masted,  lead-color  steamer  (blockade  runner)  was  discovered  on  shore,

Report  of  Commander  Frailey,  XT.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  information 
regarding  the  attempted  destruction  of  a  blockade  runner  off  Fort 
Campbell,  N.  C. 

U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City, 

Off  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  March  15,  1864. 
Sir  :  I  regret  to  report  that  shortly  after  daylight  yesterday  morning 
a  large  side- wheel  steamer,  which  had  doubtless  passed  in  by  the  ves¬ 
sels  of  the  squadron  during  the  night,  was  discovered  on  or  near  the 
beach  on  the  west  point  of  Oak  Island,  the  officer  of  the  watch,  Acting 
Ensign  R.  Wilkinson,  at  or  about  G  a.  m.  being  directed  to  it  by  the 
steamer  Aries,  which  vessel  was  engaged  firing  at  her  until  driven  off 
by  the  batteries  in  the  vicinity  and  a  number  of  Whitworth  guns 
which  had  been  quickly  brought  to  the  scene  of  action. 

In  the  evening,  on  the  return  of  the  State  of  Georgia  and  Aries  to 
their  stations,  both  vessels  opened  a  fire  upon  the  stranded  vessel,  but 
without  any  success,  as  in  a  few  minutes  a  very  heavy  fire  was  opened 
upon  both  by  numerous  batteries  of  greater  range,  which  compelled 
them  to  withdraw,  without,  however,  either  vessel  receiving  anyjnjury. 

During  the  night  the  enemy  succeeded  in  floating  the  vessel  and 
getting  her  safely  into  the  river.  Weather  very  hazy. 

Acting  [Volunteer]  Lieutenant-Commanding  Devens,  of  the  Aries, 
reports  having  seen  her  at  5  o’clock  from  his  night  station  No.  7,  ran  in 
to  cut  her  oft,  when  she  ran  upon  the  beach.  His  report  and  an  extract 
from  his  log  herewith  accompanies  this. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jas.  Madison  Frailey, 
Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads. 

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Aries, 

Off  Western  Bar,  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  March  14,  1864. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  statement  in  regard  to 
the  steamer  driven  on  shore  by  this  vessel,  and  also  enclose  the  remarks 
of  the  officer  in  charge  of  the  deck  at  the  time. 

At  5  a.  m.  saw  a  steamer  bearing  north  from  night  station  No.  7,  which 
station  was  occupied  for  the  night  by  this  vessel;  stood  in  to  cut  her 
off’,  when  she  ran  upon  the  beach,  about  1  mile  below  Fort  Campbell. 
Got  the  boats  ready  to  board  her,  when  we  saw  a  large  number  of 


552 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


troops  and  several  pieces  of  artillery  coming  down  t^ie»  beach  from  the 
direction  of  the  fort.  At  5: 20  a.  m.  opened  fire  on  her;  at  the  same  time 
rebels  opened  fire  upon  us  from  the  beach  above  and  below  the  steamer 
with  several  Whitworth  guns,  the  shell  all  falling  close  to  us  or  going 
over  us.  At  0:10  a.  m.,  having  had  reason  to  believe  two  shells  had 
struck  her,  one  through  her  bow  and  one  through  her  just  forward  of 
the  wheelhouse,  I  deemed  it  prudent  to  withdraw,  and  ran  out  and 
reported  all  the  circumstances  to  the  senior  officer  present.  She  is  a 
long,  low,  side- wheel  steamer,  and  looks  very  much  like  the  A.  1).  Vance, 
which  grounded  here  in  January.  The  rebels  fired  43  shell  at  us. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  F.  Devens,

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Plusser,  JJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  rumored 
progress  on  Confederate  ironclad  under  construction  in  the  Roanoke 
River. 


IT.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Plymouth,  N.  C.,  March  16,  1864. 

Sir.  Your  communication  of  the  1st  instant,  in  reply  to  mine  of  the 
20th  ultimo,  was  received  last  night. 

General  Wessells  has  written  me  to-day  about  the  immediate  obstruc¬ 
tion  ot  the  Roanoke,  and,  I  presume,  will  need  the  light-boats  now  here. 
I  received  information  to-day  from  an  old  steamboat  captain,  just  front 
the  vicinity  of  the  ironclad  on  the  Roanoke,  that  she  will  be  ready  to 
be  brought  down  to  Williamston  on  the  1st  of  April.  He  says  she  has 
two  layers  of  iron;  that  they  are  drilling  the  iron  night  and  day,  and 
pushing  her  forward  to  completion  as  rapidly  as  possible.  He  had  a 
conversation  with  the  pilot  engaged  to  bring  her  down,  and  gathered 
trom  him  that  the  attack  on  Plymouth  was  to  be  made  from  below. 
Ihe  pilot  asked  him  if  Ryan’s  Thoroughfare  was  obstructed  with  piles. 
He  replied  that  he  did  not  know,  but  had  heard  that  it  was.  The  pilot 
remarked  that  it  was  of  no  importance,  that  they  had  scows  prepared 
to  go  ahead  of  the  ironclad,  and,  under  cover  of  her  guns,  to  remove 
any  obstructions.  He  said  they  were  greatly  afraid  we  had  torpedoes 
in  the  river.  1 

My  informant  has  returned  to  find  out  more  about  her,  and  promises 
to  give  me  early  intelligence  of  her  movements.  He  deems  her  verv 
formidable.  If  she  has  but  3  inches  of  iron,  as  I  have  been  informed 
by  others  our  present  foree  here  should,  unless  we  are  very  unfortu¬ 
nate,  easily  defeat  her;  yet,  it  would  be  but  prudent  to  insure  her 
destruction,  if  not  inconvenient  to  increase  it  by  a  few  heavv  suns'  Her 
plating  may  be  thicker  than  we  think. 

In  my  report  of  the  explosion  of  the  Southfield's  100-pounder,  I  rec¬

Washington,  March  17, 1864. 

The  following  is  from  headquarters,  Army  of  the  Potomac,  March  16, 
and  forwarded  for  the  information  of  Major-General  Butler,  by  order  of 
the  Secretary  of  War: 

The  following  intelligence  received  from  scouts  just  returned  is  sent  for  your 
information : 

The  enemy  are  making  large  preparations  for  the  capture  of  Norfolk ;  large  details 
are  made  from  Pickett’s  division  to  work  on  the  gunboats  now  building  at  Richmond. 
The  work  is  pushed  night  and  day,  and  it  is  expected  three  gunboais  will  be  finished 
in  three  or  four  weeks.  They  are  also  building  floats  or  rafts  to  carry  guns  to  move 
down  the  James  River  with  their  fleet.  Longstreet  is  to  have  command  on  the 
Blackwater  for  the  main  attack  on  Norfolk.  His  whole  command  is  expected  at 
Petersburg;  his  force  is  estimated  at  15,000.  Pontoons  have  been  sent  from  Rich¬ 
mond  to  Petersburg.  A  feint  will  be  made  on  Williamsburg  with  a  force  of  3,000 
infantry  and  some  cavalry  and  artillery;  and  for  this  purpose  Ford’s  [Forge?] 
Bridge  over  the  Chickahominy  is  being  rebuilt.  The  whole  information  is  brought 
by  a  man  named  Black,  whom  our  scouts  brought  back  with  them,  and  who  repre¬ 
sents  himself  as  having  been  sent  by  Union  men  in  Richmond  to  communicate  the 
above  and  other  information  to  the  War  Department.  He  will  be  sent  up  to-morrow 
with  an  officer.  Our  scouts  report  that  J.  E.  B.  Stuart  is  collecting  a  cavalry  force 
at  Fredericksburg  to  make  a  raid  on  our  rear,  and  is  only  waiting  for  the  Rappa¬ 
hannock  to  become  fordable  to  cross  at  or  near  Fredericksburg.  They  also  report 
the  enemy  sending  supplies  and  ammunition  in  great  quantities  over  both  railroads, 
uniting  at  Hanover  Junction,  to  Lee’s  army. 

Geo.  G.  Meade, 

Major-General. 

Major-General  H.  W.  Halleck. 

March  16,  1864 — 11  p.  m.

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Flusser,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
progress  of  the  Confederate  ram  under  construction  in  the  Roanoke 
River. 

U.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Plymouth,  N.  C.,  March  18,  1864. 

Sir:  General  Wessells  sent  me  word  night  before  last,  just  as  he 
stepped  on  board  the  mail  boat  for  Roanoke  Island,  that  a  man  was  just 
down  from  Hamilton  who  had  been  on  board  tlie  rebel  ironclad,  and 
that  in  two  hours  I  might  get  him  on  board  to  interrogate  him.  The 
adjutant-general  rode  out  to  the  lines  to  bring  him  in,  but  he  had 
already  started  for  his  house,  some  10  or  12  miles  off,  and  no  one  knew 
its  situation  or  whereabouts.  A  report  in  town  to-day,  said  to  be  trace¬ 
able  to  him,  represents  the  ironclad  at  Hamilton,  with  a  large  force  of 
soldiers,  and  2,000  soldiers  at  Williamston.  Further,  tlie  floating  bat¬ 
tery,  about  which  I  had  heard  nothing  for  a  long  time  and  hoped  had 
died  a  natural  death,  is  said  to  be  very  near  completion.  The  present 
report  makes  her  octagonal,  with  7  inches  of  iron,  lined  with  two  tiers 
of  cotton  bales.  The  ram,  or  whatever  it  may  be  called,  is  also  said  to 
have  7  inches  of  plating.  I  think  the  reporters  are  putting  on  the  iron 


556 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


rather  heavy.  I  am  inclined  to  believe  her  armor  Is  not  more  than 
stated  in  one  of  my  former  letters — 3  inches. 

The  people  in  the  country  above  and  below  us,  who  have  better 
means  than  we  possess  of  gaining  information,  anticipate  an  early  and 
severe  attack  by  land  and  water  here. 

I  should  like  very  much  to  have  the  new  guns  for  the  Southfield 
mounted.  She  is  badly  shorn  of  her  strength. 

The  vessels  will  be  ready  to  sink  by  Monday.  I  have  a  torpedo 
prepared  for  each  one.  General  Wessells  has  said  he  would  supply 
powder  if  I  would  construct  them.  I  hope  they  may  be  successful.  It 
will  be  difficult  to  sink  the  vessels  in  proper  positions,  owing  to  the 
strong  current.  I  have  suggested  a  plan  to  the  general,  who  is  doing 
the  business.  I  shall  aid  him  if  he  requests  assistance. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be  sir.  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  W.  Flusser, 
Lieutenant-  Commander . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads.

instructions  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee , 
U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  limits  seaward  of  the  blockade. 

Navy  Department,  March  19, 1864. 

Sir:  Your  letter  of  the  9th  instant  is  received,  stating  that  immedi¬ 
ately  upon  the  receipt  of  the  Department’s  letter  of  February  27,  decid¬ 
ing  that  the  limits  of  the  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron  were 
just  outside  of  the  line  occupied  by  the  blockading  vessels,  with  right 
of  pursuit  beyond  that  line,  you  had  immediately  recalled  the  fast 
steamers  stationed  off  the  extensive  shoals  off  the  Capes  of  Lookout 
and  Fear;  also  those  in  the  tracks  of  the  blockade  runners  between  the 
principal  inlets  on  the  coast  of  North  Carolina  and  their  depots  at  Ber¬ 
muda  and  Nassau. 

Your  letter  of  February  27  having  raised  the  question  of  limits  sea¬ 
ward,  there  seemed  to  be  no  other  decision  possible  than  that  they 
should  [cruise]  beyond  the  line  occupied  by  the  blockading  vessels.  At 
the  time  this  decision  was  made  the  Department  was  aware,  and  was 
gratified  to  find,  that  you  had  followed  the  plan,  long  since  adopted  by 
Rear-Admiral  Farragut  and  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey  with  a  much 
smaller  force,  of  placing  some  of  your  vessels  well  to  seaward ;  and  this 
plan  being  in  successful  operation  and  your  limits  seaward  being  beyond 
the  position  occupied  by  these  vessels,  it  is  not  understood  why  you 
should  have  acted  so  hastily  in  bringing  your  vessels  inshore  unless  you 
are  of  opinion  that  the  blockade  can  be  more  rigidly  enforced  there. 
The  Department  does  not  propose  to  suggest  any  particular  positions 
for  your  vessels,  having  great  confidence  in  your  judgment  and  zeal  for 
the  public  service. 

If  the  Shenandoah,  by  authority  delegated  to  you  by  the  Department, 
has  been  sent  toward  Bermuda  and  is  acting  under  your  orders,  she  is 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


557 


not  an  independent  command.  If  there  is  reasonable  ground  for  believ¬ 
ing  that  blockade  running  can  be  more  effectually  suppressed  by  send¬ 
ing  any  of  your  steamers  in  the  track  of  such  vessels  bound  from 
Bermuda  to  Nassau,  you  are  authorized  to  make  such  disposition  of 
your  command. 

The  Department  does  not  consider  that  you  would  be  beyond  the  lim¬ 
its  of  your  command,  subject  to  the  disability  contemplated  by  the  third 
clause  of  the  third  section  of  the  act  for  the  better  government  of  the 
Navy,  while  you  are  temporarily,  by  authority  of  the  Department,  per¬ 
sonally  present  in  a  vessel  in  the  Potomac  Kiver. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  recruits. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  March  19,  1864. 

Sir  :  General  Butler  informs  me  that  he  has  300  mariners  in  one  regi¬ 
ment  whom  he  is  ready  to  transfer  to  me  for  the  naval  service  at  any 
time.  I  have  verbally  requested  that  this  may  be  done  at  once. 

He  has  also  some  30  prisoners  at  Point  Lookout  who  are  willing  to 
enlist  in  the  Navy,  and  whom  he  considers  reliable  men. 

These,  by  the  Department’s  rule  for  distribution,  are  not  needed  here 
at  present. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Babcock,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
transfer  of  recruits  from  the  Army  to  the  Navy. 

U.  S.  S.  Morse, 

Off  Yorktown,  Va.,  March  20,  1864. 

Sir:  General  Wi star  informs  me  that  in  a  few  days  there  will  be 
from  75  to  100  soldiers  transferred  to  the  Navy  at  this  place,  and  he 
states  he  is  willing  to  assist  me  in  every  way  possible  to  get  these 
men  to  fill  up  the  complement  of  the  different  vessels  at  this  point. 
He  says,  if  you  will  make  arrangements  with  General  Butler,  he  thinks 
this  can  be  accomplished  without  going  through  the  regular  form  of 
sending  these  men  to  the  rendezvous  to  be  transferred  to  the  Navy. 

I  would  respectfully  request,  if  this  arrangement  meets  with  your 
approbation,  that  I  may  be  allowed  to  have  these  men  to  distribute 
among  the  vessels  at  this  point  which  are  short  of  complement  of  crew. 
I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Neivport  News,  March  21,  1864. 

Sir:  When  this  ship  goes  North  for  repairs  I  propose,  if  it  is  not 
disapproved  by  the  Department,  to  transfer  her  marine  guard  to  other 
vessels  of  the  squadron. 

The  St.  Lawrence  needs  a  small  marine  guard,  as  the  prisoners  of  the 
squadron  must  be  placed  on  her,  as  Commodore  Livingston  thinks  they 
can  not  be  safely  accommodated  on  the  Brandywine  at  Norfolk.  The 
Malvern,  which  will  be  the  temporary  flagship,  will  also  need  marines, 
and  the  commanding  officers  of  several  vessels  desire  to  have  a  small 
marine  guard.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  urging  the  need  of  light- 
draft  ironclads  for  operations  against  Richmond. 

Confidential.]  TJ.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  March  21,  1864. 
Sir  :  I  enclose  a  copy  of  a  confidential  communication  from  General 
Butler,  dated  17th  instant. 

Not  doubting  that  a  vigorous  campaign  will  be  opened  against  Rich¬ 
mond  this  spring,  I  trust  that  the  Department  will  be  able  to  provide 
me  with  some  ironclads  whose  draft  will  allow  me  to  cooperate  with  the 
Army. 

The  Roanoke  can  not  go  up  the  James  River  out  of  sight  of  Newport 
News,  nor  the  Atlanta  within  sight  of  City  Point.

Confidential.]  II.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Newport  News,  March  22,  1864. 

Sir:  General  Butler,  under  date  of  21st  instant,  encloses  to  me  a 
copy  of  a  statement  made  to  him  by  a  scout  whom  he  sent  to  Hamil¬ 
ton,  N.  C., which  is  in  substance  as  follows:  That  he  heard  at  Hamilton, 
where  he  was  for  half  an  hour  only,  that  the  ironclad  building  on  the 
Roanoke  River  was  aground  at  a  point  about  10  miles  below  Hamilton 
aud  25  above  Plymouth,  on  the  Roanoke,  and  that  the  rebels  had  taken 
all  the  guns  off  it  and  removed  them.  Its  draft  is  about  17  feet.  In 
the  vicinity  of  Hamilton  there  was,  he  learned,  a  regiment  of  infantry, 
and  about  1,500  cavalry  conscripting  and  foraging  through  the  coun¬ 
try.  He  heard  nothing  about  the  number  of  troops  at  Weldon  or  any 
other  point  in  that  vicinity.  In  regard  to  Pickett’s  division,  that  he 
had  about  15,000  effective  men  in  the  State  of  North  Carolina.  Nearly 
all  the  negroes  had  been  taken  into  the  interior  of  the  State. 

General  Butler  writes  me  that  he  will  send  a  copy  of  this  statement 
to  the  commanding  officer  at  Plymouth,  with  instructions  to  communi¬ 
cate  it  to  the  senior  naval  officer  there.  He  proposes  that  a  little  expe¬ 
dition  be  organized  to  destroy  this  ironclad,  and  I  desire  that  you  will 
arrange  the  details  of  a  suitable  expedition  with  the  commanding  offi¬ 
cer  at  Plymouth  (General  Wessells)  and  carry  it  out,  if  you  deem  it 
practicable,  without  further  instructions  from  me. 

If  you  need  more  gunboats  than  you  have  under  your  command  at 
Plymouth,  inform  Commander  Davenport,  in  confidence,  of  the  plan, 
and  ask  him  to  send  you  the  necessary  force.  I  desire,  however,  that 
the  knowledge  of  the  affair  be  confined  to  as  few  persons  as  possible. 

Respectfully,  yours, 


S.  P.  Lee, 
Acting  Rear-Admiral. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Flusser, 

U.  S.  8.  Miami,  Plymouth,  N.  C.

Sir:  On  the  20th  instant  the  New  Berne  left  here  for  New  York 
encountered  a  heavy  gale  and  returned,  and  is  still  here. 

We  have  now  a  severe  northeast  wind  and  snowstorm. 

The  Calypso ,  with  two  heavy  guns  on  her  deck  for  the  Southfield  will 
leave  for  Beaufort  as  soon  as  the  weather  clears  off.

mington,  in  proportion  to  their  crews.

of  the  Department’s  order  requiring  them  to  be  sent  up  for  the  Iroquois.

Off  Newport  News ,  Va .,  March  23,  1864. 

Representations  are  made  that  prize  steamers  are  turned  over  to  the 
U.  S.  marshal  in  such  bad  condition  from  carelessness  as  lessens  their 
appraised  value  and  increases  the  expense  to  Government  when  they 
are  taken  into  the  service. 

Prize  masters  are  strictly  required  to  take  special  care  to  have  prize 
vessels  (especially  the  engines  and  boilers,  which  must  not  be  allowed 
to  freeze  up  or  rust)  turned  over  to  the  U.  S.  marshal  free  of  tilth  and 
in  good  police. 

It  is  expected  that  prizes  will,  on  their  arrival,  undergo  a  naval 
inspection.

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Flusser ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
rumored  presence  of  the  Confederate  ironclad  at  Williamston ,  N.  C. 

U.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Plymouth,  N.  C.,  March  24,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  information  to-day,  which  would  seem  to  be  reliable,  to 
the  effect  that  the  ironclad  on  this  river  is  at  Hamilton,  and  that  the 
rebels  are  removing,  or  have  removed,  the  torpedoes  they  had  placed 
in  the  [Roanoke]  River  below  Williamston.  It  is  also  stated  that  their 
boat  is  80  feet  long,  and,  something  more  serious,  that  her  armor  is  4£ 
inches  instead  of  3,  as  formerly  represented.  We  should  have  the 
guns  for  the  Southfield  immediately,  as  we  do  not  know  when  we  will 
be  attacked.  The  land  force  (rebel)  near  us  has  been  lately  increased 
and  their  lines  closed  to  prevent  information  reaching  us.  I  think  we 
may  expect  an  early  attack.  Please  send  Southfield’s  guns  at  once. 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

0.  W.  Flusser, 
Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Commander  H.  K.  Davenport, 

Senior  Naval  Officer,  Sounds  of  North  Carolina. 


Boat  expedition  to  Swansboro  and  Bear  Creek,  March  24-26,  1864. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  reports. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  April  2,  1864. 

Sir:  I  transmit  enclosed  a  report  (with  its  enclosure)  dated  27th 
ultimo,  from  Commander  B.  M.  Dove,  of  the  failure  of  an  expedition 
arranged  by  Colonel  Jourdan,  of  the  Army,  commanding  at  Beaufort, 
and  himself,  with  the  reasons  of  this  failure. 

The  object  of  this  expedition  was  the  capture  or  destruction  of  two 
schooners  near  Swansboro  and  the  capture  of  the  force  and  supposed 
battery  on  the  south  end  of  Bogue  Island  [Banks]. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


563 


The  force  employed  consisted  of  about  200  soldiers  and  45  sailors. 
They  were  embarked  on  tbe  Britannia  on  the  24th  ultimo,  and  two 
flats,  a  launch  (with  a  howitzer),  and  two  small  boats  were  taken  in  tow 
to  land  them. 

They  arrived  off  Bogue  Inlet  about  11  p.  m.,  by  which  time  the 
weather,  which  was  fair  at  the  time  of  starting,  had  changed;  a  strong 
S.  E.  wind  came  up  with  heavy  swells.  But  two  boats  got  inside; 
others  grounded  in  the  attempt  and  got  off  and  returned  to  the 
Britannia  with  difficulty.  The  two  that  had  succeeded,  being  unsup¬ 
ported,  also  returned. 

In  a  second  attempt  one  of  the  launches  got  into  Bear  Inlet  and 
proceeded  up  Bear  Creek.  The  party  succeeded  in  burning  a  schooner 
and  brought  off  about  twenty  contrabands. 

They  were  not  able  to  return  to  the  Britannia ,  owing  to  the  high 
wind  and  sea,  and  she  was  obliged  to  seek  an  offing.  At  daylight  on 
the  morning  of  the  26th  she  stood  in  toward  the  bar,  fired  guns  to 
attract  attention,  but  saw  nothing  of  the  fiat,  and  returned  to  Beau¬ 
fort  about  noon. 

The  losses  were  one  flat,  two  launches,  and  two  small  boats  stove. 

A  negro,  who  refused  to  leave  the  launch  when  ordered,  was 
drowned.  The  howitzer  was  saved,  but  all  the  ammunition  lost. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Bear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


[Enclosure.] 


U.  S.  Naval  Station, 
Beaufort ,  N.  C .,  March  27,  1864. 

Sir:  A  well-planned  expedition  by  Colonel  Jourdan  and  myself  was 
frustrated  by  circumstances  beyond  our  control. 

The  colonel’s  scouts  reported  two  schooners  near  Swansboro,  one  cot¬ 
ton  loaded,  the  other  from  Bermuda.  It  was  gotten  up,  therefore,  for 
the  capture  or  destruction  of  these,  as  also  to  capture  the  force  and  sup¬ 
posed  battery  on  the  south  end  of  Bogue  Island  [Banks). 

The  colonel,  with  his  staff'  and  about  200  soldiers,  also  parties  of  15 
sailors  each  from  the  Cambridge,  Keystone  State,  and  Florida,  embarked 
on  board  the  Britannia  on  the  afternoon  of  the  24th  instant.  She  took 
in  tow  for  landing  them  two  schooner-rigged  fiats,  a  launch  with  how¬ 
itzer,  and  two  small  boats,  and  sailed  about  sunset;  fine  weather  and 
bright  prospects. 

They  arrived  off'  Bogue  Inlet  about  11  p.  m.  and  disembarked  the 
troops,  the  sailors  managing  the  fiats  and  launches.  By  this  time  the 
weather  became  overcast,  wind  raised  from  the  S.  E.,  and  a  heavy  swell 
came  on.  Several  of  the  boats  grounded,  not  being  able  to  find  the 
channel.  Gunner  |S.  D.j  Hines,  with  his  boat  and  another,  got  inside, 
but,  the  others  not  being  able  to  follow,  he  returned  after  landing. 

With  much  difficulty  the  boats  were  gotten  oft' again  and  the  men 
safely  on  board  the  Britannia.  TLie  wind  and  sea  became  tremendous 
and  nothing  else  could  be  done  except  to  give  attention  to  the  vessel. 

In  a  second  attempt  one  of  the  schooners,  with  Lieutenant  [T.  F.] 
King,  [jr.],  of  the  Army,  with  40  soldiers  and  20  sailors,  went  into  Bear 
Inlet  and  up  Bear  Greek,  where  they  burned  one  schooner  and  brought 
off  some  twenty  or  more  contrabands. 


564 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Not  being  able  to  return  to  the  Britannia ,  slie  stood  up  Bogue  Sound 
and  arrived  safely  at  Moreliead  City  at  4  a.  m.  of  the'' 26  th. 

The  howitzer  and  carriage  were  gotten  out  of  the  launch,  but  the  sea 
was  too  heavy  for  them  and  they  broke  adrift,  were  driven  high  up  on 
the  beach  badly  stove. 

After  weathering  the  gale  the  Britannia  returned  about  noon  of 
the  26th. 

One  flat,  the  launch,  and  the  two  boats  were  lost.  One  contraband 
was  drowned  in  consequence  of  his  not  obeying  orders  to  leave  the  liat. 
The  ammunition  of  the  howitzer  was  also  lost. 

Enclosed  is  Lieutenant  Commanding  Huse’s  report. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benjamin  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads. 


[Subenclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Britannia, 
Beaufort ,  [ N .  0.  ],  March  28,  1864. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  orders,  having  received  on  board  Colonel 
Jourdan,  with  a  detachment  of  200  of  the  One  hundred  and  fifty-eighth 
Regiment  New  York  State  Volunteers,  also  parties  of  12  men  from  the 
[J.  S.  steamers  Cambridge,  Keystone  State,  and  Florida,  1  started  at  5 
p.  m.  24th  instant  for  Bogue  Inlet,  having  in  tow  two  lighters,  one 
launch,  and  one  small  boat.  At  7  p.  m.  turned  the  outer  buoy;  weather 
line,  with  light  easterly  wind.  At  10:30  came  to  off  Bogue  Inlet  and 
commenced  embarking  troops  and  sailors.  At  11 : 20  p.  m.  last  boat  left 
the  ship ;  all  the  sailors  in  the  boats  being  under  the  command  of  Acting 
Master  Joseph  S.  Cony. 

At  2  a.  m.  (25th)  a  boat  returned,  reporting  the  launch  and  some  other 
boats  unable  to  cross  and  aground  among  the  breakers.  At  daylight 
all  the  boats  returned  to  the  ship,  only  three  having  succeeded  in  get¬ 
ting  inside;  weather  looking  threatening  and  easterly  swell  making 
fast.  At  7  a.  m.  one  lighter,  with  a  party  of  soldiers  under  Captain 
[William]  Cuff  and  0  sailors  under  Acting  Ensign  M.  E.  Waudell, 
crossed  the  bar  and  made  an  attempt  to  reach  a  schooner  said  to  be 
loaded  with  cotton  lying  about  6  miles  above  Swansboro.  At  the  same 
time  another  lighter,  with  a  party  of  soldiers  under  Lieutenant  King 
and  a  party  of  sailors  under  Acting  Ensign  [E.  A.]  Small,  of  the  Cam¬ 
bridge,  left  the  ship  on  an  expedition  up  Bear  Inlet.  At  10 :  20  the  lighter 
in  charge  of  Acting  Ensigu  Waudell  returned  to  the  ship,  having  been 
fired  upon  by  the  enemy  from  the  banks  of  the  river  near  Swansboro, 
and  being  unable  to  effect  a  landing  without  considerable  loss.  At  11 
a.  m.  the  lighter  was  sent,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  [A.  J.]  Lowell, 
with  a  party  of  sailors  and  soldiers,  to  support  the  other  lighter;  wind 
and  sea  rising  fast. 

At  1:30  the  lighter  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Lowell  returned  to 
the  ship;  sea  running  high,  with  fresh  gale  from  S.  E.;  took  the  men 
from  the  lighter  in  a  small  boat  with  line;  got  all  on  board  safely  except 
one  negro,  who  refused  to  leave  and  remained  to  steer.  Wind  and  sea 
still  increasing,  we  stood  out  for  an  offing,  hauled  launch  alongside, 
and  succeeded  in  getting  the  12-pounder  rifle  howitzer  out;  was  obliged 
to  cut  her  adrift  soon  after,  her  towline  becoming  foul  of  our  rudder; 
ran  a  line  with  buoy  attached  to  try  and  save  the  negro,  but  he  did  not 
avail  himself  of  it.  The  lighter  soon  broke  adrift,  the  foremast  to  which

565 


the  liawser  was. made  fast  being1  carried  away.  The  [negro]  was  drowned 
while  attempting  to  come  on  board  on  the  hawser,  which  still  remained 
fast  to  the  wreck.  The  other  lighters,  at  this  time  (3  p.  m.),  lying  at 
anchor  inside  the  bar,  unable  to  cross  on  account  of  the  surf. 

At  4:30  we  came  to  with  both  anchors,  60  fathoms  chain;  blowing  a

20th  instant,  at  daylight,  wind  having  moderated,  stood  in  for  the

Laid  to  until  9  a.  m.,  and,  seeing  nothing  of  her,  got  underway  for

Wm.  F.  Spicer, 

Commander. 

Acting  Bear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  off  Neicport  News. 


[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Cambridge, 
Beaufort,  N.  C.,  March  27,  1864. 

Sir:  Obedient  to  your  order  to  join  an  expedition  fitted  out  at  this 
place  against  Swansboro  and  Bear  Creek,  1  beg  to  report: 

That  I  joined  the  forces  to  be  sent,  consisting  of  200  infantry  and 
cavalry  and  about  50  seamen,  and  proceeded  in  the  U.  S.  S.  Britannia, 
with  two  flats,  one  launch,  and  two  cutters  in  tow,  and  proceeded  to 
Bogue  Inlet.  Arrived  there  at  9  p.  m.  and  disembarked  the  troops 
into  the  lighters  and  other  boats  and  proceeded  into  the  inlet.  It 
being  very  dark  and  the  pilot  who  was  to  guide  us  into  the  inlet  being 
but  imperfectly  acquainted,  we  missed  the  channel  and  nearly  all  the 
boats  got  aground,  when  we  were  obliged  to  lighten  the  heavier  boats 
and  return  to  the  steamer,  which  caused  great  delay  and  occupied  till 
daylight  and  caused  a  total  failure  of  our  original  plans.  It  was  then 
decided  by  the  officers  in  command  of  the  expedition  to  send  a  day 
expedition  with  the  flats  to  do  what  could  be  done.  Accordingly  one 
flat  was  sent  into  Bogue  Inlet  with  soldiers  and  a  detachment  of  sea¬ 
men  from  the  Britannia,  in  charge  of  officers  of  the  regiment  and  an 
acting  ensign  of  the  Britannia,  and  another  with  56  soldiers  and  20 
seamen,  in  charge  of  Lieutenant  King  and  other  officers  of  the  troops 
and  myself,  to  operate  against  Bear  Inlet.  We  left  the  steamer  at  7 


566 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


a.  m.,  passed  safely  through  the  inlet,  and  found  our  way  up  Bear 
Creek,  where  we  found  a  small  schooner  at  anchor,  which  we  destroyed, 
as  it  was  not  possible  to  take  her  out,  as  also  some  other  rebel  prop¬ 
erty.  We  then  divided  our  forces,  Lieutenant  King  taking  20  men 
and  8  seamen,  going  eastward  to  another  creek,  and  myself  taking  the 
remainder  to  work  the  flat  round  to  the  place  to  which  they  were 
going,  which  I  did  and  arrived  at  noon  and  found  the  other  flat  at  the 
inlet,  from  which  I  got  a  boat  and  four  men  to  assist  in  bringing  oft 
the  other  party.  The  wind  had  increased  and  blowing  almost  a  gale 
from  the  southeast,  and  the  other  flat,  fearing  it  might  be  getting  too 
rough  to  pass  the  bar,  returned  to  the  Britannia ,  by  which  I  sent  word 
that  I  could  not  come  off'  till  nearly  night,  if  then.  I  sent  the  two 
boats  in  search  of  our  party  and  found  them,  and  at  3  p.  in.  got  them 
all  on  board,  also  a  large  number  of  contrabands.  At  this  time  it  was 
blowing  furiously  from  the  southeast,  and  the  flood  tide  had  made  it 
impossible  to  go  over  the  bar,  so  we  concluded  to  try  to  work  our  way 
through  the  sound  to  Beaufort,  fortunately  having  secured  a  pilot 
among  the  contrabands  captured.  At  5  p.  m.  we  got  underway  and 
proceeded,  working  our  way  through  to  Swansboro  by  dark,  where  we 
got  aground.  Landed  and  destroyed  some  property;  got  our  flat  afloat 
again,  proceeded  and  arrived  at  Morehead  City  at  4  a.  m.  of  the  27th, 
having  a  large  number  of  contrabands  and  one  rebel  prisoner  on  board, 
and  losing  no  one  of  our  party.  We  were  obliged  to  leave  many 
negroes  at  the  landing  at  starting,  as  our  boat  was  overcrowded. 

I  am,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  A.  Small, 

Acting  Ensign ,  U.  8.  Navy. 

Commander  W.  F.  Spicer, 

Commanding  U.  8.  8.  Cambridge.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  transmitting  proposed 
acts  relative  to  the  personnel  of  the  Navy. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va .,  March  25,  1864. 

Sir  :  In  view  of  the  proposed  changes  in  the  organization  of  the  Navy, 
by  a  codification  of  the  laws  which  have  heretofore  governed  it,  I  beg 
leave  to  suggest  to  the  Department,  for  its  consideration,  a  more  com¬ 
plete  organization  of  the  staff  of  the  commander  in  chief  of  a  fleet  or 
squadron  and  the  establishment  of  a  naval  law  department  for  the 
Navy,  as  contained  in  the  enclosed  proposed  acts. 

Experience  has  proved  to  me  the  necessity  of  a  chief  of  staff  of  the 
commander  in  chief  of  a  fleet  or  squadron,  whose  duties  shall  be 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


567 


similar  to  those  of  the  adjutant-general  of  our  army  in  the  held,  and 
that  he  should  have  rank  and  pay  commensurate  with  the  character 
and  extent  of  the  duties  he  is  called  upon  to  perform. 

The  great  increase  in  the  personnel  of  the  Navy,  with  the  consequent 
frequency  of  naval  courts  martial  and  courts  of  enquiry,  imperatively 
demands  the  appointment  of  a  chief  judge  advocate  of  the  Navy,  who 
should  be  a  regularly  educated  naval  officer,  informed  in  the  law,  and 
1  recommend  the  proposed  measure  to  the  careful  attention  of  the 
Department. 

The  frequent  accidents,  incidents,  breaches  of  good  order  and  dis¬ 
cipline  occurring  in  every  beet  or  squadron,  which  can  only  be  reached 
and  punished,  and  therefore  restrained,  by  the  judgment  of  courts- 
martial,  demand  the  appointment  of  a  judge-advocate  for  such  fleet  or 
squadron,  who  should  be  attached  to  the  staff  of  the  commander  in 
chief,  and  whose  duties  should  be  similar  to  those  of  a  judge-advocate 
of  an  army  in  the  field. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Bear- Admiral ,  Gomdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  T).  G.

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Flusscr ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  giving  information 
regarding  Confederate  ironclad,  in  the  Roanoke,  and  expected  attack 
upon  New  Berne  and  Plymouth. 

U.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Plymouth,  N.  C.,  March  27,  1864. 

Sir:  We  have  been  awaiting  an  attack  here  for  some  days,  bnt  the 
latest  information  seems  to  point  to  a  postponement  on  the  part  of  the 
rebels.  I  think  we  have  at  length  something  reliable  from  the  ironclad 
up  this  river.  I  examined  a  man  who  has  been  at  work  as  a  ship  car¬ 
penter,  and  was  sent  from  her  about  three  months  since  to  the  hospital 
at  Wilmington,  sick.  He  states  that  she  is  152  feet  long,  34  feet  beam, 
has  two  propellers,  is  pierced  for  six  guns;  draft,  from  6  to  8  feet;  0 
feet  depth  of  hold;  her  gun  deck  about,  or  nearly,  flush  with  the  water; 
6  feet  between  decks,  with  an  iron  shield  from  4  to  5  inches  thick,  and 
40  feet  long,  with  sides  aucl  ends  about  amidships  of  her  length.  When 
he  left  her  boiler  was  not  in.  The  dimensions  given  above,  with  the 
exception  of  length  and  breadth  of  beam,  are  judged  by  the  eye.  The 
man  seems  to  be  honest,  has  been  kindly  treated  by  us,  and,  I  think, 
tells  the  truth.  The  vessel  has  a  keel  of  5  inches.  The  placing  of  the 
hulks  has  been  delayed  longer  than  I  anticipated.  By  request  of 
General  Wessells,  I  am  sinking  them  to-day.  Each  one  carries  a  tor¬ 
pedo,  to  be  exploded  by  percussion.  I  hope  they  will  be  in  position  by 
night.  I  forgot  to  mention  that  from  the  knuckle  of  the  shield  of  the 
ram,  the  plating  runs  down  for  5  feet  and  joins  the  hull,  and  that  her 
stem  is  covered  with  a  piece  of  heavy,  sharp  iron,  0  to  10  inches  thick. 
I  enclose  a  longitudinal  and  sectional  draft  through  the  shield. 

#  #  #  #  *  *  * 

It  is  the  wish  of  the  enemy  to  pass  through  Ryan’s  Thoroughfare 
and  attack  from  below,  thus  avoiding  the  fire  of  the  two  forts,  Gray 
and  Worth,  both  constructed  mainly  for  her  benefit,  one  carrying  a 
100  pounder  and  the  other  a  200-pounder,  bearing  on  the  water. 
####*** 

I  enclose  copy  of  a  note  from  General  Wessells,  received  this  alter - 
noon,  upon  which  I  based  my  assertion  that  the  attack  at  this  place 
would  probably  be  deferred  some  time.  I  can  not  think  why  they 
should  postpone  it,  unless  they  are  waiting  for  the  completion  of  the 
floating  battery  on  the  Roanoke,  which,  I  think,  will  prove  a  more 
formidable  antagonist  than  the  ram — that  is,  .she  can  not  be  run  down, 
and  will  stand  more  hammering  of  shot.  She,  however,  will  have  to 
approach  from  above,  and  I  will  leave  her  to  the  tender  mercies  of  the 
forts. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

0.  W.  Flusser, 
Lieutenant- Commander. 


Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads. 


[En^’osure.] 


Plymouth,  March  27, 1864. 

Dear  Captain:  I  have  just  had  an  interview  with  a  man  just  from 
Kinston  who  has  recently  resigned  from  the  Confederate  service  as  a 
lieutenant  in  the  Forty-first  North  Carolina  Cavalry  and  who  passed 
Foster’s  Mills  yesterday.  His  statement  is  clear  and  full,  and  I  am 
disposed  to  give  it  great  weight.  He  avers  that  there  is  no  change  in 


570 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


affairs  in  Foster’s  Mills;  that  the  Thirty-fifth  is  stilk there  and  at  Ham¬ 
ilton;  that  Pool’s  battalion  is  also  at  the  latter  place;  that  it  is  the 
design  to  attack  New  Berne  and  Plymouth  simultaneously;  that  Gen¬ 
eral  Hooker  says  they  will  have  New  Berne  within  two  months;  he  has 
been  on  board  the  gunboat  at  Kinston;  that  she  has  three  plates  of 
iron,  draws  about  0  feet,  and  has  two  heavy  guns;  that  she  intends  to 
run  by  the  forts  if  possible;  he  knows  nothing  of  our  ram,  but  observed 
she  was  completed.  He  enquired  if  the  Thoroughfare  was  blocked, 
and  says  there  is  no  intention  of  approaching  direct.  He  says  no 
attack  will  be  made  Avithin  five  or  six  weeks,  and  he  believes  not  within 
two  months;  that  at  Kinston  they  are  not  ready;  are  building  at 
Moseley  Hall  a  number  of  launches  similar  to  those  used  at  New 
Berne  some  time  ago.  He  was  with  the  army  at  the  late  attack  on 
New  Berne;  was  sent  with  his  company  to  cut  the  wires  on  the  Beau¬ 
fort  railway,  and  got  lost  in  the  swamps.  He  says  the  Seventeenth  is 
ordered  back  to  Hamilton;  there  is  a  court-martial  going  on  at  Kins¬ 
ton  and  several  colonels  are  being  tried  for  misconduct  at  New  Berne. 

This  man’s  statement  is  so  open  and  unreserved  that  I  believe  it, 
particularly  as  I  am  informed  as  to  his  antecedents.  I  hear  nothing 
from  the  hulks. 

Yours,  truly,  Wessells. 

Captain  Flusser, 

U.  S.  8.  Miami.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Barclay ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  an  exchange  of 
shots  with  a  boat,  in  James  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Jones, 

James  River ,  Va.,  March  38,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  this  morning  at  6:45  a.  m.  1  saw  a  boat 
pulling  along  the  southern  shore,  about  2  miles  above  Smithfield  Neck, 
with  six  men  in  it.  1  immediately  steamed  up  abreast  other;  the  men 
in  the  boat  running  her  ashore  and  disappearing  among  the  bushes.  I 
sent  two  armed  boats,  thinking  that  there  might  be  some  mail  matter 
left  in  what  I  supposed  was  a  rebel  mail  boat.  On  approaching  her 
several  volleys  were  fired  into  our  boats.  I  immediately  fired  seven 
shells,  but  can  not  tell  with  what  effect. 

I  send  with  this  the  executive  officer,  Acting  Ensign  G.  W.  Adams, 
who  had  charge  of  the  boats,  to  make  his  report. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  O.  Barclay, 
Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  II.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  report  of

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  March  29,  1864. 

Sir:  The  Department  will  recollect  that  an  expedition  under  my 
command,  sent  by  its  direction  up  James  River  last  July,  took  posses¬ 
sion  of  Fort  Powhatan,  thoroughly  destroyed  its  magazines,  barracks, 
and  all  platforms  for  guns,  and  cut  away  all  the  sodding,  of  which 
there  was  a  great  deal  and  well  done,  leaving  the  fresh  earthworks  to 
be  exposed  to  the  effects  ot  the  weather. 

On  Sunday,  the  27tli  instant,  I  received  a  confidential  communication 
from  General  Butler,  enclosing  a  copy  of  a  statement  he  had  received, 
representing  that  the  enemy  had  removed  all  the  guns  and  men  from 
Die  wry’s  Bluff  to  Fort  Powhatan  and  still  threatened  to  attack  Noi- 
folk,  and  that  this  information  came  “direct  from  Richmond,  from  our 
incndSi^ 

Yesterday  morning,  2Sth  instant,  I  dispatched  the  Commodore  Morris, 
Lieutenant  J.  P.  Fyfle,  commanding,  with  the  Commodore  Barney 
(Acting  Master  Williams),  and  the  Shokokon  (Acting  Master  W.  B. 
Sheldon),  with  orders  to  proceed  to  Fort  Powhatan  and  ascertain  it 
the  enemy  occupied  it.  These  gunboats  returned  this  morning,  and 
Lieutenant  Fyfle  reports  that  he  found  Fort  Powhatan  in  the  condition 
I  left  it  last  fall,  except  that  it  was  much  wasted  by  the  action  of  the 
frost  and  rains  since.

Powhatan  at  5: 30  p.  m.,  remained  there  an  hour,  then  steamed  down 
the  river  again  as  tar  as  J amestown  Island,  where,  at  9 :  30,  we  anchored. 
This  morning  at  5:30  got  underway  again,  and  at  10  returned  to  this 
anchorage.
