Report  of  Acting  Master  Sheldon,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  an  attack  upon 
a  party  of  Confederates  near  l)ay7s  Point,  James  River. 

IT.  S.  S.  Shokokon, 

Off  Newport  News,  March  29,  1864. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  submit  the  following  report: 

On  the  morning  of  the  28th  instant  I  received  orders  from  Lieuten¬ 
ant  Fyfte,  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  Commodore  Morris,  to  relieve  the 
IT.  S.  S.  Commodore  Jones  on  advanced  picket  duty  near  White  Shoal 
James  River  ;  also  to  keep  lookout  for  any  of  the  enemy  in  the  vicinity 
of  Hay’s  Point,  on  the  west  bank  of  the  river.  At  9:30  a.  m.  saw  a 
party  of  about  100  infantry  at  the  last-meutioned  point,  who  seemed 
to  be  watching  our  movements.  I  steamed  up  to  about  2,000  yards 
opened  on  them  with  our  two  30-pounder  Parrotts  with  15-second  fuze’ 
making  very  fair  shots,  every  shell  exploding  near  and  among  them! 
lhe  enemy  taking  shelter  in  a  piece  of  woods  on  the  bank  of  the  river 
1  steamed  m  as  near  as  the  depth  of  water  would  allow,  being  about 
l,o()0  yards  distant.  I  used  both  the  two  Parrotts  and  24  pounder 
howitzers  with  shrapnel.  In  a  few  minutes  succeeded  in  driving  them 
out  of  their  shelter  and  beyond  Tange.  1  could  not  tell  whether  any 
were  killed  or  wounded,  but  the  general  impression  was  that  there 

must  have  been  some,  tor  our  shells  exploded  among  them  several 
Lim  es. 

Lnclosed  I  send  a  report  of  ammunition  expended. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  B.  Sheldon, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding.

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  March  30,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  obedience  to  your  order  of 
yesterday,  I  went,  with  the  fourth  and  fifth  cutters  with  32  men  and 
Acting  Master  Pierson  and  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Jarvis,  and  reported 
to  Captain  Williams,  of  the  Commodore  Barney,  to  cooperate  with  him 
in  an  expedition  to  Ghuckatuck  Greek,  the  object  of  which  was  to 
capture  Lieutenant  Roy  and  27  men  of  his  command. 

At  11  p.  m.  we  started  from  the  Barney  with  four  boats  and  60  men 
and  officers.  We  landed  near  Cherry  Grove,  and  captured  20  rebel 
soldiers  with  all  their  arms  and  equipments,  but  did  not  succeed  in 
capturing  Lieutenant  Roy,  he  being  absent  from  his  post. 


574 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


I  feel  it  my  duty  to 'mention  the  brave  conduct  of»  the  officers  and 
men  under  my  command.  Owing  to  the  storm  and  bad  state  of  our 
road  the  men  of  the  expedition  suffered  severely,  but  they  bore  it 
with  a  zeal  and  cheerfulness  that  was  surprising;  I  would  not  wish 
better  men. 

I  also  have  to  report  the  loss  of  one  revolver  and  one  sword  bayonet 
belonging  to  this  ship,  from  accident  and  not  carelessness. 

I  would  also  wish  to  state  to  you  at  this  time  that  I  will  volunteer  to 
act  either  as  a  scout,  spy,  take  command  of  a  raid  on  the  enemy,  or  act 
in  any  position  where  I  can  be  of  service  on  shore,  and  I  consider 
myself  a  very  proper  person  to  act  in  either  capacity,  having  seen 
seventeen  years  in  active  service  in  different  countries  and  services  as 
a  man  of  war  at  sea  and  on  shore. 

Very  respectfully, 


Chas.  B.  Wilder,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Williams,  II.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Barney. 

U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Barney, 
Nansemond  River ,  Va.,  March  30,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  arrival  of  U.  S.  S. 
Shokokon  on  the  evening  of  29th  instant,  an  expedition  under  my 
charge,  consisting  of  32  men,  with  two  boats  from  U.  S.  S.  Minnesota , 
and  23  men,  with  two  boats  from  this  vessel,  proceeded  to  Blinkhorn’s 
Creek,  on  the  west  side  of  the  river.  After  landing,  we  proceeded  to 
a  distance  of  about  2  miles,  and  met  with  a  citizen  and  a  negro,  whom 
we  took  as  guides.  We  then  returned  to  boats  and  proceeded  to 
Chuekatuck  Creek.  We  landed  at  the  head  of  the  creek,  and  at  a  dis 
tance  of  about  a  half  a  mile  met  with  a  citizen  and  his  son,  whom  we 
also  took  to  guide  us  to  the  headquarters  of  Lieutenant  Boy,  where  we 
arrived  at  about  4  a.  m.  of  the  30th  instant.  We  immediately  sur¬ 
rounded  two  houses  (the  headquarters)  and  demanded  instant  surren¬ 
der,  a  demand  with  which  they  complied,  the  result  of  which  was  the 
capture  of  2  sergeants  and  18  privates  (Confederate),  with  small  arms, 
etc.,  without  tiring  a  shot.  Acting  Masters  Wilder  and  Pierson  had 
charge  of  Minnesota's  boats’  crews,  and  both  behaved  with  the  utmost 
coolness  and  bravery.  I  must  give  them  the  whole  credit  of  the  cap¬ 
ture.  Mr.  Bodgers  (pilot  of  this  vessel)  piloted  the  boats  up  and  down 
river  and  deserves  great  praise.  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Auld,  of  this 
vessel,  had  charge  of  the  boats,  and  displayed  the  utmost  coolness  and 
courage.  Acting  Third  Assistant  Engineers  Leftler  and  Shannon 
also  acted  with  great  courage  and  bravery.  I  would  also  respectfully 
call  your  attention  to  John  Cross  (yeoman),  who  had  charge  of  the  flag, 
and  did  his  whole  duty  to  my  entire  satisfaction.  The  petty  officers 
and  crews  of  both  vessels  did  their  duty  nobly.  Should  I  again  have 
the  honor  of  an  expedition  under  my  charge,  I  will  feel  confidence  with 
such  another  set  of  men  with  me. 

I  am  very  sorry  that  we  did  not  take  more  boats,  as  we  could  have 
captured  the  whole  signal  corps  of  17  men,  if  we  had  had  accommoda¬ 
tion  to  bring  them  off  to  the  vessel.  The  following  are  the  names  and

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Adniiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  Neics ,  Va.,  March  31,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  on  the  night 
of  the  29th  instant,  during  the  prevalence  of  a  violent  storm,  an  expe¬ 
dition  consisting  of  two  boats  and  23  seamen  from  the  U.  S.  S.  Commodore 
Barney ,  under  the  command  of  Acting  Master  Williams,  commanding 
that  vessel,  with  two  boats  and  32  seamen  of  this  ship,  commanded 
by  Acting  Master  Wilder,  of  the  Minnesota ,  ascended  the  Cliuckatuck 
Creek  and  effected  a  landing  at  a  place  called  Cherry  Grove.  It  was 
known  that  in  that  vicinity  was  stationed  a  company  of  rebel  soldiers, 
whose  capture  was  the  object  of  the  expedition.  Procuring  a  guide, 
the  party  made  their  way  to  the  house  in  which  the  objects  ot  their 
search  were  sheltered,  and  by  a  careful  disposition  of  the  force  succeeded 
in  surprising  and  capturing  20  soldiers  ot  the  rebel  Army,  with  their 
arms  and  equipments.  With  their  prisoners  the  party  returned  to 
their  boats,  and  brought  them  safely  to  the  Commodore  Barney,  lying  in 
the  Nansemond. 

I  have  transferred  the  prisoners  to  General  Butler  and  the  arms 
captured  with  them  have  been  transferred  to  the  naval  ordnance  depot. 

Acting  Masters  Williams  and  Wilder  speak  in  commendable  terms  of 
the  conduct  of  the  officers  and  men  engaged  in  this  exploit,  and  it 
gives  me  pleasure  to  commend,  the  energy  and  zeal  displayed  by  these 
officers  in  planning  and  carrying  out  to  a  successful  termination  an 
expedition  of  no  little  difficulty. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

IT.  S.  S.  Commodore  Barney, 
Nansemond  River ,  Virginia ,  April  1,  1864. 

Sir:  In  regard  to  the  expedition  (under  my  charge)  of  March  29,  I 
would  respectfully  inform  you  that  Mr.  Wright  (a  gentleman  of  whose 
Union  sentiments  I  am  strictly  confident)  kindly  offered  his  assistance 
to  guide  us  from  his  residence  at  Blinkhorn  Creek  to  the  headquarters 
of  Lieutenant  Boy  at  Chuckatuck;  and  through  his  timely  aid  in  so 
doing  may  be  attributed  the  result  of  our  victory  being  so  easy,  as  I 
consider  that,  had  we  been  one  hour  later,  although  our  victory  would 
have  been  complete,  there  would  have  been  loss  of  life,  as  it  would  have 
been  daylight,  and  they  (I  believe)  on  being  aware  of  our  coming  would 
have  made  a  determined  resistance. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  M.  Williams, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Bear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee,

U.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Plymouth ,  N.  G.,  March  30,  1864. 

Sir  :  When  I  wrote  you  concerning  the  report  of  General  Butler  s 
scout,  on  the  subject  of  which  your  last  dispatch  to  me  was  written,  I 
stated  that  1  felt  confident  of  the  falsity  of  the  story. 

I  am  now  enabled  to  declare  beyond  possibility  of  doubt  that  the 
whole  affair  was  a  fabrication,  without  the  slightest  approach  to  truth. 
The  records  of  the  provost-marshal’s  and  adjutant-general’s  offices  at 
this  place  show  that  James  arrived  at  Plymouth  on  the  15th  instant; 
that  he  obtained  a  pass  to  go  outside  the  lines  on  the  16tli  instant  for 
the  purpose  of  purchasing  cotton,  etc. ;  that  he  returned  within  three 
hours  and  stated  that  he  had  been  6  miles  beyond  our  lines,  but,  hear¬ 
ing  that  the  rebel  soldiers  were  thick  in  the  vicinity,  returned.^  That 
day  he  left  Plymouth  for  Roanoke  Island.  On  Sunday  last,  -btli,  he 
was  again  here  and  again  was  outside  of  the  lines  for  a  few  houis. 
Without  knowing  him  I  saw  him  in  the  cabin  of  the  steamei  General 
Berry  while  I  and  other  officers  were  going  up  to  see  how  they  were 
getting  on  with  sinking  the  hulks  above  here.  He  was  lying  on  a 
bench  in  the  cabin,  with  his  hat  over  his  eyes,  listening  to  the  conver¬ 
sation  of  the  officers.  General  Butler  will  do  well  not  to  trust  him 

t °I  was  at  General  Wessells'  office  to-day  during  the  examination  of 
two  of  our  cavalrymen  who  escaped  from  the  rebels  near  Warrenton, 
in  this  State,  by  jumping  from  the  cars.  They  were  en  route  to 

Americus,  Ga.  .  ,, 

One  of  these  men  was  very  intelligent  and  told  Ins  story  confidently, 
seeming  to  have  a  good  knowledge  of  the  country  through  which  he 
had  passed  and  a  retentive  memory  for  facts  and  dates.  On  their  way 
to  this  place  they  were  concealed,  housed,  fed,  and  guided  by  negioes. 
About  twelve  days  since  they  stopped  for  the  night  at  the  house  ol  a, 
negro  man,  who  told  them  that  he  had  worked  m  the  navy  yard  at 
Halifax  ever  since  the  establishment  of  the  yard ;  that  the  ram  was  not 
finished,  and  he  thought  would  not  be  before  July ;  that  she  still  was 
at  Halifax,  and  had  never  been  moved  from  there.  1  le  stated  that  by 
the  contract  she  should  have  been  finished  by  the  4tli  of  this  month. 
He  said  they  were  putting  iron  on  her,  but  that  not  so  many  men  were 
now  employed  as  had  been  formerly.  This  story  agrees  very  well  with 
that  of  the  lieutenant,  about  which  I  wrote  you  some  time  since,  and 
who  stated  that  the  attack  on  this  place  would  not  take  place  tor  six 
weeks  or  two  months.  I  think  the  negro  is  wrong  in  deferring  the 
probable  completion  of  the  vessel  so  long.  It  is  probable  she  is  now 
nearly  or  quite  finished.  Another  story  from  Bertie  is  that  she  was  at 
Hamilton,  but  hearing  of  our  placing  torpedoes  in  the  river  returned 
to  Halifax  to  have  a  spur  placed  forward  to  explode  them  without  col 
lision  on  her  part.  I  believe  now  she  is  yet  at  Halifax.  Work  upon 
her  is  done  by  fits  and  starts;  sometimes  a  large  force  is  employed,  and 
then  again  nearly  everyone  will  be  ordered  away. 

They  now  anticipate  a  movement  up  country  by  us.  Troops  have 
been  telegraphed  for  to  meet  us,  and  others  who  had  been  ordered  away 
from  this  neighborhood  have  had  their  orders  countermanded  This 
report  arises  merely  from  the  running  backward  and  forward  of  t 
steamers  engaged  in  sinking  the  hulks.  Extravagant  reports  of  our 
Senglh  have  been  sent  on  to  higher  authority.  It  is  declared  that  we 
are  landing  on  the  Roanoke  with  40,000  men,  ana  the  rebs  generally 

are  badly  scared.

command  of  the  guard  at  Hog  Island  (of  whom  Major  White  received 
his  information),  who  informed  me  that  the  steamer  Tamaulepas  came  in 
the  inlet  on  the  26th  of  March  and  left  on  the  morning  of  the  28tli,  bound 
(as  he  was  informed  by  some  of  the  crew,  who  came  on  shore)  to  Hew 
Oi  leans.  The  Tamaulepas  is  a  stern  wheel  boat,  commonly  called  u  wheel¬ 
barrow,”  of  iron  hull,  was  loaded  very  deep,  and  the  only  suspicion  that 
Lieutenant  ihrockmorton  had  of  her  was  that  she  was  too  deep  in  the 
water,  and  the  crew  were  foreigners,  and  that  the  Government,  in  his  opin¬ 
ion,  would  not  send  such  a  vessel  to  sea.  Ho  one  went  on  board  of  her  as 
the  lieutenant  says  it  was  too  rough  to  board  her,  but  my  opinion  is  he 
was.afraid  to  board  her,  but  went  to  Eastville,  [  V a. J,  and  reported  to  Maior 
White.  I  thmk  there  were  no  just  grounds  for  any  suspicions  of  the  ves¬ 
sel,  as  the  Government,  m  my  opinion,  has  sent  as  poor  sea  boats  to  sea  as 
the  Tamaulepas.  On  the  31st  I  attempted  to  cross  the  bar  and  return 
to  Newport  Hews,  but  the  wind  was  easterly,  and  a  heavy  ground  swell 
setting  m,  made  the  sea  break  all  the  way  across  the  bar,  so  as  not  to 
be  sate  to  cross.  In  the  evening  the  wind  commenced  to  blow  a  gale

Navy  Department,  0.  S.  A., 

Richmond ,  September  10, 1863. 

Sir:  Your  letter  of  the  18th  of  July,  from  Jacksonport,  Ark.,  reached 
me  a  few  days  ago. 

You  inform  me  that  a  certain  party  “  desires  to  obtain  proper  author¬ 
ity  from  the  Confederate  Government  to  undertake  the  destruction  of 
gunboats,  transports,  etc.,  for  such  per  centum  of  the  value  of  the  boats 
destroyed  as  may  be  offered,  etc.” 

There  is  no  legislation  of  which  I  am  aware  that  satisfies  precisely 
the  conditions  required. 

The  act  of  the  6th  of  May,  1861,  recognizing  the  existence  of  war  with 
the  United  States  and  providing  for  privateering,  is  not  construed  to 
permit  privateering  on  inland  waters. 

A  reference  to  the  law  for  the  establishment  of  a  volunteer  navy,  a 
copy  of  which  1  enclose  herewith,  will  show  you  that  it  can  not  be  made 
to  embrace  the  parties  to  which  you  refer. 

To  facilitate  organizations  of  parties  to  operate  as  you  propose,  in 
boats  or  otherwise,  against  the  enemy  on  our  Western  rivers,  they  could 
be  received  into  the  Navy  if  they  shipped  regularly  in  accordance  with 
existing  laws,  and  then  assigned  to  duty  under  an  acting  master  upon 
those  rivers. 

In  this  case,  however,  they  would  form  part  of  the  Regular  Navy  estab¬ 
lishment,  drawing  its  pay  and  subsistence. 

I  infer  from  your  letter  that  such  is  not  the  object  of  the  parties  in 
question,  but  that  they  desire  to  organize  in  smali  parties  to  operate  as 
independent  river  guerrilla  parties  under  their  own  leaders,  and  to  look 
to  prize  money,  or  reward  from  the  country  for  destroying  enemy’s  prop¬ 
erty,  to  defray  expenses,  etc.,  using  an  appointment  from  the  Govern¬ 
ment  to  secure  to  them  their  rights  of  prisoners  of  war  if  captured. 

J udging  from  what  you  say  that  you  have  not  the  acts  of  Congress 
at  hand,  I  enclose  copies  of  two  acts,  one  of  which  possibly  serves  the 


desired  purpose. 

T he  President  has  authority  to  make  such  an  arrangement  as  you  refer 
to,  and  I  would  suggest  that  parties  wishing  to  engage  in  the  enterprise 
presen  t  to  him  their  names,  purpose,  and  terms,  either  directly  or  through 
your  obedient  servant. 

Very  respectfully, 

S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Colonel  E.  C.  Cabell,  C.  S.  Army, 

Headquarters  Price’s  Army ,  Jacksonport,  Ark. 


[Subenclosure.] 

An  Act  to  provide  for  local  defense  and  special  service. 

Section  1.  The  Congress  of  the  Confederate  States  do  enact,  That 
the  President  be.  and  he  is  hereby,  authorized  to  accept  the  services 
of  volunteers  of  such  kind  and  in  such  proportion  as  he  may  deem 
expedient,  to  serve  for  such  time  as  he  may  prescribe,  for  the  defense 
of  exposed  places  and  localities,  or  such  special  service  as  he  may  deem 
expedient. 

Section  2.  And  such  forces  shall  be  mustered  into  the  service  of 
the  Confederate  States,  for  the  local  defense  or  special  service  aforesaid, 
the  muster  roll  setting  forth  distinctly  the  services  to  be  performed; 
and  the  said  volunteers  shall  not  be  considered  in  actual  service  until 


582 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


thereunto  ordered  by  the  President,  and  they  shalLbfc  entitled  to  pay 
or  subsistence  only  for  such  time  as  they  may  be  on  duty,  under  the 
orders  of  the  President,  or  by  his  direction. 

Section  3,  Such  volunteer  forces  when  so  accepted  or  .ordered  into 
service,  shall  be  organized  in  accordance  with,  and  subject  to  all  the 
provisions  of  the  act  entitled  “An  act  to  provide  for  the  public  defense,” 
approved  March  G,  1861,  and  may  be  attached  to  such  divisions, 
brigades,  regiments,  or  battalions  as  the  President  may  direct,  and 
when  not  organized  into  battalion  and  regiments  before  being  mustered 
into  service,  the  President  shall  appoint  the  field  officers  of  the  bat¬ 
talions  and  regiments,  when  organized  as  such  by  him. 

Approved  August  21,  1861. 

An  Act  to  authorize  the  formation  of  volunteer  comj>anies  for  local  defense. 

The  Congress  of  the  Confederate  States  of  America  do  enact,  That 
for  the  purpose  of  local  defense  in  any  portion  of  the  Confederate 
States,  any  number  of  persons,  not  less  than  twenty,  who  are  over  the 
age  of  forty-five  years,  or  otherwise  not  liable  to  military  duty,  may 
associate  themselves  as  a  military  company,  elect  their  own  officers, 
and  establish  rules  and  regulations  for  their  own  government,  and 
shall  be  considered  as  belonging  to  the  Provisional  Army  of  the  Con¬ 
federate  States,  serving  without  pay  or  allowances,  and  entitled,  when 
captured  by  the  enemy,  to  all  the  privileges  of  prisoners  of  war. 

Provided ,  That  such  company  shall,  as  soon  as  practicable,  transmit 
their  muster  roll,  or  list  of  the  names  of  the  officers  and  privates 
thereof,  to  the  Governor  of  the  State,  the  commanding  general  of  the 
department,  or  any  brigadier  general  in  the  State'  or  Confederate 
service,  to  be  forwarded  to  the  Secretary  of  War;  but  the  President, 
or  commander  of  the  district,  may,  at  any  time,  disband  such  com¬ 
panies;  Provided.  That  in  the  States  and  districts  in  which  the  act 
entitled  “An  act  to  further  provide  for  the  public  defense,”  approved 
April  16,  1802,  and  the  acts  amendatory  thereof  have  been  suspended, 
persons  of  any  age,  resident  within  such  States  or  districts,  may  vol¬ 
unteer  and  form  part  of  such  companies  so  long  as  such  suspension 
may  continue;  Provided,  That  no  person  shall  become  a  member  of 
said  company  until  he  shall  have  first  taken  the  oath  of  allegiance  to 
the  Confederate  States  of  America  in  writing,  a  copy  of  which  shall  be 
filed  with  the  muster  roll  for  said  company,  as  above  prescribed. 

Approved  October  13,  1S62.

Report  of  Commander  Dove,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  attempted  de¬ 
struction  of  the  light  house  on  Cape  Lookout. 

U.  S.  Naval  Station, 
Beaufort,  N.  C.,  April  5,  1864. 

Sir  :  An  attempt  was  made  to  destroy  tlie  light-house  on  Cape  Look¬ 
out  last  Sunday  night,  [3d],  but  it  was  only  partially  successful. 

It  was  made  by  four  or  five  mischievous  persons.  Two  kegs  of 
powder  were  exploded  in  it,  which  shattered  the  glasses,  set  fire  to  the 
building,  and  stove  in  the  oil  cans. 

A  party  of  soldiers  and  boat’s  crew  from  the  Badger  were  sent  over 
in  the  small  steamer  North  State,  and  repaired  the  damages  sufficiently 
to  keep  the  light  going,  but  not  so  bright  as  usual.  I  supplied  the 
necessary  od  to  keep  it  up  until  it  can  be  refurnished  by  the  proper 
department. 

There  are  but  two  blockaders  in  port  at  present,  the  Butaiv  and 
Maratanza.  The  latter  is  ready  to  sail,  but  I  have  directed  Lieuteuant- 
Commander  Haxtuu  to  remain  until  the  arrival  of  another,  so  as  not  to 
leave  the  harbor  without  sufficient  protection. 

The  schooner  Ann'S.  Cannon,  a  collier,  picked  up  the  anchor  and  45 
fathoms  of  chain  which  were  lost  by  the  prize  steamer  Ceres,  of  which 
I  took  possession.  Her  captain,  G.  W.  Feuimore,  claims  salvage  on 
them,  but  I  did  not  think  it  within  my  authority. 

The  steamer  City  of  Jersey  having  lost  her  anchor  on  Sunday  night, 
off  Cape  Lookout,  her  captain  applied  to  me  for  assistance,  and  1  let 
him  have  the  one  which  had  just  been  recovered.  It  seemed  to  be  a 
matter  of  necessity,  and  he  has  given  every  assurance  that  it  will 
either  be  returned  here  or  delivered  up  at  New  York  on  his  arrival 
there. 

Verv  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benj.  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads. 


Confidential  letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  the 
Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  regarding  general  matters. 

Confidential.]  [U.  S.  S.]  Minnesota,  April  4,  1864. 

Sir:  Yours  of  the  1st  instant  came  to-day.  Undoubtedly  ironclads 
and  some  other  vessels  must  be  needed  here  for  the  approaching 
campaign. 

Should  not  ironclads  for  the  Gulf  be  sent  either  from  the  Mississippi 
Biver  or  Charleston  ? 

We  return  to  the  Army  sailors  who  can  not  pass  the  examination. 

I  thank  you  heartily  for  the  promise  of  more  vessels  for  W ilmington 
when  you  get  the  seamen  now  to  come  promptly  from  the  Army. 

You  say  what  a  pity  that  Cushing’s  undaunted  bravery  and  good 
luck  can  not  be  put  to  a  useful  purpose  in  a  manner  to  tell  upon  the 
enemy.  Please  explain  this.  I  have  always  encouraged  his  dash,  and 
am  ever  ready  to  do  so.  What  can  he  now  do?  He  is  urging  me  to 
let  him  cruise  off  for  prizes.  He  went  into  Cape  hear  Biver  to  get 
prizes.  I  am  rejoiced  that  he  returned  with  such  eclat  to  the  Mont/i- 
cello.  Pity  he  did  not  get  a  prize  then.  Well,  very  well,  that  the 


584  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


enemy  did  not  get  a  chance  to  surprise  the  Monticello  by  returning  in 
her  boats. 

He  thinks  that  the  fort  on  Bald  Head  may  be  surprised  by  the  block- 
aders.  Will  you  in  any  manner,  even  by  a  “Go  it  Ned”  (after  the 
fashion  of  the  Attorney  and  Lord  Codrington),  justify  the  attempt? 
The  idea  is  taking  and  the  thing  is  possible,  though  Nelson  failed  in 
such  an  effort.  But  I  like  enterprises,  and  have  always  encouraged 
them.  Is  this  what  you  hint  at? 

I  have  a  good  idea  of,  and  good  feeling  for  this  youngster. 

Give  me  your  mind  in  the  matter. 

The  Richmond  ironclads  are  designed  to  act  between  Drewry’s  Bluff 
and  the  city.  If  you  will  give  the  right  means  for  the  James  River 
route  to  Richmond,  it  can  and  will  be  taken.  It  is  now  the  time  to  do 
this  big  thing.  Jo  Johnston’s  report,  which  General  Grant  tells  me 
he  believes  is  entirely  true,  shows  the  weakness  of  the  rebels. 

The  upper  James  is  the  point  for  naval  cooperation,  and  now  is  the 
time. 


Respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee. 

Hon.  G.  V.  Fox, 

Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Flusser,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  giving  rumors 
regarding  expected  movements  of  the  enemy. 

IT.  S.  S.  Miami, 
Plymouth,  N.  C.,  April  6,  1864. 

Sir:  Yours  of  31st;  of  March  in  answer  to  mine  of  27t.h  ultimo  is  at 
hand. 

1  to-day  received  a  letter  from  Bertie  County  in  which  I  am  advised 
to  prepare  for  an  attack,  as  one  will  soon  be  made  by  laud  and  water. 
My  correspondent  reports  a  large  force  in  Martin  County,  near  here,  and 
6,000  more  men  on  the  way  down  from  Garysburg. 

Nevertheless,  from  all  the  reports  General  Wessells  and  I  receive 
from  other  sources,  I  am  inclined  to  believe  him  deceived  by  the  boast¬ 
ful  talk  of  the  rebel  soldiers  and  others  from  whom  he  obtains  his 
information. 

The  rebel  lines  above  us  are  closed;  they  permit  no  one  to  pass. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


587 


The  reason  assigned  for  this  by  men  whose  opinions  are  of  value  is 
that  they  fear  an  advance  by  us;  that  every  man  they  can  spare  has 
been  sent  or  is  under  orders  to  Richmond,  and  that  they  desire,  by 
admitting  no  one  within  their  lines,  to  hide  their  weakness  from  us. 

They  have  intended  the  withdrawal  of  the  troops  from  this  State 
for  some  time.  I  mean  that  it  is  part  of  a  well-considered  plan.  In 
view  of  this,  to  prevent  an  advance  by  us  on  Weldon  and  to  protect 
the  fisheries  on  the  Chowan  River,  a  ten-gun  battery  was  thrown  up, 
some  weeks  since,  at  Wintou.  Recently,  three  or  four  weak  regiments 
have  been  stationed  there.  From  Weldon  to  Richmond  the  railroads 
are  in  possession  of  the  rebel  Government.  No  civilians  are  permitted 
on  the  cars,  but  soldiers  are  being  pressed  forward  night  and  day. 
Immense  depots  are  being  established  in  the  vicinity  of  Richmond. 

I  have  the  information  about  the  roads,  depots,  etc.,  from  General 
Wessells.  Where  he  obtained  it  I  do  not  know,  but  he  deems  it  reliable, 
and  he,  I  think,  is  always  correct. 

He  certainly  possesses  the  art,  in  a  greater  degree  chan  anyone  else 
I  know  of,  of  sifting  evidence,  reconciling  or  rejecting  conflicting  sto¬ 
ries,  and  seizing  the  truth  and  the  important  from  out  a  wordy  mass  of 
seeming  irrelevant  talk.  We  have  sunk  sis  or  seven  hulks  with  a  tor¬ 
pedo  on  each,  but  still  require  two  to  fill  the  entire  channel.  General 
Wessells  has  written  to  General  Peck  to  procure  them. 

The  schooner  Comet  I  have  turned  into  a  hospital  for  skin  diseases, 
several  of  the  men  having  caught  scabies.  I  could  not  obtain  a  place 
for  them  on  shore. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient 
servant, 

C.  W.  Flusser, 
Lieutenant- Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  off  Newport  News.

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,

Sir  :  Fill  up  your  coal  of  best  quality,  take  in  other  necessary  sup¬ 
plies  at  Beaufort,  and  proceed  to  cruise  between  the  meridians  of  73°

Keep  your  abstract  log  and  forward  it  from  Beaufort  on  returning 
there  to  coal.  Pay  particular  attention  to  the  trim  of  the  Keystone 
State.  Do  not  let  the  officers  and  men  crowd  forward  in  chasing. 
Economize  your  fuel.  Night  chasing  is  rarely  successful.  Be  sure  and 
keep  enough  coal  to  return  with  in  bad  weather.  Time  your  position 
on  the  track  between  the  points  named  accordingly. 

Wishing  you  success,  I  am,  respectfully,  yours,

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Lieutenant  Gushing , 
U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  8.  S.  Monticello,  to  cruise  on  the  outside 
blockade  off  Wilmington,  N.  C. 


Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News,  Vo.,  April  7,  1864. 

Sir:  Yon  are  hereby  assigned  to  duty  o:i  the  outside  blockade  of 
Wilmington. 

Your  duty  will  be  to  intercept  inward-bound  blockade  runners  which 
hover  off  Cape  Lookout  Shoals  with  a  view  to  run  in  at  night,  after 
making  Cape  Lookout  light,  when  they  shape 'a  course  for  New  Inlet, 
and  to  intercept  outward-bound  blockade  runners  from  New  Inlet  to 
Bermuda.  Their  course  is  supposed  to  be  direct,  i.  e.,  E.  §  S.,  but 
since  the  publication  of  my  report  about  the  station  of  the  Sassacus 
they  may  shape  another  course.  You  will  not  blockade  farther  east¬ 
ward  than  the  meridian  of  74°.  On  this  course  you  should  aim  to  be 
at  daylight  at  a  point  where  the  blockade  runner  would  likely  be, 
allowing  her  the  speed  of  12  knots  an  hour  from  New  Inlet,  whence 
she  will  probably  depart  at  one  hour  before  high  tide  on  that  bar. 
Keep,  therefore,  an  accurate  tide  table  showing  time  of  high  water  on 
that  bar. 

Report  to  me,  when  you  put  into  Beaufort,  the  result  of  your  expe¬ 
rience. 

You  will  receive  herewith  Coast-Survey  Sheet  No.  3,  of  the  Atlantic 
coast  of  the  United  States,  and  Blunt’s  Chart  of  the  west  side  of  the 
Atlantic  Ocean. 

Steam  moderately  going  to  your  station.  When  on  it,  be  always 
ready,  especially  at  daylight,  to  chase  to  the  most  advantage.  Do  not 
allow  officers  and  men  to  crowd  forward  in  chasing. 

Pay  particular  attention  to  the  trim  of  the  Monticello ,  the  cleaning 
of  your  fires  (which  should  be  done  to  the  most  advantage  and  not 
all  at  once),  and  to  the  quality  of  your  coal,  of  which  you  should  have 
a  picked  supply. 

Direct  your  prizes,  if  any,  to  touch  here  to  coal  and  report  to  me, 
leaving  blanks  as  to  the  prize  court  to  which  the  prize  is  to  be  sent  in 
your  instructions  to  the  prize  master,  and  in  your  report  to  the  Depart¬ 
ment  and  the  district  judge.  The  blanks  I  will  fill  in  here  and  inform 
you  of  the  destination  of  the  vessel. 

The  red  field  is  your  ground,  the  north  and  south  strip  for  in-runners, 
and  the  east  and  west  strip  for  out-runners.  Snake  these  sections  by 
day  under  low  steam. 

Send  me  your  abstract  log  when  you  go  into  Beaufort  for  coal. 

Respectfully,  yours, 


S.  P,  Xjee 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Gomdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Confidential  letter  from  the  Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting 
Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  cutting-out  expeditions. 


Washington,  April  8,  1864. 

Admiral:  I  have  yours  of  the  4th  instant.  Porter  tells  us  that  not 
an  ironclad  he  has  is  tit  to  be  out  of  the  river,  and  at  Charleston 
they  might  possibly  spare  two  on  an  emergency.  The  duty  there  is 
terrible;  gales  continually,  and  torpedo  boats.  Few  people  dream  of 
the  effort  required  to  keep  that  harbor  closed  to  blockade  running. 
What  I  meant  about  Cushing  was  that  it  was  a  pity  [that]  so  much 
luck  and  dash  had  not  brought  fruits  equal  to  the  risk.  You  notice 
the  Department  never  finds  fault  with  these  exploits.  I  believe  they 
ought  to  be  encouraged.  To  be  sure,  the  people  will  say,  when  he  is 
captured,  “  Damn  fool.”  The  Department  will  not.  I  have  been  read¬ 
ing  this  new  English  naval  history,  and  I  find  their  wars  abounded 
in  rash  coast  attacks  and  cutting-out  expeditions  of  all  kinds;  they 
were  encouraged  aud  formed  a  bright  page  of  naval  history.  You  may 
be  very  sure  that  the  Department  will  not  find  any  fault  with  any  dasli- 
iug  expeditions  that  give  reasonable  hope  of  a  result  injurious  to  the 
enemy,  even  though  they  fail  occasionally. 

See  how  much  they  make  out  of  John  Taylor  Wood’s  exploits — a 
solemn  vote  of  thanks  and  everybody  cheerful  over  the  capture  of 
three  tugs.  I  am  sure  I  do  not  blame  them  for  being  happy,  for  I  have 
groaned  over  the  loss  constantly,  because  it  was  disgraceful  to  us  in 
each  case.  Going  into  the  river  to  destroy  a  blockade  runner  about  to 
sail  is  a  most  happy  idea,  and  most  serious  to  the  enemy,  because  cot¬ 
ton  and  dispatches  would  be  burned.  The  first  officer  that  destroys 
one  in  this  way  I  think  I  can  promise  shall  go  up  several  numbers  on 
the  list,  according  to  the  new  law,  and  if  it  is  Cushing  we  can  add  his 
former  exploits  and  give  him  thirty  numbers  up.  I  think  we  should  all 
gain  credit  for  such  an  affair. 

G.  V.  Fox. 


Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads. 


We  are  beginning  to  get  a  few  sailors  in  INew  York.  We  have  writ¬ 
ten  to  the  War  Department,  confidentially,  to  say  that  we  have  a 
rumor  that  an  army  is  to  Ire  moved  up  James  River,  and  that  such  a 
movement,  to  be  successful,  requires  naval  cooperation ;  we  must  have 
the  12,000  sailors.  The  1,000  potato  diggers  are  extra,  and  taken 
because  we  won’t  refuse  auy  human  being  physically  sound.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  II.  8.  Navy ,  stating  the  uses  for 

additional  light-draft  vessels. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  April  8 ,  1864. 

Sir:  If  tlie  three  high-pressure  light  draft  screws  of  Captain  Forbes 
are  adapted  to  towing,  they  would  be  quite  useful  in  this  squadron  for 
other  than  such  secret  service  as  picket  duty  on  the  Wilmington  bars,  or 
for  expeditions  where  surprise  is  intended,  though  it  was  for  such  serv¬ 
ice  they  were  first  recommended  to  and  desired  by  me.  It  is  very  desir¬ 
able  to  have  one  or  two  of  them  at  Beaufort  to  patrol  the  approaches 
from  the  sounds  to  that  harbor  and  prevent  surprise  by  boats  to  the 
vessels  there,  to  move  the  colliers  to  the  blockaders,  to  sound  the  bar 
after  blows,  and  to  deliver  and  receive  our  navy  pilots  at  Beaufort. 

Two  of  them  would  be  useful  here  to  patrol  the  shallow  waters  of  the 
eastern  shore  counties  and  prevent  rebel  raids  there;  to  keep  the 
oystermen  within  their  limits,  and  for  towing  purposes. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Oomdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Lieutenant-  Commander  Braine ,  U.  S.  Navy,  giving  information 
regarding  salt  works  near  Lockwood' s  Folly  Inlet ,  and  the  evasion  of 
the  blockade  of  Wilmington. 

U.  S.  S.  Vicksburg, 

Off  Lockwood's  Folly  Inlet ,  April  8,  1864. 
Sir:  I  beg  leave  to  give  you  the  following  information:  This  morn¬ 
ing  about  8  a.  m.,  whilst  steaming  to  the  eastward,  a  boat  was  discov¬ 
ered  inshore  near  Shallotte  Inlet.  I  ran  toward  her  and  picked  her  up ; 
a  man  came  off  named  Francis  Storrne;  he  is  a  native  of  Belgium,  and 
produced  papers  to  that  effect.  He  has  been  in  the  United  States  about 
three  years,  most  of  that  time  in  Virginia.  He  states  that  in  the 
vicinity  of  Lockwood’s  Folly  Inlet,  where  he  has  been  making  salt, 
there  were  some  200  men  stationed  there  as  picket  guard,  but  at  present 
there  are  12  men,  the  balance  having  left  about  March  25  for  Fairfax 
Court-House  [Fairfax  County,  or  Orange  C.  H.|,  Orange  Couuty,  Va. 
He  says  that  the  salt  made  at  this  inlet  amounted  to  about  7  barrels

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy,  advising  repairs  to  the 

Norfolk  navy  yard. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va .,  April  9 ,  1864. 

Sir:  The  Norfolk  navy  yard  differs  from  other  navy  yards  in  these 
important  respects: 

1st.  It  has  been  burned  down  and  is  a  mere  wreck. 

2d.  It  is  an  expansion  of  the  machine  shop  for  repairing  the  vessels 
of  this  squadron  removed  from  Fortress  Monroe. 

3d.  It  lies  within  the  limits  of  the  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squad¬ 
ron,  is  in  some  sense  a  command  within  a  command,  and  is  its  principal 
and  necessary  and  convenient  depot  for  repairs  and  supplies. 

If  this  burned  and  blockaded  yard  were  in  full  repair,  probably  it 
could,  not  answer  all  the  necessities  of  this  squadron,  and  to  the  extent 
that  it  can  now  do  so,  it  is  obviously  advantageous  to  the  public  interest 
that  its  limited  meaus  should  be  so  applied  rather  than  to  the  improve¬ 
ment  of  vessels  for  other  service  just  from  Northern  ports.  Steamers 
from  the  roads  can  reach  Washington  or  Baltimore  in  about  half  a  day, 
and  Philadelphia  or  New  York  in  one  day.  At  these  points  the  facili¬ 
ties  are  good,  and  returning  or  sending  steamers  not  of  this  squadron 
to  such  points  will  have  good  effect  all  round. 

If  these  views,  in  whole  or  in  part,  meet  the  approval  of  the  Depart¬ 
ment — to  whose  consideration  they  are  most  respectfully  submitted — I 
trust  that  the  corresponding  action  may  be  had. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Nortiv  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C .

York  River ,  Virginia. 


U.  S.  S.  Mystic, 

Off  Yorktown ,  Va.,  April  9,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  morning  of  the  7th  I  got 
underway  and  proceeded  up  York  Biver  by  request  of  General  Wis- 
tar,  to  cooperate  with  a  small  force  of  cavalry  which  he  sent  up  by 
land  for  the  purpose  of  scouring  Poquetank  [Potopotank]  Greek  and 
vicinity,  where  there  were  reported  to  be  armed  boats  awaiting  an 
opportunity  to  attack  the  oystermen.  Before  leaving,  I  left  an  armed 
boat  here  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Kelleher,  to  attend  to 
the  guard  duty.  I  then  took  on  board  a  lieutenant  and  20  men  from 
the  One  hundred  and  forty  eighth  New  York  Begiment  and  arrived 
opposite  the  creek  at  8  a.  m.  In  advance  of  the  cavalry  I  sent  in  three 
armed  boats  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  Meader,  my  executive  officer, 
also  towing  two  skiffs  with  the  infantry.  In  obedience  to  my  orders,  he 
landed  the  troops  on  both  sides  of  the  creek  and  made  a  thorough 
search,  capturing  oue  large  pontoon,  eight  skiffs,  one  large  sailboat, 
and  rowboat,  also  six  marine  compasses,  and  fifty-eight  new  oyster 
tongs.  After  making  a  thorough  search  about  the  creek  and  vicinity, 
where  I  thought  there  could  be  any  possible  chance  for  secreting  boats,

J  W.  Wright,

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  Neivs,  Ya .,  April  9,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  last  night  about  2  o’clock,  while  riding  to 
the  ebb  tide,  a  dark  object  was  discovered  slowly  passing  the  ship 
about  200  yards  distant.  It  was  thought  to  be  a  boat,  and  hailed ;  to 
the  hail  was  answered  “Roanoke.”  By  this  time  it  was  directly  abeam, 
seemingly  without  any  power  of  locomotion.  The  officer  of  the  deck 
promptly  gave  orders  to  the  tug  astern  to  go  and  examine  it,  and  repeated 
his  orders  several  times  before  getting  any  reply,  and  while  endeavor¬ 
ing  to  have  this  order  executed,  the  object,  a  “David,”  approached 
the  ship  just  abaft  the  port  main  chains  and  exploded  a  torpedo  under 
her,  the  “David”  making  off  in  the  direction  of  the  Nansemond  River. 
Several  muskets  and  a  round  shot  were  fired  at  it  and  every  effort  made 
to  send  in  pursuit,  but  the  tug  Poppy  had  failed  to  keep  the  required 
lookout  and  also  had  allowed  her  steam  to  go  down,  which  was  not  dis¬ 
covered  until  the  “David”  had  disappeared.  Vessels  were  sent  in 
search,  but  failed  to  find  her.  I  submit  the  accompanying  report  of 
Acting  Ensign  Birtwistle,  officer  of  the  deck  at  the  time  specified.  It 
is  difficult  to  say  how  far  the  ship  maybe  damaged,  although  she  mani¬ 
fests  no  leak.  The  shock  was  quite  severe  and  I  should  be  glad  to  have 
a  survey  to  ascertain  the  extent  of  injury  sustained. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  H.  Upshur, 

Lieutenant- Commander,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Minnesota.

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  April  9,  1864. 

Sir  :  At  1.45  this  morning,  while  in  charge  of  the  deck,  the  quarter¬ 
master  directed  my  attention  to  a  boat  adrift  a  little  forward  of  the 
port  beam  and  about  150  yards  distant,  and  while  passing  to  the  port 
side  of  the  bridge  the  sentry  at  the  gangway  hailed  her.  She  answered 
“Boanoke.”  I  then  hailed  her,  and  could  not  make  out  her  reply.  1 
went  down  off  the  bridge  and  hailed  her  from  the  quarter.  She 
answered  “  Boanoke.”  1  told  him  not  to  come  alongside.  She  answered 
“  Aye!  aye!”  1  hailed  the  tug  Poppy  three  times  and  told  him  to  see 
what  that  boat  was.  He  said  “Aye !  aye !  ”  I  thought  the  boat  was 
nearing  us,  and  I  could  not  see  any  oars.  I  sent  a  messenger  to  call 
you,  sir,  and  ordered  the  boat  to  keep  off  or  I  would  fire  into  him.  I 
repeated  the  order,  but  discovered  that  she  was  nearing  us  fast.  I  then 
ordered  the  Poppy  twice  to  run  that  boat  down. 

I  then  saw  the  glimmer  of  a  light;  the  quartermaster  said  he  could 
hear  her  puff.  I  jumped  to  a  convenient  gun,  called  for  help  to  train 
it;  the  sentries  on  the  gangways  and  forward  fired  three  shots  at  her; 
but  before  I  could  fire  the  gun,  she  was  inside  of  range.  I  jumped  back 
from  the  gun  and  the  explosion  followed.  I  then  met  you  at  the  cabin 
hatch,  and  in  answer  to  your  enquiry  said  it  was  a  torpedo.  Men  were 
rushing  on  deck,  the  drum  beat  to  quarters,  and  I  went  forward  and 
fired  a  shell  from  a  IX-inch  gun  in  my  division.  After  the  explosion  I 
thought  sure  the  Poppy  would  capture  her,  or  I  would  have  remained 
at  the  quarter-deck  guns.  The  rest,  sir,  you  saw. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully, 

James  Birtwistle, 

Acting  Ensign. 

Lieutenant-Commander  J.  H.  Upshur, 

Commanding  U.  8.  Flagship  Minnesota. 


U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  April  12,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  would  most  respectfully  submit  the  following  circumstances  in 
order  to  exonerate  myself  as  much  as  possible  from  the  blame  attached 
to  me:  On  Friday  night,  the  8th  instant,  I  was  ordered  to  drop  astern 
of  the  Minnesota  with  the  tug,  of  which  I  was  in  command,  and  hang  by 
a  hawser;  this  I  did.  Here  I  would  particularly  request  your  consid¬ 
eration  :  I  had  so  arranged  the  watches  that  I  should  always  be  on  deck 
from  4  o’clock  in  the  morning  until  8  o’clock  at  night.  It  being  after  8 
o’clock  on  the  night  in  question,  after  seeing  the  tug  properly  secured 
I  intended  to  go  below,  but  before  doing  so  I  went  to  the  engine  room 
and  told  the  engineer  of  the  watch  to  have  everything  ready  to  start  at 
a  moment’s  notice,  adding  that  I  did  not  know  the  moment  we  would 
be  called  upon  to  perform  some  errand.  He  replied  “Aye!  aye!”  I 
then  told  the  officer  of  the  deck,  Mr.  [T.  S,]  Sullivan,  to  keep  a  good 
lookout  and  answer  all  hails  from  the  Minnesota,  and  to  call  me  if  any¬ 
thing  occurred.  After  the  watch  had  been  reported  to  me  on  deck,  I 
went  below.  I  lay  down  on  the  settee  in  the  cabin  without  undressing, 
in  order  to  be  on  hand  as  quickly  as  possible.  I  was  suddenly  roused  up 
about  2  o’clock  in  the  morning  by  some  noise.  I  rushed  on  deck  and 
found  they  had  been  hailing  us  from  the  ship  to  come  alongside.  On 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


595 


going  forward  I  saw  a  boat  on  our  port  bow ;  soon  afterward  I  was  ordered 
from  the  Minnesota  to  run  her  down.  I  jumped  into  the  pilot  house,  and 
with  the  firm  impression  that  everything  was  ready  to  start  the  tug,  I 
ordered  the  hawser  to  be  cast  off  and  rang  one  bell  to  go  ahead.  To  my 
astouishmentl  found  the  engine  wasnot  started,  and  I  went  to  the  engine 
room  to  ascertain  the  cause.  (Meantime  the  hawser  had  been  cast  off 
and  the  boat  was  drifting  astern.)  I  told  the  engineer  to  try  and  turn 
over  the  engine,  and  I  must  do  him  the  justice  to  say  that  he  made 
every  effort  to  do  so,  but  in  vain.  He  told  me  he  had  only  a  few  min¬ 
utes  before  pumped  up  the  boiler.  As  soon  as  sufficient  steam  could  be 
got  up,  lobeyed  the  order  to  come  alongside  the  Minnesota.  Before 
sufficient  steam  could  be  got  up,  the  boat  which  I  saw  had  disappeared. 

I  regret  sincerely  the  above  unfortunate  circumstances  which  pre¬ 
vented  me  from  executing  the  orders  given  me,  and  which  accorded  so 
well  with  my  feelings,  that  of  bringing  to  speedy  punishment  the  per¬ 
petrators  of  a  deed  as  daring  as  it  was  vicious. 

Trusting  that  the  reasons  I  have  given,  as  well  as  my  endeavor  to  do 
my  duty  faithfully  on  all  occasions,  will  relieve  me  from  the  imputation 
of  negligence  under  which  I  now  labor, 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Isaac  Miller, 

Acting  Ensign  and  Pilot ,  late  in  command  of  U.  S.  8.  Poppy.

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


IJ.  S.  Steam  Tug  Poppy,  April  12,  1864. 

Sir:  The  following  are  the  facts  concerning  this  vessel  during  the 
night  of  the.Stli  instant:  Between  the  hours  of  9  and  10  p.  m.  I  turned 
in,  as  has  been  the  custom,  while  lying  securely  moored  alongside  or 
astern  of  the  Minnesota.  I  soon  fell  asleep,  and  was  conscious  of  noth¬ 
ing  till  I  was  half  aroused  by  a  call  from  the  Minnesota ,  and  which  was 
immediately  followed  by  the  explosion  of  the  torpedo.  I  immediately 
sprang  to  the  wheel  and  saw  the  torpedo  boat  lying  about  amidships 
of  the  ship,  and,  as  near  as  I  could  judge,  about  30  or  40  feet  distant 
from  the  frigate  and  30  or  40  yards  from  the  tug.  I  was  hailed  from 
the  ship  and  ordered  to  let  go  and  run  her  down.  I  wished  them  to  let 
go  our  lines,  but  was  ordered  to  let  go  ourselves.  We  had  from  30  to  40 
fathoms  of  the  hawser  coiled  on  the  house.  I  ordered  the  watch  to  let 
go  the  line  and  rang  to  go  ahead,  when  I  was  answered  by  the  engineer 
that  he  had  no  steam.  All  were  aroused  by  the  shock  of  the  explo¬ 
sion,  and  when  I  rang  up,  the  captain  stood  by  the  wheelhouse  door  on 
deck  and  hailed  the  officer  of  the  deck,  and  told  him  that  he  thought 
it  was  the  picket  boat  from  Norfolk,  as  it  resembled  her  very  much  in 
the  gloom  of  the  night.  Prom  the  time  that  I  sprang  to  the  wheel  and 
parleyed  with  the  officer  of  the  deck  regarding  the  hawser  till  I  rang 
up,  which  was  probably  all  done  in  one  or  two  minutes,  the  boat  lay 
motionless.  When  I  struck  the  bell  she  sheered  off  in  direction  of  the 
Nansemond  and  gave  her  full  steam,  judging  by  her  exhaust  and  the 
sparks  from  her  smokestack;  she  was  soon  lost  sight  of  in  the  darkness. 
During  this  time  the  engineer  was  eudeavoring  to  raise  his  steam,  and 
by  the  time  that  he  had  steam  we  were  something  like  three-quarters 
of  a  mile  astern.  I  knew  nothing  of  the  state  of  the  tires  or  the 
quantity  of  steam  at  the  time.  Had  we  had  steam  I  think  that  we 


596 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


would  have  run  her  down;  at  any  rate,  we  should  have  done  all  in 
that  direction  that  was  possible  for  us  to  do. 

While  1  have  been  in  the  tug  it  has  been  customary  to  sleep  while 
lying  secure  alongside  or  astern,  thinking  nothing  wrong,  and  having 
a  good  watch  on  deck  to  answer  all  hails  from  the  ship,  and  when 
hailed  have  never  been  found  wanting  before  as  to  steam  or  anything 
else.  We  have  never  received  orders  to  keep  guard  for  the  Minnesota , 
and  when  cruising  in  the  river  on  picket  have  always  received  positive 
orders  not  to  go  below  the  Roanoke ,  ironclad,  except  to  make  a  circle 
around  her  occasionally.  During  the  winter  we  have  cruised  from 
between  the  wharf  at  Newport  News  and  the  Roanolce ,  and  latterly, 
while  on  picket,  have  received  orders  to  run  across  the  river  between 
the  Roanoke  and  Atlanta.  These  orders  we  have  strictly  obeyed,  and 
by  them  have  always  supposed  that  no  danger  was  apprehended  to  the 
Minnesota ,  but  to  the  ironclads.  Captain  Miller,  from  the  time  that 
he  came  on  deck,  did  all  that  lay  in  his  power  to  get  steam  on  and 
give  chase  to  the  enemy. 

Most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Henry  M.  Pishon, 

Acting  Master’s  Mate. 

Fleet  Captain  Barnes. 


U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 

Off  N ewport  News,  Va.,  April  14 ,  1864. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  verbal  order  of  14th  instant,  I  respectfully 
submit  the  following  statement: 

Agreeably  to  the  orders  of  the  senior  engineer  in  charge,  I  had  20 
pounds  of  steam,  the  quantity  maintained  while  lying  alongside  the 
flagship. 

On  being  hailed  I  immediately  gave  orders  to  spread  fires  (which 
were  promptly  obeyed),  at  the  same  time  opening  my  steam  jet. 

Beturning  to  the  engine  room,  I  received  two  bells  (to  back),  which 
was  done,  the  engine  running  slowly.  An  order  to  “go  ahead”  was 
next  sent  to  me  and  obeyed,  but  very  slowly,  as  the  steam  was  rapidly 
falling.  Perceiving  this,  and  unable  to  stem  the  tide,  I  was  compelled 
to  stop  the  engine  until  the  necessary  amount  of  steam  was  restored. 

The  sole  cause  of  this  loss  of  steam  was  due  to  the  fact  that  I  was 
obliged  to  feed  my  boilers  about  five  minutes  prior  to  the  order  to  get 
underway  to  keep  the  same  (steam)  down,  not  being  permitted  to  blow 
when  lying  by  the  flagship. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  Speirs, 

Acting  Third  Assistant  Engineer,  U.  S.  Tug  Poppy. 

Fleet  Captain  Barnes, 

North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Sir:  I  respectfully  submit  the  following  report  concerning  the  explo¬ 
sion  of  a  torpedo  and  the  state  of  this  vessel  on  that  morning: 

At  or  about  12:30  on  the  night  of  the  8th  I  turned  in,  being  off 
watch,  and  slept  until  awakened  by  the  explosion  of  the  torpedo.  On

597 


hurrying  to  the  engine  room  I  found  that  the  bell  had  been  rung  to  go 
ahead  and  that  there  were  but  20  pounds  pressure  of  steam  on  the 
gauge,  and,  the  water  in  the  boiler  being  cold  (as,  in  obedience  to  order 
of  Fleet  Engineer  Garvin  not  to  blow  off  steam,  we  were  compelled  to 
keep  pumping  and  blowing),  this  was  not  sufficient  to  work  the  engine. 
The  engineer  on  watch  was  exerting  himself  to  the  utmost  to  get  up 
steam,  aided  by  the  captain  and  myself,  as  soon  as  there.  Notwithstand¬ 
ing  we  were  nearly  half  an  hour  before  we  had  steam  enough  to  work 
the  boat.  Previous  to  the  order  of  fleet  engineer  we  had  orders  from 
the  captain  to  keep  up  steam  at  all  times  sufficiently  to  work  the 
engines;  and  20  pounds  are  sufficient  if  the  pressure  can  be  kept  up. 
Our  boiler  is  too  small  to  keep  up  the  pressure  to  the  nicety  the  order 
demands  at  all  times,  and  at  that  time  we  were  unfortunately  caught. 

All  officers  and  men  did  their  best  to  assist  in  raising  steam  in  time, 
and  are  deeply  chagrined  at  their  failure. 

In  speaking  of  the  order  not  to  blow  off  steam,  we  were  not  to  blow 
through  the  safety  valve,  but  through  the  surface  blow,  in  order  to 
avoid  noise. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Martin  Boggons,

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va . ,  April  13,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  carefully  investigated  the  facts  and  circumstances 
attending  and  causing  the  failure  on  the  part  of  the  tug  Poppy  to  com¬ 
ply  with  the  orders  given  to  and  received  by  the  officers  of  that  vessel 
to  run  down  and  destroy  the  rebel  torpedo  boat  which  attacked  the 
Minnesota  on  the  morning  of  Saturday,  the  9th  instant. 

I  have  examined  all  the  officers  of  the  Poppy  and  caused  written 
statements  to  be  made  from  each  of  them  as  to  all  the  facts  coming 
within  their  personal  knowledge,  and  from  a  comparison  of  their  state¬ 
ments  and  their  written  reports  the  following  facts  are  adduced: 

The  tug  was  lying  astern  of  the  Minnesota,  secured  by  a  hawser  from 
the  tug.  °No  watch  was  on  deck  known  to  any  of  the  officers.  General 
directions  had  been  given  for  an  anchor  watch  to  auswer  hails  from  the 
Minnesota,  and  an  order  had  been  given  by  the  captain  of  the  tug  that 
steam  should  be  ready  to  move  at  any  moment.  When  the  torpedo 
boat  struck  the  ship  there  was  no  one  ready  to  respond  to  the  order  to 
run  the  boat  down  until  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Pishon,  whose  watch  it 
was,  and  Acting  Ensign  Miller,  in  charge  of  the  tug,  aroused  from 
sleep  by  the  shock  and  repeated  hails,  took  the  wheel  and  rang  the 
bells  to  start  the  engine.  The  tug  had  been  lying  with  fires  banked, 
and,  by  all  accounts,  the  boiler  had  but  a  few  minutes  before  been 
pumped  up  with  cold  water.  The  gauges  showed  20  pounds  of  steam, 
but  as  soon  as  the  throttle  was  opened  and  the  jet  put  on  the  steam  ran 
down  to  4  or  5  pounds  and  the  engine  could  not  be  turned.  The  haw¬ 
ser  which  held  the  tug  was  slipped  from  the  tug  some  40  or  50  fathoms, 
running  over  the  side  from  the  place  where  it  was  coiled,  and  the  tug 
drifted  helplessly  astern  with  the  ebb  tide  about  half  an  hour,  during 
which  time  the  torpedo  boat  made  off  toward  the  Nansemond  side  of 
the  river  and  disappeared  in  the  darkness.  A  half  hour  had  passed 
from  the  time  of  the  explosion  of  the  torpedo  before  the  Poppy  had 
steam  enough  to  move.

Previously  to  this  night  the  Poppy  had  been  employee!  as  a  picket 
boat  around  the  Boanolce ,  with  instructions  to  run  down  and  ram  any¬ 
thing  of  a  suspicious  character  which  was  seen  approaching  or  floating 
near,  and  it  appears  that  when  not  so  employed  about  the  ironclads 
the  officers  had  improperly  conceived  that  no  vigilance  was  required 
from  them.  Upon  the  night  in  question  the  tug  Young  America  was 
guarding  the  Atlanta ;  the  tug  Violet ,  just  returned  from  the  navy  yard, 
where  she  had  been  under  repairs,  was  guarding  the  Boanolce  against 
torpedoes,  and  the  Poppy  was  retained  at  the  Minnesota  in  the  place 
of  the  Mount  Washington ,  previously  employed  on  that  duty,  and  then 
absent  for  repairs. 

Written  orders  assigning  these  tugs  to  this  special  duty  had  been 
issued  with  a  view  to  meeting  this  species  of  attack,  and  there  is  no 
reason  or  excuse  for  the  failure  of  the  Poppy  promptly  to  respond  to 
the  call  made  upon  her  to  run  the  torpedo-  boat  down,  a  duty  which 
she  could  easily  have  performed  had  she  been  in  a  condition  to  move 
and  her  commanding  officer  vigilant.  That  she  was  not  in  such  con¬ 
dition  is  the  fact,  and  the  responsibility  of  the  failure  rests  upon  her 
commanding  officer,  Acting  Ensign  Isaac  Miller,  Acting  Master’s  Mate 
Pishon  (the  officer  of  the  deck),  and  Acting  Third  Assistant  Engineer 
James  Speirs,  the  engineer  in  charge.  Had  they  performed  their  duty 
a  vigilant  watch  would  have  been  kept,  steam  would  have  beeu  ready, 
and  the  capture  or  destruction  of  the  torpedo  boat  would  have  been 
accomplished. 

There  were  at  the  time  of  this  occurrence  three  acting  master’s 
mates  and  three  engineers  attached  to  the  tug  Poppy ,  besides  Acting 
Ensign  Miller,  who  was  in  command.  The  senior  engineer  was  absent 
on  leave  of  absence. 

Acting  Ensign  Miller  has  heretofore  exhibited  much  zeal  and  intel¬ 
ligence  in  the  performance  of  his  duty,  and  I  have  always  regarded 
him  as  an  intelligent  and  callable  officer,  peculiarly  fitted  for  the  posi¬ 
tion  he  has  held.  I  enclose  herewith  the  written  statements  of  Mr. 
Miller,  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Pishon,  and  Third  Assistant  Engineers 
Speirs  and  Boggons,  of  the  Poppy. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant. 

John  S.  Barnes,

The  tug  Violet  is  assigned  to  the  Boanolce. 

The  tug  Young  America  is  assigned  to  the  Atlanta. 

The  tug  Cohasset  or  H.  Brinker  is  assigned  to  the  Minnesota. 

These  tugs  are  to  be  kept  underway  from  sunset  to  sunrise,  and  dur¬ 
ing  thick  and  foggy  weather  by  day,  with  a  good  head  of  steam  up  (a 
regular  watch  of  officers  and  men,  battery  clear  and  provided),  from  f>0 
to  100  yards  astern  of  these  steamers,  respectively,  all  ready  for  ram¬ 
ming  and  running  down,  and  are  to  ram  and  run  down  without  waiting 
for  further  orders  any  “David”  or  torpedo  or  other  suspicious  vessel  or 
boat  approaching  the  vessel  to  which  the  tug  is  assigned.  These  tugs 
are  to  be  kept  for  this  special  service  and  to  do  no  other  duty,  and 
they  are  to  have  bold  and  trustworthy  officers  in  charge  of  them  and 
faithful  engineers.

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  April  15,  1864. 

Sir  :  In  compliance  with  your  order  to  inform  you  in  writing  as  to 
the  nature  and  time  of  the  order  I  passed  to  the  senior  engineer  of  the 
II.  S.  steam  tug  Poppy,  I  would  respectfully  state  that  I  have  been  fre¬ 
quently  requested  to  give  orders  to  the  tugs  to  stop  blowing  off  steam. 
Whenever  this  request  has  been  made  1  have  always  informed  the 
officers  that  it  could  not  be  done  and  at  the  same  time  have  the  tugs 
ready  for  instant  use. 

The  last  request  of  this  kind  was  made  to  me  about  a  month  since 
by  the  executive  officer  of  this  ship,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant 
Charles  B.  Wilder,  tvlio  informed  me  that  the  tug  Poppy  made  so  much 
noise  by  blowing  off  steam  that  his  orders  and  those  of  the  officer  of 
the  deck  could  not  be  heard.  I  informed  Mr.  Wilder  that  I  would  see 
the  senior  engineer  of  the  Poppy  (when  she  returned  with  the  mail) 
and  ascertain  what  could  be  done. 

On  the  return  of  that  vessel  I  sent  for  Acting  Assistant  Engineer 
John  Evans,  who  was  in  charge,  and  enquired  whether  he  could  not 
avoid  so  much  blowing  off  through  the  safety  valve  (while  alongside 
this  vessel)  by  feeding  and  blowing.  He  informed  me  that  he  did 
blow  and  feed  as  much  as  he  could  and  keep  steam  to  be  ready  to  move ; 
that  the  Poppy  was  carrying  the  mail,  and  it  was  impossible  to  know 
at  what  moment  the  bell  might  ring  to  get  underway.  I  told  him  he 
was  doing  right,  and  if  he  could  not  keep  ready  without  blowing  then 
lie  would  have  to  continue  it,  but  to  avoid  raising  the  safety  valve 
higher  than  was  absolutely  necessary. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benjamin  F.  Garvin, 

Fleet  Engineer,  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Acting  Bear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Additional  report  of  Captain  Barnes,  II.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  a  drawing  of  torpedo  boat. 

Flagship  Agawam, 

James  River ,  May  24 ,  1S64. 

Sir:  Upon  the  14th  instant  I  had  an  opportunity  of  observing 
closely  a  torpedo  boat  of  the  enemy  when  under  a  flag  of  truce,  which 
was  the  one  undoubtedly  employed  by  the  enemy  in  the  attempt  to 
blow  up  the  Minnesota. 

Hunter  Davidson,  formerly  of  the  U.  S.  Navy,  was  in  command  of 
the  craft  at  the  time  of  that  attempt  and  when  I  observed  it. 

The  simplicity  of  construction  and  its  great  efficiency  as  a  weapon 
of  war  for  torpedo  purposes,  reconnoitering,  and  picketing  in  rivers, 
induce  me  to  describe  the  boat  in  the  hope  that  several  of  them  may 
be  built  and  furnished  the  squadron  under  your  command. 

The  boat  is  a  propeller,  of  about  30  to  40  feet  in  length,  of  sharp 
model,  moves  rapidly  under  steam,  and  turns  with  great  quickness. 
Her  engine  is  covered  with  boiler  iron,  making  a  low,  cupola-shaped, 
musket-proof  house,  which  also  protects  the  .fireman,  engineer,  and  one 
or  two  sitters.  There  is  a  washboard  extending  around  the  sides  and 
covering  the  forward  part,  leaving  an  open  cuddy  for  sitters  and  the 
pilot,  who  steers  the  craft  with  a  small  wheel.  Upon  the  top  of  the 
stem  there  is  a  roller,  or  sheave,  over  which  passes  the  guy  to  the  tor¬ 
pedo  staff  and  by  which  the  torpedo  is  raised  or  lowered  by  means  of 
a  winch  in  the  cuddy.  On  a  stem  at  the  water’s  edge  is  a  goose  neck, 
to  which  the  torpedo  staff  is  attached.  The  accompanying  drawing- 
will  more  fully  explain  the  machine.* 

I  have  no  doubt  but  that  the  various  torpedo  boats  called  “Davids,” 
and  which  have  been  so  often  reported  as  submerged  and  cigar  shaped, 
are  all  of  similar  construction.  It  would  be  very  difficult  to  discern 
this  boat  at  night  at  a  short  distance.  The  many  reports  which  have 
been  made  by  those  whose  observations  were  confined  to  glimpses  at 
night  under  exciting  circumstances,  could  hardly  give  a  correct  idea  of 
the  real  appearance  and  construction  of  the  vessel. 

Verv  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  S.  Barnes, 

Fleet  Captain. 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Abstract  log  of  the  IJ.  S.  S.  Minnesota. 

April  .9,- 1864. — At  1:45  a.  m.  discovered,  as  I  thought,  a  boat  drift¬ 
ing  by  on  the  port  beam.  Hailed  her  several  times.  She  answered 
“lioanoke.”  I  ordered  her  to  keep  off  or  I  would  tire  into  her.  Hailed 
the  Poppy ,  who  was  hanging  astern,  but  received  no  answer.  The 
object  by  this  time  was  steering  straight  for  the  ship  and  coming  rap¬ 
idly;  could  not  see  or  hear  any  oars;  ordered  the  Poppy  to  see  what 
she  was,  hailing  her  three  times,  and  the  third  time  received  an  answer. 
I  then  called  Captain  Upshur.  I  then  discovered  the  object  to  be  a 
little  steamer;  ordered  the  Poppy  to  run  her  down,  and  endeavored  to 
lire  a  gun  at  her,  when  she  struck  the  ship  abaft  the  main  chains,  and 
a  tremendous  explosion  followed.  She  then  backed  off  and  steamed  off 
toward  the  mouth  of  the  Nansemond  Eiver.  Pired  a  shell  at  her  from 
one  of  the  IX-inch  guns.  Sounded  the  pumps  and  found  the  ship  not 
making  water.  Called  the  small  vessels  and  sent  them  to  warn  the 
other  vessels  of  the  tleet  and  to  search  for  the  torpedo  boat. 

April  11.— From  midnight  till  4  a.m.:  Captain  Fyffe,  of  the  Commo¬ 
dore  Morris,  reported  having  chased  the  infernal  machine,  and  that  the 
Dawn  fired  a  gun  at  it  aud  made  signal  of  alarm. 


Extract  from  the  report  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  of  the  Confederate  States,  April  30,  1864. 

On  the  night  of  the  9tli  instant  Lieutenant  Commanding  Hunter 
Davidson,  in  command  of  the  torpedo  boat  Squib ,  with  six  officers  and 
men,  ran  through  the  enemy’s  fleet  off  Newport  News,  attacked  the 
flagship  Minnesota,  exploding  a  torpedo  against  her,  and  returned  in 
safety  under  a  heavy  tire.  The  extent  of  the  injury  inflicted  upon  the 
ship  has  not  yet  been  ascertained,  but  it  is  believed  to  be  serious.  The 
cool  daring,  professional  skill,  and  judgment  exhibited  by  Lieutenant 
Davidson  in  this  hazardous  enterprise  merit  high  commendation  and 
confer  honor  upon  a  service  of  which  he  is  a  member.  A  copy  of  his 
report  is  herewith  submitted. 


[Telegram.] 

Turkey  Island, 

Via  Drewry's  Bluff,  April  11,  1864. 

Passed  through  the  Federal  fleet  off  Newport  News  and  exploded 
53  pounds  of  powder  against  the  side  of  the  flagship  Minnesota  at  J  a.  m., 
9th  instant.  She  has  not  sunk,  and  I  have  no  means  yet  of  telling  the 
injury  done.  My  boat  and  party  escaped  without  loss  under  the  tire  of 
her  heavy  guns  and  musketry  and  that  of  a  gunboat  lying  to  her  stern.

Search  for  the  U.  S.  Army  steamer  Scott. 

[Telegram.] 

Navy  Department,  April  11,  1864. 

Captain  of  steamer  Clark  reports  having  fallen  in  with  the  army 
steamer  Scott  off  Capes  ot  Virginia.  He  laid  by  her  over  two  days,  and 
finally,  after  parting  all  his  hawsers,  lost  her  in  a  gale.  She  must  now 
be  some  distance  southeast  of  Cape  Henry.  She  has  lost  her  rudder, 
and  is  short  of  provisions. 

Send  what  vessels  you  have  at  your  disposal  in  search  of  her. 

Gideon  Welles,

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Simmons,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Dawn. 


U.  S.  S.  Dawn, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  April  14,  1864. 
Sir  :  1  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  your  orders  of 
the  11th,  3 : 30  p.  in.,  I  proceeded  with  the  Dawn  to  search  for  and  relieve 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


605 


the  steamer  Scott ,  said  to  be  southeast  from  Cape  Henry.  After  coaling 
I  proceeded  to  sea,  steering  S.  E.  and  S.  S.  E.  until  reaching  latitude 
36°  10'  N.  and  longitude  75°  15'  W.  I  then  changed  my  course  to 
S.  W.,  thinking  the  Scott  might  have  run  on  the  beach.  At  12  noon 
spoke  the  schooner  Henry  N.  Morse,  from  south  of  Cape  Hatteras.  She 
had  seen  nothing  of  a  disabled  steamer.  At  12 : 30  spoke  schooner  J.  C. 
Baxter,  but  she  had  seen  nothing  of  the  Scott.  At  3  p.  in.,  Cape  Hatteras 
bearing  S.  by  W.,  distant  30  miles,  Bodie’s  Island  W.  S.  W.  8  miles, 
changed  the  course  to  N.  N.  W.  and  ran  close  along  the  beach,  but  saw 
nothing  of  the  steamer  on  shore.  At  10  p.  in.,  Cape  Henry  light  bearing 
N.  W.,  distant  10  miles,  changed  the  course  to  S.  E.  until  0  a.  m.  on  the 
13th,  then  changed  the  course  to  E.  by  S.  until  8  a.  in.,  being  then  in 
latitude  3G°  15'  N.,  longitude  75°  00'  W.,  24  miles  east  of  Cape  Hatteras. 
Changed  the  course  to  JST.  1ST.  W.  at  2  p.  m.,  Hog  Island  light  bearing 
N.  N.  W.,  distant  10  miles.  Atthis  time,  feeling  confident  that  the  Scott 
w  as  not  in  the  vicinity  mentioned  in  the  dispatch,  I  concluded  to  return 
to  this  place,  and  to  my  regret  report  that  I  could  not  find  the  missing 
steamer. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  W.  Simmons, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Dawn. 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  S.  P.  Lee,

Bevort  of  Acting  Bear- Admiral  Lee ,  JJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  expedition  up 
York  Biver  near  Potopotank  Creek. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  April  11 ,  1864. 

Sir  :  Acting  Master  [William]  Wright,  U.  S.  S.  Mystic ,  reports,  under 
date  of  9th  instant,  that  on  the  7th  instant  he  proceeded  up  York  Biver 
by  General  Wistar’s  request  to  cooperate  with  a  small  party  of  cavalry 
sent  by  him  to  scout  the  vicinity  of  Poquetank  [Potopotank]  Creek, 
where  armed  boats  were  reported  to  be  concealed.  The  Mystic,  with  a 
small  body  of  infantry  on  board,  arrived  opposite  the  creek  in  advance 
of  the  cavalry,  and  sent  in  three  armed  boats  and  two  skiffs  with  the 
soldiers. 

They  landed  on  both  sides  the  creek  and  succeeded  in  capturing  and 
bringing  off  1  large  pontoon,  11  boats,  8  skiffs,  0  compasses,  and  58  new 
oyster  tongs.  No  resistance  was  encountered  nor  any  of  the  enemy 
seen. 

After  further  search  for  any  boats  that  might  be  secreted,  the  party 
reembarked,  and  the  Mystic  returned  to  her  anchorage  at  the  mouth  of 
York  Biver. 

I  have  directed  Lieutenant-Commander  Babcock  to  send  these  cap¬ 
tured  articles  to  Washington  with  proper  witnesses,  as  in  the  former 
case. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Bear- Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Simmons ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding 
the  escape  of  a  steamer  in  James  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Dawn, 

James  River ,  April  11,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  respectfully  report  to  you  that  on  the  night  of  Sunday,  April 
10,  at  11  p.  m.,  this  ship  being  then  on  picket  duty,  the  officer  of  the 
deck  reported  to  me  strange  lights  on  the  south  shore  of  James  River, 
near  Pagan  Creek.  I  at  once  went  on  deck.  Upon  taking  my  night 
glasses  I  saw  sparks  as  if  coming  from  the  smoke  pipe  of  a  steamer, 
and  immediately  after  saw  what  I  supposed  was  a  boat,  about  25  feet 
long,  steering  about  southeast  toward  Chuckatuck  River  [Creek].  I 
beat  to  quarters  at  once,  and  fired  one  20-pound  shell  at  the  boat.  A 
heavy  squall  of  wind  and  rain  coming  up  at  the  time  1  lost  sight  of  him. 
The  strange  boat  was  moving  very  rapidly  at  the  time.  The  steamer 
Commodore  Morris  coming  in  hail,  I  made  my  report  to  him  and  he  said 
he  would  report  to  you  at  once. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  W.  Simmons, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Lawn. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Commander  Davenport ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  detention  of 
the  U.  S.  S,  Tacony  at  New  Berne ,  N.  C. 

U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne,  N.  C.,  April  12,  1864. 

Admiral:  In  reply  to  your  letter  of  the  6th  instant,  directing  me  to 
send  the  Tacony  to  Hampton  Roads  for  repairs,  I  beg  leave  to  say  that 
1  have,  in  connection  with  Carpenter  Paul,  made  an  inspection  of  that 
vessel  and  tind  that  she  requires  no  repairs  that  can  not  be  done  here. 

As  regards  her  wheel  ropes,  I  think  the  trouble  arises  from  the  short¬ 
ness  of  the  tillers.  Carpenter  Paul  concurs  with  me  in  this  opinion. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Flusser  having  written  that  you  directed  him 
to  apply  to  me  for  the  Lockwood  or  Ceres,  I  have  sent  the  latter  vessel 
to  Plymouth. 

After  consultation  with  General  Peck,  I  think  it  necessary  that  the 
Tacony ,  or  a  vessel  other  size,  should  be  stationed  here  for  the  present, 
I  have,  therefore,  concluded  not  to  send  her  away  until  I  receive  further 
orders  from  you. 

I  trust  that  this  will  meet  with  your  approval. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  K.  Davenport, 

Commander  and  Senior  Naval  Officer  in  Sounds  of  North  Carolina. 

Acting  Pear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

rebel  ram  is  several  miles  below  Rainbow  Bluff;  that  she  is  accompa-

nied  by  a  land  force  of  11,000  men,  and  that  an  attack  will  be  made

in  use  as  a  hospital,  was  to-day  cleared  of  the  sick  and  delivered  to  the 
quartermaster  to  be  filled  with  earth  and  bricks,  preparatory  to  sink¬ 
ing  to-morrow.  On  the  Miami  I  shall  rig  a  spar,  projecting  from  the 
bow,  and  another  from  the  stern,  carrying  a  torpedo  each,  the  one  con¬ 
taining  70  pounds  of  powder  ancl  the  other  50  pounds. 

If  we  get  to  close  quarters  they  may  prove  destructive. .  The  rebels 
fancy  the  Roanoke  in  this  vicinity  [is]  filled  with  torpedoes,  and  have 
exhibited  ingenuity  in  preparing  to  remove  or  explode  them.  They 
have,  we  are  informed,  attached  long  iron  hooks  to  the  under  side  of 
stout  rafts,  which  are  to  be  brought  down  by  the  rapid  current,  and 
which  might  very  well  remove  torpedoes  anchored  in  the  stream,  if 
there  were  any  there. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  W.  Flusser, 
Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  off  Newport  Neics.

Navy  Department, 

Washington,  April  7,  1864. 

Sir  :  Lieutenant-General  Grant  lias  asked  for  two  more  ironclads  to 
be  sent  to  Hampton  Roads  within  ten  days.  The  ironclad  batteries 
Onondaga  and  Tecumseli  have  been  directed  to  leave  New  York  on 
Monday  or  Tuesday  next.  The  Tecumseli  has  no  crew,  but  by  taking 
out  from  all  the  other  vessels  the  few  hands  on  board  of  each,  I  believe 
she  will  not  be  detained  beyond  the  time  indicated  by  the  Lieutenant- 
General.  This  Department  has  not  been  informed  of  the  duty  expected 
of  these  ironclads,  or  whether  additional  naval  force  is  required,  which 
would  be  the  case  in  the  event  of  an  army  being  sent  as  far  as  City 
Point.  Public  rumor  points  to  a  movement  of  this  kind,  which  can  not 
be  successful  unless  a  cooperating  naval  force  is  kept  in  James  River. 
Twice  the  number  of  steamers  required  have  been  ready  for  two 
months,  excepting  the  crews.  I  bring  this  subject  again  to  your 
notice,  because  the  legislation  of  Congress  has  placed  in  your  hands 
the  providing  of  seamen  for  the  Navy,  and  the  Department  must  await 
your  action,  whatever  may  be  the  exigency  which  coming  events  impose 
upon  the  Navy. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Hon.  E.  M.  Stanton, 

Secretary  of  War.
