by  orders  from  him  sent  (at  4  p.  m.)  the  second  cutter  in  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  G.  P.  St.  John  and  10  men  to  report  to  him.  At  4:30 
p,  m.  got  underway  and  proceeded  to  Station  No.  4.  At  dark  I  sent  in 
first  cutter  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  and  Executive  Officer  R.  W.

with  12  men,  to  march  up  the  beach  to  Masonboro  Inlet  and  capture 
all  pickets  they  might  find,  and  to  hold  the  point  on  the  south  side  of 
the  inlet  to  protect  the  boats  returning  from  the  sound,  the  Howquah 
proceeding  up  the  beach  in  3  fathoms  of  water  to  shell  the  beach  in 
case  of  an  attack  from  the  southward. 

At  10  p.  m.  our  pickets  were  fired  upon  by  the  cavalry.  Not  being 
able  to  surround,  fired  upon  them.  One  man  was  seen  to  fall,  but  was 
carried  off  by  his  companions.  They  followed  them,  finding  his  rifle. 
At  10:15  p.  m.  signals  were  made  to  shell  the  beach  southward,  and  I 
commenced  shelling.  At  10:35  p.  m.  signals  were  made  to  cease  firing. 
At  10:45  first  cutter  returned  with  11  conscripts,  and  immediately 
returned  for  the  rest  of  our  men.  At  11:20  all  boats  returned  on 
board,  having  accomplished  the  duty  sent  to  perform  without  loss  or 
accident.  In  submitting  this  report  I  can  not  say  too  much  in  praise 
of  the  coolness  of  the  officers  and  good  conduct  of  the  men. 

I  am,  sir,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

J.  W.  Balch, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  V.  S.  S.  Howquah. 

Captain  B.  F.  Sands,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Senior  Officer,  Off  Wilmington ,  N.  C. 


Report  of  Major-General  Whiting,  C.  S.  Army. 

Headquarters  Department  op  Cape  Fear, 

Wilmington,  N.  C.,  April  22,  1864. 

General:  Nine  barges  of  the  enemy,  piloted  by  a  renegade,  lauded 
last  night  at  Masonboro,  at  the  State  salt  works,  which  they  destroyed. 
They  carried  off  a  number  of  conscripts  or  employes.  I  do  not  much 
regret  the  matter,  as  the  State  salt  works  have  always  been  a  nest  of 
traitors,  and  more  than  suspected  of  holding  intercourse  with  the 
enemy,  but  I  have  no  doubt  at  all  that  the  attempt  was  made  in  con¬ 
sequence  of  information  transmitted  to  the  enemy  of  the  withdrawal 
of  my  movable  force. 

On  the  12th  instant  I  had  directed  General  Martin  to  occupy  the 
belt  of  sounds  opposite  Masonboro  Inlet,  but  the  recent  movement  of 
troops  prevented  it.  It  has  always  been  my  custom  to  guard  these 
points  strongly,  as  of  very  great  importance  to  the  secxxrity  of  the  com¬ 
mand.  The  enemy  carried  off  a  number  of  willing  prisoners.  They 
are  capable  of  giving  much  information.  You  will  see  by  the  enclosed 
copy  of  a  letter  to  the  governor,  my  opinion  of  the  works  and  the 
people  engaged  on  them.  The  whole  affair  strongly  illustrates  the 
necessity  of  keeping  here  at  least  a  brigade  at  all  times.  The  men 
carried  off  were  in  the  habit  of  daily  visiting  the  city  to  haul  and  dis¬ 
pose  of  salt,  are  fully  aware  of  the  late  movements  and  of  every 
exposed  condition,  and  will  no  doubt  give  all  the  information  they  have 
to  the  enemy. 

If  your  operations  will  not  permit  you  to  leave  a  brigade  with  me,  I 
beg  you  will  present  this  to  the  Department,  which  has  been  fully 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


678 

advised  of  the  circumstances  of  tin's  command.  I  have  not  at  present 
sufficient  force  to  perform  the  heavy  garrison  duties  of  the  city. 

Yery  respectfully, 

W.  H.  0.  Whiting, 

Major-  General. 

General  G.  T.  Beauregard, 

Weldon ,  N.  G. 


[Enclosure.] 

Headquarters  Department  of  the  Cape  Fear, 

Wilmington ,  N.  C.,  April  22 ,  1864. 

Sir:  Last  night  tlie  enemy  landed  at  the  State  salt  works  and 
destroyed  one  of  them,  taking  off  a  number  of  the  conscripts.  I  do 
not  regret  it.  I  consider  that  the  whole  affair  was  done  with  the  com¬ 
plicity  and  on  the  information  of  parties  engaged  there.  The  enemy 
undoubtedly  were  made  aware  of  the  withdrawal  ot  Martin’s  brigade. 
The  establishment  has  long  been  a  nuisance,  and  the  circumstantial 
evidence  of  their  intercourse  with  the  enemy  is  very  strong,  and  com¬ 
bined  with  the  known  character  of  many  of  the  conscripts,  is  sufficient 
to  induce  me  to  remove  what  the  enemy  have  spared.  In  this  connec¬ 
tion  I  respectfully  refer  to  my  letter  of  22d  ultimo  to  you.  If  the 
works  are  regarded  as  indispensable  to  the  State  it  will  be  necessary 
to  remove  them  to  Gape  Fear  River.  Ho  more  salt  works  will  be  per¬ 
mitted  on  Masonboro  Sound.  The  enemy  left  a  number  of  letters  to  be 
distributed. 

Very  respectfully, 

W.  H.  C.  Whiting, 

Major-  General. 

His  Excellency  Governor  Vance, 

Raleigh. 


Reconnoissanee  in  vicinity  of  Myrtle  Sound ,  North  Carolina ,  April 

22,  1864. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  lee,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  giving  results. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Hampton  Roads,  Virginia ,  April  27,  1864. 

Sir:  Captain  Sands,  IJ.  S.  S.  Fort  Jackson,  reports  under  date  of 
22d  [23d]  instant  he  sent  the  Niphon  to  reconnoiter  in  the  vicinity  of 
Myrtle  Sound  and  obtain  information,  if  practicable,  of  the  number  and 
disposition  of  the  enemy.  A  cutter  and  a  dingey  were  dispatched  from 
the  Niphon.  The  latter,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Borden,  was  car¬ 
ried  across  the  beach  and  into  the  sound,  while  the  cutter,  in  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  Semon,  both  officers  attached  to  the  Niphon,  picketed 
the  beach.  Acting  Ensign  Borden  crossed  the  sound  without  being 
discovered  by  the  enemy’s  pickets,  and  running  up  a  small  creek, 
landed  about  10: 15  p.  m.,  conducted  by  J.  H.  Pucket,  the  refugee  pilot 
who  guided  the  expedition  which  destroyed  the  State  salt  works  on  the 
21st  instant.  He  proceeded  to  the  house  of  Acting  Lieutenant  E.  H. 
Davis,  of  the  Masonboro  Home  Guard,  who  was  known  to  be  favorable 
to  our  cause.  He  came  off'  with  the  party  after  making  arrangements 
to  obtain  information  from  his  friends  at  frequent  intervals. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  679 

The  information  obtained  from  him  is  substantially  as  follows:  That 
the  present  force  in  Fort  Fisher  and  the  batteries  adjacent  consists  of 
about  1,000  men;  the  force  in  and  around  Wilmington,  about  2,000 
men,  General  Beauregard  and  General  Whitney  [W.  H.  C.  Whiting] 
commanding,  in  addition  to  which  some  300  conscripts,  who  had  been 
employed  at  the  salt  works,  were  sent  there  after  these  works  were 
destroyed;  that  Wilmington  could,  in  his  opinion,  be  taken  with  little 
difficulty  now,  by  landing  troops  at  Masonboro  and  marching  across. 
The  distance  is  short  and  the  road  good  and  undefended. 

The  batteries  at  Wilmington  mount  but  about  tenor  fifteen  guns, 
and  they  old-fashioned  smoothbores.  He  does  not  state  their  cal¬ 
iber.  When  the  firing  at  the  salt  works  on  the  21st  was  heard  at  Wil¬ 
mington  it  was  supposed  there  that  an  attack  on  that  place  was 
intended,  and  troops  that  had  been  dispatched  to  Swansboro  and  the 
sounds  were  recalled.  The  number  of  these  is  not  stated,  nor  whether 
they  are  included  in  the  estimate  given  of  the  troops  at  Wilmington 
and  vicinity. 

I  have  informed  General  Butler  of  this  man’s  statement,  and  repre¬ 
sented  to  him  that  the  presence,  of  a  general  so  highly  esteemed  as 
Beauregard,  the  sending  of  troops  from  Wilmington  to  Swansboro,  the 
recent  attack  on  Plymouth,  and  the  increase  of  rebel  force  in  the 
eastern  part  of  North  Caroliua,  seems  to  indicate  their  determination 
to  push  the  campaign  with  vigor,  possibly  to  attack  both  Beaufort  and 
New  Berne,  and  that  in  view  of  these  facts  an  increase  of  military 
force  at  Morehead  City  and  Fort  Macon  appeared  requisite. 

The  garrison  at  the  latter  place  is  so  weak  that,  at  the  commanding 
officer’s  request,  Commander  Dove  sent  60  sailors  from  the  blockaders 
there  in  the  harbor  to  assist  in  manning  it.  Immediately  upon  being 
informed  of  this  by  him,  however,  I  directed  him  to  return  the  men  at 
once  to  their  vessels,  as  the  already  small  crews  could  not  bear  this 
diminution. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Bloclcading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Captain  Sands,  IT.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Breck, 

U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Niphon, 

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Jackson, 

Off  New  Inlet ,  Gape  Fear  River ,  April  23 , 1864. 

Sir  :  Yesterday  evening  I  sent  the  Niphon  to  No.  4  station  and  along 
the  beach  to  the  northward  to  make  a  reconnoissance  in  the  sound  for 
information  [IJ  supposed  could  be  obtained  from  friends  on  the  mainland, 
and  I  herewith  enclose  the  report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant 
Breck,  accompanied  by  that  of  Acting  Ensign  H.  S.  Borden,  who  had 
charge  of  the  party. 

I  would  respectfully  bring  to  your  notice  the  zeal  and  energy  evinced 
by  Acting  Ensign  Borden  upon  all  occasions  of  enterprise,  and  I  name 
him  as  one  deserving  promotion. 

Mr.  Davis,  the  refugee  officer  from  the  home  guard,  North  Carolina, 
states  that  when  the  shells  exploded  in  the  salt  works  it  was  thought 
in  Wilmington  that  we  had  landed  in  force  at  Masonboro,  to  march  on 


680  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

former  city,  and  expresses  were  immediately  sent  off  to  recall  troops 
that  liad  been  sent  toward  Swansboro  and  the  sounds,  and  may  have 
the  effect  of  interfering  with  the  threatened  attack  upon  New  Berne 
and  Washington,  N.  C.  He  also  states  that  General  Beauregard  was 
at  Wilmington  with  General  Whiting.  That  the  morning  after  our  raid 
all  the  conscripts  left  by  us  after  the  destruction  of  the  works  and 
State  property  (some  300)  were  marched  off  to  Wilmington  for  the 
Army,  as  the  work  of  salt  making  for  the  State  was  spoiled. 

Very  respectfully,  etc.,  your  obedient  servant,

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Niphon, 

Off  New  Inlet ,  North  Carolina,  April  23,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  sent  the  second  cutter  of  this 
ship  on  shore  at  Big  Hill  under  the  command  of  Acting  Ensign  E.  N. 
Semon,  and  a  small  dingey  from  the  Fort  Jackson,  to  carry  across  the 
beach  over  to  the  sound."  Mr.  Borden,  the  executive  officer,  volunteered 
to  go  in  her  with  Mr.  Pucket  and  see  what  information  could  be  had; 
to  establish  a  regular  communication  with  the  shore.  I  enclose  his 
report  to  me.  The  expedition  returned  at  midnight,  having  been  suc¬ 
cessful  in  all  respects,  and  we  are  to  have  news  from  the  shore  every 
three  days.  Mr.  Borden  also  brought  off  with  him  Eli  H.  Davis,  a 
lieutenant  in  the  Masonboro  Home  Guard.  Mr.  Davis  says  that  the 
destruction  of  the  salt  works  by  the  expedition  was  entire.  Their  daily 
average  of  salt  was  about  500  bushels,  they  being  the  principal  salt 
works  in  the  State.  Yesterday  one  company  of  artillery  and  800 
infantry  of  the  Fiftieth  North  Carolina  Begiment  came  down  to  the 
sound  to  protect  the  sawmill  owned  by  Government.  Mr.  Davis  says 
there  are  at  Fort  Fisher  and  the  batteries  near  about  1,000  men — the 
Twenty-sixth  North  Carolina  and  one  company  of  Georgia  cavalry. 
About  Wilmington  and  in  vicinity  there  are  some  2,000  troops,  consist¬ 
ing  of  General  Whiting’s  division,  Fiftieth  North  Carolina,  and  small 
detachments  from  other  regiments  doing  provost  duty.  Most  of  the 
troops  formerly  stationed  at  Wilmington  have  left.  Thinks  Wilming¬ 
ton  could  be  taken  easily  by  troops  landed  at  Masonboro,  it  being  but 
a  short  distance,  a  good  road,  and  not  defended.  The  batteries  have 
but  few  pieces,  not  more  than  ten  or  fifteen  altogether,  and  they  are 
old-fashioned  smoothbore.  Farmers’  crops  are  very  bad  and  provisions 
very  scarce  and  dear;  out  of  the  reach  of  all  except  the  rich.  People 
are  tired  of  secession  and  would  be  glad  to  see  us  in  possession  of  the 
country.  There  was  a  great  excitement  at  Wilmington,  as  they  expected 
an  attack  from  the  party  burning  the  salt  works.  Only  three  blockade 
runners  at  Wilmington;  do  not  know  their  names.  Mr.  Davis  is  the 
brother-in-law  to  Mr.  Bowen,  pilot  of  the  Nansemond ,  The  man  that  I 
am  in  communication  with  has  promised  me  a  sketch  of  Fort  Fisher, 
which  I  shall  have  in  a  few  days. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  B.  Breck, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Niplion. 

Captain  B.  F.  Sands, 

Senior  Officer  Present.

[Subenclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Niphon, 

Off  New  Inlet,  North  Carolina ,  April  23,  1864. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  orders,  on  tbe  night  of  the  22d  of  April  I  pro¬ 
ceeded  with  the  second  cutter  and  dingey  on  a  reconnoissance  across 
Myrtle  Sound  to  the  mainland,  to  gain  information  in  regard  to  the 
strength  and  position  of  the  rebels.  About  9 : 30  in  the  evening  landed 
on  the  beach,  took  the  dingey  and  carried  her  across  the  beach  to  the 
sound,  and  with  the  pilot,  2  men,  and  myself  proceeded  to  the  main¬ 
land.  Owing  to  pickets  being  stationed  at  several  points  along  the 
sound  on  the  mainland,  it  was  necessary  to  proceed  very  cautiously. 
By  so  doing,  I  got  across  without  being  discovered,  and  about  10:i5 
entered  Sandy  Bun,  a  small  creek;  went  up  about  one-fourth  of  a  mile 
and  landed.  Leaving  the  2  men  in  the  dingey,  the  pilot  and  myself 
proceeded  to  Lieutenant  Davis’s  house,  about  a  mile  and  a  quarter  from 
the  boat.  Upon  arriving  at  the  house,  the  pilot  went  to  the  window 
and  awoke  Mr.  Davis,  who  got  up  immediately.  He  informed  us  where 
the  pickets  were  stationed,  the  nearest  being  about  500  yards  from  his 
house.  We  transacted  our  business  as  soon  as  possible  and  jiroceeded 
to  the  boat.  Mr.  Davis  went  to  one  of  the  neighbors,  a  confidential 
man,  about  a  mile  from  his  house,  held  an  interview  with  him,  and  then 
both  of  them  met  us  at  the  boat.  Mr.  Davis  took  the  opportunity  to 
escape  with  us.  I  made  arrangements  to  hold  communication  with  the 
parties  on  shore,  who  will  keep  the  fleet  posted  in  regard  to  all  military 
movements,  etc.,  the  present  force  in  Fort  Fisher  being  about  1,000 
men. 

Too  much  praise  can  not  be  given  to  Acting  Ensign  E.  N.  Semon, 
who  went  in  the  second  cutter  and  picketed  the  beach  while  I  was 
across  the  sound.  Everything  being  carried  out  successfully,  I  pro¬ 
ceeded  back,  hauled  the  dingey  across  the  beach  again,  and  got  on 
board  the  vessel  at  2 : 15  a.  m.  of  the  23d. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  S.  Borden, 

Acting  Ensign  and  Executive  Officer  U.  8.  8.  Niphon. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  J.  B.  Breck, 

Commanding  U.  8.  8.  Niphon,  off  New  Inlet,  North  Carolina 


Instructions  from  Acting  Bear- Admiral  Lee,  U.  8.  Navy,  to  Commander 
Dove,  U.  8.  Navy,  regarding  affairs  in  Beaufort  Harbor,  N.  C. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  April  22,  1864. 

Sir:  Your  No.  56,  of  the  20th  instant,  is  received.  I  desire  that  you 
immediately  withdraw  the  GO  sailors  you  have  sent  to  Fort  Macon  and 
return  them  to  their  vessels;  and  referring  also  to  your  statement  that 
if  the  Ninth  Vermont  Begiment  is  driven  in  it  will  be  necessary  to  send 
a  strong  party  to  man  the  intrenchments  back  of  Morehead  City,  I 
would  remind  you  that  the  Navy  has  nothing  to  do  with  military  affairs 
and  arrangements.  General  Butler  has  the  charge  of  such  defensive 
and  offensive  operations,  and  I  wish  you  to  leave  them  entirely  to  him 
or  the  officers  he  may  place  in  charge. 

If  it  should  become  necessary  to  remove  the  ordnance  vessels  from 
Beaufort  Harbor,  you  can  take  them  outside  the  bar,  but  this  is  only  to 
be  done  if  absolutely  necessary.

possible.  Notify  their  commanding  officers  and  give  them  every  facility

The  rebel  ram  is  125  feet  long,  and  draws  8  feet  of  water;  armed  with 
four  30-pounders.  She  will  have  done  all  the  mischief  before  we  can

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Gdptain  Smith ,  U.  S. 
Navy ,  to  assume  command  in  the  sounds  and  attach  the  C.  S.  ram  Albe¬ 
marle. 


Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  April  23 ,  1864—1  p.  m. 

Sir:  The  Navy  Department,  by  telegraphic  dispatch  of  this  date, 
directs  me  to  send  you  to  assume  command  in  the  sounds  of  North  Oaro- 
liua  for  the  purpose  of  attacking,  at  all  hazards,  the  rebel  ram  there  in 
the  best  manner  to  insure  its  destruction  by  running  it  down  with  the 
double-enders,  or  in  any  other  manner  which  my  judgment  or  yours 

may  suggest.  . 

The  Miami  (Commander  Renshaw)  and  the  Tacony  (Lieutenant-Com¬ 
mander  Truxtun)  are  nowin  the  sounds.  The  Sassacus  (Lieutenant- 
Commander  Roe)  was  sent  there  last  night.  You  will  take  the 
Mattabesett  (Commander  Febiger)  and  the  Wyalusing  (Lieutenant-Com¬ 
mander  Queen)  with  you,  and  leave  with  all  practicable  dispatch, 
availing  yourself  of  the  present  high  tides  to  enter  the  sounds. 

I  send  with  you  two  officers  who  have  served  in  the  sounds,  and 
whose  local  knowledge  will  be  useful  to  you. 

I  enclose  a  copy  of  my  instructions*  of  21st  instant  to  Commander 
Davenport  for  your  information  and  guidance,  unless  you  find  occasion 
to  vary  them  for  a  more  promising  plan  of  attack. 

Attacking  the  ram  will,  to  some  extent,  intimidate  it,  and  by  getting 
alongside  of  it,  in  or  near  contact,  and  on  each  side,  holding  position, 
and  by  firing  at  the  center  of  its  ports,  whether  open  oi  shut,  and  on 
its  roof,  you  will  disable  and  capture  it.  Your  guns  should  have 
double  breeching,  and  be  loaded  with  heavy  charges  (say  from  15  to  18 
pounds  of  powder  for  the  IX-inch  guns)  and  solid  shot,  and  they  should 
be  so  depressed  as  to  tire  as  near  a  perpendicular  line  to  the  slope  of 
the  roof  as  practicable. 

If  all  hands  lie  down  when  the  guns  are  fired,  they  will  escape  the 
rebound  of  broken  parts  from  the  shot. 

At  the  time  of  this  attack  if  some  shell  were  thrown  down  the  ram’s 
smokestack,  she  might  thus  be  disabled. 

The  advantage  of  getting  alongside  and  on  each  side  of  her  is  that 
you  prevent  her  from  ramming,  and  have  a  controlling  lire  upon  her 
roof  and  ports. 

Her  ports  and  stern  are  her  weak  points. 

Even  if  her  ports  are  kept  closed,  as  in  her  attack  on  the  Miami’s  and 
Southfield's  bows,  you  can,  if  alongside  of  her,  fire  through  them  and  into 
her,  and  if  her  roof  is,  as  described,  of  railroad  iron  with  a  thin  plating 
over  it,  the  mechanical  difficulty  of  securing  this  is  such  that  it  will 
loosen  and  fly  off  under  the  concussion  of  your  heavy  fire,  while  the 
inside  nuts  ami  bolts  will  act  like  canister  on  her  deck,  and  the  con¬ 
cussion,  especially  if  her  ports  are  shut,  will  shock  and  demoralize  her 
crew,  giving  you  a  complete  victory. 

Besides  you  may  force  her  ashore,  where  the  faliing  freshet  in  the 
Roanoke  may  leave  her. 

Be  sure  and  not  have  the  neutral  point  of  your  wheelhouses  opposite 
her  ports. 

Your  wheelhouses  should  be  abaft  or  forward  of  her  roof — better 
abaft. 

The  Department  seems  to  prefer  ramming. 


See  p.  669. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  685 

This  ram  is  reported  to  be  of  the  usual  Merrimack  model ;  if  so,  heavy 
logging  and  a  knuckle  ironed  over  make  her  sides  strong.  But  ram¬ 
ming  under  high  speed  may  drive  it  in,  or  you  may  drive  her  ashore  or 
mount  her  ends  (especially  if  in  the  sounds  with  some  sea)  and  sink  her. 

Intrusted  by  the  Department  with  the  performance  of  this  signal 
service,  I  leave  (with  the  expression  of  my  views)  to  you  the  manner  of 
executing  it. 

All  assaults  are  exposed  service,  but  this  assault  has,  with  much  real 
risk,  less  than  appears. 

Wishing  you  success  and  promotion, 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee,

The  ram  is  said  to  have  two  screws  and  to  turn  short.  Her  blow  is

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy ,  transmitting  correspond¬ 
ence  regarding  the  defenses  in  the  sounds  of  North  Carolina. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  April  24,  1864. 

Sir:  General  Butler  read  me  this  evening  his  dispatch*  making  the 
surrender  of  Plymouth  the  result  of  want  of  naval  defense  ot  its 
Hanks — meaning  against  the  rebel  ram  and  the  riflemen  in  the  steam¬ 
boat  Cotton  Plant. 

The  Navy  had  nothing  to  do  with  the  planning,  placing,  or  fighting 
the  extensive  and  expensive  fortifications  which  the  Army  had  erected 
for  the  defense  of  Plymouth,  Washington,  and  New  Berne,  by  land 
and  water. 

There  are  three  earthen  works  on  the  riverside  at  Plymouth — one 
in  the  lower  part  and  the  other  two  above  this  small  town,  and  they 
should  not  need  wooden  gunboats  to  defend  them. 

General  Butler  told  me  at  Plymouth  last  fall  that  he  did  not  care  for 
the  ram,  and  that  the  fortifications  ought  to  be  sufficient  to  hold  the 
place. 

A  few  days  since  he  informed  me  that  he  had  ninety  days’  supplies 
at  Plymouth.  The  garrison  there  was  about  2,200  strong. 

Nothing  can  be  more  ungenerous  and  unjust  than  to  make  the  Navy 
responsible  for  the  occupation  or  surrender  of  this  fortified  town. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

General:  Permit  me  to  renew  my  previous  suggestions  in  favor  of

Our  present  policy  of  occupying  detached  posts  struck  me  last  fall, 
and  more  so  now  than  then,  as  being  expensive,  insecure,  and  subject¬ 
ing  us  to  attack  in  detail,  whereas  if  we  occupied  one  good  position, 
the  concentration  of  our  land  and  naval  forces  would  better  enable  us 
to  act  our  part  of  prosecuting  the  war.  Naval  movements  necessarily 
follow  army  policy  in  this  matter,  as  we  can  not  withdraw  our  assist¬ 
ance  whilst  you  need  it  in  the  occupation  of  a  place. 

Matters  are  taking  the  same  critical  turn  here  as  in  the  sounds. 
The  enemy  are  trying  to  cut  off  our  positions  in  detail  and  to  reoccupy

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Ya.,  May  1 ,  1863. 

General:  I  had  the  honor  to  receive  on  the  27th  ultimo  your  inter¬ 
esting  and  instructive  communication  of  the  22d  ultimo,  giving  your 
views  respecting  the  occupation  of  posts  within  the  limits  of  your 
command. 

It  was  only  in  connection  with  the  occupation  of  such  posts  by  the 
Navy  as  a  part  of  their  defense  that  the  subject  claimed  my  official 
attention.  I  meant  in  my  communication  of  the  17th  to  refer  only  to 
positions  in  the  sounds  of  North  Carolina  and  not  to  Port  Macon  and 
Beaufort  Harbor,  the  defense  of  which,  and  of  Ilatteras  Inlet,  is  of 
obvious  necessity. 

As  to  Boanoke  Island,  I  supposed  it  best  that  the  abandoned  rebel 
works  there  should  be  razed  and  the  obstructions  in  Croatan  Sound 
removed.  Then  such  observation  or  police  as  should  prevent  attempts 
at  reconstruction  might  answer,  but  even  if  reoccupied  by  the  enemy, 
we  could,  if  there  were  not  too  many  other  places  to  guard,  concentrate 
and  dislodge  them. 

But  this  position  does  not  receive  naval  occupation  at  present,  and 
therefore  is  only  referred  to  in  view  of  future  demands. 

Your  views  in  respect  to  New  Berne,  Washington,  and  Plymouth 
possess  great  force.  Thej^  would  require  considerable  military  defenses, 
however,  to  accomplish  all  you  have  in  view.  They  are  sickly  places, 
Plymouth  especially.  The  enemy  can  build  gunboats  on  the  Tar, 
above  Washington,  and  on  the  Boanoke,  above  Plymouth,  though 
their  facilities  would  be  better  at  the  towns,  if  they  held  them.  The 
question  with  us  is,  How  many  places  can  we  profitably  hold,  comparing 
the  advantage  with  the  expense  of  possession?  We  do  not  hold  Eliza¬ 
beth  City,  Eden  ton,  Hertford,  Winfield,  etc.,  nor  does  the  enemy  derive 
any  visible  advantage  from  having  access  to  them. 

My  general  view  of  our  policy  is  to  take  places  which  the  enemy  has 
fortified,  to  level  his  works  of  defense,  and  then  to  leave  these  places 
as  they  were  before  the  rebellion,  unless  they  are  of  particular  military 
importance,  in  which  case  they  would  require  and  justify  proper  de¬ 
fenses.  Where  a  place  is  held,  it  seems  to  me  that  the  military  occu¬ 
pation  ought  to  be  as  complete  as  practicable  in  itself,  and  when  this 
cannot  be  done,  the  occupation  becomes  one  of  questionable  propriety 
to  the  extent  that  gunboats  are  permanently  needed  for  its  defense. 

I  do  not  desire  or  attempt  to  interfere  with  your  military  plans,  and 
1  fully  appreciate  the  good  spirit  in  which  you  favor  me  with  your  views. 
It  is  certainly  my  wish  and  purpose  to  cooperate  heartily  with  you.  I 
shall  be  glad  if  this  interchange  of  ideas  will  lead  to  such  an  examina¬ 
tion  of  the  subject  as  will  show,  in  connection  with  each  necessary 
military  occupation,  precisely  what  kind  and  extent  of  naval  force  is 
required  in  the  sounds.

It  appears  to  me  that  the  naval  part  of  oar  policy5  there  is  to  have 
such  a  force  as  can  cooperate  in  expeditious  with  the  army,  and  in  the 
meantime,  by  cruising  and  as  guard  vessels,  preserve  the  blockade  and 
the  police  of  the  waters. 

Should  the  enemy  build  gunboats  on  the  rivers  above  the  towns,  the 
naval  force  should  be  sufficient  to  destroy  his  vessels  before  they  unite 
or  after  they  have  combined. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  very  respectfully,  yours,

General  Foster  informed  me  on  his  arrival  at  Fortress  Monroe  to 
succeed  General  Dix  that  half  the  gunboats  in  the  sounds  might  be 
withdrawn,  they  being  no  longer  necessary  here  for  military  purposes,

Proposed,  joint  expedition  against  Richmond. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  lee,  IJ.  S.  Navy. 

Confidential.] 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Newport  News ,  Va.,  April  25,  1864. 

Sir:  General  Butler’s  plan  requires  a  powerful  cooperating  naval 
force  to  cover  his  landing,  protect  his  position,  and  keep  open  his  com¬ 
munications.  His  plan  is  so  dependent  on  naval  support,  and  requires 
so  much  of  it,  that  the  naval  force  should  be  so  sufficient  as,  under  cir¬ 
cumstances,  to  insure  his  safety. 

The  enemy  have  three  ironclads,  a  number  of  small  gunboats  and 
torpedo  boats,  and,  it  is  believed,  some  rams. 

Four  ironclads  capable  of  ascending  the  upper  James  is  the  least 
number  necessary.  Two  more  such  ironclads  would  be  only  prudent 
provision  for  the  security  of  the  army. 

We  should  have  ten  or  a  dozen  good  double-enders,  several  more 
good  tugs,  two  more  good  steam  transports  (light  drafts  of  speed  like 
the  Mary  Ann  would  answer  this  purpose),  and  three  or  four  ordnance 
schooners. 

I  say  nothing  of  ironclad  rams  and  torpedo  vessels,  only  because  it 
will  be  impracticable  now  to  obtain  them. 

A  careful  consideration  of  the  situation  would  soon  satisfy  the 
Department  that  the  force  I  ask  for  is  only  a  proper  provision  to  meet 
the  necessities  of  the  case. 

The  army  preparation  is  progressing  rapidly,  judging  from  the 
arrival  ot  troops  from  the  South,  and  I  fear  delay  will  be  experienced 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  691 

from  tlie  want  of  naval  preparation.  This  movement,  considering  its 
character,  lias  been  sprung  rather  suddenly. 

1  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Gomdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  G. 

P.  S.— -I  am  just  informed  by  General  Butler  that  the  expedition  is 
to  be  ready  for  the  30th  instant. 


Letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  IT.  S.  N  avy,  to  Major-General  Butler,  TJ.  S.  Army. 

Confidential.]  Flagship  Minnesota, 

Newport  Neics,  Va.,  April  25,  1864. 

General  :  I  will  thank  you  to  inform  me  of  the  extent  and  charac¬ 
ter  of  the  joint  expedition  which  you  propose  to  make,  showing  the 
exact  service  which  you  expect  the  navy  to  render,  the  time  when  and 
the  points  to  which  the  different  military  and  naval  movements  are  to 
be  made,  and  the  assistance  which  the  army  will  give  the  navy  in 
taking  and  holding  the  different  positions  deemed  necessary  (which 
should  be  named),  the  number  and  kind  of  transports  requiring  convoy 
and  protection,  where  to,  and  when.  In  a  word,  to  give  me  such  fuil 
and  perfect  information  in  writing  as  will  enable  the  Navy  Department 
fully  to  understand  the  nature  of  the  service  to  be  performed,  to  ascer¬ 
tain  its  ability  to  furnish  the  means  needed,  and  to  enable  me  to  make 
timely  professional  dispositions. 

I  send  this  by  Fleet  Captain  Barnes,  my  chief  of  staff,  and  solicit  an 
early  reply. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Gomdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Major-General  B.  F.  Butler, 

Gomdg.  Dept,  of  Virginia  and  North  Carolina,  Fortress  Monroe. 


Letter  from  Major-General  Butler,  U.  S.  Army,  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Confidential.]  Headquarters  18th  Army  Corps, 

Dept,  of  Virginia  and  North  Carolina, 

Fortress  Monroe,  April  25,  1864. 

Admiral  :  As  I  had  the  honor  to  suggest  to  you  in  a  personal  inter¬ 
view,  in  which  we  had  the  pleasure  of  interchanging  views  upon  the 
subject,  it  is  intended  to  land  at  City  Point  and  above  on  the  south 
side  of  James  River,  below  a  place  called  Osborne’s  at  the  head  of 
Farrar’s  Island,  a  force  of  30,000  to  35,000  men,  with  the  necessary  sup¬ 
plies,  artillery,  and  trains. 

To  this  purpose  it  is  proposed  to  use  the  Appomattox  as  far  up  as 
Port  Walthall  as  a  convenient  rendezvous  for  transports. 

To  move  this  force  will  take  a  fleet  of  about  fifty  transports,  beside* 
some  thirty  schooners  and  barges  for  landing  and  other  purposes. 

From  this  position  it  is  contemplated  to  move  along  the  south  side  of 

the  James  River  upon  Richmond,  in  cooperation  with  General - ’s 

army. 

To  effect  this  landing  and  keep  the  position,  it  is  expected  that  the 
navy  will  hold  the  James  River  above  Farrar’s  Island  and  the  Appo¬ 
mattox  above  Port  Walthall  free  from  all  attacks  by  rebel  water  craft, 


692 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


at  all  hazards,  as  upon  this  depends  the  success,  and  indeed  the  safety 
of  the  expedition. 

In  order  to  prevent  annoyance  by  the  enemy  as  well  of  the  transports 
as  the  naval  vessels,  it  is  prepared  to  seize  and  hold  Fort  Powhatan 
and  Wilson’s  Wharf,  nearly  opposite  each  other  on  the  James  River, 
which  are  supposed  to  be  the  only  bluffs  or  high  points  below  City 
Point  from  which  we  can  be  substantially  annoyed  by  the  enemy’s  light 
artillery  or  sharpshooters. 

It  is  proposed  to  start  a  flying  column  on  board  transports,  with 
means  of  effecting  a  landing,  and  seize  Wilson’s  Wharf  and  Fort 
Powhatan  and  leave  an  adequate  force  there  to  intrench  the  same, 
thence  proceeding  upward  to  seize  City  Point  and  commence  landings 
on  both  sides  of  the  Appomattox,  while  the  navy  take  and  hold 
Osborne’s,  as  indicated  above. 

The  navy  will  be  expected  to  cover  the  landings  at  each  of  the  places 
indicated  by  its  guns,  and  to  aid  by  a  flanking  fire  the  army  in  holding 
its  positions  until  intrenched. 

As  the  movement  is  to  be  in  the  nature  of  a  surprise,  it  will  be 
necessary  for  the  naval  vessels  to  go  up  with  the  leading  column  of 
army  transports  with  the  utmost  celerity,  so  that  the  several  positions 
indicated  may  be  taken  both  by  the  land  and  naval  forces  before  the 
enemy  can  concentrate  opposition. 

The  commanding  general  offers  the  use  of  the  armed  boats  of  the 
army,  being  of  very  light  draft,  to  precede  the  naval  force  and  draw¬ 
ing  the  river  for  torpedoes  or  obstructions,  as  their  loss  (if  so  unfortu¬ 
nate)  would  not  be  so  serious  as  a  loss  of  more  valuable  naval  vessels 
with  their  armament;  to  be,  if  desired,  under  your  orders. 

It  is  required  by  the  commanding  general  of  the  army  that  the  joint 
expedition  must  be  ready  for  this  movement  at  a  date  not  later  than 
the  30th  instant. 

Alter  the  landing  is  effected,  in  the  ulterior  operations  as  well  as 
before,  the  army  will  expect  to  render  all  the  aid  and  cooperation  in  its 
power  to  the  navy  to  enable  it  to  clear  the  river  of  water  craft  and 
obstructions,  and  to  receive  that  hearty  and  genial  cooperation  from 
the  navy  which  the  commanding  general  has  always  had  the  good  for¬ 
tune  to  receive  from  the  navy,  such  as  protecting  his  water  transporta¬ 
tion  and  covering  his  flanks  when  lying  on  the  river,  so  that  the  great 
objective  point,  the  capture  of  Richmond,  may  be  the  joint  enterprise 
of  the  united  services  of  the  army  and  navy. 

I  believe,  admiral,  I  have  answered  each  one  of  the  propositions 
contained  in  your  note  of  to-day  with  as  much  particularity  and  dis¬ 
tinctness  as  the  subject-matter  will  admit,  and  upon  which  and  every 
point  and  part  of  which  I  would  desire  to  interchange  views  with 
you  in  person,  and  to  do  so  will  hold  myself  in  readiness  to  meet  you 
when  and  where  you  will  honor  me  with  an  appointment  for  that  pur¬ 
pose. 

I  desire  specially  to  call  your  attention  to  the  question  whether  you 
can  hold  the  point  at  Osborne’s  as  against  the  rebel  water  craft,  as  that 
is  vital,  or  whether  I  shall  make  provision  to  aid  you  by  sinking 
obstructions  in  the  channel  or  such  other  devices  as  engineering  skill 
shall  suggest. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benjamin  F.  Butler, 

Major-  General ,  Commanding. 

Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Flagship  Minnesota.

Letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Major-General  Butler,  U.  S.  Army. 

Confidential.]  Hampton  Roads,  Virginia,  April  27, 1864. 

General  :  I  received  late  on  the  night  of  this  date  your  confidential 
communication  of  the  25th  instant,  referring  to  our  previous  interview 
and  giving  me  more  fully  your  views  respecting  the  movements  you 
contemplate,  and  including  the  Appomattox  to  Port  Walthall  as  part 
of  the  base  of  your  operations.  This  plan  was,  in  our  interview  yes¬ 
terday  with  the  Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  modified  in  this,  that 
you  abandoned  the  idea  of  landing  troops  or  sending  your  transports 
above  City  Point  on  James  River. 

I  have  the  Onondaga ,  and  I  expect  also  three  monitor  ironclads,  and 
with  these  I  shall  be  able  to  cooperate  with  you  as  far  up  James  River 
as  this  draft  and  the  depth  of  water  will  allow  them  to  go,  viz,  to 
Trent’s  Reach,  in  which  there  are  but  8^  feet  of  water.  Our  ironclads 
can  not  enter  or  operate  in  the  Appomattox,  but  I  can  cooperate  with 
you  in  small  wooden  vessels  to  Broadway,  and  perhaps  as  high  as  Point 
of  Rocks,  if  there  are  no  obstructions  in  the  river,  or  rifle  pits  on  the 
banks  to  drive  the  men  from  their  guns  on  these  open-deck  vessels,  or 
batteries  with  which  such  vessels  can  not  contend. 

The  ironclads  can,  barring  accidents,  average  5  knots  per  hour  to 
Harrison’s  Bar,  which  is  50  miles  above  Newport  News.  They  require 
high  water  by  day  to  cross  that  bar.  The  river  at  Harrison’s  Bar, 
before  City  Point,  in  the  Appomattox,  and  from  City  Point  to  Farrar’s 
Island,  requires  to  be  examined  for  torpedoes,  and  if  we  meet  with  no 
resistance  this  can  be  done  by  day,  and  in  part  of  a  day. 

I  thankfully  accept  the  offer  of  your  light-drafts  to  act  under  my 
orders  in  the  performance  of  this  important  duty. 

The  engineering  device  of  defense  by  obstructions  (the  means  of 
making  which  you  kindly  propose  to  provide)  above  the  ironclads  in 
James  River  would  materially  aid  in  preventing  the  success  of  attempts 
to  blow  them  up,  and  of  surprise  by  torpedo  vessels  and  fire  rafts. 
The  confusion  and  loss  which  would  inevitably  ensue  among  your  numer¬ 
ous  transports  crowded  in  the  river,  in  the  event  of  such  an  alarm, 
would  be  very  serious. 

I  would  suggest  Trent’s  Reach  or  Dutch  Gap  as  a  good  location  for 
such  obstructions. 

1  do  not  see  clearly  how  such  a  movement  can  be  made  a  surprise,  as 
the  enemy  has  a  signal  corps  in  operation  along  James  River. 

I  would  respectfully  suggest  that  the  occupation  of  Dutch  Gap,  which 
is  high  and  narrow,  would  be  a  great  advantage  to  us,  and  that  a  body 
of  skirmishers  to  laud,  clear,  and  picket  the  bluffs  on  the  left  bank, 
between  Eppes  Island  and  Farrar’s  Island,  would  be  a  very  desirable 
protection  to  the  gunboats  against  sharpshooters  and  torpedo  operators. 

The  wooden  gunboat  force  expected  is  not  so  large  as  I  have  desired. 
It  will,  however,  I  hope,  be  sufficient  to  give  the  convoy  required  and 
assist  the  ironclads  in  covering  the  landings  contemplated. 

Be  assured,  general,  that  intelligent  and  hearty  cooperation  is  the 
first  wish  of  myself,  and  will  be  the  effort  of  the  officers  and  men  of 
my  command. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  serv¬ 
ant, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Actg.  Bear- Admiral,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Major-General  Benjamin  F.  Butler, 

Comdg.  Dept,  of  Virginia  and  North  Carolina,  Fortress  Monroe.

Report  of  Commander  Davenport ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  presence  in 
the  sounds  of  Brigadier- General  Graham ,  U.  S.  Army. 

XL  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne ,  N.  C.,  April  25 ,  1864. 
Admiral:  Brigadier-General  Graham  is  here,  and  as  he  ranks  me  I 
should  like  to  be  informed  who  commands  the  gunboats  in  the  sounds. 
You  are  aware  that  your  predecessor  appointed  me  as  a  commander  and 
senior  naval  officer  in  the  sounds  of  North  Carolina.  I  can  not  under¬ 
stand  how  anyone  can  be  afloat  in  the  sounds  not  belonging  to  the 
Navy  who  has  an  independent  command. 

I  simply  call  this  to  your  attention.  I  have  not,  nor  do  I  intend  to, 
if  possible,  have  the  slightest  jar  with  the  Army.  Will  you  be  good 
enough  to  inform  me  how  I  stand  with  army  gunboats'? 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  K.  Davenport, 

Commander ,  etc. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Commander  Davenport ,  IT.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  orders  issued  to 

officers  under  his  command. 

U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne ,  N.  G.,  April  25,  1864. 

Admiral  :  In  reply  to  your  letter  of  the  21st  instant,  I  have  to  inform 
you  that  I  have  sent  Lieutenant-Commander  Truxtun  to  Albemarle 
Sound,  with  orders  not  to  let  the  ram  come  out  of  the  Roanoke  River. 
I  have  no  torpedoes,  and  do  not  know  how  to  make  them. 

I  think  it  best  that  Commander  Renshaw  should  remain  at  Washing¬ 
ton.  We  are  expecting  an  attack  there  hourly,  and  he  is  so  well 
acquainted  there  that  he  could  not  well  be  spared. 

I  think  that  Captain  French  will  do  well  in  the  Miami,  and  I  have 
ordered  him  to  remain  in  command  of  her. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  K.  Davenport, 

Commander  and  Senior  Naval  Officer  in  Sounds  of  North  Carolina. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  French,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding 
the  arrival  of  launches  from  the  Chowan  River,  prepared  for  coopera¬ 
tion  with  the  Confederate  ram. 

U.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Albemarle  Sound ,  North  Carolina,  April  25,  1864. 
Sir  :  After  sending  my  dispatch  this  morning  I  went  on  board  the 
Massasoit  and  proceeded  to  Edenton,  in  company  with  the  U.  S.  S. 
Ceres,  to  put  the  women  and  children  ashore.  I  communicated  with 
the  shore,  and  learned  from  Mr.  Bond  and  Mr.  Bland,  two  very  reliable 
gentlemen,  that  last  Thursday  night  there  were  thirteen  launches 
brought  down  from  Cold-rain  [Colerain],  on  Chowan  River,  about  25 
miles  above,  each  being  armed  with  a  howitzer,  and  the  whole  manned 


696 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


by  300  men,  which  are  intended  to  cooperate  with  the  ram,  and  I  learn 
that  they  are  now  quartered  in  the  mouth  of  the  Casliie  River  and 
Simon  [Salmon]  Creek. 

Being  in  possession  of  this  information  I  deem  it  proper  to  dispatch 
the  Massasoit  with  this  letter  to-night.  Under  the  circumstances  I  con¬ 
sider  it  improper  to  send  boats  on  picket  at  the  mouth  of  the  river.,  and 
I  have  ordered  the  steamers  to  be  kept  underway  at  night. 

In  my  communication  to-day  I  requested  that  you  would  send  the 
General  Jesup  back,  if  possible,  but  if  you  have  not  obtained  her,  I 
beg  to  call  your  attention  to  the  necessity  of  having  one  or  two  more 
steamers  as  soon  as  possible.  My  object  in  making  the  suggestion  for 
more  boats  is,  that  I  may  be  able  to  keep  a  more  extended  line  and 
watch  the  movements  at  the  mouth  of  both  rivers,  and  not  that  1  am 
afraid  of  being  captured.  I  did  not  have  time  to  make  the  reconnois- 
sance  proposed,  but  I  learned  at  Edenton  that  a  battery  had  been 
erected  at  the  mouth  of  Chowan  River,  on  its  left  bank.  I  shall  go  up 
in  the  morning,  and  if  I  And  the  enemy  at  work,  or  guns  in  position,  I 
shall  shell  them  out. 

Please  send  the  Massasoit  back  immediately. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  A.  French, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant. 

Lieutenant-Commander  W.  T.  Truxtun, 

U.  8.  8.  Tacony ,  Roanolce  Island ,  North  Carolina.

vessels  of  his  command. 


U.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne ,  N.  C.,  April  25 ,  1864. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  semimonthly 
statement  of  the  disposition  of  vessels  in  the  sounds  for  term  ending  at 
date: 

April  11. — The  Ceres  left  for  Plymouth. 

April  15. — The  Tacony  left  for  Plymouth. 

April  17. — The  Seymour  arrived  from  Roanoke  Island. 

April  18. — The  Tacony  arrived  from  Plymouth.  The  Seymour  sailed 
for  Roanoke  Island. 

April  19. — The  Southfield  was  sunk  by  rebel  ram. 

April  20. — The  Ceres  arrived  from  Plymouth. 

April  22. — Seymour  arrived  from  Roanoke  Island.  Ceres  sailed  for 
Albemarle  Sound. 

April  24. — Seymour  sailed  for  Roanoke  Island.  The  Tacony ,  Miami , 
and  Whitehead  are  in  Albemarle  Sound.  The  Louisiana  and  Valley 
City  are  at  Washington.  The  Hetzel ,  Commodore  Hull ,  and  Lockwood 
are  at  New  Berne.  The  Seymour  is  at  Roanoke  Island,  and  the  Granite 
is  at  Hatteras  Inlet. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  K.  Davenport, 

Commander  and  Senior  Naval  Officer  in  Sounds  of  North  Carolina .

Report  of  Acting  Master  Sheldon,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  chase  of  a 
boat  in  James  River  and  engagement  with  the  enemy. 

U.  S.  S.  Shokokon, 

TJp  James  River,  April  26,  1864. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  submit  the  following  report: 

At  3:30  p.  m.  this  day,  saw  a  boat  under  sail  steering  out  from  the 
shore  about  the  vicinity  of  Day’s  Point  (James  River),  apparently  for 
the  purpose  of  crossing  the  river.  I  immediately  started  in  pursuit. 
The  boat  on  discovering  us  to  be  in  chase  of  her,  turned  back  and  ran 
in  by  Rock  Wharf.  I  steamed  up  to  abreast  of  the  wharf,  and  not  seeing 
anyone,  I  cautiously  steamed  inshore  for  the  purpose  of  discovering 
torpedoes,  if  any  should  be  there;  got  to  within  350  yards  of  the  shore, 
when  we  received  a  volley  of  musketry  from  a  concealed  enemy  in  the 
woods  on  the  bank  of  the  river,  and  for  a  short  time  they  kept  up  a 
very  sharp  tire.  I  immediately  returned  their  tire  with  our  30-pounder 
Parrotts  and  howitzers,  throwing  shell  and  shrapnel  in  where  they  were 
concealed ;  in  a  short  time  silenced  their  tire,  saw  them  leave  and  take 
shelter  behind  a  blutf,  where  we  could  not  reach  them.  No  one  was 
hurt  on  this  ship,  although  many  of  their  shot  passed  across  the  deck 
and  several  struck  the  side ;  could  not  tell  whether  any  of  the  enemy  were 
hit,  as  the  brush  hid  them  from  our  view. 

Officers  and  men  behaved  well.  I  should  suppose  by  the  rapidity  of 
their  tire  that  there  were  from  50  to  75  of  the  enemy  at  the  time  they 
opened  on  us. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  B.  Sheldon, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Captain  G-.  Gansevoort, 

Senior  Officer  off  Newport  News,  Va.

II.  S.  S.  Fort  Jackson, 

Off  Fortress  Monroe,  April  26,  1864. 

Sir:  In  my  communication  of  17th  instant,  informed  you  that  I  had 
detained  the  Mount  Vernon  temporarily  at  New  Inlet,  to  strengthen 
the  blockade  there.  On  the  25th,  other  vessels  having  arrived  from 
Beaufort,  I  relieved  her  from  that  detention  and  she  is  now  on  the  out¬ 
side  blockade,  in  conjunction  with  the  Monticello ,  to  intercept  Bermuda 
runners. 

When  I  left  New  Inlet  there  were  present  there  the  following  vessels: 
Tuscarora,  Kansas,  Cambridge ,  Niphon,  Howquah,  and  Falikee.  The 
Grand  Gulf  expected  there  that  evening.  The  Calypso  had  reported, 
and  I  detained  her  for  the  Western  Bar,  where  were  the  Dacotali,  Mar- 
atanza ,  Aries,  and  Emma.  The  Vicksburg  expected  daily. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 


B.  F.  Sands,

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Captain  Sands,  TJ.  S. 
Navy,  in  view  of  the  weakened  condition  of  the  Wilmington  blockade  on 
account  of  the  defense  of  Beaufort  Harbor,  N.  C. 

Flagship  Minnesota, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  April  26,  1864. 
Sir:  Send  to  General  Butler,  with  lists,  the  refugees  and  the  persons 
captured  near  Wilmington  on  the  21st  instant,  and  inform  the  general 
that  I  will  write  to  him  on  the  subject. 

Then  proceed  to  the  Gosport  navy  yard  with  the  Fort  Jackson,  ask 
Commodore  Livingston  in  my  name  to  give  you  every  facility  to  coal, 
and  take  in  your  supplies  with  dispatch,  when  return  to  Beaufort. 
Confer  with  and  instruct  Commander  Dove  and  make  the  necessary 
naval  disposition  from  without  and  within  for  insuring  the  safety  of 
thgt  harbor  against  boat  raids  or  land  attacks  by  the  enemy.  Use  for 
this  purpose  only  so  much  of  the  blockading  force  as  may  be  absolutely 
necessary.  The  blockade  must  be  effectively  kept ;  meanwhile  I  have

699 


desired  Captain  Smith  to  send,  if  he  can  possibly  spare  them,  the  Com¬ 
modore  Barney  (ferryboat,  well  armed)  and  one  or  two  light  vessels 
from  the  sounds  to  aid  in  the  protection  of  Beaufort  Harbor. 

The  sailors  from  our  already  weakly  manued  blockaders,  which  Com¬ 
mander  Dove  had  sent  to  Fort  Macon  and  the  forts  at  Morehead  City, 
I  have  ordered  him  to  have  returned  to  their  vessels,  and  these  sent 
back  to  the  blockade,  reserving  one  or  two  only,  unless  more  are  abso¬ 
lutely  necessary  for  the  defense  of  Beaufort. 

I  regret  to  hear  from  you  that  there  are  nine  blockaders  detained  in 
Beaufort,  and  that  there  are  but  three  vessels  off  Wilmington;  this  is 
very  wrong.  It  is  of  the  utmost  public  account  that  the  blockade 
of  W  ilmington  should  be  very  good  at  this  time  when  supplies  are  of  so 
much  consequence  to  the  enemy.  Let  Captain  Frailey,  or  some  other 
vigilant  officer,  have  charge  of  the  defense  of  Beaufort,  if  you  think 
it  best  to  be  off  Wilmington  in  person,  which  I  think  is  the  preferable 
plan. 

I  have,  and  shall  again,  call  General  Butler’s  attention  to  the  great 
importance  of  providing  proper  military  means  for  the  security  of 
Beaufort  Harbor,  and  I  have  asked  him  to  put  some  of  the  light  army 
gunboats  at  the  disposition  of  the  Navy  for  this  purpose.  Do  the  best 
with  the  naval  means  at  command  to  keep  the  blockade  of  Wilmington 
strictly  to  provide  for  the  security  of  Beaufort. 

Return  with  dispatch. 

Respectfully,  yours, 


S.  P.  Lee, 

A ctg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Captain  Smith ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Mattabesett, 

of  arrival  in  Pamlico  Sound. 

IT.  S.  S.  Mattabesett, 

Pamlico  Sound,  April  26,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  arrived  here  this  morning,  having  been  delayed  by  a  southeast 
gale,  in  which  the  Wyalusingwas  somewhat  strained,  and  could  scarcely 
be  kept  free  by  her  pumps.  Had  the  gale  continued  six  hours  she  would 
have  lightened  at  the  expense  of  guns  and  ammunition. 

This  vessel  made  better  weather,  but  the  contract  ironwork  proved 
very  defective  and  the  copper  below  the  first  streak  hangs  in  rags,  and 
in  several  places  is  entirely  gone.  The  eccentric  is  also  out  of  order, 
and  the  vessel  can  be  propelled  but  one  way.  The  ram  has  not  been 
seen  since  her  first  exploit,  but  from  what  information  I  can  gather  here, 
she  is  guarding  Plymouth.  I  am  on  the  Swash,  and  expect  to  get  over 
the  next  tide.  The  Sassacus  succeeded  in  crossing  this  morning,  and 
was  bound  for  New  Berne. 

The  Miami  and  Tacony  are  off  Plymouth ;  the  Hetzel  and  Valley  City 
are  at  New  Berne. 

The  engineer  of  the  Onondaga  is  perfectly  acquainted  with  the  con¬ 
struction  of  the  engines  of  these  vessels,  and  as  the  machinery  of  the 
Onondaga  is  in  perfect  order,  and  the  first  assistant  a  valuable  and  intelli¬ 
gent  engineer,  I  should  be  pleased  if  you  would  allow  Mr.  Henderson  to

Report  of  Commander  Davenport ,  U,  S.  Navy ,  regarding  expected  attack 

from  all  points. 

FT.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne ,  N.  C .,  April  26 ,  1864. 

Admiral  :  The  Sassacus  and  Commodore  Barney  arrived  this  morn¬ 
ing,  and  I  received  your  letters. 

I  think  that  Commander  Benshaw  can  be  of  more  service  at  Wash¬ 
ington  than  in  Albemarle  Sound. 

General  Palmer  informed  me  this  morning  confidentially  that  he 
intended  to  withdraw  most  of  the  force  from  Washington,  leaving  only 
enough  to  make  a  show.  I  have  directed  Commander  Benshaw  to  send  all 
the  stores  belonging  to  the  Navy,  including  ammunition,  to  this  place. 

From  the  best  information,  the  enemy  is  very  active  in  his  movements, 
and  we  expect  an  attack  from  all  points  at  any  moment. 

I  enclose  you  two  general  orders  from  the  army. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  K.  Davenport, 
Commander ,  V.  S.  Navy ,  etc. 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  S.  P.  Lee,

Letter  from  Acting  Bear- Admiral  Lee ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Major-General 
Butler,  V.  S.  Army ,  regarding  indications  of  a  vigorous  campaign  by 
the  enemy  in  North  Carolina. 

Flagship  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron, 

Hampton  Roads,  Virginia,  Axnil  27,  1864. 
General:  Captain  Sands,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Fort  Jackson,  reports 
to  me  that  on  tbe  night  of  the  22d  instant  he  sent  two  boats  on  shore 
near  New  Inlet  to  reconnoiter  Myrtle  Sound  and  vicinity  and  obtain 
information  in  regard  to  the  strength  and  position  of  the  enemy.  The 
party  was  guided  by  a  refugee  named  Pucket,  who  was  picked  up  some 
days  previously,  and  acted  also  asguidein  the  expedition  that  destroyed 
the  State  salt  works  near  Masonboro  on  the  21st  instant.  The  officer 
in  charge  of  the  party  was  conducted  by  this  man  to  the  house  of  a 
lieutenant  in  the  Masonboro  Home  Guard  named  Eli  H.  Davis,  who 
came  off  with  them  and  furnished  the  following  information  in  sub¬ 
stance  :  That  the  present  force  in  Fort  Fisher  and  the  batteries  adjacent 
consists  of  about  1,000  men,  and  the  force  in  and  around  Wilmington 
about  2,000,  General  Beauregard  and  General  Whiting  commanding; 
in  addition  to  which  some  300  conscripts,  who  had  been  employed  at 
the  salt  works,  were  sent  there  after  these  works  were  destroyed;  that 
Wilmington  could,  in  his  opinion,  be  taken  with  little  difficulty  now  by 
lauding  troops  at  Masonboro  and  marching  across.  The  distance  is 
short  and  the  road  good  and  undefended.  The  batteries  at  Wilming¬ 
ton  mount  but  about  ten  or  fifteen  guns,  and  they  u  old-fashioned  smooth¬ 
bores.”  He  does  not  state  their  caliber.  When  the  firing  at  the  salt 
works  on  the  21st  was  heard  at  Wilmington  it  was  supposed  there  that 
an  attack  on  that  place  was  intended,  and  troops  that  had  been  dis¬ 
patched  to  Swansboro  and  the  sounds  were  recalled.  The  number  of 
these  is  not  stated,  nor  whether  they  are  included  in  the  estimate  given 
of  the  troops  at  Wilmington  and  vicinity. 

Mr.  Davis  further  says  that  the  high  prices  of  provisions  and  conse¬ 
quent  suffering  have  made  the  people  tired  of  the  war,  and  that  many 
of  them  will  be  glad  to  see  our  forces  in  possession. 

I  desire  to  call  your  serious  attention  to  these  statements.  The  pres¬ 
ence  at  Wilmington  of  a  general  so  highly  esteemed  by  the  rebels  as 
Beauregard,  the  sending  of  troops  from  Wilmington  to  Swansboro,  the 
recent  attack  on  Plymouth,  and  the  increase  of  the  force  of  the  rebels 
in  all  the  eastern  part  of  North  Carolina  indicate,  I  think,  their  deter¬ 
mination  to  push  the  campaign  in  that  region  with  vigor,  possibly  to 
attack  both  Beaufort  and  New  Berne. 

The  presence  of  the  enemy  at  Swansboro  has  made  an  increase  of  the 
force  at  Fort  Macon  and  Morehead  City  requisite,  and  Commander 
Dove,  commanding  naval  station  at  Beaufort,  lias  taken  men  from  the 
blockading  vessels  to  man  these  points.  But  the  necessities  of  the 


702 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


blockade  and  the  weakness  of  the  crews  of  the  blockading  vessels  has 
compelled  me  to  order  that  these  men  be  returned  to  their  ships. 

The  possession  of  Beaufort  and  New  Berne  is  of  such  manifest  impor¬ 
tance  that  I  deem  it  necessary  only  to  call  your  attention  to  the  condi¬ 
tion  of  affairs  in  that  region. 

I  shall  issue  orders  to  the  senior  officer  off  Wilmington  to  use  every 
exertion  to  obtain  information  and  to  forward  it  as  soon  as  received. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee, 

Act.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Major-General  B.  F.  Butler,

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Break,  U.  8.  Navy,  regarding  an 
engagement  near  Masonboro  Inlet ,  North  Carolina ,  April  27  and  29, 
1864. 

U.  S.  S.  Niphon, 

Off  New  Inlet ,  North  Carolina,  April  29,  1864. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  morning  of  April  27, 
while  close  inshore  near  Masonboro  Inlet,  discovered  a  boat,  stood  for 
her,  found  8  negro  refugees  in  her,  one  of  which  shipped  on  board  this 
vessel  for  three  years,  the  other  7  were  transferred  on  board  the 
IT.  S.  S.  Fahkee  at  the  request  of  Acting  Master  [F.  B.]  Webb,  who 
shipped  them  for  three  years.  While  taking  on  board  these  refugees 
six  pieces  of  field  artillery  opened  on  us,  but  the  shell  fell  short.  We 
immediately  went  to  quarters,  threw  shell  among  them  and  drove  them 
away,  two  of  our  shell  exploding  in  the  steam  sawmill  on  shore  and  set 
it  on  lire.  On  the  morning  of  the  29th  the  enemy  opened  lire  on  us 
with  two  Whitworth  guns,  the  shot  passing  over  us;  stood  inshore  and 
shelled  them  and  also  a  company  of  cavalry,  who  were  driven  away 
into  the  woods. 

There  appears  to  be  a  large  body  of  the  enemy  located  at  Masonboro. 
The  refugees  state  that  there  is  great  excitement  at  Wilmington,  and 
on  Sunday  last  when  they  left  that  place  all  the  citizens  were  under 
arms,  expecting  an  attack. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  B.  Breck, 

Commanding  TJ.  8.  8.  Nip hon. 

Commander  W.  A.  PARKER, 

Senior  Officer  Present.

Report  of  Commander  Davenport,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  affairs  in  Alhe- 

marle  Sound ,  and  transmitting  orders  to  Lieuteoiaoit-Comonaoider  Roe, 

U.  S.  Navy. 

IT.  S.  S.  Hetzel, 

Off  New  Berne ,  N.  C.,  April  28,  1864. 

Admiral:  I  am  in  receipt  of  your  letter  of  the  22d  instant. 

There  is  no  news  of  importance  from  Albemarle  Sound.  The  Tacooiy 
returned  to  this  place  this  morning  to  repair  boilers.  A  boiler  maker 
has  been  sent  from  Philadelphia  to  do  the  work,  and  Captain  Truxtun 
came  here  for  better  facilities. 

I  have  sent  the  Sassacus  to  Albemarle  Sound.  I  enclose  a  copy  of 
my  orders  to  Lieutenant-Commander  Itoe. 

General  Palmer  has  decided  to  evacuate  Washington,  [FT.  C.],  and  as 
this  is  rather  a  delicate  movement  to  be  executed  in  the  face  of  the 
enemy,  I  have  decided  to  keep  Commander  Eenshaw  here  until  the 
troops,  citizens,  and  stores  are  all  removed.  Agreeably  to  General 
Palmer’s  request,  I  have  sent  the  Coonmodore  Barney  and  Commodore 
Hull  there  to  render  what  assistance  they  can,  to  give  our  troops  confi¬ 
dence,  and  intimidate  the  enemy. 

I  understand  they  were  hard  pushed  at  Washington  last  night,  the 
enemy  being  in  large  force.  I  expect  New  Berne  will  be  attacked  as 
soon  as  they  get  through  there. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

as  senior  officer.

the  Roanoke  River  and,  in  case  she  should  get  out,  to  destroy  her.

enclosed  letter  from  him,  and  keep  me  constantly  advised  of  the  state

Headquarters  District  of  North  Carolina, 

New  Berne,  N.  C.,  April  27,  1864. 

Sir:  I  yesterday  made  you  acquainted  with  my  plans  for  evacuating 
Little  Washington.  Transports  were  sent  there  to  bring  away  the 
forces  and  stores  as  quietly  as  possible.  This  morning,  however,  heavy 
firing  has  been  reported  in  the  direction  of  Washington,  [N.  C.J,  and  it 
may  be  that  they  are  attacked  there. 

If  you  have  a  gunboat  that  can  be  spared  to  go  to  Washington,  I 
will  be  much  obliged  to  you  if  you  would  send  her.  She  could  be  use¬ 
ful  in  carrying  dispatches  up,  and  she  may  be  very  much  needed,  either 
for  assisting  in  the  defense  or  in  the  bringing  away  of  the  men  and 
stores. 

If  you  will  direct  Captain  Renshaw  to  let  his  forces  assist  in  remov¬ 
ing  the  guns  and  in  bringing  them  here,  it  would  materially  assist  us, 
as  we  have  but  four  transports  now  here. 

Very  respectfully, 


I.  N.  Palmer, 

Brigadier-  General ,  Commanding. 

Commander  H.  K.  Davenport,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Naval  Forces ,  Sounds  of  North  Carolina.

U.  S.  S.  Louisiana, 

Off  Washington ,  [N.  C.},  April  28 ,  1864. 
Sir  :  The  Valley  City  could  have  been  sent  to  New  Berne  in  two  hours 
after  the  receipt  of  your  orders,  but  the  enemy  have  been  harassing 
our  lines  to  some  extent,  so  I  thought  it  prudent  to  keep  her  for  a  short 
time. 

The  Barney  has  arrived,  but  draws  too  much  water  to  come  up  and 
take  extra  guns  on  board;  the  Valley  City  the  same,  but  the  best  means 
shall  be  used,  although  it  is  quite  an  undertaking  to  move  great  guns 
with  the  enemy  about  us.  The  interests  of  the  Government  shall  be 
strictly  looked  to. 

I  am,  sir,  with  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  T.  Eenshaw,

Report  of  Lieutant- Commander  Babcock,  U.  8.  Navy ,  of  search  for  obstruc¬ 
tions  and  torpedoes  in  Pamunkey  and  Mattapony  rivers ,  Virginia. 

U.  S.  S.  Morse, 

Off  Yorktown,  Va.,  April  29,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  respectfully  report  that  yesterday,  by  the  request  of  Major- 
General  Smith,  commanding  army  forces  at  Yorktown,  got  underway, 
taking  the  Mystic  in  company  and  leaving  the  Crusader  as  guard  vessel 
off  Yorktown,  and  proceeded  up  the  river  for  the  purpose  of  finding  out 
if  it  was  clear  from  obstructions,  torpedoes,  etc.,  to  West  Point,  [Va.). 

1  was  informed  by  good  authority  that  torpedoes  had  been  placed 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


707 


only  a  few  days  since  near  the  wharves  both  in  the  Pamunkey  and 
Mattapony  rivers.  Arrived  at  the  mouth  of  the  Mattapony  Eiver  at  6 
p.  m.  and  proceeded  up  to  Shepherds  [Sheppard’s]  Landing;  found 
everything-  clear  for  lauding  troops.  Came  again  down  the  Mattapony 
Eiver  and  anchored  in  the  mouth  of  the  Pamunkey  Eiver,  the  Mystic 
anchoring  below. 

This  morning  at  5  a.  in.  again  got  underway,  swept  with  our  boats 
around  the  wharf  at  West  Point,  and  proceeded  up  the  Pamunkey 
Eiver  about  4  miles;  found  no  obstructions  whatever. 

At  10  a.  m.  returned  again  to  Yorktown  with  this  vessel  and  Mystic , 
and  reported  the  facts  to  Major-General  Smith. 

Being  short  of  coal,  Major-General  Smith  very  kindly  lent  me  the 
amount  I  needed. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  A.  Babcock,

[U.  S.  S.]  Louisiana, 

Off  Washington ,  N.  C.,  April  29,  1864. 

My  Dear  Davenport  :  I  am  fearful  that  some  demonstration  will 
be  made  on  New  Berne,  so  I  will  send  the  Valley  City,  as  she  may  be 
of  some  service.  She  can  carry  but  little  and  that  I  will  put  on  board 
for  the  army.  She  has  also  our  ammunition  on  board.  Colonel  Dut¬ 
ton  will  take  passage  in  her  with  a  rebel  deserter  who  has  given  us 
some  information,  such  as  it  may  be  worth.  The  enemy  appears  to 
have  left  us.

Flagship  Minnesota,

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Babcock,  U.  S.  Navy,  of  cooperation 
with  the  army  in  the  occupation  of  West  Point,  Va.,  April  30-May  1, 
1864. 

U.  S.  S.  Morse, 

Off  IF est  Point ,  Mattapony  River,  May  2,  1864. 
Sir  :  I  respectfully  report  that,  having  telegraphed  to  you  on  the 
evening  of  the  29th  ultimo  that  some  troops  were  about  to  proceed  from 
Yorktown  to  West  Point,  and  that  Major-General  Smith  requested  the 
aid  of  the  gunboats  to  cover  his  landing  and  protect  them  while  at  this 
point,  when,  on  the  morning  of  the  30th,  I  received  your  communi¬ 
cation  by  the  Shawsheen,  I  was  ready  then  to  proceed  up  the  river. 
For  some  reason  unknown  to  me  the  transports  were  not  ready  to 
leave  Gloucester  Point  until  late  in  the  afternoon  of  the  30tli.  At  4 
a.  m.  on  the  morning  of  the  1st  instant  got  underway,  followed  by  four 
transports,  carrying  some  2,500  troops.  The  Shawsheen  during  the 
night  having  been  obliged  to  haul  her  fires  for  slight  repairs  to  her 
boiler,  I  left  her  at  Yorktown  with  orders  to  follow  as  soon  as  possible. 
After  being  underway  the  General  Putnam  arrived  from  Hampton 
Roads;  communicated  with  her,  ordering  her  to  bring  up  the  rear. 
Arrived  at  West  Point  at  9  a.  m.  and  came  to  anchor  off  the  wharf,  cov¬ 
ering  the  landing  of  the  troops  who  were  disembarking  from  the  trans¬ 
ports.  The  troops  at  once  marched  out  some  2  miles  and  took  posses¬ 
sion  of  the  intrenchments  which  were  thrown  up  by  General  Gordon 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


711 


some  twelve  months  since.  I  then  stationed  the  General  Putnam  and 
Shawsheen  in  different  positions  in  the  Pamuukey  River  for  covering 
our  troops  and  resisting  any  attack  which  might  be  made  by  the 
enemy.  Proceeded  with  this  vessel  into  the  Mattapony  River,  taking 
a  station  where  my  guns  would  sweep  the  whole  plain  before  the 
intrenchinents.  While  lying  in  the  Pamunkey  River  picked  up  three 
refugees  from  Richmond  in  a  canoe;  turned  them  over  to  Colonel 
Henry,  commanding  army  forces  at  this  place. 

Not  needing  further  the  services  of  the  Shawsheen ,  ordered  her  to 
proceed  to  Hampton  Roads  and  report  to  you.  I  send  by  her  a  torpedo 
which  had  drifted  down  the  river,  and  was  picked  up  on  the  beach  at 
Yorktown  by  Patrick  McCall  (seaman),  one  of  my  gig’s  crew,  on  the 
29th  ultimo. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  A.  Babcock,

Flagship  Minnesota,

Sir  :  General  Butler,  under  date  of  28th  instant,  informs  meas  follows : 

Later  information  brought  to  me  puts  Beauregard’s  advance  at  Petersburg  on  their 
way  to  Richmond  and  Lee’s  army  in  Virginia. 

Captain  [Haswell  C.]  Clarke,  of  my  staff,  has  just  come  up  and  reports  the  rebel 
troops  are  leaving  North  Carolina.  Plymouth  is  evacuated  and  Little  Washington 
and  New  Berne  are  relieved  from  all  threats  of  operations. 

And  you  inform  me  that  there  are  always  one  or  two  blockaders  at 
Beaufort  coaling  or  repairing.  Such  being  the  case  the  arrangements 
proposed  in  my  communication  of  26th  instant  will  be  unnecessary 
until  the  emergency  contemplated  shall  arise. 

Blockaders  must  not  be  detained  at  Beaufort  longer  than  the  time 
necessary  to  coal  and  repair,  except  upon  an  emergency  that  shall 
justify  such  detention. 

Respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  Lee,

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Braine,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
capture  of  the  British  schooner  Indian. 

U.  S.  S.  Vicksburg, 

Lat.  32°  45'  N.,  Long.  78°  W.,  April  30,  1864. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  morning,  at  4 : 30  a.  m.,  I  dis¬ 
covered  a  sail  to  the  eastward  and  gave  chase;  boarded  her,  and  found 
her  to  be  the  English  schooner  Indian,  belonging  to  Nassau,  New 


712  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

Providence.  I  found  no  name  on  lier  stern,  and  tliatvshe  had  no  cargo 
save  1  hogshead  of  palm  oil,  said  to  have  been  picked  up  at  sea,  and 
I  also  found  that  she  had  kept  no  log  book.  Her  master,  J .  M.  Celeste, 
claims  to  be  bound  from  Belize,  Honduras,  to  Havana;  says  he  could 
not  get  into  Havana, owing  to  northerly  winds;  claims  to  have  drifted 
past  Havana ;  he  then  ran  his  vessel  into  Indian  Key,  coast  of  Florida, 
from  whence  he  sailed  22d  April,  1864;  since  then  he  claims  to  have 
drifted  510  miles  in  the  Gulf  Stream,  unable  to  get  to  Havana.  His 
crew  state  that  they  have  been  lying  in  this  vicinity  waiting  lor  an 
opportunity  to  run  the  blockade.  I  deem  him  suspicious  from  these 
facts  and  from  the  position  I  boarded  him,  latitude  32°  45'  N.,  longi¬ 
tude  78°  W.,  an  excellent  position  to  run  into  one  of  the  North  Caro¬ 
lina  inlets.  I  hud  also  that  in  November,  1863,  he  sailed  from  Nassau, 
New  Providence,  to  Matamoras,  where  he  took  in  a  cargo  of  cotton, 
intending  to  go  to  Havana,  but,  owing  to  a  gale  of  wind,  went  to  Cam¬ 
peche.  There  repairing  his  schooner,  he  proceeded  to  Belize,  Honduras, 
from  whence  he  last  sailed,  going  into  Indian  Key,  a  blockaded  portion  of 
the  coast  of  Florida.  His  crew  list  is  imperfect,  and  one  man  on  board 
not  accounted  for.  When  chased  by  me  he  stood  to  the  northward  and 
eastward  with  the  current,  when  he  could  h#ve  stood  to  the  southward 
and  westward.  I  do  not  think  he  ever  intended  to  go  to  Havana,  but 
running  into  Indian  Key  and  failing  to  get  a  cargo,  has  run  up  the 
coast  intending  to  try  and  enter  one  of  the  North  Carolina  inlets. 

I  have  sent  this  vessel  to  Washington,  If.  C.,  in  charge  of  Acting 
Master’s  Mate  Robert  B.  Elder,  with  a  prize  crew  of  six  persons ;  also  the 
master  and  cook  of  the  prize.  I  have  sent  a  copy  of  the  above  to 
Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

D.  L.  Braine, 
Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  1).  C.

Headquarters  Armies  of  the  United  States, 

Culpeper  Court-House,  Va.,  April  28,  1864. 

General  :  If  no  unforeseen  accident  prevents,  I  will  move  from  here 
on  Wednesday,  the  4th  of  May. 

Start  your  forces  the  night  of  the  4th,  so  as  to  be  as  far  up  James 
River  as  you  can  get  by  daylight  the  morning  of  the  5th,  and  push 
from  that  time  with  all  your  might  for  the  accomplishment  of  the 
object  before  you. 

Should  anything  transpire  to  delay  my  movement,  I  will  telegraph 
you.  Acknowledge  the  receipt  of  this  by  tolegraph. 

Everything  possible  is  now  being  done  to  accumulate  a  force  in 
Washington  from  the  Northern  States  ready  to  reinforce  any  weak 
point. 

I  will  instruct  General  Halleck  to  send  them  to  you  should  the  enemy 
fall  behind  his  fortifications  in  Richmond.  You  will  therefore  keep  the 
headquarters,  Washington,  advised  of  every  move  of  the  enemy  so  far 
as  you  know  them. 

I  am,  general,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

U.  S.  Grant,

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Breck,  JJ.  S.  Na  vy ,  giving  infor¬ 
mation  received  from  a  refugee  regarding  affairs  at  Wilmington  and 
vicinity. 


U.  S.  S.  Niphon, 

Off  New  Inlet,  North  Carolina,  May  1 ,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  2  o’clock  on  this  date,  I  took 
off  the  beach  Charles  Wesley,  a  bright  mulatto,  who  states  that  he  left 
Fort  Fisher  about  three  hours  before  we  took  him  off,  aud  that  he  was 
servant  to  Colonel  Lamb,  commanding  Fort  Fisher.  He  states  that 
the  garrison  of  Fort  Fisher  is  the  Thirty- sixth  North  Carolina  Regi¬ 
ment,  of  about  800  men,  and  that  General  [N.  G.]  Evans’s  division  of 
6,000  men  has  been  ordered  to  Wilmington  and  to  Forts  Caswell  and 
Fisher;  tli at  General  Beauregard  is  in  command  of  Wilmington  and 
its  defenses;  General  Hampton  has  been  ordered  to  command  the  cav¬ 
alry  force  of  the  Department. 

The  Half  Moon,  or  Gatlin,  is  to  be  be  made  into  a  twelve-gun  battery, 
the  guns  being  now  on  their  way  from  Columbia,  S.  C.  The  ironclad 
North  Carolina  intends  to  come  out  if  she  can  get  over  the  bar,  but,  as 
she  draws  15  feet,  they  think  it  doubtful.  The  ironclad  Raleigh  is  on 
shore  about  8  miles  up  the  river  from  Fort  Fisher,  and  it  is  thought 
she  will  not  get  oft;  she  draws  16  feet.  Both  the  Raleigh  and  North 
Carolina  are  very  slow.  Four  blockade  runners  have  arrived  within 
the  last  six  days;  one  of  them,  the  Lucy,  . was  loaded  with  Enfield 
ritles  and  big  guns.  On  Tuesday  last  the  cotton  yards  were  set  fire  to, 
aud  >5,000  to  20,000  bales  were  burned  up  belonging  to  the  Confederate 
Government.  The  cigar  torpedo  steamer  was  burned  at  the  same  time,

and  all  the  material  in  the  shipyard;  this  steamer  was  built  of  cedar. 
I  have  shipped  this  man,  Charles  Wesley,  for  the  service.

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Babcock ,  U.  < S'.  Navy ,  of  experiments 
tvith  torpedoes  found  on  York  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Morse, 

Off  West  Point ,  Mattapony  River ,  May  2 ,  1864. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  report  that  last  night  some  soldiers  found  in  a 
deserted  house  at  this  place  four  torpedoes  (similar  to  the  one  I  send 
you),  ready  to  place  in  the  river.  Colonel  Henry  (commanding  army 
forces  at  this  place)  gave  me  one  to  experiment  with.  Placed  it  under 
an  old  wharf,  in  about  7  feet  of  water,  anchoring  it  3  feet  below  the 
surface,  with  a  line  attached  leading  to  the  shore.  When  ready,  by 
hauling  on  the  line  exploded  the  torpedo,  the  force  of  the  powder  throw¬ 
ing  a  large  volume  of  water  nearly  75  feet  in  the  air  and  breaking  some 
heavy  timbers.  I  am  informed  there  is  a  rebel  party  in  these  rivers 
employed  in  putting  them  down  to  destroy  the  gunboats.  They  are 
very  dangerous  to  handle,  on  account  of  the  force  of  the  spiral  spring, 
which,  if  it  happened  to  slip  while  arranging,  would  certainly  destroy 
the  boat  and  crew.  The  torpedo  I  send  you  is  full  of  powder,  but 
the  air  chamber  leaks,  as  water  ran  from  it  some  time  after  it  was 
picked  up. 

I  also  send  you  what  remains  of  the  exploded  torpedo,  it  having  been 
anchored  by  this  part. 

I  have  swept  several  times,  but  as  yet  have  not  been  able  to  find  any, 
although  I  am  informed  a  great  many  have  been  put  down. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  A.  Babcock, 

Lieutenant-  Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads.
