Detailed  report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  French,  IT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Miami,  transmitting  additional  reports. 

U.  S.  S.  Miami, 

Off  Mouth  Roanoke  River,  North  Carolina ,  May  6,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following-  report  of  the  engagement 
with  the  rebel  ironclad  ram  Albemarle  and  [the  steamer]  Bombshell: 

Yesterday  at  1  p.  in.  I  got  underway,  in  company  with  the  Commodore 
Hull,  Ceres,  and  army  transport  Trumpeter,  and  proceeded  from  our 
picket  station  off  Edenton  Bay  across  to  the  mouth  of  the  Roanoke  for 
the  purpose  of  putting  down  torpedoes.  When  within  a  short  distance 
of  the  buoy  at  the  mouth  of  the  river  the  rebel  ram  Albemarle  was  dis¬ 
covered  coming  down  the  river,  accompanied  by  the  Cotton  Plant  and 
Bombshell,  the  last  two  steamers  laden  with  troops.  1  immediately 
dispatched  the  Trumpeter  to  give  you  the  earliest  notice  of  their 
appearance. 

The  vessels  under  my  command  were  ordered  to  steam  in  line  slowly 
down  the  sound,  at  such  a  distance  that  the  enemy’s  movements  could 
be  watched.  We  dropped  down  to  Bluff  Point,  the  enemy  following 
determinedly.  As  soon  as  you  came  up  I  steamed  ahead,  ready  to  fol¬ 
low  your  movements  and  engage  the  enemy.  At  twenty  minutes  to  5 
I  opened  lire  with  solid  shot  and  continued  firing  rapidly,  with  good 
range.  The  ram  was  struck  by  us  at  almost  our  first  fire,  and  I  have 
to  report  throughout  the  action  excellent  firing  by  both  divisions  of 
this  ship.  I  saw  the  Sassacus  running  into  the  ram,  and  immediately 
headed  for  them  both,  with  the  intention  of  exploding  under  the  ram 
the  torpedo  rigged  on  my  bow.  Before  I  could  get  to  her,  however,  the 
Sassacus  became  disabled  and  dropped  down  from  her;  the  ram  had 
changed  her  course  and  I  could  not  work  to  advantage  on  account  of 
the  fire  of  our  own  vessels.  I  still  kept  up  a  fire  when  it  could  be  done 
without  exposing  the  other  vessels  of  our  fleet. 

After  we  had  been  firing  about  an  hour  you  ordered  me  to  run  up  to 
the  ram  and  use  the  torpedo.  I  steamed  ahead,  still  keeping  up  a 
rapid  fire,  until  we  got  within  the  ship’s  length  of  her.  I  used  every 
endeavor  to  get  at  her,  bow  on,  but  the  Miami  proving  herself  so 
unwieldy  and  so  very  bad  to  steer,  the  enemy  (who  was  probably  well 
aware  of  our  purpose)  succeeded  in  keeping  clear  of  us  by  going  ahead 
and  backing  and  turning. 

We  did  not  cease  our  fire,  however,  all  this  time.  The  enemy  struck 
us  three  or  four  times  while  within  this  close  range;  one  shot,  which 
passed  through  the  after  part  of  the  cabin,  came  very  near  disabling 
our  rudder. 

I  dropped  down  from  her  and  reported  to  you  the  reason  why  I  could 
not  get  my  torpedo  to  work.  You  then  ordered  me  to  follow  the  Wya- 
lusing  in  order;  I  did  so,  keeping  up  a  fire  which  I  believe  was  more 
effective  than  at  any  previous  time,  as  I  am  confident  one  of  our 
shot  struck  the  upper  part  of  her  port  while  open,  if  it  did  not  pass 
into  her  interior.  Owing  to  the  danger  of  getting  aground,  and  the 
fact  of  the  ship’s  handling  so  badly,  1  deemed  my  fire  more  effectual, 
at  close  range,  to  be  on  one  side  of  her  than  to  attempt  to  pass  clear 
around  her. 

For  more  than  ten  minutes  we  poured  solid  shot  upon  her  as  rapidly 
as  we  could  fire. 

I  then  dropped  astern  to  give  the  vessels  coming  up  an  opportunity 
to  pass  and  engage  her.  It  was  then  growing  dark;  the  ram  steamed 
up  to  the  Roanoke  River,  and  the  firing  soon  ceased  on  both  sides.

U.  S.  S.  Miami,  May  6 ,  1864. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  submit  the  following  report  of  damages  received 
by  this  vessel  in  hull,  etc.,  during  the  engagement  with  the  rebel  ram 
Roanoke  [Albemarle],  in  Albemarle  Sound  on  the  afternoon  of  5th 
instant: 

One  shot  struck  smokestack  and  passed  through,  scattering  frag¬ 
ments  over  quarter  deck.  One  struck  starboard  wheelhouse  and  carried 
away  hand  rail,  passing  through  port  quarter  boat,  tearing  away  her 
planking.  One  shell  struck  under  the  starboard  counter,  passed 
through,  cutting  away  hanging  knee  under  after  beam,  and  bursting  in

away  two-thirds  of  the  second  after  beam  and  hanging  knee  on  port 
side,  starting  two  outside  planks  and  started  the  decks  up  under  pivot 
gun  and  knocked  down  the  cabin  bulkhead,  making  a  total  wreck  of 
the  tiller  room. 

The  ship  is  very  much  shaken  from  the  effects  of  the  rapid  firing, 
making  about  5  inches  of  water  per  hour.  Several  shots  and  shells 
passed  over  our  top  gear,  but  did  but  little  damage  save  cutting  away 
smokestack  guys.  During  the  engagement  off  Plymouth  with  the  same 
vessel  the  ram  ran  under  our  port  bow  and  scarred  the  planking  for 
several  feet.  Within  14  inches  of  the  water  a  shell  from  gun  No.  3  struck 
the  ram,  rebounded  and  exploded,  cutting  away  port  forward  boat 
davit,  and  fragments  passing  through  deck  forward  of  boiler  and  star¬ 
board  waist,  and  cutting  away  port  smokestack  guy  and  passing 
through  smokestack. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

Henry  S.  Buckless, 

Carpenters  Mate.

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Barrett,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Whitehead. 


17.  S.  S.  Whitehead, 

Off  Roanoke  River ,  North  Carolina ,  May  6 ,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  part  taken  by  this  vessel 
during  the  engagement  of  yesterday  (5th)  with  the  rebel  ironclad  ram 
Albemarle  and  gunboat  Bombshell. 

In  obedience  to  a  general  signal  made  by  the  flagship  Mattabesett ,  I 
weighed  anchor  at  3: '30  and  proceeded  up  the  Albemarle  Sound,  fol¬ 
lowing  the  U.  S.  S.  Wyalusing. 

The  rebel  ram,  accompanied  by  two  steamers,  was  soon  discovered, 
apparently  steaming  toward  us.  Went  to  quarters  immediately  and 
prepared  for  action.  At  4:30  the  action  became  general  between  the 
leading  vessels,  Mattabesett,  Sassacus ,  and  Wyalusing,  and  the  ram 
Albemarle. 

Owing  to  the  superior  rate  of  speed  of  the  above-named  vessels,  I  was 
unable  to  bring  my  vessel  into  action  until  after  the  rebel  steamer 
Bombshell  had  surrendered.  The  rebel  steamer  Cotton  Plant,  with  a 
number  of  launches  in  tow,  having  succeeded  in  making  her  escape, 
my  attention  Avas  then  directed  to  the  ram,  upon  which  I  opened  fire 
with  the  100-pounder  rifle,  using  solid  shot,  first  at  a  distance  of  1,000 
yards,  but  it  was  soon  lessened  to  400  yards. 

The  ram  meanwhile  commenced  to  retreat  toward  Eoanoke  River. 

Being  ordered  by  you  to  take  my  position  astern  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Miami 
and  follow  up  the  attack  closely,  I  immediately  took  the  position 
assigned,  but  finding  that  I  could  not  use  the  100-pounder  rifle  effec¬ 
tively,  1  steamed  ahead  of  the  Miami  and  on  a  course  parallel  to  that 
which  the  rebel  steamer  was  making,  until  I  approached  within  200 
yards  of  her.  At  this  distance  we  succeeded  in  making  some  excellent 
shots,  the  projectiles  used  being  solid,  chilled-end  shot,  which  must 
have  made  a  serious  impression  on  the  iron  armor  of  the  ram,  as  I 
judged  from  the  appearance  of  the  plating  on  her  when  viewed  through 
a  glass. 

Keeping  the  ram  on  my  starboard  beam,  I  ran  ahead  of  and  across 
her  bows,  making  a  circuit  about  her. 

Notwithstanding  the  heavy  fire  which  was  concentrated  on  the  rebel 
ironclad  by  our  vessels,  she  succeeded  under  the  cover  of  approaching 
darkness  to  make  good  her  escape  up  the  Roanoke  River.  Having 
ceased  firing  at  7:30  p.  m.,  we  came  to  anchor  off  the  mouth  of  the 
river  at  8  with  the  fleet.  I  have  no  casualties  to  report.  Ammunition 
expended,  17  solid  shot,  rifle  100-pounder,  and  170  pounds  of  cannon 
powder. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gf.  W.  Barrett, 

Acting  Ensign,  Commanding. 

Captain  Melancton  Smith, 

Senior  Naval  Officer,  Sounds  of  North  Carolina. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Josselyn,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Commodore  Hull. 

IJ.  S.  S.  Commodore  Hull, 

Off  Roanoke  River ,  North  Carolina,  May  6,  1864. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  part  taken  by  this  vessel  in  the 
action  of  the  5th  instant  with  the  rebel  ram. 


756 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


I  first  sighted  the  ram  at  half  past  1  o’clock  p.  m.,vC&ming  out  of  the 
river  in  company  with  two  steamers,  distant  about  2  miles.  In  accord¬ 
ance  with  previous  instructions  I  retreated  slowly  down  the  sound, 
keeping  out  of  range  of  her  guns  until  the  flagship  came  up,  when  I 
fell  into  line  astern  of  the  Miami.  About  5  o'clock  I  fired  several  shots 
from  my  pivot  guns  at  the  ram,  striking  it  once  or  twice. 

At  half  past  0  I  engaged  the  ram  at  close  quarters,  firing  shell  from 
my  pivot- and  broadside  guns,  many  of  which  struck  the  vessel,  effectu¬ 
ally  preventing  the  opening  of  her  ports.  As  I  steamed  ahead,  in 
passing  the  ram’s  bow,  I  paid  out  a  large  seine  for  the  purpose  of  foul¬ 
ing  his  propeller,  but  though  encompassing  the  ram  it  did  not  have  the 
desired  effect. 

I  ceased  firing  when  it  became  too  dark  to  distinguish  the  enemy. 

I  can  not  speak  too  highly  of  my  officers  and  crew,  many  of  the  latter 
being  for  the  first  time  under  fire.  This  vessel  was  not  struck,  and  I 
have  no  casualties  to  report. 

Enclosed  is  a  list  of  ammunition  expended. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Francis  Josselyn, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Captain  Melancton  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Senior  Officer,  Sounds  of  North  Carolina.

Abstract  log  of  the  TJ.  S.  S.  Commodore  Hull. 

May  5,  1864. — At  5:30  a.  m.  steamed  up  the  sound.  At  6  saw  some¬ 
thing  up  in  Edeuton;  steamed  over  to  it;  found  it  to  be  a  fishing  boat; 
got  no  information.  Ran  back  and  anchored  near  the  Miami.  From  S 
to  12:  Picketing  off  Roanoke  River.  At  10  got  ready  to  send  armed 
boats  up  the  Roanoke  River  to  sink  torpedoes.  Started  to  tow  the 
boats  to  the  mouth  of  the  Roanoke.  When  near  the  month,  the  rebel 
ram  Roanolce  [ Albemarle ],  accompanied  by  the  rebel  steamers  Cotton 
Plant  and  Bombshell,  came  out  and  started  in  chase  of  us.  Took  up  all 
boats  and  ste'amed  slowly  down  the  sound  in  the  direction  of  the  fleet, 
keeping  the  ram  and  steamers  at  an  equal  distance  behind  us;  the  fleet 
below  bound  toward  us.  At  4:30  p.  m.  the  fleet  arrived,  formed  line 
of  battle,  flagship  ahead,  and  ran  up  to  the  enemy.  At  4:40  the  Mat- 
tabesett  opened  fire  on  the  ram  and  the  engagement  became  general. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  757 

At  4 : 45  the  rebel  steamer  Bombshell  surrendered.  At  4 : 50  the  Sassacus 
ran  down  the  ram,  going  nearly  over,  sinking  her  most  out  of  sight,  but 
she  soon  came  up,  apparently  not  much  hurt.  The  Sassacus  being  dis¬ 
abled  while  in  contact  with  the  ram,  was  obliged  to  retire  at  5:30,  the 
rest  ot  the  boats  keeping  up  a  brisk  tire  at  the  enemy  all  the  time,  the 
ram  making  for  the  Roanoke  River  as  fast  as  she  could.  At  6:30  ran 
across  the  ram’s  prow,  keeping  up  a  brisk  fire  to  keep  her  from  opening 
her  ports.  Ran  a  seine  across  her  bow  so  that  it  might  catch  in  her 
screw,  but  it  did  not  succeed.  At  8  sent  on  picket.  From  8  to  12  mid¬ 
night:  A  ind  S.  W  .,  sky  clear.  Weather  hazy.  All  quiet.  On  picket 
near  the  mouth  of  the  Roanoke  River.  Expended  in  the  engagement 
77  rounds  of  ammunition — 58  rifle,  19  howitzer.

TJ.  S,  S.  Sas'-acus. 

IT.  S.  S.  Mattabesett, 

Albemarle  Sound ,  May  9,  1864. 

Sir:  I  would  respectfully  inform  you  that  I  had  an  examination  of 
the  boilers  of  the  Sassacus ,  and  enclose  you  a  report  from  Chief  Engi¬ 
neer  Stewart  of  its  disabled  condition  and  the  impossibility  of  making 
the  necessary  repairs  at  this  place. 


758  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

Both  elevating  screws  of  the  rifle  guns  are  broken  and  the  hurters 

of  both  carried  away.  ... 

The  guard  to  forward  rudder  was  broken  by  the  collision  with  the 
Albemarle ,  and  they  have  not  been  able  to  detach  the  lower  fastenings 
from  the  stem,  which  makes  it  impossible  to  steer  her. 

I  have  ordered  Lieutenant-Commander  Roe  to  take  his  vessel  below 
the  Swash  in  clear  water,  where  he  will  be  able  to  work  to  better 
advantage,  and  report  to  me  when  he  has  remedied  the  above-mentioned 

difficulties.  . 

I  would  recommend  that  she  be  brought  to  Norfolk  for  repairs,  anil 
would  seriously  urge  the  importance  of  having  a  few  boiler  makers  at 
New  Berne  to  do  what  necessary  work  may  be  required  afloat  until  the 
Albemarle  has  been  captured. 

I  have  directed  Commander  Davenport  to  communicate  all  matters 
of  importance  direct,  that  you  may  receive  the  earliest  intelligence  of 
all  movements  at  New  Berne,  as  I  consider  my  presence  here  of  the 
first  importance  to  secure  the  control  of  the  sound. 

There  is  no  coal  at  Roanoke  Island,  and  I  have  been  obliged  to 
charter  a  schooner  and  send  her  to  New  Berne  for  some  to  supply  me 
at  this  point. 

The  officers  captured  in  the  Bombshell  state  that  the  Albemarle ,  iron¬ 
clad,  has  but  four  guns;  the  men,  that  she  has  but  two. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Melanoton  Smith,

U.  S.  S.  Wyaltjsing, 
Albemarle  Sound ,  May  9,  1864. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  I  have  carefully  examined  the  boil¬ 
ers  and  engines  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Sassacus ,  and  have  the  honor  to  report 
that  the  starboard  boiler  has  been  penetrated  by  a  100-pounder  rifle 
shot,  the  projectile  entering  on  the  forward  side  about  7  feet  from  the 
front  and  14  inches  from  the  top,  then  passing  diagonally  through,  car¬ 
rying  away  in  its  course  braces,  T  iron,  and  dry  pipes,  then  passing 
out  through  the  after  side  about  3  feet  from  the  front,  tearing  away  the 
side  sheet  for  2  feet  in  height  and  about  8  inches  in  width.  This  boiler 
is  entirely  useless,  and  can  not,  in  my  opinion,  be  repaired  here. 

The  port  boiler  is  in  good  condition,  with  the  exception  of  a  few 
unimportant  leaks;  steam  is  now  on  it,  and  in  smooth  water  the  ship 
can,  in  my  opinion,  steam  7  or  8  knots  per  hour,  provided  the  stem, 
which  is  now  partly  carried  away,  be  removed,  as  it  now  lies  along¬ 
side.  Her  movement  would  be  very  slow — probably  not  more  than 
4  knots  per  hour. 

The  engine  is  in  good  order  and  ready  for  immediate  use. 

The  starboard  wheel  has  been  injured  by  contact  with  the  rebel  ram, 
but  not  very  seriously. 

I  am,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  H.  Stewart, 

Chief  Engineer,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Captain  M.  Smith, 

Commanding  Naval  Forces  in  the  Sounds  of  North  Carolina,

Report  of  Captain  Smith.,  II.  S.  Navy,  forwarding  information  regarding  the  injuries  sustained 

by  the  C.  S.  S.  Albemarle. 

U.  S.  S.  Mattabesett, 
Albemarle  Sound ,  May  10,  1864. 

Sir:  I  beg  respectfully  to  transmit  tbe  following  intelligence  just 
received  from  a  Union  man  residing  at  Edenton,  N.  0.,  with  which 
place  I  have  this  day  communicated;  and  I  also  dispatched  an  officer 
of  the  Southfield ,  having  an  intimate  acquaintance  with  facilities  for 
obtaining  information,  up  the  Middle  River,  to  make  a  reconnoissance 
in  a  boat : 

A  man  came  from  Plymouth  night  before  last,  and  he  stated  that  the  ram  was  to 
have  come  out  yesterday  at  10  a.  m.  Some  rebel  sympathizers  think  he  will  not 
come  out  for  some  time.  Only  one  shot  penetrated  her  armor.  Every  shot  that 
struck  dented  her  iron  considerably.  The  Sassacus  injured  him  severely  when  she 
struck  him,  making  a  large  hole  on  his  water  line.  She  also  disabled  his  100-pounder 
Brooke  rifle.  The  ram  had  hut  two  guns,  one  working  at  each  end  of  him. 

On  his  house  (on  the  top)  he  has  a  trapdoor,  4  feet  square,  for  ventilation.  They 
could  not  keep  it  open  with  safety,  as  they  were  afraid  it  would  he  observed  and 
fired  into. 

It  is  the  opinion  of  those  who  pretend  to  know  something  about  it,  that  the  ven¬ 
tilation  is  imperfect,  and  in  consequence  he  can  not  fire  his  guns  fast,  as  the  smoke 
would  suffocate  the  crew.  The  destination  of  the  ram  was  New  Berne. 

There  is  a  battery  on  the  Chowan,  at  Eden  Ferry.  The  Union  people  at  Edenton 
hope  that  a  gunboat  will  he  sent  to  that  place  often,  as  the  moral  support  they 
would  receive  by  it  would  he  great.  The  signal  will  always  he  given  when  it  is  safe 
to  land. 

It  is  said  by  some  that  it  is  the  intention  of  the  authorities  to  put  more  iron  on 
him  before  he  comes  out  again,  hut  Mr.  Bond  thinks  they  have  not  the  facilities  for 
doing  it  at  Plymouth.  The  shot  which  penetrated  his  armor  lodged  in  the  wood¬ 
work.  It  is  the  general  opinion  of  the  knowing  secesh  that  the  ram  put  hack  on 
account  of  the  damage  done  to  his  gun,  and  for  no  other  reason,  hut  he  burned  a 
quantity  of  bacon  to  get  steam  to  effect  his  escape.  One  good  boat  from  him  drifted 
on  shore  at  Roberts’  Fishery. 

If  a  substantial,  fast  tugboat,  with  an  improvised  prod,  could  be 
sent  me,  I  could  destroy  him  with  much  less  expense  to  the  Govern¬ 
ment  than  the  sacrifice  I  shall  be  compelled  to  make  in  wooden  vessels 
to  accomplish  the  object. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Melancton  Smith, 

Captain  and  Senior  Officer  in  Sounds  of  North  Carolina. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Bloclcading  Squadron.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Roe,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  injuries\to  the  guns  of  the  U.  S.  S. 

Sassacus. 

(J.  S.  S.  Sassacus, 

Hatteras  Inlet ,  North  Carolina ,  May  17,  1864. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  report  tliat  in  the  engagement  on  the  5th  instant 
with  the  rebel  ironclad  Albemarle ,  all  the  pivot  gun  elevating  screws 
broke  in  two,  including  the  spare,  in  the  early  part  of  the  engagement. 

I  also  report  that  the  rear  hurter  of  the  forward  pivot  slide  was 
carried  away.  This  was  done  by  firing  the  gun  only  partly  run  out, 
which  was  imperative,  owing  to  the  close  proximity  of  the  vessel.  The 
officer  of  this  gun  was  endeavoring  to  put  a  shot  into  the  enemy’s  open 
port.  The  gun,  if  run  out,  would  fire  over  the  port,  and  on  account  of 
its  length  had  to  be  run  in.  It  was  fired  precisely  at  the  same  moment 
the  enemy  fired,  and  our  shot  struck  the  port  sill  of  the  ironclad,  broke 
into  pieces,  one  portion  flying  back  and  lauding  on  our  decks,  and  the 
other  portion  passed  into  his  port.  The  guns  were  so  close  that  the 
burned  powder  from  the  ironclad’s  gun  blackened  the  bows  of  the  Sas¬ 
sacus.  Also  the  rear  hurter  of  the  after  pivot  was  carried  away.  This 
was  done  by  the  great  haste  of  the  gun  captain  to  fire  as  the  ironclad 
swept  alongside,  and  the  compressors  were  not  brought  to,  and  perhaps 
[the]  gun  was  not  run  all  the  way  out.  This  shot  struck  the  armor  of 
the  enemy,  and  it  was  reliably  reported  to  me  that  it  penetrated  it.  If 
so,  it  is  the  only  shot  that  did,  as  the  IX-inch  solid  shot  alongside  of 
it  flew  into  the  air  with  a  bound,  leaving  no  more  impression  than  a 
pea  would  have  done. 

I  think  that  the  injury  to  the  hurters  may  be  excused,  as  those  shots 
were  of  vital  importance.  But  the  loss  of  the  elevating  screws  was  a 
severe  one.  My  men  worked  the  guns  by  holding  them  up  by  hand¬ 
spikes  under  the  breech,  to  their  great  danger,  as  they  were  of  course 
fired  at  all  the  depression  we  could  get.  If  these  guns  were  furnished 
with  good  quoins,  as  recommended  in  ordnance  instructions,  it  would 
be  very  useful.  But  these  screws  can  not  be  relied  upon  at  all  after 
two  or  three  fires,  when  the  gun  is  disabled.  In  consequence  of  this, 
some  of  the  guns'  crew  and  an  officer  were  injured,  and  I  lost  the  good 
service  of  my  most  valuable  guns  at  a  supreme  moment,  when,  perhaps, 
one  lucky  shot  would  have  settled  my  antagonist  for  a  full  due. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

F.  A.  Roe, 
lieutenant- Commander. 

Commander  H.  A.  Wise, 

Chief  of  Bureau  of  Ordnance ,  Navy  Dept.,  Washington,  D.  C.

'  Report  of  Captain  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  C.  S.  S.  Bombshell. 

U.  S.  S.  Mattabesett, 
Albemarle  Sound ,  North  Carolina,  May  24,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  rebel  steamer 
Bombshell,  with  33  prisoners,  on  the  5th  of  May,  1804,  by  the  vessels 
under  my  command,  during  the  engagement  with  the  rebel  ram  Albe¬ 
marle. 

The  Bombshell  was  originally  an  armed  U.  S.  steamer  sunk  by  the 
rebel  batteries  at  Plymouth  ou  the  18th  of  April  last,  during  the  attack 
upon  that  place,  and  was  subsequently  raised,  fitted  out,  and  accompa¬ 
nied  the  ram  as  a  consort. 

The  vessels  entitled  to  share  iu  the  capture  are  the  Mattabesett, 
Wy aiming ,  Sassacus ,  Miami,  Commodore  Hull,  Ceres ,  and  Whitehead. 

Acting  Master’s  Mate  John  Woodman,  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Ceres,  has  been 
sent  as  prize  master,  with  the  necessary  papers  and  witnesses,  to  the 
U.  S.  district  judge  for  the  southern  district  of  New  York. 

Full  reports  from  the  commanders  of  the  vessels,  with  a  list  of  the 
prisoners,  have  been  forwarded  to  Bear  Admiral  Lee,  with  a  duplicate 
of  the  survey  and  appraisal  of  the  vessel. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Melancton  Smith, 

Captain  and  Senior  Officer  in  Sounds  of  North  Carolina. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  I).  C. 


Letter  of  congratulation  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Captain  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy. 


Navy  Department,  May  25,  1864. 

Sir:  I  have  had  great  satisfaction  in  receiving  and  perusing  your 
report  as  the  senior  officer  present  and  the  reports  of  the  commanding 
officers  of  the  several  vessels  that  were  engaged  in  the  encounter  with 
the  rebel  ironclad  ram  Albemarle  and  her  tender  on  the  afternoon  of  the 
5th  instant  in  Albemarle  Sound. 

The  Department  congratulates  all  of  the  officers  and  men  of  the 
United  States  Navy  who  participated  in  this  remarkable  contest 
between  wooden  gunboats  and  a  formidable  armored  vessel,  in  which 
the  latter  was  forced  to  retreat  to  prevent  capture,  and  it  particularly 
thanks  you  for  your  vigilant  and  gallant  use  of  the  means  placed  at 
your  command  to  thwart  the  designs  of  the  rebels  to  regain  control  of 
the  sounds  of  North  Carolina. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 


Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Captain  Melancton  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy,

Report  of  Captain  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  armor  and  construction  of  the  C.  S.  S. 

Albemarle. 

U.  S.  S.  Mattabesett, 
Albemarle  Sound,  North  Carolina,  June  1,  1864. 

Sir  :  The  information  obtained  from  the  four  men,  deserters  from  the 
ironclad  Albemarle,  referred  to  in  my  letter  of  the  30th  instant,  differs 
somewhat  from  the  reports  heretofore  received  as  regards  the  description 
of  the  armor  and  the  construction  of  that  vessel. 

The  prow  is  a  solid  wedge  of  iron,  3  feet  in  length  and  2  in  breadth 
on  the  upper  end,  resembling  in  form  an  inverted  hawk’s  bill,  and  is 
completely  submerged,  even  when  the  vessel  is  light.  The  armor  con¬ 
sists  of  2-inch  iron  plates  (English),  6  inches  wide,  placed  longitudinally 
over  14  inches  of  wood.  A  second  course  of  the  same  width  and  thick¬ 
ness  runs  vertically  over  the  sides  of  the  casemates  and  is  turned  down 
at  an  acute  angle  to  form  the  plating  of  the  hull  under  water,  and  these 
ends  are  secured  by  a  horizontal  plate  of  the  former  dimensions. 

The  bottom  of  the  ram  is  flat,  and  the  form  of  the  hull  under  water 
is  nearly  identical  with  the  outside,  the  kuuckle  forming  a  complete 
guard  around  the  vessel,  and  the  angle  under  water  causing  a  shot  to 
glance  downward  in  the  same  manner  that  one  is  thrown  upward  on 
striking  the  casemate.  He  has  but  one  [twoj  propeller  and  can  carry 
fuel  for  five  or  six  days. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


763 


In  tlie  engagement  of  the  5th  the  Albemarle  was  struck  on  the  case¬ 
mates  by  54  solid  shot,  and  the  only  damage  sustained  was  two  timbers 
broken,  the  port  shutters  damaged  or  carried  away,  one  gun  disabled 
(by  the  first  shot),  some  plating  knocked  off  of  the  ends  and  sides,  and 
the  stack  riddled.  The  Sassacus  effected  no  injury  whatever  when  she 
ran  into  the  ram,  and  it  was  generally  thought  on  board  that  it  was  aq 
accidental  collision,  or  that  she  was  armed  with  a  torpedo  that  had 
failed  to  explode. 

I  do  not  intend  to  attack  the  ram  in  Eoanoke  River  with  the  gun¬ 
boats,  believing  that  any  such  attempt  would  be  attended  with  serious 
disaster,  if  it  did  not  give  the  ram  complete  control  of  the  sound.  If 
disposed  to  meet  me  in  a  fair  fight,  I  am  prepared  to  engage  him  any 
hour,  night  or  day. 

I  have  interfered  somewhat  with  the  rebel  ferry  at  the  mouth  of  the 
Chowan  by  taking  their  boats,  one  of  which  was  a  new  one  that 
belonged  to  the  Southfield. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Melancton  Smith, 

Captain  and  Senior  Officer  in  Sounds  of  North  Carolina. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

anything  fouling  her  propellers,  as  they  were  protected,  in  what  man¬ 
ner  he  does  not  know  positively,  but  thinks  by  an  iron  basket.  He

Eeport  of  Captain  Smith,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  collision  between  the  U.  S.  S.  Sassacus  and  the 

C.  S.  S.  Albemarle. 

LT.  S.  S.  Mattabesett, 
Albemarle  Sound ,  North  Carolina ,  June  4,  1864. 

Sir:  Your  order  of  May  17,  through  Rear-Admiral  Lee,  directing  a 
full  report  to  be  furnished  of  the  collision  of  the  Sassacus  with  the  rebel 
ram  Albemarle ,  together  with  a  diagram  showing  the  position  of  the 
two  vessels,  is  received,  and  1  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following- 
report :  & 

One  report  from  Lieutenant-Commander  Roe  has  already  been  for¬ 
warded  to  Admiral  Lee,  and  I  retained  two,  one*  from  himself  and  the 
other  from  his  executive  officer,  to  avoid  multiplying  testimony  that 
appeared  to  me  to  be  much  exaggerated,  but  both  reports  are  now 
enclosed. 


*  See  p.  737, 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


765 


Lieutenant- Comm ander  Boe  states  that  lie  “  struck  the  ram  Albemarle 
fairly,  just  abaft  her  beam,  at  about  9  or  10  knot  speed.  The  blow 
jarred  and  careened  her  so  much  that  the  water  bowed  freely  over  her 
decks.”  His  executive  officer  states  that  “We  had  a  start  of  300  or 
400  yards  and  were  making  about  11  knots  when  we  struck  her  with  our 
prow  at  right  angles  on  the  starboard  quarter,  at  the  junction  of  her 
after  casemate  with  the  hull,  forcing  her  side  under  water  2  or  3  feet.” 

It  is  my  impression  that  the  Sassacus ,  when  within  400  yards  of  the 
ram,  had  stopped  her  engines  and,  when  fairly  pointed,  commenced 
steaming  toward  him,  making  it  apparent  that  she  intended  to  try  the 
effect  of  ramming.  I  remarked  to  Captain  Febiger  at  that  time,  “How 
slow  she  moves,”  and  in  a  few  moments  she  struck,  as  represented, 
fairly  and  nearly  at  right  angles,  causing  the  water  to  flow  over  the 
deck  aft. 

I  subsequently  called  Lieutenant-Commander  Boe’s  attention  to  the 
statement  made  by  him  in  reference  to  the  rate  of  speed,  which  he  evi¬ 
dently  estimated  by  the  number  of  revolutions,  without  considering  the 
short  distance  he  had  to  run,  from  a  dead  stand,  to  reach  the  ram;  but 
as  he  was  not  disposed  to  make  the  correction,  although  I  had  taken 
the  report  on  board  for  that  purpose  as  well  as  to  examine  his  injuries, 
I  forwarded  it  as  it  was.  I  should  judge,  from  the  slight  injury  the 
vessel  sustained  and  the  short  distance  that  the  Sassacus  was  from  the 
ram  when  heading  for  him,  that  her  speed  did  not  exceed  5  knots.  The 
Albemarle ,  as  I  have  since  learned,  did  not  sustain  the  slightest  injury 
from  the  collision. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Boe  also  states :  “  I  put  three  rifle  shot  into  her 
port,  and  the  muzzles  of  two  of  her  guns  were  badly  broken.”  This  is 
evidently  a  mistake,  as  the  Albemarle  has  but  two  guns,  each  one  work¬ 
ing  in  three  ports,  and  not  a  man  on  board  was  injured.  The  muzzle 
of  one  gun  was  broken,  and  the  four  deserters  from  the  ram  report  that 
it  was  damaged  in  the  early  part  of  the  action,  on  the  port  side,  but 
they  continued  to  use  it  through  the  engagement. 

The  stems  of  the  double-enders,  as  well  as  the  rudder  guards,  are 
nearly  perpendicular,  are  very  frail,  and  are  not  calculated  to  run  up 
on  the  deck.  Had  they  been  curved  I  am  of  the  opinion  that  the  Sas¬ 
sacus  would  have  brought  sufficient  weight  upon  the  deck  to  have  sunk 
him. 

I  herewith  enclose  a  diagram*  of  the  position  of  the  Sassacus  and  Albe¬ 
marle  at  the  time  of  collision  and  after  they  had  been  separated  by  the 
ram’s  steaming  ahead.  I  have  sent  also  to  Bear  Admiral  Lee  a  frag¬ 
ment  of  a  solid  shot  fired  from  the  100-pounder  rifle  of  the  Sassacus 
when  close  alongside,  proving  that  the  various  reports  heretofore  made 
of  the  invulnerability  of  the  ram  have  not  been  much  exaggerated. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Melancton  Smith, 

Captain  and  Senior  Officer  in  Sounds  of  North  Carolina. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  1>.  C.

U.  S.  S.  Sassacus. 

Albemarle  Sound,  North  Carolina,  May  5,  1864 — 10  p.  m. 

Sir  :  1  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report  of  the  part  taken 
by  this  vessel  in  the  action  this  afternoon  with  the  rebel  ironclad 
ram  Albemarle  and  rebel  gunboat  Bombshell.

At  4:35  we  commenced  firing  at  the  ram  and  gunboat,  both  opening 
on  us  about  the  same  time.  In  a  few  moments  after  the  beginning  of 
the  engagement  the  Bombshell  hoisted  the  white  flag  and  we  steamed 
alongside  of  her;  she  surrendered  at  about  5  o’clock.  We  ordered  her 
to  anchor,  which  she  did,  and  then  steamed  for  the  ram,  running  at 
full  speed,  and  struck  her  on  her  starboard  side  just  abaft  her  case¬ 
mate.  I  could  not  see  whether  we  did  her  much  damage  or  not.  We 
carried  away  our  prow  and  false  stem,  but  did  no  serious  injury  to  our¬ 
selves.  The  ship  does  not  leak  a  drop.  She  fired  two  shots  through 
us,  one  just  before  we  struck  her,  which  passed  through  our  starboard 
bow  and  out  on  our  port  side,  and  another  about  three  minutes  after¬ 
wards,  while  our  bow  was  on  her  deck,  which  passed  through  our 
starboard  boiler,  scalding  all  the  men  in  the  fire  room  and  the  chief 
engineer,  Mr.  Hobby,  who  was  at  the  starting  bar  at  the  time. 

While  we  were  alongside  of  her,  our  bow  resting  on  her  deck,  we 
fired  two  solid  shot,  one  100-pounder  and  one  IX-inch,  into  her  forward 
port,  knocking  off  the  muzzle  of  her  forward  gun.  The  muzzle  of  her 
after  gun  was  broken  off'  when  we  struck  her.  After  we  separated  I 
noticed  what  appeared  to  me  like  a  shot  hole  through  her  roof  just 
over  her  forward  broadside  port.  A  fragment  of  one  of  our  own  solid 
shot  rebounded  onto  our  deck.  This  was  not  a  chilled-iron  shot. 

Our  100  pounders  were  disabled  by  the  breaking  of  the  elevating 
screws  early  in  the  fight,  and  we  had  to  use  handspikes  under  them. 
Three  screws  were  broken. 

The  man  stationed  in  the  foretop  threw  six  hand  grenades,  two  of 
which  went  into  her  hatch  on  top  her  roof. 

No  men  were  killed  or  wounded  by  shot  or  rifles,  although  the  enemy 
poured  a  steady  fire  into  us  from  rifles  while  we  were  alongside  of  him. 

We  were  alongside  of  him  for  about  ten  minutes.  The  officers  and 
men  behaved  splendidly,  but  I  cau  not  help  mentioning  Acting  Ensign 
[William  H.]  Mayer  for  his  coolness,  he  standing  on  the  forward  pivot 
carriage  directly  in  front  of  the  enemy’s  gun  and  under  a  heavy  fire  of 
musketry,  we  being  then  about  15  feet  distant  from  .her,  and  firing  a 
shot  into  her  forward  port.  In  speaking  of  forward  port  I  mean  her 
forward  broadside  port.  The  first  loader  and  first  sponger  of  the  for¬ 
ward  pivot — Peter  Kelly,  seaman,  and  Peter  Hoyt,  seaman — displayed 
great  coolness  in  loading  their  gun  under  a  heavy  fire  of  rifles.  We 
kept  np  a  constant  fire  on  the  enemy  until  compelled  to  drop  out  of 
action. 

Yerv  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  W.  Muldaur, 

Acting  Master ,  Executive  Officer. 

Lieutenant-Commander  F.  A.  Roe, 

Commanding  Steamer  Sassacus.

[Enclosure.] 

Statement  of  John  T>.  Patrick,  seaman,  lately  belongin' /  to  the  C:  S.  ram  Albemarle,  taken 
before  Fleet  Captain  John  S.  Barnes,  U.  S.  Navy,  June  26,  1864. 

Flagship  Malvern, 

James  River ,  June  27,  1864. 

I  was  on  board  the  Albemarle  upwards  of  two  months.  I  formerly 
belonged  to  the  gunboat  North  Carolina,  at  Wilmington,  and  left  her 
in  the  launches.  When  the  Bombshell  was  raised,  I  went  on  board  of 
her  and  remained  on  her  until  about  two  hours  before  the  fight,  and 
was  then  sent  for  in  a  small  boat  and  brought  on  board  the  Albemarle 
as  she  was  coming  down  the  river.  I  was  second  front  leverman  at  the ' 
after  gun,  and  it  was  a  Brooke  100-pounder  rifle. 

The  Albemarle  had  two  guns,  just  alike.  We  expected  to  go  to  New 
Berne  to  meet  the  Neuse  at  the  time  the  army  attacked.  We  did  not 
expect  to  have  a  fight  with  the  gunboats,  as  they  had  run  away  when 
the  Albemarle  came  down  on  Plymouth.  We  did  know  that  there  were 
three  new  vessels,  but  did  not  know  what  kind  of  vessels  they  were. 
There  were  several  vessels  lying  near  the  mouth  of  the  river  as  we  came 
down,  which  steamed  away  from  us,  and  we  followed  them  on  down  the 
sound  for  about  10  miles,  when  we  made  out  that  the  gunboats  were 
going  to  fight  us.  We  fired  our  bow  gun  as  a  signal  for  battle.  The 
Cotton  Plant  was  ordered  back  to  the  Roanoke  River  and  the  Bombshell

the  port  shutters  were  knocked  away  except  one;  no  shots  came  in  the

Sassacus  knocked  off  four  plates  at  the  edge  of  the  water;  they  were 
only  secured  by  three  or  four  bolts;  the  blow  was  a  glancing  one.  We

Captain  Cooke  saw  the  smoke  or  steam  coming  out  of  her  and  told  us 
not  to  fire  at  her  any  more,  as  she  had  surrendered  or  was  sinking.  We 
then  fired  at  the  other  boats.  The  wheel  ropes  parted  and  she  swung 
around.  I  looked  out  the  port  and  saw  she  was  going  up  the  river 
again.  The  rudderhead  was  wrenched  off  and  gave  much  trouble. 
There  was  a  large  piece  of  plating  hanging  over  the  bows,  shot  off, 
which  balanced  the  rudder;  this  was  cut  off  after  dark  up  the  river. 
She  would  not  steer  at  all,  running  first  into  one  bank  and  then  the 
other.  I  think  twenty-five  shots  broke  the  iron ;  two  broke  through 
the  wood  inside;  three  men  wounded;  seven  plates  knocked  off;  no 
leak  more  than  ordinary  0 

She  was  very  hot  inside.  The  men  were  nearly  exhausted.  She  could 
not  have  held  out  an  hour  longer.  She  draws  8  feet;  plating  8  [4] 
inches  thick  above  water,  under  water;  crew  about  TO  men.  The 
smokestack  was  shot  away  and  we  could  make  no  steam.  Our  failure 
to  get  to  New  Berne  was  laid  partly  to  that.  Mr.  Shelby  [Shelly]  said 
they  must  have  a  new  one  of  a  different  kind.  They  all  thought  it  was 
impossible  to  get  to  New  Berne  unless  the  Neuse  came  to  meet  them 
halfway.  Nearly  all  the  bacon,  lard,  and  butter  was  burned,  the  bulk¬ 
head  also,  to  raise  steam  to  get  back  with.  They  are  making  a  smoke¬ 
stack  now,  to  shove  up  a  piece  at  a  time  as  it  is  shot  away.  Our  coal 
was  all  hard  coal.  The  crew  never  live  on  board ;  they  sleep  under  a 
shed  in  hammocks,  with  a  watch  on  board.  She  is  very  rough  and 
confined;  no  room  except  just  to  work  two  guns  and  steer  her.  They 
say  she  will  now  go  8  or  9  knots.  She  has  two  screws  worked  with 
one  engine. 

I  belong  to  Nashville,  Tenn.  I  am  a  seaman;  sailed  from  New 
Orleans  to  Bermuda  and  to  Galveston.  I  have  been  in  the  rebel  service 
since  1861.  I  enlisted  in  the  regulars  in  .Tennessee  and  went  to 
Charleston.  I  was  there  during  all  the  fighting,  until  the  evacuation 
of  Morris  Island.  I  was  stationed  at  No.  1  gun  on  the  sea  face  parapet. 
There  was  considerable  damage  done  the  fort;  several  shot  came 
through  the  wall,  and  the  casemates  were  very  much  damaged.  I  was 
stunned  by  a  shot  which  struck  the  brick  tower  and  buried  me  in  the

Lieutenant  Blake  was  arresred  and  was  to  be  tried  for  saying  he  hoped 
it  would  never  go  off,  as  it  was  too  bad  to  blow  people  up  in  that  way; 
it  was  not  Christian.  They  tried  to  raise  the  torpedo  afterwards,  but 
could  not  do  it. 

After  leaving  Charleston  I  came  to  Wilmington  and  entered  the 
Navy,  and  went  on  the  North  Carolina  about  seven  months.  Captain 
Muse  then  commanded  her.  He  died  and  Porter  took  her.  He  was 
the  executive  officer.  She  is  a  ram,  four  guns,  just  like  those  at  Rich¬ 
mond.  Her  engines  are  very  bad,  always  out  of  repair.  The  Raleigh 
was  run  on  a  bank  by  the  captain  purposely.  He  thought  it  would 
not  hurt  her;  when  the  tide  fell  her  back  broke.  They  set  fire  to  her 
and  burned  all  the  woodwork  out  of  her.  They  have  but  the  North 
Carolina  now;  she  never  got  down  far  without  breaking  something 
and  had  to  be  towed  back.  I  have  heard  that  she  escorts  blockade 
runners  out,  but  don’t  know  it.  Don’t  know  how  much  she  draws. 

The  Albemarle  had  no  torpedoes,  but  she  is  having  one  fitted  now. 


Report  of  Commander  Cooke,  C.  S.  Navy,  commanding  C.  S.  S.  Albemarle. 

C.  S.  S.  Albemarle, 
Plymouth ,  N.  C.,  May  7,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  your  order  of 
the  5th  instant  I  left  here  at  meridian  of  that  day,  together  with  the 
prize  steamer  Bombshell ,  as  tender,  and  the  Cotton  Plant ,  to  convoy  to 
Alligator  River.  As  soon  as  we  reached  the  mouth  of  Roanoke  River 
we  discovered  six  of  the  enemy’s  gunboats  in  the  sound,  about  10  miles 
distant.  They  immediately  got  underway  and  stood  down  the  sound 
E.  N.  E.,  until  we  had  run  about  10  miles,  when  three  more  gunboats, 
double-enders,  of  a  much  more  formidable  class,  carrying  from  ten  to 
twelve  guns  each,  made  their  appearance. 

Perceiving  the,  unequal  contest  in  which  we  were  compelled  to 
engage,  I  immediately  prepared  for  action.  The  enemy  steamed  up  in 
two  columns,  half  , a  mile  apart,  delivering  his  broadsides  as  he  passed 
us;  two  of  his  largest  and  swiftest  vessels  breaking  off  from  the  column, 
bore  rapidly  down  upon  the  Bombshell  and  pouring  in  their  broadsides 
forced  her  to  surrender.  The  third  or  fourth  shot  fired  by  the  enemy 
broke  off  20  inches  of  the  muzzle  of  the  after  gun  of  the  Albemarle.  The 
action  lasted  from  twenty  minutes  to  5  till  after  dark,  when  they  hauled 
off.  One  of  their  largest  and  heaviest  boats  endeavered  to  run  us  down, 
but  failed  in  the  attempt,  although  she  struck  us  heavily  on  the  star¬ 
board  quarter.  I  think  we  succeeded  in  sinking  her,  as  we  gave  her  two 
shots  while  she  was  hung  to  us,  which  must  have  passed  through  her. 
The  rapidity  of  the  firing  caused  such  a  dense  smoke  that  I  was  unable 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


771 


to  ascertain  tlie  damage  done  to  the  enemy,  but  I  think  1  am  safe  in 
saying  that  we  sunk  one  of  their  most  formidable  boats,  and  severely 
crippled  two  others.  The  contest  was  a  very  severe  one,  lasting  about 
three  hours.  The  disadvantages  under  which  I  labored,  from  the  tiller 
giving  way,  and  the  impossibility  of  producing  steam  enough  to 
maneuver  the  vessel  to  advantage,  prevented  me  from  inflicting  much 
greater  damage  than  we  did.  The  smokestack  was  riddled  to  such  an 
extent  as  to  render  it  useless,  and  so  great  was  my  extremity  at  one 
time  that  I  was  forced  to  tear  down  the  bulkheads,  throw  in  all  of  my 
bacon,  lard,  and  other  combustible  matter,  to  produce  steam  sufficient 
to  bring  me  back  to  the  river.  I  can  not  speak  too  highly  of  the  officers 
and  crew,  especially  of  the  following-named  men,  viz,  John  Benton, 
James  Cullington,  J.B.  Cooper,  H.  A.  Kuhn,  John  Smith,  II.  P.  Hay, 
Thomas  Wroten,  John  Steely,  and  T.  Nichols.  The  pilot,  J.  B.  Hopkins, 
deserves  great  credit  for  the  manner  in  which  he  maneuvered  the  ves¬ 
sel,  and  bringing  her  safely  back  to  port.  Since  the  engagement  I 
have  ascertained  by  flag  of  truce  that  there  was  no  one  hurt  on  the 
Bombshell. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  W.  Cooke, 
Commander ,  0.  3.  Navy. 

Commander  R.  F.  Pinkney, 

Commanding ,  etc.

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  3.  3.  Ceres. 

April  17 ,  1864. — At  anchor  off  Plymouth,  N.  C.,  near  the  flagship. 
At  5: 40  p.  in.  got  underway  and  proceeded  up  the  river.  At  0:15, 
when  passing  the  blockade  a  short  distance  above  Fort  Gray,  the  rebels 
opened  on  us  from  artillery  and  sharpshooters  at  short  range.  At 
0: 25  had  passed  the  rebel  batteries;  while  passing  returned  their  fire 
as  fast  as  possible.  Casualties,  2  killed  and  6  wounded.  A  shell 
exploded  in  boat  on  port  quarter;  one  shot  struck  on  port  quarter  about 
6  inches  above  the  water  line  and  abreast  of  the  magazine,  but  did  not 
go  through  the  outer  planking.  One  shell  entered  the  port  gangway, 
passed  through  one  brace  of  the  gallows  frame,  exploded  in  the  ward¬ 
room  gangway.  Were  struck  in  numerous  other  places  by  bullets  and 
pieces  of  shell.  At  0: 45  p.  m.  anchored  in  Roanoke  River  near  the 
Whitehead ,  at  the  upper  blockade,  7  miles  above  Plymouth.  At  8:35 
got  underway  and  proceeded  down  the  river;  ran  the  fire  of  the  rebel 
batteries  and  sharpshooters  which  lined  the  bank  of  the  river  above 
Fort  Gray.  At  9  anchored  near  the  Miami ,  off  Plymouth.  At  9 :  30

April  18. — At  daylight  the  rebels  made  an  unsuccessful  assault  on

Roanoke  River.  Employed  in  getting  up  spiles  from  the  blockade  to 
make  a  passage  through  to  the  Roanoke  River  above  the  rebel  bat¬ 
teries.  At  4:30  p.  m.  sent  a  boat  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate

from  the  Whitehead.  Employed  in  dragging  spiles  out  of  the  block¬ 
ade  in  the  Thoroughfare.  At  7  p.  m.,  to  make  sure  that  we  had  removed 
enough  spiles,  we  passed  through  the  channel  made  in  the  blockade, 
and  at  7 :  30  started  on  our  return  to  Plymouth  by  way  of  the  Oashie

ship  Miami.  At  10:45  went  alongside  of  the  coal  wharf  and  com¬ 
menced  coaling. 

April  19. — At  3  a.  m.  saw  the  flashes  of  musketry  apparently  around 
Fort  Gray.  Immediately  after  a  shell  passed  over  the  fort  from  some 
vessel  up  the  river.  At  3 : 10  the  rebel  ram  made  her  appearance,  com¬ 
ing  down  the  river.  Immediately  cast  off  from  the  wharf,  went  to 
quarters,  and  proceeded  down  the  river  to  the  flagship  and  communi¬ 
cated  with  her.  The  ram  ran  between  the  Miami  and  the  Southfield , 
sinking  the  latter  vessel,  at  which  time  this  vessel  drifted  ashore, 
caused  by  a  temporary  disaster  to  the  engine.  While  ashore  the  Miami 
and  Whitehead  passed  us  on  their  way  down  the  river.  As  soon  as  the 
engine  was  in  working  order  we  backed  off  and  up  the  river  a  short 
distance,  when  we  picked  up  the  Southfield’s  gig,  in  which  were  3 
officers  and  4  men  who  escaped  from  the  Southfield  when  she  went 
down.  We  then  proceeded  down  the  river  and  passed  the  Miami  and 
kept  her  company  to  the  mouth  of  the  river.  A  5 : 15  passed  out  of  the 
Roanoke  River,  and  in  company  with  the  Miami  and  Whitehead  pro¬ 
ceeded  toward  Edenton.  At  7:45  the  Miami  anchored  off  Edenton. 
At  8:30  a.  m.  took  on  board  the  body  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Flusser 
and  the  wounded  from  the  Miami  and  proceeded  toward  Roanoke 
Island.  At  7 : 30  p.  m.  got  aground  off  Roanoke  Island  landing.  Sent 
mails  and  dispatches  on  shore.  At  9:30  got  afloat  and  proceeded 
toward  New  Berne.

for  assistance  by  order  of  Commander  Almy.  Lowered  the  second  and

At  10  steamer  Daylight  arrived  and  came  to  anchor  on  our  starboard

September 24.— At  1  p. m.  sent  all  boats,  with  all  the  prisoners,  on  board 
the  Iroquois  for  transportation  to  New  York. 

October  12. — On  blockade  oft'  Wilmington,  N.  C.  At  5 : 45  a.  m.  sighted 
a  steamer  on  fire  on  the  shore.  At  6  communicated  with  the  steamer 
Nansemond  and  learned  from  her  that  the  steamer  on  fire  was  run  on 
[shore]  by  her,  and  after  trying  to  get  her  off,  but  finding  they  could 
not,  they  set  fire  to  her.  She  was  the  blockade  runner  Douro.  At  3:30 
p.  m.  received  on  board  five  prisoners  from  the  JSfansemond ,  captured  in 
the  blockade  runner  Douro. 

December  6. — At  daylight  saw  a  large  white  steamer  on  shore  near 
Bald  Head  light.  The  Aries  stood  for  her  to  board  her,  followed  by  the 
tug  Violet.  At  G :  55  a.  m.  the  steamer  was  set  on  fire  amidships  by  the 
rebels.  At  7:10  the  Violet  went  alongside  of  her,  when  Fort  Caswell 
and  the  battery  to  the  S.  W.  opened  fire  on  the  Aries  and  Violet.  At 
7:50  the  Violet  left  the  steamer,  came  alongside,  and  reported  the 
“steamer  on  shore  was  loaded  with  bales,”  but  could  not  discover  her 
name.  Three  guns  from  Smith’s  Island  opened  fii’e,  but  without  any 
effect,  upon  our  vessels.  At  10  received  on  board  from  the  Aries  the 
papers  of  the  blockade  runner  Ceres, from  Bermuda, bound  to  Wilming¬ 
ton,  N.  C.  At  12: 15  p.  m.  lowered  second  cutter,  in  charge  of  Acting 
Ensign  William  Swasey,  and  picked  up  two  boxes  containing  sides  of 
bacon,  which  had  drifted  from  the  blockade  runner  on  shore;  brought 
them  on  board  and  served  it  out  to  the  ship’s  company. 

December  7. — At  G  a.  m.  the  steamer  which  was  on  fire  the  night  before 
drifted  toward  us;  got  all  ready  to  slip  chain.  At  6: 30  the  Violet  took 
a  line  to  the  Ceres  and  kept  her  in  good  anchoring  ground.  At  7:30 
made  signals  for  the  Maratanza  to  keep  underway  and  send  men  to  the 
Ceres  to  put  out  the  fire  and  get  her  anchors  and  chains  clear  for  anchor¬ 
ing.  At  8:30  the  Ceres  came  to  astern  of  us  with  port  anchor;  ordered 
the  tug  Violet  to  go  alongside  and  try  to  extinguish  the  fire.  The  first 
assistant  engineer  of  the  Aries  came  on  board  and  reported  the  engines 
of  the  Ceres  apparently  in  good  order.  At  11  the  party  returned  from 
the  Ceres,  having  done  all  that  they  could,  assisted  by  boats  from  the 
Maratanza,  with  hose  from  the  tug  Violet,  to  extinguish  the  fire. 

December  20. — At  G  a.  m.  made  two  strange  sails  on  the  port  bow; 
stood  for  one  of  them.  At  7  fired  a  blank  cartridge  at  the  chase.  At 
9:15  came  up  to  her  and  sent  Acting  Ensign  Sam  Harding,  jr.,  on  board 
of  her.  She  proved  to  be  the  schooner  Sallie ,  of  Nassau,  from  Harbor 
Island, bound  to  Baltimore,  loaded  with  salt  and  snuff.  At  9  a.  m.  sent 
Acting  Ensign  F.  Wallace  with  hawser  to  the  schooner  Sallie ;  also  sent 
Acting  Master’s  Mate  Staufield  with  three  men  as  a  prize  crew  to  take 
charge.  At  10 : 30  started  ahead  with  the  schooner  in  tow.

March  1. — At  sea.  At  7:10  a.  m.  discovered  a  steamer  making  black 
smoke  bearing  N.N.E. ;  gave  chase,  and  at  7 : 45  sent  down  yards.  From

At  8:20  tired  a  shot  across  her  bow  and  hoisted  the  ensign;  steamer 
showed  no  colors  and  hove  over  bales  of  cotton.  At  8:30  strange 
steamer  hove  to.  At  8:35  stopped  the  engine;  sent  Lieutenant  Kemptf 
and  Third  Assistant  Engineer  McGrath  on  board  of  her.  She  proved 
to  be  the  blockade  runner  Scotia ,  from  Wilmington,  bound  to  Nassau, 
loaded  with  cotton.  At  9:30  transferred  the  crew  of  the  Scotia  to  this 
ship;  sent  a  marine  guard  on  board  the  prize  steamer  Scotia.  At  noon, 
latitude  32°  44'  N.,  longitude  77°  12'  W.  At  3:30  p.  m.  sent  a  prize 
crew  on  board  the  prize  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  J.  M.  C.  Eeville. 
At  3:50  p.  m.,  everything  being  ready  on  board  the  prize,  she  parted

mate,  cook,  and  steward,  and  a  family  consisting  of  2  ladies,  1  man,  and 
a  child,  north  in  her. 

March  8.— Sent  at  5  p.  m.  36  prisoners,  which  we  captured  in  the  prize 
steamer  Scotia,  with  their  baggage,  on  board  the  Violet.  At  5:30  p.  m. 
Fort  Macon  N.  h  W.,  4  miles.

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Monticello. 

February  19,  1864. — At  4  p.  m.  sighted  the  blockading  fleet.  At  5:20 
came  to  anchor  and  captain  went  on  board  the  flagship. 

February  21. — At  9:30  p.  m.  the  batteries  opened  fire  on  us.  Cut 
away  the  hawser  and  anchored  farther  to  the  southward.  At  10  the 
gig  and  first  cutter,  armed  and  manned,  left  the  ship  and  proceeded 
up  the  channel  toward  Fort  Caswell. 

February  22.— At  3:45  a.  m.  the  boats  returned  to  the  ship,  they 
having  succeeded  in  passing  the  batteries  at  the  entrance  of  the  river 
unobserved,  and  proceeded  upward  to  Smith ville.  The  gig  was  com¬ 
manded  in  person  by  Lieutenant  Cushing,  the  first  cutter  by  Acting 
Ensign  C.  A.  Pettit,  second  cutter  by  Acting  Ensign  J.  E.  Jones,  C.  A. 
Martine,  second  assistant  engineer,  and  Acting  Master’s  Mates  How- 
orth  and  C.  Croton. 

February  24.— At  2.  a.  m.  a  boat  exhibition,  consisting  of  the  gig, 
Captain  Cushing  in  charge;  first  cutter,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign 
C.  A.  Pettit;  second  cutter,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  J.  E.  Jones; 
dingey,  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  George  [F.]  Goodrich;  the 
total  crew  consisting  of  45  men,  started  to  try  and  capture  a  battery 
on  Oak  Island.  Pulled  in  to  the  beach  and  were  discovered  and  fired 
upon.  Captain  Cushing  gave  the  order  to  retreat  and  we  returned  to 
the  ship. 

February  28. — At  4:45  p.  m.  the  rebels  opened  fire  on  the  ship  from 
the  beach  on  Smith’s  Island;  returned  their  fire  with  100-pounder  and 
30-pounder  rifies.  At  extreme  elevation  our  shells  all  fell  short,  while 
several  shots  of  the  enemy  passed  over  the  ship. 

March  6.  At  5  a.  m.  made  a  vessel  on  the  port  beam,  distant  about 
three-quarters  of  a  mile,  supposed  it  to  be  a  blockade  runner.  Star- 
boarded  the  helm  and  challenged  her.  On  her  answering’  my  chal¬ 
lenge,  put  the  helm  aport  to  keep  on  my  course,  thinking  she  was  at

April  22. — At  sea.  At  4.  p.  m.  sent  a  boat  on  board  the  schooner

Abstract  log  of  the  TJ.  S.  S.  Mount  Vernon. 

May  11,  1863. — Off  New  Inlet.  At  10  a.  m.  the  enemy  opened  fire  on 
us  at  a  distance  of  4  miles.  One  shot  fell  a  few  [yards]  astern,  the 
other  100  yards  outside  of  us.  The  guns  being  wet,  could  not  return 
the  fire. 

May  13. — At  daylight  observed  3  steamers  going  over  the  bar  at  New 
Inlet — 1  small  screw  steamer,  1  large  paddle  steamer,  also  1  large  paddle 
steamer,  painted  a  dark  color,  with  every  appearance  of  being  a  gun¬ 
boat.  Observed  the  Niphon  fire  a  shot  toward  them.  Forts  opened 
fire ;  stood  off  to  the  Iroquois. 

May  18. — A  heavy  mist  overhanging  the  land;  objects  not  very 
plainly  to  be  observed.  At  2:55  weighed  anchor  and  stood  up  and 
down  the  beach.  Daylight — a  thick  haze  overhanging  the  land.  Stood 
in  for  Fort  Fisher.  At  4:25  discovered  a  steamer  directly  under  the 
guns  of  Fort  Fisher.  This  steamer  resembled  the  Mount  Vernon  in 
every  respect,  except  that  she  had  a  small  house  on  deck  between  the 
funnel  and  the  mainmast;  her  decks  were  crowded  with  men,  and  she 
looked  as  though  she  might  be  a  gunboat,  though,  on  account  of  the 
haze,  no  guns  could  be  discerned.  At  4:30,  appearing  to  discover  us, 
she  hoisted  a  large  rebel  flag  and  stood  rapidly  inside  the  bar.  The 
State  of  Georgia  coming  up  from  the  southward,  fired  two  shot  at  her, 
but  they  fell  far  short.  This  steamer  had  apparently  been  at  anchor 
under  the  fort  all  night.  Stood  off  to  the  Iroquois  and  reported  the 
facts  of  the  case  to  the  senior  officer. 

May  22. — At  4:10  a.  m.  observed  the  Penobscot  and  a  long,  low 
steamer  between  her  and  the  shore,  standing  southward;  started 
toward  them;  steamer  ran  under  the  fort.  At  4: 15  Penobscot  opened 
fire;  stood  toward  her  as  near  inshore  as  the  pilot  could  be  persuaded 
to  go,  say  1 A  miles.  At  4 : 20  Fort  Fisher  opened  a  heavy  fire.  Penob¬ 
scot  stood  offshore  and  made  signal. 

June  5. — At  8 : 30  a.  m.  observed  one  of  the  enemy’s  steamers  stand¬ 
ing  down  the  river  toward  New  Inlet.  At  9  enemy’s  steamer  crossed 
the  bar  at  New  Inlet  and  stood  to  the  northward  as  far  as  Fort  Fisher. 
Got  underway,  cleared  for  action,  and  stood  in  for  the  enemy.  At 
9:15  the  Iroquois  and  State  of  Georgia  to  the  northward  opened  fire. 
Steamed  back  to  New  Inlet.  At  9:20  opened  fire  from  pivot  gun. 
At  9:25  the  steamer  crossed  the  bar.  Fort  Fisher  opened  fire  on  us. 
Stood  offshore.  Expended  10  pounds  cannon  powder,  one  100-pounder 
Parrott,  25- second  shell. 


778  NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

June  7. — At  9  observed  a  sail;  signaled  to  Iroquois  and  Florida  and 
stood  in  chase.  At  10  the  Shokolcon  stood  past  the  rebel  batteries  and 
crossed  Caroline  Shoal,  going  close  to  the  beach.  The  enemy  did  not 
fire  until  she  turned  to  come  out,  when  they  opened  fire  without  effect. 

June  14. — At  4:05  a.  m.  discovered  a  large  steamer,  supposed  be  the 
Gornubia ,  running  in  at  New  Inlet. 

June  15. — Stood  toward  Fort  Fisher.  At  3:50  a.  m.  [observed]  a 
large  steamer  propeller,  one  mast,  two  smokestacks,  running  in  at  New 
Inlet. 

June  16. — Observed  the  enemy’s  steamer  coming  over  the  bar.  State 
of  Georgia  fired  a  shot  from  her  pivot  gun  toward  steamer.  Fort  Fisher 
fired  7  shot,  all  outreaching  ours. 

June  17. — Discovered  a  steamer  going  over  the  bar  at  New  Inlet. 
Fort  Fisher  fired  a  shot  which  struck  State  of  Georgia ,  wounding  3 
men.  At  9  p.  m.  discovered  a  steamer  coming  over  the  bar,  steering 
about  S.  S.  W. ;  stood  in  chase.  At  9:  10  steamer  discovered  us,  stood 
back  N.  W.,  and  ran  over  Caroline  Shoal.  Followed  him  as  long  as  the 
water  would  permit.  At  9:  50  stood  off  and  anchored. 

June  IS. — At  4  a.  m.  discovered  the  steamer  which  we  had  chased 
last  night,  and  also  the  schooner  which  had  been  inside  the  bar  for 
some  time,  ashore  on  the  Caroline  Shoal  near  Zeek’s  Island.  Com¬ 
municated  with  the  State  of  Georgia.  At  5  stood  in  to  reconnoiter  the 
position  of  the  vessels.  At  5 :  30  fired  a  shot  from  the  pivot  gun,  which 
fell  short  half  a  mile.  At  the  same  time  a  shot  was  fired  at  us  from 
the  new  sand  mound  battery;  fell  within. 50  yards  of  us. 

June  19. — At  daylight  the  schooner  was  yet  ashore  at  the  mouth  of 
New  Inlet,  but  the  steamer  had  gone,  supposed  up  to  the  city  for 
repairs.  Heard  heavy  firing  on  the  south  side  of  Frying  Pan  Shoals. 

June  25. — Weighed  anchor  and  stood  toward  Fort  Fisher.  Discov¬ 
ered  a  side- wheel  steamer,  two  smokestacks  and  two  masts,  running  in 
at  New  Inlet.  At  3  p.  m.  Fort  Fisher  fired  two  shots  at  us,  both  fall¬ 
ing  short.  Two  small  steamers  cruising  on  the  bar. 

June  27. — At  daylight  discovered  a  large  side-wheel  steamer  ashore, 
just  inside  the  bar  at  New  Inlet.  The  enemy  began  firing  from  the  two 
casemate  forts  south  of  Fort  Fisher,  firing  0  shot  toward  us,  6  in  other 
directions,  and  4  blank  cartridges.  Stood  in  toward  New  Inlet  Bar. 
At  sunset  steamer  still  ashore  inside  the  bar. 

June  29. — Expended  10  pounds  cannon  powder,  one  100-pound  sand 
shot,  firing  at  a  schooner. 

July  12. — Discovered  that  the  Penobscot  had  driven  a  steamer 
ashore  and  had  commenced  firing  to  drive  the  enemy  off.  At  8 :  05  a.  m. 
took  up  a  position  to  the  northward  and  westward  of  the  woods  on 
Smith’s  Island  and  opened  fire  on  the  enemy  whenever  they  could  be 
seen.  During  the  morning  observed  squads  of  armed  men  marching 
toward  the  steamer;  also  noticed  a  steamer  cross  from  Fort  Caswell  to 
Smith’s  Island,  the  fleet  on  the  west  side  of  the  island  keeping  up  a 
heavy  fire  on  the  woods.  From  meridian  to  4  p.  in.:  Shelling  the 
northwest  end  of  Smith’s  Island  at  intervals.  Beceived  orders  from 
the  Iroquois  to  keep  firing  whenever  the  enemy  could  be  seen.  At  3, 
finding  the  enemy  coming  in  force,  set  the  steamer  on  fire.  At  3:10 
opened  fire  on  the  steamer,  the  •  Sacramento ,  Ghocura ,  Victoria ,  and 
Violet  in  sight  on  the  south  side  shelling  the  woods.  At  3:30,  the 
enemy,  having  got  their  artillery  in  position,  commenced  firing  at  us. 
Their  shots  were  promptly  returned  by  the  State  of  Georgia ,  Mount 
Vernon,  and  Penobscot.  At  4  hauled  off  and  stood  to  the  northward.

July  15. — Discovered  a  steamer  ashore  on  the  bar  at  New  Inlet,  a 
propeller,  two  masts,  one  smokestack.  A  towboat  communicated  with 
the  steamer  on  the  bar.  Fort  Fisher  fired  7  shots  at  us,  3  passing 
over  us.  Returned  the  fire  once  from  the  pivot  gun;  shot  fell  in  Fort 
Fisher.  Expended  one  10-pound  charge  cannon  powder,  one  100- 
pounder  10-second  shell. 

J uly  16. — At  4:30  a.  m.  saw  a  long,  low  side- wheel  steamer,  with  two 
masts  and  two  smokestacks,  bearing  !3.  W.  Started  ahead  full  speed 
to  cut  her  off  from  the  inlet,  but  did  not  succeed.  Fired  two  shots  at 
her  from  the  pivot  gun.  Expended  20  pounds  cannon  powder,  two  10- 
second  100-pounder  shell. 

July  24. — At  midnight  tho  Iroquois  passed  within  hail.  At  1 : 30  a.  m. 
saw  two  rockets  thrown  up  to  the  northward;  saw  the  flash  of  guns 
and  heard  shells  bursting  in  the  air;  stood  to  the  northward  at  full 
speed.  Cleared  ship  for  action.  Sent  up  rocket  to  attract  attention. 
Could  notfind  from  where  the  firing  proceeded.  At  daylightthe  Iroquois 
in  sight,  apparently  in  chase.  Learned  from  the  brig  Perry  that  they 
had  fired  fourteen  guns  at  a  steamer  running  out. 

July  25. — Stood  in  chase  of  a  vessel  bearing  N.  E.  At  12:15  p.  m. 
the  Iroquois  made  signal;  stood  for  her.  At  1  the  captain  wrent  on 
board.  Passed  withiu  hail  of  the  Iroquois  and  were  informed  of  the 
capture  by  her  of  the  rebel  steamer  Merrimac. 

August  1. — At  5:30  a.  m.  discovered  that  the  enemy  had  succeeded 
in  getting  the  steamer  Kate  (driven  ashore  at  Smith’s  Island  by  the 
Penobscot  July  12)  afloat,  and  were  towing  her  with  small  boats  toward 
Fort  Fisher.  At  5:45  made  signal  to  the  Iroquois  “I  wish  to  com¬ 
municate  with  you.”  Receiving  permission,  stood  up  and  reported  the 
circumstance;  received  an  order  to  go  in  and  cut  her  out  or  destroy 
her,  and  on  the  way  to  stop  at  the  [James]  Adger  and  inform  Commander 
Patterson  that  he  was  to  assist  us.  At  6:20  communicated  with 
the  Adger ;  stood  inshore,  the  Iroquois  following.  At  7  commenced 
firing.  At  7:05  a  shot  from  Fort  Fisher  passed  over  us  and  we  were 
immediately  opened  upon  by  all  the  batteries.  One  battery  of  Whit¬ 
worth  artillery  was  placed  about  300  yards  from  the  steamer  and  was 
very  troublesome.  At  7 : 15  received  orders  from  the  Iroquois  to  make 
an  attempt  to  cut  her  [the  steamer]  out.  Called  away  and  manned  two 
boats,  which  boarded  ier  and  slipped  the  cables  (the  enemy  having  let 
go  both  anchors  and  deserted  her).  The  Iroquois  and  James  Adger 
steamed  out  of  range.  Steamed  up  alongside  of  the  steamer  and 
boarded  her;  made  fast  a  hawser  and  backed  out  into  3^  fathoms 
water;  turned  out  and  steamed  offshore  with  the  Kate  in  tow.  At  the 
time  we  ran  alongside  of  the  Kate  she  was  in  a  quarter  less  3  fathoms 
of  water  and  about  300  yards  from  the  beach  where  the  Whitworth 
battery  was  planted.  This  battery  kept  up  a  constant  fire  on  us, 
striking  us  four  times.  One  shot  entered  the  starboard  side,  passed 
through  the  engine  room,  cutting  First  Class  Fireman  E.  II.  Peck  in 
twain,  and  lodged  in  the  engine  tool  chest,  cutting  up  many  of  the  tools. 
One  shot  cut  away  port  fore-rigging,  another  cut  away  the  fore-topmast 
rigging,  and  another  cut  away  the  fore-galf.  Expended  10-pound 
charge  cannon  powder,  6 -pound  charge  cannon  powder,  Parrott  shell, 
100-pounder,  32-pounder  shell.

August  5. — Observed  two  steamers,  one  a  side-wlieel  steamer  with 
walking  beam,  the  other  a  screw,  move  down  the  river  and  take  posi¬ 
tion  near  Fort  Fisher.  At  7  p. m.  left  the  ship;  ordered  the  Niphon  to 
send  a  boat  on  the  bar.  At  8  cast  loose  the  battery,  armed  and 
equipped  the  men,  and  stood  ready  for  action.  At  1:30  the  Niphon1  s 
boat  sent  up  a  rocket,  immediately  followed  by  another  from  the 
Niphon;  we  answered  the  rockets  and  stood  to  the  southward,  the 
rockets  going  up  in  that  direction.  At  midnight,  not  seeing  anything, 
stopped  the  engine  and  lay  to. 

August  7. — From  midnight  to  4  a.m.:  Discovered  a  rebel  steamer 
standing  across  our  stern;  stood  for  her  full  speed,  but  the  steamer 
was  evidently  gaining  on  us.  A  transport  steamer  crossed  the  bows 
of  the  rebel;  he  turned  and  stood  down  across  our  bows,  and  it 
appears  that  until  this  moment  he  had  not  discovered  us,  for  as  he 
observed  us  he  turned  again  and  stood  offshore.  Fired  two  broadsides 
into  him,  but  he  stood  on  as  before  and  soon  distanced  us.  We  sent 
up  fore  and  main  yards  and  topmasts  and  set  all  sail,  but  at  3  a.  m. 
we  lost  sight  of  him.  At  8:10  a.  m.  the  captain  returned  ou  board 
(from  the  Niphon) ;  stood  down  to  the  reef.  The  side-wheel  steamer 
yet  inside  the  inlet,  but  the  propeller  gone. 

November  7.— At  5  a.  m.  weighed  anchor  and  steamed  down  the  bay, 
Delaware  (from  Philadelphia  navy  yard). 

November  13. — At  sea.  At  9 : 15  a.  m.  observed  a  two-masted  schooner 
apparently  at  anchor  and  showing  no  colors.  Proceeded  toward  her, 
and  when  within  half  a  mile  of  her  sent  two  armed  boats  to  board 
her.  Found  her  to  be  the  schooner  Alice  Webb,  of  New  York,  dis¬ 
charged,  scuttled,  and  abandoned,  lying  in  3  feet  water  in  the  breakers. 
As  we  approached  her  the  ship  fired  4  shots  at  her,  viz,  2  from  the 
bow  chaser,  1  from  IX-inch,  and  one  from  the  stern  chaser.  First  shot 
was  fired  at  9:  45  a.  m.  Expended  from  IX-inch  guns  1  15-second  and 
1  5-second  shell,  from  20-pounder  1  5-second,  1  10-second,  and  1  percus¬ 
sion  shell  to  clear  the  guns.  At  10:35  started  ahead,  course  S.W. 
Latitude  at  meridian,  34°  37'  X.  From  9  a„  m.  to  noon  ran  W.  S.  W. 
8-^-  miles  and  S.  W.  by  W.  18  miles. 

December  16. — At  8:45  a.  m.  got  underway  and  proceeded  out  of 
Beaufort  Harbor.  At  9:15  crossed  the  bar  in  company  with  U.  S.  S. 
New  Berne.  At  9:  30  the  pilot  left  the  ship.  Shaped  the  ship’s  course 
along  the  land.  At  11:50  observed  a  schooner  at  the  entrance  of  Bear 
Inlet.  At  12  m.  called  all  hands  to  quarters  and  stood  for  the  schooner. 
At  12:30  p.  m.  anchored  in  4^  fathoms  water,  center  of  Bear  Inlet 
bearing  X.  W.  Launched  all  the  boats,  manned  and  armed  them,  and 
sent  Acting  Master  E.  W.  White  to  board  and  bring  the  schooner  out 
if  possible,  but  if  not,  to  burn  and  destroy  her.  At  1:40  p.  m.  the 
boats  returned  to  the  ship  and  Acting  Master  White  reported  that 
they  had  scuttled  and  set  fire  to  the  schooner  O.  O.  Bigelow,  the  crew 
having  run  her  aground  and  abandoned  her  a  few  moments  before  they 
got  on  board.  He  also  reported  that  she  was  without  cargo,  but  had 
dunnage  laid  apparently  for  the  storage  of  cotton.  Hoisted  up  all  the 
boats  and  proceeded  on  for  Xew  Inlet.  At  5:35  p.  m.  came  to  anchor 
off  Wrightsville. 

December  20. — At  11:50  a.  m.  saw  a  steamer  bearing  S.  E.  standing 
toward  us.  Between  and  9  and  11  heard  ten  heavy  guns  from  8.  W. 
At  1  p.  m.  steamed  up  to  the  Fort  Jackson  and  commanding  officer 
went  on  board  of  her.  At  2  p.  m.  steamed  down  to  the  W.  S.  W.  At  4

strange  sail  bearing  S.  W.  by  S.j  half  an  hour  afterwards  discovered  a

March  5,  1864. — At  daylight,  Fort  Fisher  bearing  N.  W.  by  1ST.,  the 
following  vessels  in  sight:  Fort  Jackson ,  T-uscarora ,  Britannia ,  and 
Nansemond  to  the  N.  E.  and  the  Peterlioff  to  the  S.  W.,  all  underway. 
Saw  a  screw  steamer  in  New  Inlet  with  two  masts  and  one  funuel 
between  masts,  sharp  bows,  no  bowsprits,  apparently  an  iron  vessel, 
English  ensign  ou  the  flagstaff  aft.  At  6:50  a.  m.  came  to  anchor  with 
a  hedge,  south  point  of  Smith’s  Island  bearing  S.  W.  At  8  a.  m.  the 
Cambridge  and  Niplion  in  sight  N.  E.  At  9:15  saw  a  strange  steamer 
in  sight  bearing  S.  E.  £  S.  At  9:50  senior  officer  made  signal,  went 
within  hail,  received  men  from  the  Fort  Jackson.  Also  received  orders 
to  change  our  station  from  No.  3  to  No.  5.  At  10:30  steamed  down 
toward  the  Peterlioff  and  communicated  with  her.  At  12:35  p.  m.  a 
battery  on  the  south  end  of  Smith’s  Island  opened  fire  on  us  and  the 
Peterlioff,  shots  striking  all  around  us.  Steamed  to  our  day  station. 

March  6. — At  4  a.  m.  got  underway  and  steamed  to  northward  and 
eastward.  At  sunrise  H.  S.  steamers  Tuscarora ,  Nansemond ,  Florida , 
and  Monticello  in  sight,  all  underway.  At  6:35  a.  m.  discovered  the 
U.  S.  S.  Peterlioff  sunk  near  Zeek’s  Island,  having  been  run  down  by 
the  U.  S.  S.  Monticello  at  5:45  a.  m.  At  the  same  time  saw  a  strange 
steamer  inside  steaming  toward  Fort  Fisher;  hailed  the  Monticello  and 
offered  assistance,  but  none  was  required;  then  steamed  toward  our  sta¬ 
tion.  At  7:45p.  m.  came  to  anchor  in  5|  fathoms  water  on  small 
bower;  bent  the  slip  rope  on;  Bald  Headlight  bearing  N.  W.  by  W. 
Officers  of  the  deck,  lookouts,  and  engineers  armed  with  loaded  rifles. 
Discovered  for  the  first  time  that  the  rebels  had  established  a  fixed 
light  in  the  Bald  Head  light- house. 

March  7. — From  1:30  p.  m.  to  2:30  p.  m.  a  rebel  battery  on  beach  6 
miles  to  the  nothward  of  Fort  Fisher  practicing  at  target  with  big  guns. 
At  4  p.  m.  a  large  side-wheel  sea  steamer  with  three  masts,  and  four 
river  steamers  in  sight  in  the  river.  At  6:15  p.  m.  started  ahead  and 
stood  toward  the  Peterlioff.  At  7  the  gig  and  third  cutter,  with  10 
men  each,  armed,  were  sent  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  E.  W.  White 
to  cut  away  the  masts  of  the  Peterlioff  and  to  bring  off  or  destroy  her 
guns.  The  Niphon  lying  near  us  also  sent  boats  for  the  same  purpose. 
After  the  boats  got  alongside  the  wreck,  considerable  sea  running,  and 
found  her  so  submerged  that  there  was  10  feet  of  water  above  the  spar 
deck.  Signal  lights  and  fires  burning  along  the  beach.  At  10 : 55  masts 
of  the  Peterhoff  fell;  weather  very  dark  all  night,  and  could  see  but  a 
short  distance. 

March  8. — At  12:15  a.  m.  boats  returned  from  the  wreck  of  the  Peter- 
hoff  after  having  cut  away  the  masts  and  rigging  and  spiking  all  the 
guns  that  could  be  got  at  and  throwing  them  overboard  and  unbend¬ 
ing  and  cutting  away  all  her  sails  above  water,  and  leaving  nothing  of 
the  wreck  remaining  above  water  except  the  smokestack.

April  24,  4863. — Navy  yard,  Boston.  At  9: 30  a.  m.  received  crew  on

May  5. — At  8  p.  m.  spoke  the  Iroquois ,  who  ordered  us  to  come  to

May  6. — At  8:30  p.  m.  steamed  inshore  to  within  1  mile  of  the  rebel 
batteries.  Cruised  inside  the  bar  all  this  watch. 

May  7. — At  10  a.  m.,  being  opposite  the  rebel  batteries,  saw  a  steamer 
moving  along  the  inside  channel.  The  pivot  gun  was  trained  on  her 
and  fired  at  a  distance  of  3,500  yards  by  the  first  lieutenant,  the  shell 
dropping  close  in  her  wake.  A  shell  was  also  fired  from  the  howitzer. 

May  13. — At  daylight  discovered  three  steamers  8  miles  off,  bearing 
X.  E.,  off  the  mouth  of  the  harbor.  One  was  a  steamer  of  about  1,000 
tons,  three  masts  and  two  funnels,  the  other  two  of  about  800  tons,  two 
masts,  one  funnel.  Immediately  got  underway  to  head  them  off;  fired 
the  bow  pivot  at  the  large  one,  but  the  shot  fell  short;  found  we  were 
getting  within  range  of  the  rebel  batteries,  who  opened  fire  on  us  and 
fired  six  shots,  and  we  had  the  mortification  of  seeing  them  pass  [into] 
the  harbor. 

May  22. — At  4  a.  m.  saw  a  vessel  inshore  and  made  chase.  Proved 
to  be  the  Penobscot ;  she  fired  several  shot  and  received  several  from 
the  battery.  Hauled  off  and  soon  found  him  after  us.  At  5  a.  m.  the 
Fenobscot  made  signal  to  us  fora  surgeon,  which  we  answered,  and  S3nt 
one  on  board.  Our  boat  returned  and  brought  information  that  she 
[Penobscot]  had  received  a  shot  which  killed  the  surgeon  and  wounded 
his  steward. 

May  25. — At  3:30  a.  m.  got  underway  and  stood  in  toward  shore. 
From  4  to  8  a.  m.  ran  in  for  the  batteries,  which  fired  on  us,  when  we 
put  about  and  stood  toward  the  flagship;  then  returned  to  our  station 
and  anchored.  At  5  p.  m.  all  hands  drilled  with  muskets  and  swords. 
At  9  ]>.  m.  got  underway  and  stood  X.  W.  by  X.  into  5£  fathoms  water, 
and  then  steered  parallel  with  the  coast  to  a  light,  which  we  fired  at 
twice  with  the  Parrott  and  once  with  the  howitzer,  one  shell  bursting 
directly  over  the  rebel  works. 

July  12. — From  8  to  12  meridian,  firing  from  Smith’s  Island  at  the

the  fleet  still  shelling  the  beach  on  Smith’s  Island. 

July  13. — At  4  a.  in.  fired  two  shots  from  the  20-pounder  Parrott  and
