for  our  station  and  prize  stood  for  Boston. 

August  1. — At  6  a.  m.  the  fleet  got  underway  and  stood  inshore,  firing 
constantly.  We  immediately  got  underway  and  stood  S.  W.  by  S. 
toward  them,  and  sighted  a  steamer  ashore  on  Smith's  Island.  At  7 
the  Mount  Vernon  stood  alongside  of  her  and  towed  her  oft-.  She  proved 
to  be  the  steamer  Kate ,  of  London.  On  our  passage  up  to  the  fleet  the 
fort  and  adjacent  batteries  fired  at  us  six  times,  all  falling  short. 

August  17. — At  daylight  fort  bore  S.  W.,  the  Minnesota ■  S.  E.  by  S., 
she  being  the  only  blockader  visible.  Saw  a  large  steamer  on  the  bar 
about  1  mile  from  the  fort.  At  5  a.  in.  saw  a  large  double-stacked,  side- 
wheel  steamer  standing  for  the  harbor  from  the  southward ;  alsoasmaller 
steamer,  painted  a  dark  lead  color,  standing  in  from  the  same  direc¬ 
tion,  both  being  within  range  of  the  rebel  batteries.  At  6,  the  tide 
being  at  half  flood,  steamer  got  off  the  bar  and  stood  for  the  harbor. 
She  was  a  large  screw  steamer,  from  1,500  to  2,000  tons,  pierced  for  six 
guns,  three  on  each  side,  painted  lead  color,  bark  rigged,  having  lower 
masts,  short  topmasts  and  topgallant  masts,  smokestack  forward  of 
mainmast,  and  painted  lead  color;  lower  and  topsail  yards  crossed 
and  white  scrollwork  on  stern.  She  was  a  finely  modeled  vessel,  of 
great  sheer,  and  had  every  appearance  of  being  a  fast  sailer. 

August  IS. — At  4:45  a.  m.  saw  a  steamer  bearing  N.  by  W.,  steering 
S.,  and  close  on  shore.  Gave  chase,  and  when  near  she  was  run  on 
shore  and  immediately  deserted  by  her  crew  with  boats  and  landed 
on  shore.  We  lowered  away  second  cutter  with  armed  crew,  Third 
Assistant  Engineer  William  Mason,  Acting  Ensign  E.  N.  Semon,  and 
in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  and  Executive  Officer  W.  W.  Crowninshield, 
sent  them  on  board  with  instructions  to  set  her  on  fire.  At  5:30  the 
Shokokon  communicated  and  commenced  shelling  the  shore  as  the  rebels 
were  coming  toward  the  steamer.  We  let  go  our  port  anchor  in  5£ 
fathoms  water.  Sea  and  gale  increasing,  the  boat  was  swamped  shortly 
after  getting  alongside  the  prize.  We  then  sent  two  more  boats  to  the 
prize,  with  lines  attached  to  haul  them  off,  and  in  charge  of  Acting 
Master’s  Mate  John  Paige.  When  close  by  was  capsized  and  the  crews 
taken  prisoners  by  the  rebels  on  shore.  During  the  time  a  constant 
and  rapid  fire  of  musketry  was  kept  up  on  the  boats  and  the  ship,  cut¬ 
ting  away  our  running  rigging,  penetrating  the  decks  and  sides  of  the 
ship  in  several  places.  At  0  a.  m.  a  rifle  battery  opened  fire  upon  us, 
the  shot  and  shell  passing  over  us  all  the  time.  The  sea  rising  very 
high,  we  weighed  anchor  and  commenced  shelling  the  shore.  The 
Shokokon  sent  a  boat  to  the  prize  and  rescued  two  of  our  men  when 
they  jumped  overboard.  W.  W.  Crowninshield,  executive  officer,  set 
fire  to  the  prize  with  the  men  under  his  charge.  When  we  could  ren¬ 
der  them  no  more  assistance,  they  jumped  overboard  and  swam  on 
shore  and  were  taken  prisoners.  Seeing  the  prize  well  on  fire  and  in 
flames,  and  that  her  destruction  was  certain,  at  12  meridian  we  pro¬ 
ceeded  to  the  Minnesota.  At  12  meridian  came  to  with  both  anchors; 
mustered  crew.  The  following  articles  were  lost-.  First  and  second 


784

cutter,  captain’s  gig,  5  revolvers,  9  pistols,  11  cutlasses,  1  battle-ax. 
Expended  during  the  engagement  54  shell  from  32-pounder,  32  howitzer 
shell,  26  Parrott  shell,  all  with  charges;  95  rifled  cartridges,  10  musket 
cartridges,  50  revolver  cartridges.  The  prize  proved  to  be  the  English 
steamer  Hebe,  of  London,  cargo  consisting  of  coffee,  dry  goods,  medi¬ 
cine,  liquors.  On  arriving  at  the  flagship  discovered  our  ship  making 
considerable  water.  The  donkey  pumps  were  constantly  working  after 
the  firing  ceased. 

August  23. — At  4:30  a.  m.  stood  S.  W.;  saw  a  steamer  in  under  the 
Mound ;  supposed  her  to  be  going  in.  At  5  a.  m.  stood  for  the  flagship. 
At  7:30  beat  to  quarters.  At  8:30  firing  commenced  from  the  whole 
fleet.  At  8 : 45  the  Minnesota  sent  boats  with  marines  toward  the  shore, 
when  the  rebels  opened  fire,  firing  six  shots,  two  at  us,  one  passing  and 
bursting  near  the  foremast,  the  other  passing  under  our  spanker  boom 
near  the  wheel,  bursting  a  few  feet  on  our  port  quarter  in  the  water. 
At  8:  50  a.  m.  the  Minnesota  fired  a  shell,  which  was  supposed  to  have 
blown  up  one  of  their  (rebels)  two  guns  on  shore.  At  same  time  the 
admiral  recalled  his  boats  and  made  signal  to  the  Western  World ,  who 
immediately  stood  for  her  station.  A  large  number  of  men  were 
reported  to  be  running  toward  Fort  Fisher.  We  followed  them  up, 
firing  into  them,  wounding  many,  when  they  soon  disappeared.  Ammu¬ 
nition  expended  during  the  engagement,  27  shell  for  Parrott  and 
charges;  23  howitzer;  72  32-pounder  shell ;  50  rifle  charges. 

August  31. — At  6 : 40  a.  m.  a  battery  of  heavy  guns  opened  fire  on  us, 
being  W.  N.  W.  about  14  miles  south  of  the  wreck.  Shot  and  shell  fell 
short. 

September  7. — At  1  p.  m.  beat  to  quarters  and  opened  fire  upon  a  block¬ 
ade  runner  lying  to  an  anchor  outside  and  close  to  Aew  Inlet  under 
the  guns  of  the  rebel  batteries.  Fired  15  rounds  from  the  20  pounder 
Parrott  and  drove  her  inside.  At  1:45  ceased  firing  and  returned  to 
our  station. 

September  8. — At  4  a.  m.  stood  S.  W.  At  dawn  of  day  saw  two 
steamers — one  on  the  bar,  very  long,  two  white  smokestacks,  2  masts, 
side- wheel,  tonnage  about  900  tons ;  the  other  oft' Fort  Fisher,  side-wheel, 
double  smokestacks,  two  masts,  tonnage  about  000  or  700  tons.  One 
appears  to  be  an  armed  vessel  of  four  broadside  guns.  Both  are  flying 
the  Confederate  flag;  seem  waiting  for  tide  to  go  in.  Stood  to  S.  W. ; 
had  a  good  view  of  the  rebel  steamers.  Captain  went  on  board  the 
flagship  and  returned  at  10  a.  m.  Stood  to  S.  W.,  fired  15  rounds  from 
20-pounder  Parrott  at  two  steamers  lying  under  Fort  Fisher.  At  11 : 30 
ceased  firing.  At  2:50  p.  m.  was  fired  at  from  Fort  Fisher.  The  shot 
fell  short. 

September  9. — At  5  a.  m.  saw  a  side- wheel  steamer  with  white  smoke¬ 
stack,  very  long,  two  small  masts,  fore-and-aft  rig;  tonnage,  250;  seen 
inside  of  Zeek’s  Island  steaming  up  the  river;  undoubtedly  came  in  on 
the  south  side.  The  rebel  steamer  that  was  run  on  shore  by  the  steamer 
Nansemond  had  steam  up  and  a  tug  alongside;  did  not  succeed  in  get¬ 
ting  off'.  At  8  a.  m.  saw  a  steamer  inside  of  Zeek’s  Island,  side-wheel 
and  black  smokestack,  a  slanting  house  fore  and  aft,  sharp  at  both 
ends,  painted  white  or  light  lead  color;  by  all  appearances  looked  like 
a  ram.  The  tug  returned  with  a  large  lighter  in  tow  to  take  cargo  out 
of  rebel  steamer  ashore.  At  4  p.  m.  commenced,  in  company  with  the 
Nansemond ,  to  fire  at  the  rebel  steamer  ashore  under  Fort  Fisher. 
We  fired  1  10-second  32-pounder  shell,  1G  15-second  and  1 10-second  20- 
pounder  rifle  shell.  The  fort  and  Mound  opened  fire  on  us  and  fired 
repeatedly.  At  4 : 45  ceased  firing  and  stood  for  the  flagship.

September  10. — At  5:  30  p.  m.  the  rebel  steamer  got  off  ground  and  a 
salute  was  fired  from  the  fort. 

September  16. — At  5  a.  m.  saw  a  steamer;  stood  for  her  and  discov¬ 
ered  her  to  be  a  blockade  runner  on  shore  off  Fort  Fisher;  fired  a  gun 
at  her  and  stood  for  the  flagship;  stood  toward  the  fort.  At  11  com¬ 
menced  firing  on  the  steamer  ashore,  which  was  flying  the  English  flag. 
Fired  16  rounds  from  the  20  pounder  Parrott  gun  and  struck  her  twice, 
upon  which  she  was  immediately  deserted  by  her  crew  in  boats.  The 
forts  returned  the  fire  for  about  half  an  hour;  their  shot  and  shell  fell 
short;  7  of  our  shells  exploded  shortly  after  leaving  the  gun.  At  6 
p.  m.  mustered  crew  at  quarters;  cleared  for  action.  At  6:40  weighed 
anchor  and  stood  for  the  bar.  At  7  sent  second  cutter  with  armed  crew 
in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  27.  Larsen,  in  company  with  a  boat  from  the 
Iron  Age,  to  destroy  and  set  fire  to  the  blockade  runner  ashore  off  Fort 
Fisher,  with  instructions  not  to  board  her  if  the  sea  was  breaking  so 
heavy  against  her  as  to  endanger  the  safety  of  the  boats.  At  10  p.  m. 
the  boats  returned,  having  failed  to  set  the  steamer  on  fire,  the  surf 
breaking  too  heavy  for  the  boats  to  get  alongside. 

October  10. — Saw  a  sail  27.  27.  W.,  which  proved  to  be  a  blockade 
runner.  The  Niphon,  in  company  with  the  Connecticut  and  Shenandoah, 
got  underway  immediately,  steamed  inshore  and  commenced  shelling 
her  and  shelled  her  until  in  close  proximity  to  the  forts,  when  they 
opened  fire  from  all  their  batteries.  We  steamed  in  as  far  as  prudent, 
and  finding  she  was  too  far  in  to  be  cut  off,  steamed  back  to  our  anchor¬ 
age.  During  the  time  several  shots  from  the  batteries  came  in  close 
proximity  to  all  the  vessels.  While  engaged  we  fired  2  32-pounder 
5-second  shell  and  4  10  second  20-pounder  Hotchkiss  shell. 

October  21. — At  1:30  a.  m.  firing  and  rockets  were  seen  to  the  north¬ 
ward  ;  gave  chase  and  beat  to  quarters.  Saw  a  blockade  runner  chased 
by  the  Nansemond.  Opened  fire  on  her,  and  when  she  found  there  was 
no  escape  she  was  run  ashore.  Sent  in  an  armed  boat  in  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  27.  Larsen,  who,  in  company  with  officers  and  men  from 
the  Nansemond,  set  her  on  fire  after  vainly  endeavoring  to  get  her  off. 
From  4  to  6  a.  m. :  Stood  along  inshore  in  sight  of  the  blockade  runner, 
during  which  time  the  Nansemond  saw  another  vessel,  which  she  chased 
to  sea.  At  6  a.  m.  commenced  firing  shot  and  shell  into  the  blockade 
runner,  which  proved  to  be  the  British  steamer  Venus.  Continued 
firing  until  8  a.  m.  The  Iron  Age  came  down  the  coast  and  commenced 
firing.  Continued  firing  until  about  8 : 30,  then  sent  a  boat  in  to  set  her 
on  fire  forward,  where  the  first  fire  failed  to  burn.  The  Iron  Age  also 
sent  in  a  boat  for  the  same  purpose.  She  was  set  on  fire  and  completely 
destroyed.  The  boat’s  crew  brought  off  some  small  articles,  including 
some  specie.  During  the  time  of  firing  we  expended  19  5-second 
32-pounder  shell,  2  10  second  32-pounder  shell,  28  percussion  20-pounder 
Parrott  shell;  23  5-second  20-pouuder  Parrott  shell,  and  25  12-pounder 
rifled  howitzer  shell. 

November  8. — Blockading  off  27ew  Inlet.  At  2  a.  m.  saw  rockets  fired 
to  the  northward;  stood  in  for  the  beach.  At  2  beat  to  quarters.  At 
2:15  saw  the  rebel  steamer  Cornubia  and  fired  at  her;  she  was  run 
ashore.  Sent  Acting  Ensign  H.  S.  Borden  with  a  boat’s  crew  on  board; 
also  sent  Acting  Ensign  E.  27.  Semon  in  charge  of  a  boat  on  shore  to 
bring  off  the  boats  belonging  to  the  blockade  runner,  which  the  pas¬ 
sengers  and  crew  had  used  to  land  with.  The  James  Adger  was  in  the 
meantime  trying  to  tow  her  off,  while  the  Niphon  was  shelling  the  beach. 
At  3: 30  a.  m.  the  prize  was  got  afloat.  At  4: 30  the  Cornubia’’ s  boats

were  brought  off  from  the  beach  and  hoisted  to  the ’davits  and  one 
towing  astern.  The  boats  contained  some  baggage  and  clothing  left 
there  by  those  who  left  the  blockade  runner.  At  daylight  saw  some

at  with  grape  and  canister.  Expended  2  32-pounder  5-second  shell  6, 
grape  and  2  canister;  6  20-pounder  time  shell. 

November  9. — At  12:25  a.  m.,  being  to  the  northward  of  the  Big  Hill, 
saw  a  blockade  runner  close  to  the  beach.  Gave  chase  and  beat  to 
quarters.  Kept  up  a  continued  fire  upon  her,  several  shots  taking 
effect.  Running  along  the  beach  at  full  speed,  sending  up  rockets  all 
the  time.  The  blockade  runner  being  very  fast,  was  gaining  upon  us  and 
at  last  was  lost  sight  of.  As  the  Niphon  got  within  range  of  the  Half 
Moon  battery  the  rebels  opened  lire  upon  us.  Nothing  more  was  seen 
of  the  steamer  nor  of  any  of  the  blockading  fleet.  Fire  was  opened 
from  Fort  Fisher.  Stood  to  the  northward  again  and  beat  the  retreat. 
At  3  saw  a  steamer,  gave  chase,  beat  to  quarters,  and  fired  one  gun. 
The  steamer  stood  seaward  and  was  lost  sight  of.  At  5 : 25  a.  m.,  being 
off  Masonboro  Inlet,  saw  a  steamer  to  the  northward,  coming  down  the 
coast.  Gave  chase  and  beat  to  quarters.  At  5 : 30  opened  tire  upon 
her.  She  now  stood  directly  for  us  at  full  speed,  evidently  with  the 
intention  of  running  us  down.  The  helm  was  put  hard  astarboard,  all 
the  starboard  guns  were  tired  directly  into  her,  and  the  vessels  were 
brought  nearly  side  by  side,  coming  in  collision  at  the  bows,  carrying 
away  our  bowsprit  and  stem,  and  doing  some  other  damage  to  the  ves¬ 
sel.  At  the  moment  of  the  collision  the  steamer  was  boarded,  carried, 
a  hawser  hove  on  board  and  made  fast.  In  five  minutes  from  the  time 
of  firing  the  first  gun  she  was  in  our  possession  and  a  prize  to  the 
Niphon,  no  other  vessel  being  in  sight.  Stood  south  and  eastward. 
At  5:  55  saw  one  of  the  blockaders;  made  signal  973,  which  was  an¬ 
swered.  At  6 : 50  the  answering  vessel  proved  to  be  the  U.  S.  S.  Shen¬ 
andoah.  The  captured  vessel  was  the  Ella  and  Annie ,  of  Charleston, 
S.  C.  At  8  came  to  an  anchor.  At  8: 30  the  Shenandoah  came  up  and 
let  go  her  anchor.  In  the  collision  the  kedge  anchor  was  carried  away 
and  the  barometer  kuocked  down  and  broken.  At  8 : 30  the  captain  of 
the  Ella  and  Annie  was  brought  on  board.  At  9:15  the  Shenandoah 
signaled  the  Niphon.  Captain  Breck  went  on  board  the  Shenandoah. 
At  10  the  captain  of  the  Ella  and  Annie  was  sent  on  board  the  Shen¬ 
andoah.  From  12  m.  to  4  p.  m.  the  prisoners  of  the  prize  were  received. 
A  prize  crew  was  sent  on  board  the  steamer  Ella  and  Annie.  At  5 : 30 
she  stood  to  sea. 

November  10. — At  8  a.  m.  came  to  anchor  in  Beaufort  Harbor.  From 
8  to  12  m.:  At  washing  down  decks,  they  were  found  to  leak  badly, 
supposed  to  be  occasioned  by  the  collision  with  the  steamer  Ella  and 
Annie.  At  2:30  p.  m.  the  prisoners  captured  on  board  the  Ella  and 
Annie  were  sent  on  board  the  New  Berne;  the  crew  were  sent  away  in 
irons.  At  3  sent  two  pair  of  hand  irons  on  board  the  New  Berne. 

November  15.-— At  1: 45  p.  m.  hove  up  anchor  and  stood  out  to  sea. 

November  20. — Came  to  off'  navy  yard,  Boston. 

February  6 ,  1864. — Blockading  off  New  Inlet,  North  Carolina.  At  1 
p.  m.  boat  exercise.  At  1 : 30  spoke  the  Cambridge ,  got  underway,  and 
stood  for  Masonboro,  and  commenced  firing  into  a  blockade  runner 
ashore  there.  At  3 : 30  ceased  tiring.  Sent  a  boat  in  to  ascertain  what 
damage  the  steamer  had  received.  Ammunition  expended:  9  32- 
pounder  5  second  and  15  32-pounder  10-second  shell,  and  2  32-pounder 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  787 

shot;  15  20-pounder  time  shell;  9  12-pounder  percussion  shell.  At  5 
p.  m.  the  second  cutter  and  second  launch  boarded  the  Dee,  blockade 
runner,  ashore,  burning,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  H.  S.  Borden, 
executive  officer.  The  boats  returned  at  sundown. 

February  7.— At  2  p.  m.  stood  in  for  the  wreck  of  the  steamer  Dee. 
At  3  arrived  there  and  came  to  by  kedge.  Sent  two  boats  in  to  destroy 
some  lead,  etc.  The  Cambridge  also  sent  in  two  boats. 

February  23. — At  10:30  beat  to  quarters  and  stood  inshore  and  fired 
at  some  cavalry  on  the  beach.  Expended  2  32-pounder  5-second  shell 
and  1  grape;  6  20-pouuder  time  shell  and  1 12-pounder  percussion  shell. 
At  2  p.  m.  sent  a  boat  with  an  armed  crew  ashore  to  get  some  sand. 
Shelled  some  horsemen  and  expended  12  32-pounder  shell;  9  20-pounder 
shell,  and  6  12-pounder  shell. 

March  7. — At  8  p.  m.  sent  two  boats  to  destroy  the  U.  S.  S.  Peterhoff. 
At  10:30  p.  m.  received  on  board  some  sails,  blocks,  etc.,  from  the 
wreck  of  the  Peterhoff.  At  12  midnight  the  boats  took  a  line  to  the 
wreck.  Got  up  kedge  and  pulled  the  gun  off  the  forecastle. 

March  11. — At  2  saw  a  box  and  barrel  floating  about;  lowered  second 
cutter  and  second  launch  and  brought  them  on  board.  The  box  con¬ 
tained  saddles  and  the  barrel  beef.  At  4  saw  another  barrel  of  beef, 
which  was  brought  on  board. 

April  18. — At  8:30  p.  m.  lowered  the  second  cutter  with  Acting 
Ensign  H.  S.  Borden  and  E.  N.  Semon,  with  the  pilot  and  boat’s  crew, 
on  reconuoitering  expedition  up  Masonboro  Inlet.  At  10:30  second 
cutter  returned. 

April  20. — At  6  a.  m.  steamed  up  slowly  toward  Masonboro  Inlet; 
fleet  to  the  southward.  At  9 : 30  saw  mounted  rebels  on  the  beach  by 
Big  Hill;  stood  inshore;  opened  on  them  with  grape  and  shrapnel,  when 
they  retreated  toward  Fort  Fisher.  Stood  offshore. 

April  21. — From  4  to  8  p.  m. :  Two  armed  boats  came  aboard  from  the 
Fort  Jachson  and  one  from  the  Hoivquah.  Got  underway  and  stood  for 
Masonboro  Inlet,  where  we  arrived  at  7  p.  m.  Sent  six  armed  boats 
under  the  command  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  J.  B.  Breck  inshore 
to  destroy  the  State  salt  works.  At  8 : 30  p.  m.  the  State  salt  works  were 
destroyed  and  the  boats  returned  with  prisoners.  Three  of  the  boats 
belonged  to  the  Niphon,  two  to  the  Fort  Jackson,  and  one  to  the  How- 
quah.  While  the  salt  works  were  being  destroyed  the  Howquah  shelled 
the  beach  to  the  southward. 

April  27. — At  1  p.  m.  sent  a  boat  inshore  to  reconnoiter.  At  2  boat 
returned.  At  3:30  came  to  by  the  kedge,  anchored  off  Masonboro 
Inlet.  At  3:45  the  rebels  commenced  firing  at  us  with  light  artillery, 
which  fell  short.  Got  underwray  and  answered  with  20-pounder  Par¬ 
rott.  At  4 : 30  fired  three  shells  from  20  pounder  Parrott  in  one  of  their 
salt  works,  driving  the  people  into  the  woods,  the  rebels  keeping  up  a 
fire  on  us  with  field  artillery,  which  fell  short.  At  6:30  mustered  at 
quarters  and  cleared  for  action.  The  rebels  fired  occasionally,  which 
we  answered  with  20-pounder  Parrott. 

April  29. — At  5  a.  m.  got  underway  and  stood  along  the  coast.  The 
rebels  opened  fire  upon  us  with  their  Whitworth  guns;  fired  three  shot. 
Fleet  to  southward.  At  9  a.  in.  saw  some  rebels  on  the  beach ;  stood  in 
and  shelled  them  out.  At  10  ceased  firing.  Expended  9  shell  from 
the  pivot,  3  from  the  howitzer,  and  11  from  the  32-pounders.  At  10 : 20 
came  to  with  kedge  off  Big  Hill.  At  1  p.  m.  saw  people  on  the  beach 
by  the  wrecks  north  of  Masonboro;  got  underway  and  stood  for  them. 
As  we  approached,  they  ran  away.

May  7,  1863.— At  12:30  p.  m.  made  a  sail,  fired  at  her  from  the  how¬ 
itzer,  and  brought  her  to;  took  her  alongside  and  continued  down  the 
sound.  Proved  to  be  the  Tiro  Marys,  of  Edenton.  At  7  p.  m.  the 
pilot  came  on  board  from  the  Petty  Martain  and  took  us  up  the  Little 
River  some  4  miles.  From  8  to  midnight :  Put  up  the  plating  and  armed 
the  watch,  the  Petty  Martain  having  been  attacked  by  guerrillas. 

May  8. — At  4  a.  m.  all  hands  were  called  and  we  proceeded  up  the 
river  to  Nixon’s  [Nixonton].  At  5  a.  m.  went  to  quarters  and  shelled 
the  woods  as  we  went  up;  came  to  anchor  and  sent  some  boats  on 
shore.  Once  in  a  while  threw  shell  and  canister  into  the  woods. 
Boats  came  on  board  bringing  1  prisoner.  Engaged  in  helping  Union 
soldiers  removing  their  families  and  effects  on  board  their  schooner. 

May  9. — At  1  p.  m.  arrived  at  the  mouth  of  Alligator  Creek  [River], 
came  to  anchor,  and  sent  on  shore  an  expedition.  At  4:30  p.  m.  fired  a 
shell  from  Parrott  gun,  brought  the  boat  to,  and  took  her  alongside; 
stood  back  to  our  anchorage  when  our  expedition  returned.  Stood 
across  to  the  opposite  side  of  the  river  and  anchored. 

May  11. — Midnight:  Sent  launch  and  gig  on  an  expedition  with  20 
men  and  3  officers.  At  4:30  a.  m.  boats  returned,  bringing  2  prison¬ 
ers  and  large  canoe.  Steamed  back  to  Alligator  Creek,  when  we  came 
to  anchor.  From  8  to  meridian :  Took  another  canoe.  At  1  steamed 
down  the  sound;  at  2  p.  m.  fired  two  shells  from  the  Parrott  gun  at  a 
small  sloop,  brought  her  to,  and  towed  her  down  to  the  entrance  to 
Croatan  Sound,  when  we  came  to  anchor. 

May  12. — From  12  to  4  p.  m. :  Still  at  anchor  in  Alligator  Creek.  At 
3:30  p.  m.  fired  a  Parrott  shell  at  a  boat  and  brought  her  to. 

May  13. — At  3:30  a.  m.  an  expedition  landed  and  went  up  the  creek, 
captured  1  boat  and  had  a  look  about  the  premises  of  Mr.  Cooper. 
From  4  to  8  a.  m. :  Expedition  returned  and  we  proceeded  down  the 
river.  From  8  to  meridian :  Came  to  anchor  at  Alligator  Creek,  took 
our  boats  alongside,  and  got  underway.  Steamed  across  the  river; 
fired  2  Parrott  shell  at  a  vessel ;  did  not  bring  her  to.  Stood  on  our  way 
across  the  river. 

May  14. — At  10  a.  m.  anchored  at  Powell’s  Point.  At  11  captain  left 
on  an  expedition.  From  12  to  4  p.  m.  fired  3  10-pound  charges,  1  shot, 
and  2  shell  with  the  Parrott,  and  2  shell  from  the  howitzer;  did  not 
heave  her  to.  At  5  p.  in.  went  to  quarters.  At  5:30  a  boat  loaded 
with  salt  came  alongside  in  charge  of  one  of  onr  men;  took  the  salt  and 
sails  on  board,  also  2  prisoners,  Mr.  John  Johnson  and  Abel  Jarvis. 
At  0 : 30  the  captain  returned,  bringing  a  boat  with  him,  the  men  having 
escaped. 

May  17. — At  4: 30  a.  m.  made  a  sail;  went  after  her;  found  her  to 
contain  salt,  which  we  took  on  board. 

May  18. — From  8  to  12  m. :  Fired  a  Parrott  shell  at  a  boat,  brought 
her  to,  and  took  on  board  her  passengers,  who  were  bound  to  Roanoke 
Island. 

May  19. — From  8  to  meridian:  Put  our  prisoners  on  board  the  Miami, 
took  on  board  some  soldiers,  and  took  in  tow  a  launch  and  proceeded 
up  the  North  River.  From  12  to  4  p.m. :  Arrived  at  the  canal  [Albe¬ 
marle  and  Chesapeake] ;  landed  and  made  a  reconnoissance.  At  2  p.  m. 
came  on  board  and  we  started  down  the  river.  At  5  p.  m.  put  our 
launch  and  soldiers  on  board  the  Miami,  also  the  salt  we  had  captured. 

May  22. — At  4  a.  m.  called  all  hands  and  started  up  the  Blackwater, 
having  taken  on  board  25  soldiers.  At  7 : 30  turned  about  and  steamed

down  the  river.  At  3  p.  m.  entered  the  Melierrin  River  and  proceeded

May  24. — At  3  a.  m.  expedition  returned  on  board,  having  captured 
2  lieutenants  and  5  guerrillas.  At  5:30  arrived  at  Plymouth. 

May  31. — At  9  p.  m.  expedition  went  on  shore  at  mouth  of  Mekerrin 
River. 

June  1. — At  4:30  a.  m.  expedition  returned  bringing  as  prisoner  Ser¬ 
geant  White,  wko  was  proceeding  home  on  furlough.  Put  prisoners 
on  board  tke  Massasoit. 

June  23. — At  7:30  a.  m.  proceeded  up  Chowan  River.  At  8  discov¬ 
ered  a  company  of  rebel  cavalry  on  tke  banks  of  tke  river  near  Colerain; 
fired  two  shots  at  them  from  tke  rifle  gun.  Expended  2  Parrott  shell, 
2  10-pound  charges.  At  5:20  p.  m.  entered  the  mouth  of  the  Roanoke 
River. 

July  5. — At  6:35  p.  m.  got  underway  and  took  a  scow  in  tow,  loaded 
with  artillery  horses,  and  towed  it  up  river  to  wharf  abreast  Ninety- 
sixth  New  York  Volunteers’  camp.  Disembarked  the  horses,  returned 
to  Plymouth  and  loaded  scow  with  artillery  and  caissons.  From  8  to 
midnight:  Engaged  during  the  watch  transporting  troops  and  cavalry 
horses  to  the  Ninety-sixth  New  York  Volunteers’  encampment.  The 
Valley  City,  Commodore  Ferry,  and  Southfield  proceeded  up  the  river. 

July  6. — At  12 : 45  a.  m.  started  up  the  river  after  the  gunboats  which 
had  preceded  us.  At  3  came  up  with  the  Commodore  Perry,  Southfield, 
and  Valley  City,  when  we  took  the  advance  and  proceeded  up  the  river 
the  fleet  following.  From  4  a.  in.  to  meridian :  Proceeding  up  the  river, 
stopping  occasionally,  waiting  for  the  gunboats  to  come  up.  Heard 
several  reports  of  artillery  down  the  river.  Current  in  the  river  run¬ 
ning  rapidly;  much  drift  stuff.  From  meridian  to  8  p.  m. :  Proceeded 
slowly  up  the  river  against  a  strong  current,  stopping  occasionally  for 
the  other  gunboats  to  come  up.  At  3  p.  m.  arrived  abreast  of  Williams- 
ton.  Saw  a  large  force  of  rebel  infantry  and  cavalry  forming  in  line  of 
battle  in  front  of  the  town.  At  4:30  p.  m.  opened  fire  on  the  rebel 
troops.  The  Commodore  Perry  and  Valley  City  also  opened  fire  on  the 
rebel  troops  who  had  formed  in  line  of  battle  on  the  crest  of  a  hill. 
Shifted  anchorage  a  short  distance  down  the  river.  At  6:30  p.  m. 
Southfield  arrived.  At  7  p.  m.  sent  a  flag  of  truce  ashore,  ordering  the 
women  and  children  out  of  the  town,  as  the  rebels  held  it  in  force.  At 
7 : 30  fire  was  opened  on  the  town  by  the  Southfield ,  Commodore  Perry, 
and  Valley  City.  At  8  ceased  firing. 

July  7. — From  midnight  until  4  a.  m. :  Continued  to  bombard  Wil- 
liamston  during  the  watch,  firing  the  Parrott  gun  and  the  24-pounder 
howitzer  alternately  at  intervals  of  tweuty  minutes.  Fired  shrapnel 
from  the  howitzer  and  percussion  shell  from  the  Parrott  gun.  At  4: 10 
a.  m.  Captain  Flusser  ordered  to  cease  firing  and  left  the  steamer.  The 
troops  then  landed  and  occupied  the  town  under  the  fire  of  our  boats. 
At  7  the  troops  embarked  on  board  and  prepared  to  get  underway. 
At  9 : 30  weighed  anchor  and  commenced  dropping  down  the  river.  At

1 : 30  p.  m.  hove  in  the  port  cable,  turned  around,  and’  steamed  down 
the  river.  Overhauled  the  Valley  City  which  had  swung  broadside  to 
the  current.  In  trying  to  avoid  a  collision  we  ran  against  the  bank  of 
the  river,  damaging  the  dingey,  hammock  nettings,  etc.,  by  the  over¬ 
hanging  trees  and  limbs.  Anchored  and  let  the  Valley  City  precede

anchored  abreast  of  a  farm  and  Captain  Flusser  went  ashore.  At  5 
proceeded  down  the  river  and  came  to  anchor  off  Plymouth  at  5:55. 

July  23. — At  9  p.  m.  sent  a  boat  with  officer  and  armed  boat’s  crew 
to  the  Umpire  [Emperor].  Landing  to  watch  for  boats  running  the 
blockade.  At  6:40  p.  m.  entered  the  Albemarle  Sound;  lay  to  off 
mouth  of  Eoanoke  Eiver  until  dark,  when  we  steered  for  the  Chowan 
Eiver. 

July  24. — At  12:10  a.  m.  the  boat  expedition  started  to  cruise  the 
eastern  shore  for  blockade  runners.  From  4  to  8  a.  m. :  Lying  to  off 
Simon’s  [Salmon]  Creek.  At  5:30  saw  a  dense  smoke  caused  by  the 
burning  of  a  storehouse  in  the  vicinity  of  Simon’s  [Salmon]  Creek,  used 
by  the  Confederates.  Sent  boat  expeditions  ashore  at  Coleraiu,  Holly 
Landing,  and  Cannon’s  Fishery.  At  7:30  p.  m.  boats  returned. 

July  25. — At  6  p.  m.  boat  expedition  started  off,  consisting  of  one 
launch  with  howitzer  and  two  boats  with  armed  crews.  Lying  off  the 
mouth  of  Eocky  Hawk  [Eockahock]  Creek.  At  9 : 45  boat  expedition 
returned,  bringing  one  boat  that  was  captured. 

July  26. — At  4: 30  a.  m.  saw  a  number  of  transports  steering  toward 
Eoanoke  Eiver.  At  6 : 05  stood  for  them.  At  8 : 15  a.  m.  came  to  anchor 
about  3  miles  off  the  mouth  of  Eoanoke  Eiver.  Captain  returned  from 
the  Valley  City  with  a  launch;  then  went  on  board  the  steam  transport 
Escort ;  returned  at  9,  got  underway,  and  proceeded  up  the  Chowan 
Eiver.  From  meridian  to  4  p.  m. ;  Proceeding  up  the  Chowan  Eiver  in 
advance  of  the  fleet,  consisting  of  the  Valley  City ,  Commodore  Perry , 
and  nine  army  transports,  etc.  Major  General  Foster  is  on  board  the 
Escort.  At  2:30  anchored  abreast  of  Winton.  The  army  transports 
went  alongside  the  wharf  and  landed  the  troops  and  artillery. 

July  27. ■ — From  8  to  meridian :  This  morning  a  large  force  of  our  cav¬ 
alry  arrived  abreast  of  Winton  from  Norfolk.  The  army  boats  are 
engaged  in  ferrying  the  cavalry  over  the  river. 

July  29. — At  11:30  a.  m.  Captain  Flusser  came  on  board,  weighed 
anchor,  and  proceeded  up  the  river.  At  11:50  entered  the  Meherrin 
Eiver.  At  12:30  p.  m.  put  up  the  iron  plating,  called  to  quarters,  and 
ran  the  howitzerout.  At  2 : 40  arrived  and  anchored  abreast  of  Murfrees¬ 
boro.  Captains  Flusser  and  French  lauded  with  an  armed  party.  A 
company  of  soldiers  landed  from  the  Valley  City  and  marched  to  the 
town.  Acting  Master  [John  E.j  Dickinson  lauded  with  a  party  and 
destroyed  the  bridge  by  setting  it  on  fire.  From  4  to  6  p.  m. :  The  gig 
came  alongside  bringing  a  Confederate  soldier,  a  prisoner,  who  was  taken 
from  the  hospital,  convalescent.  Mr.  Dickinson  still  absent  burning 
bridge.  At  6 : 15  p.  m.  the  expedition  returned  on  board.  Proceeded 
to  the  bridge,  put  a  hawser  to  it,  and  pulled  it  down.  Anchored 
abreast  of  Cooper’s  plantation  and  brought  off  25  negroes  and  their 
furniture. 

July  30. — The  cavalry  expedition  has  returned,  and  the  army  boats 
are  ferrying  them  across  the  river. 

August  5. — At  5  a.  m.  proceeded  up  the  Pasquotank  Eiver,  following 
the  Miami.  At  8 : 30  went  on  board  the  Miami  and  took  on  board  from 
her  120  soldiers  and  some  sailors,  and  proceeded  up  the  river  to  a 
bridge  3  miles  above  Elizabeth  City.  Landed  the  forces,  with  13  men

Elizabeth  City.  Landed  the  soldiers,  who  marched  to  Camden  Court-.

August  7. — At  2  p.  m.  anchored  off  Powell’s  Point  and  sent  a  boat 
expedition  ashore.  At  3 : 30  boat  expedition  returned ;  weighed  anchor 
and  steered  for  Alligator  River.  From  4  to  6  p.  m. :  Overhauled  a  boat 
by  tiring  a  5-second  shell  from  howitzer;  took  her  in  tow  and  proceeded 
up  the  Alligator  River  in  chase  of  a  boat;  chased  boat  ashore;  came

captured  boat  came  alongside  in  charge  of  one  of  the  boat’s  crew. 

August  8. — Cruising  in  the  Alligator  River  after  blockade  runners. 

August  10. — Midnight  to  4  a.  in.:  Lying  at  anchor  in  Edenton  Bay. 
Sent  a  boat  with  armed  crew  down  the  bay  to  watch  for  boats  running 
the  blockade.  At  5:30  a.  m.  boat  returned  with  a  large  canoe  in  tow, 
which  she  had  captured.  At  9:35  a.  m.  came  to  anchor  outside  the 
bar  in  the  mouth  of  the  Scuppernong  River.  Sent  an  expedition  up 
the  Scuppernong  River  consisting  of  two  boats  from  the  Underwriter 
and  two  from  us,  with  armed  crews.  At  11  the  dingey  returned  with  a 
captured  canoe.  At  1  p.  m.  the  expedition  returned  with  two  large 
boats.  Returned  the  canoe  captured  in  the  morning  to  the  owner. 

August  14. — From  G  to  8  p.  m. :  Fitted  out  and  sent  on  shore  an  expe¬ 
dition  consisting  of  two  boats,  with  armed  crews  and  a  party  of  sol¬ 
diers,  under  the  command  of  Captain  French  and  Colonel  Cullen. 

August  15. — At  6:45  a.  m.  the  expedition  returned,  bringing  8  pris¬ 
oners,  3  of  whom  were  conflued  in  double  irons  on  board.  The  soldiers 
and  5  prisoners  were  landed  and  the  boats  returned. 

Aiigust  16. — At  3  p.  in.  came  to  anchor  about  4  miles  above  Elizabeth 
City.  Landed  troops  and  10  men,  who  marched  off  on  an  expedition. 
From  4  to  G  p.  m. :  Lying  to  an  anchor  with  guns  trained  on  the  roads. 
At  6:10  the  expedition  returned,  having  captured  38  muskets  and  76 
cartridge  boxes  and  belts,  25  bayonets,  G  bayonet  scabbards,  10  cap 
boxes.  Proceeded  down  the  river ;  came  to  anchor  at  9:20  at  mouth 
of  the  Pasquotank. 

August  17. — At  9:30  sent  a  boat  expedition  up  the  Currituck  Canal. 
From  4  to  6  p.  in.:  The  expedition  returned  having  captured  nine 
boats,  three  with  corn  on  board. 

November  6. — From  8  to  meridian:  Proceeding  up  the  Chowan  River 
in  company  with  the  Miami ,  the  fleet  of  steam  transports  following. 
At  11 : 20  passed  Holly  Landing.  At  11 : 45  called  all  hands  to  quarters 
and  put  up  the  iron  plating.  The  Miami  signalized  for  us  not  to  lire 
until  ordered.

November  7. — At  11  a.  m.  all  hands  to  quarters 'and  cleared  for 
action.  Saw  nothing  of  the  enemy.  At  11:45  steamed  back  up  the 
river  again.  At  12:30  p.  m.  arrived  abreast  of  Winton  and  was 
ordered  to  proceed  up  the  river,  the  Delaware  following,  with  Captain 
Flusser  and  General  Peck  on  board.  At  1  p.  m.  called  all  hands  to 
quarters  and  prepared  for  action.  At  3  p.  m.  fired  100  pounder  rifle 
shell  at  some  rebel  pickets  at  Eeddick’s  Landing.  At  3:30,  when  a 
short  distance  below  the  mouth  of  the  Blackwater,  turned  round  and 
proceeded  down  the  river.  At  5: 45  let  go  anchor  off  Winton. 

January  28,  1864. — Proceeding  up  Koanoke  Eiver. 

February  5. — At  9:10  a.  in.  passed  the  light  house  at  the  mouth  of 
Pamlico  Eiver  and  proceeded  on  up.  At  1  p.  m.  spoke  the  Miami  at 
anchor  off  Hill’s  Point  battery;  then  proceeded  up  the  river.  At  2: 15 
p.  m.  ran  aground  near  Washington;  got  off  with  the  assistance  of  the 
steamer  Trumpeter.  At  2 :  35  proceeded  down  the  river  and  came  to 
anchor  off  Eodman’s  Point.  From  4  to  G  p.  m. :  Proceeding  down  the 
river  until  steamer  Trumpeter  overtook  us  and  ordered  us  to  Moothes 
[Maul’s?]  Point,  to  remain  there  until  further  orders  from  Commander 
'Eenshaw.  From  6  to  8  p.  m.:  At  anchor  off  Moothes  [Maul’s?]  Point, 
firing  port  howitzer  and  Parrott  gun  alternately  at  intervals  of  thirty 
minutes  apart,  using  shrapnel  from  howitzer  and  shell  from  Parrott. 
From  8  to  midnight:  Throwing  shell  at  intervals  of  an  hour  on  the 
point  to  prevent  the  erection  of  a  battery.  Expended  2  Parrott  per¬ 
cussion  shell  and  2  shrapnel,  22  10-pound  charges. 

March  1. — From  meridian  to  4  p.  m. :  Proceeding  up  the  Chowan 
Eiver,  the  Southfield  following.  At  6:15  p.  m.  the  enemy  opened  fire 
upon  us  from  the  bluff  with  artillery  at  the  distance  of  700  yards. 
Eeturned  the  fire  effectually  with  shrapnel  and  percussion  shell.  At 
6: 45  the  enemy  were  silenced.  Proceeded  down  the  river  in  company 
with  the  Southfield ;  concealed  all  lights  and  anchored  for  the  night. 
Ammunition  expended:  5  percussion  shell,  10  shrapnel,  1  shell,  howit¬ 
zer;  5  10-pound  charges.  One  seaman  wounded  by  recoil  of  Par¬ 
rott  gun. 

March  2. — From  meridian  to  4  p.  m. :  Firing  shell  from  Parrott  gun 
on  the  bluffs  where  the  enemy  were  last  seen.  Occasionally  a  shot 
from  howitzer,  but  no  reply  from  them;  the  Southfield  firing  also.  At 
4:30  p.  m.  the  Bombshell  hove  in  sight,  coming  down  the  river.  As 
the  Bombshell  arrived  without  being  fired  at  coming  down  the  river, 
she  went  alongside  the  Massasoit,  which  took  her  in  tow,  and  we  all 
proceeded  down  the  river,  throwing  a  shell  occasionally  on  the  bluffs 
as  we  passed  down.  Ammunition  expended  during  the  day:  37  per¬ 
cussion  shell,  2  15-second  shell,  rifle;  17  shrapnel,  howitzer;  37  10-pound 
charges.  From  8  to  midnight:  Eunning  down  the  Chowan  Eiver, 
crossed  the  sound,  and  proceeded  up  the  Eoanoke  Eiver.  At  10  p.  m. 
came  to  anchor  at  the  upper  station. 

March  4.— Proceeded  up  the  river  (Chowan),  the  army  steamer  Bomb¬ 
shell  following.  When  about  a  mile  below  Petty  Shore  discovered  a 
squad  of  rebel  pickets  ou  a  road.  Fired  several  rounds  at  them  from 
howitzers  and  then  proceeded  up  the  river  to  the  bluff  at  Petty  Shore. 
Expended  2  shrapnel,  1  shell,  howitzer;  1  percussion  Parrott  shell, 
1 10- pound  charge. 

March  27.— Lying  at  anchor  abreast  Hyman’s  Ferry.  At  7  : 30  a.  m. 
the  steamers  Massasoit  and  Bombshell  came  up  the  [Eoanoke]  river 
with  six  hulks  in  tow,  and  proceeded  up  the  river  above  us  for  the  pur¬ 
pose  of  making  a  blockade  by  sinking  the  hulks  across  the  river.  At

6 : 30  p.  m.,  the  hulks  being  sunk,  our  working  party  returned  on  board. 
At  9  shitted  our  anchorage  farther  up  the  river,  nearer  the  blockade. 

April  16. — At  0:  30  a.  m.  discovered  a  Confederate  battery  of  0  guns 
at  Sharp’s  place.  At  G :  45  opened  fire  on  the  battery,  from  which  they 
returned  our  fire  by  sending  us  some  twenty-five  shots,  which  all  fell 
short.  At  9 : 20  a.  m.  weighed  anchor  and  proceeded  down  the  [Chowan] 
river.  As  we  passed  Colerain  we  fired  a  shell  at  the  bank,  but  got  no 
reply.  Expended  4  percussion  shell,  1  15-second  shell,  and  5  10-pound 
charges  for  rifle  gun. 

April  IS. — At  5  a.  m.  heavy  firing  was  heard  in  the  direction  of 
Plymouth  and  was  continued  during  the  watch.  At  9 : 15  beat  to  quar¬ 
ters  and  mustered  the  crew.  At  9 : 30  a  colored  man  arrived  from  up 
the  river  with  important  news  concerning  the  enemy.  At  10  proceeded 
down  the  river  below  Hyman’s  Ferry,  then  returned  to  our  anchorage. 
Firing  was  heard  at  intervals  during  the  forenoon.  From  meridian  to 
4  p.  m.  heard  heavy  firing  in  the  direction  of  Plymouth.  At  4 :  30  p.  in. 
a  boat  arrived  from  the  Ceres,  having  come  through  the  Thoroughfare, 
and  then  returned  down  the  river  again.  During  the  latter  part  of  the 
watch  there  was  very  heavy  firing  heard  in  the  direction  of  Plymouth. 
From  G  to  8  p.  m.  heard  heavy  fil  ing  in  the  direction  of  Plymouth.  At 
8: 10  p.  m.  discovered  lights  from  two  steamers  coming  down  the  river. 
Immediately  slipped  our  cable  and  slowly  dropped  down  the  river, 
waiting  for  the  ram  and  Cotton  Plant  to  make  their  appearance  below 
the  blockade,  which  they  soon  did.  When  we  saw  them  we  sent  up  a 
rocket  to  alarm  Captain  Flusser  at  Plymouth,  which  the  ram  answered, 
supposing  it  came  from  their  party.  When  we  came  to  the  upper 
Thoroughfare  we  ran  in,  and  in  so  doing  we  ran  aground;  ran  aline 
and  succeeded  in  getting  her  off'.  Then  we  started  for  the  blockade,  in 
which  we  stuck,  and  just  at  that  time  the  ram  and  steamer  made  their 
appearance.  As  we  lay  we  could  not  get  our  guns  to  bear,  and  conse¬ 
quently  made  up  our  minds  if  they  saw  us  to  set  fire  to  her  and  leave 
in  the  boats.  They  went  on  down  without  seeing  us  and  we  proceeded  on. 

April  19. — At  12:30  a.  m.  arrived  off'  Plymouth  and  came  to  anchor 
near  the  Miami  and  Southfield.  Captain  Barrett  reported  to  Captain 
Flusser  that  the  ram  was  coming  down  to  Warneck  [Warren  Neck]. 
Steamers  Miami  and  Southfield  were  laid  alongside  of  each  other  and 
secured  with  chains  in  that  position.  At  3:15  a.  m.  the  Ceres  came 
down  the  river  and  reported  the  ram  coming,  she  having  passed  Fort 
Gray  and  the  obstructions  in  the  river.  At  3:30  she  struck  the  South- 
field  and  became  wedged  between  her  and  the  Miami ,  both  vessels  firing 
solid  shot,  which  the  ram  returned  with  musketry.  The  Southfield 
sank  in  a  few  moments.  We  then  proceeded  slowly  down  the  river  in 
company  with  the  Miami  and  Ceres.  At  5  a.  m.  stopped  at  the  mouth 
of  the  river;  it  wms  then  daylight.  Signal  was  made  from  the  Miami. 
Captain  then  w^ent  on  board;  then  proceeded  over  to  Edenton  Bay.  At 
7  a.  m.  received  information  that  Captain  Flusser  was  killed  in  the 
engagement  with  the  ram.  At  8  stopped  off  Edenton.  At  8:30  the 
remains  of  Captain  Flusser  were  put  on  board  the  Ceres  and  sent  to 
New  Berne.  At  9  a.  m.  Captain  French  came  on  board.  We  got 
underway  and  proceeded  across  the  sound  and  anchored  at  the  buoy  at 
the  mouth  of  the  Eoanoke  Eiver.  Sent  a  boat  ashore  in  charge  of  Mr. 
Nelson,  who  brought  off  several  ladies  who  had  left  Plymouth  when  it 
was  attacked,  they  having  been  all  night  in  the  woods.  At  11 : 05  got 
underway  and  proceeded  toward  Edenton  in  company  with  steamer 
Miami.  At  9 : 15  p.  m.  stopped  off  the  mouth  of  the  Eoanoke  Eiver  and

lay  to  under  steam  to  watch  for  the  rebel  ram  if  she  came  down  the 
river. 

April  20. — At  7  p.  m.  sent  the  gig,  with  armed  crew  and  officer,  fitted 
out  for  an  expedition,  to  the  U.  S.  S.  Tacony.  Ran  the  guns  out  and 
armed  the  watch.  At  9 : 30  p.  m.  the  boat  expedition  returned  in  great 
haste,  having,  as  they  supposed,  seen  tlie  rebel  ram  and  Cotton  Plant 
coming  down  the  river.  All  hands  to  quarters,  weighed  anchor,  and 
ran  a  short  distance  out  in  the  sound,  in  company  with  the  Tacony  and 
Miami;  returned  and  stopped  near  the  buoy. 

April  29. — 12  until  4  a.  m.:  Lay  to  under  steam  below  Sandy  Point. 
At  3:  45  a.  m.  the  Ceres  gave  the  signal  of  alarm,  which  was  answered. 
Shortly  afterwards  the  Miami  made  signal  to  follow  her  down  the 
sound.  Running  down  the  sound  until  5  a.  in.,  when  we  all  turned 
round  and  proceeded  back  up  the  sound.  Ran  into  Edenton  Bay,  in 
company  with  the  Massasoit ,  and  remained  there  until  the  other  steam¬ 
ers  came  in,  when  we  anchored.  At  10:30  a.  m.  the  rebel  ram  was  seen 
coming  out  of  the  Roanoke  River.  Weighed  anchor  at  10:40  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  toward  Roanoke  River.  At  11  a.  m.  was  ordered  to  take  jiosi- 
tion  on  the  starboard  side  of  the  Miami ,  when  we  proceeded  down  the 
sound,  the  ram  following.  From  meridian  to  4  p.  m. :  Proceeding  down 
the  sound  in  company  with  the  Miami  and  Ceres,  the  rebel  ram  follow¬ 
ing.  At  10:30  p.  m.  proceeded  down  to  Croatan  Sound,  following  the 
Miami. 

May  1. — From  G  to  8  p.  m.:  At  anchor  off  Roanoke  Island.  Received 
information  of  the  ram  being  at  Alligator  River. 

May  2. — At  11a.  m.  stopped  in  Albemarle  Sound  about  a  mile  above 
Croatan  light.  At  11:30  a.  m.  brought  a  sail  boat  alongside  containing 
refugees  from  East  Lake,  Alligator  River,  who  reported  that  the  rebel 
ram  had  returned  up  the  sound  in  company  with  a  steamer  and  several 
barges  loaded  with  corn. 

May  5. — At  3  p.  m.  flagship  made  signal.  Weighed  anchor  and 
proceeded  up  the  Albemarle  Sound,  following  the  flagship.  From  4  to 
6  p.m.:  Proceeding  up  the  sound,  following  the  flagship.  Saw  near 
the  Roanoke  River  three  rebel  steamers,  viz,  the  ram,  Cotton  Plant, 
and  Bombshell;  the  latter  was  captured  from  us  at  the  fall  of  Plymouth. 
At  4:30  the  ram  opened  fire  on  the  fleet.  Went  to  quarters  and  steamed 
rapidly  toward  them  and  opened  on  the  ram  with  rifled  100-pounder  at 
long  range.  At  5  p.  m.  the  Bombshell  surrendered  to  the  fleet.  The 
fleet  continued  nearing  the  ram  and  firing  as  fast  as  possible.  At  5:30 
the  steamer  Sassacus  received  a  shot  from  the  ram  which  disabled  her; 
she  withdrew  ti  om  the  action.  The  whole  fleet  was  now  firing  very 
rapidly  at  the  ram,  hitting  her  nearly  every  shot,  but  apparently  with 
no  effect.  From  6  to  8  p.  m. :  The  rebel  ram  commenced  to  retreat  by 
steaming  toward  the  Roanoke  River.  The  commodore  then  ordered 
the  fleet  to  advance  in  line  and  endeavor  to  cut  off  her  retreat.  We 
steamed  ahead  rapidly  and  soon  took  the  advance,  followed  closely  by 
the  Commodore  Hull,  keeping  the  ram  on  our  starboard  beam.  We 
kept  up  a  steady  fire  with  solid  shot  from  the  100-pounder  rifle  at  close 
range.  Ran  ahead  and  across  the  bows  of  the  ram,  making  a  complete 
circuit  around  her.  At  7 :45  the  ram  had  reached  the  mouth  of  the 
Roanoke  River  in  spite  of  our  exertions  to  prevent  her.  At  7:50 
ceased  firing  and  anchored  oft'  the  mouth  of  the  Poanoke  River. 
Expended  17  10-pound  charges  and  17  solid  shot.

Letter  from  Major-General  Whiting ,  C.  S.  Army,  to  the  British  acting 
consul  at  Charleston,  S.  C.,  regarding  the  blockade-running  schooner 
Rarkaway. 


Headquarters  District  of  the  Cape  Fear, 

Wilmington ,  May  11,  1863. 

Sir  :  I  have  received  your  letter  of  this  date  relating  to  the  schooner 
Rarkaway,  alleged  to  belong  to  a  British  subject,  engaged  in  running 
the  blockade,  and  seized  in  this  port  by  the  military  authorities  of  the 
Confederate  States  of  America. 

I  am  not  aware  that  my  Government  has  recognized  you  as  the 
representative  of  her  Britannic  Majesty.  Her  Britannic  Majesty’s 
Government  has  certainly  not  recognized  the  Government  of  the  Con¬ 
federate  States.  I  decline,  therefore,  to  discuss  the  subject  with  you 
or  to  release  the  vessel,  but  will  forward  your  communication  to  the 
Secretai'y  of  State  and  await  orders. 

In  the  meantime,"  as  her  Britannic  Majesty’s  Government  does  not 
recognize  the  jurisdiction  of  the  Confederate  States  here,  and  the 
United  States  Government  claims  it,  perhaps  it  would  be  as  well  to 
apply  to  the  latter. 

Very  respectfully, 


W.  H.  C.  Whiting, 

Major-  General. 


H.  P.  Walker, 

Rer  Majesty's  Acting  Consul  for  the  Sta  tes 

of  North  Carolina  and  South  Carolina,  at  Charleston.

[Enclosure.] 

Halifax,  N.  C.,  September  12, 1863. 

*  *  *  After  a  careful  examination  of  a  chart  of  the  coasts  of  North 

and  South  Carolina,  I  am  persuaded  that  you  will  concur  with  me  in 
thinking  an  attack  upon  the  forts  defending  the  entrances  to  the  Cape 
Fear  Eiver  by  ironclads  impracticable  for  months  to  come. 

Within  a  week,  in  all  probability,  we  shall  have  the  equinoctial  gale, 
after  which  the  weather  becomes  unsettled  and  is  frequently  tempes¬ 
tuous. 

From  Bald  Head  light,  at  the  southwest  and  principal  entrance*  of 
the  Cape  Fear,  to  Bull’s  Bay,  in  South  Caroliua,  the  first  harbor  in  a 
southerly  direction  for  any  but  vessels  of  a  light  draft  is  a  distance  of 
GO  miles,  and  from  New  Inlet  entrance  to  Beaufort,  N.  C.,  the  nearest  in 
that  direction  of  sufficient  draft  of  water  is  80  miles. 

The  Lronsides  may  ride  out  the  gales  which  spring  up  so  suddenly  and 
with  such  force  in  the  vicinity  of  Frying  Pan  Shoals,  but  the  monitors 
can  not,  and  therefore  would  scarce  venture  an  attack  during  the  forth¬ 
coming  season. 

If  the  south  end  of  Smith’s  Island  be  as  much  neglected  as  was  the 
south  end  of  Morris  Island,  the  enemy  may  transport  guns  to  and  erect 
batteries  upon  it;  but  I  think  that  General  Whiting  lias  not  overlooked 
the  importance  of  that  position. 

[Endorsement.] 


September  28,  1863. 

Returned  with  acknowledgments  to  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy. 
General  Whiting  concurs  in  reference  to  naval  attack,  but  dreads  effort 
to  assail  by  laud. 

J.  A.  Seddon, 

Secretary.

bar  or  rip  than  at  New  Inlet.

The  naval  command  at  Drewry’s  Bluff,  composed  of  seamen  and 
marines,  is  in  a  high  state  of  efficiency,  and  the  river  obstructions  are 
believed  to  be  sufficient,  in  connection  with  the  shore  and  submarine 
batteries,  to  prevent  the  passage  of  the  enemy’s  ships. 

An  active  force  is  employed  on  submarine  batteries  and  torpedoes.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  Secretary  of  War,  request¬ 
ing  the  opening  of  the  obstructions  at  Drewry's  Bluff,  for  the  passage 
of  the  C.  S.  steamers  Richmond  and  Fredericksburg. 

Navy  Department,  C.  S.  A., 

Richmond,  January  2,1864. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  request  that  orders  may  be  given  to  the 
engineer  officers  in  charge  of  the  construction  of  the  obstructions  in  the 
James  Eiver  to  open  those  at  Drewry’s  Bluff  sufficiently  to  permit  the 
passage  of  the  ironclads  Richmond  and  Fredericksburg.  I  deem  it  highly 
important  to  the  defenses  of  the  river  that  these  vessels  should  be  below 
the  obstructions. 

I  beg  leave  to  suggest  for  your  consideration  the  expediency  of  con¬ 
structing  a  suitable  caisson  to  hold  in  readiness  to  be  sunk  in  the  space 
made  for  these  vessels,  and  which  can  be  made  by  the  time  the 
obstructions  are  removed. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  E.  Mallory, 

Secretary  Navy. 

Hon.  James  A.  Seddon, 

Secretary  of  War. 


Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Cooke,  C.  S.  Navy, 
to  superintend  the  completion  of  the  C.  S.  S.  Albemarle. 

Navy  Department,  C.  S.  A,, 

Richmond,  January  15,1864. 

Sir:  You  have  been  ordered  to  Halifax  to  take  charge  of  the  com¬ 
pletion  of  the  gunboat  Albemarle.  This  charge  has  been  made  upon 
representations  to  the  Department  that  your  acquaintance  with  the 
people  and  resources  of  the  district  in  which  the  vessel  is  being  built 
renders  you  peculiarly  qualified  for  the  duty,  and  because  the  Depart¬ 
ment  is  anxious  to  adopt  any  measure  which  looks  to  an  early  completion 
of  the  vessel. 

To  one  so  familiar  with  the  whole  subject  it  is  needless  to  dwell  upon 
the  great  importance  of  the  most  prompt  and  energetic  action  in  getting 
the  vessel  ready,  and  you  are  expected  to  leave  nothing  undone  to  effect 
this  object.  That  your  judgment  may  be  untrammeled,  you  are  relieved 
from  duty  under  Flag-Officer  Lynch,  and  will  correspond  directly  with 
this  Department. 

Notwithstanding  it  is  reported  that  there  are  as  many  men  employed  as 
can  work  to  advantage,  I  have  this  day  sent  Acting  Constructor  Graves 
with  21  men  to  report  to  you,  believing  that  their  services  will  be 


800 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


important.  You  have  been  requested  to  keep  these  men  together,  not 
only  with  the  view  of  stimulating  the  work  on  the  vessel  by  their  com¬ 
petition  with  those  already  there,  but  that  they  may  return  here  at  the 
proper  time. 

You  are  expected  to  command  the  Albemarle ,  and  you  will  push  on 
all  parts  of  the  work  upon  and  for  her  as  far  as  practicable  at  the  same 
time.  Consult  with  Constructor  Graves,  who  has  charge  of  the  work, 
and  read  him  so  much  of  this  letter  as  you  may  deem  necessary  to 
secure  his  energetic  cooperation. 

Your  ladders,  gratings,  hatches,  racks,  hammock  cloths,  hooks,  eye- 
bolts,  magazine  work,  etc.,  should  all  be  looked  after  at  once.  Your 
guns  will  be  got  in  readiness  here. 

You  will  make  a  weekly  report  of  your  progress,  and  you  will  not 
hesitate  to  adopt  any  measure  necessary  to  the  prompt  completion  of 
the  work. 

Under  Constructor  Porter’s  arrangement  with  Mr.  Elliott,  employing 
him  and  his  force  by  the  day,  it  is  clearly  his  interest  to  protract  the 
work,  a  circumstance  which  you  will  not  fail  to  note. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Commander  James  W.  Cooke,  C.  S.  Navy, 

Halifax ,  N.  C.

Unofficial  letter  from  Commander  Wood,  C.  S.  Navy,  to  Commander 
Jones,  C.  S.  Navy,  regarding  naval  affairs. 

Richmond,  February  26,  1864. 

My  Dear  Captain:  Many  thanks  for  your  kind  expressions  and 
wishes.  I  hardly  deserve  them.  As  regards  promotion,  I  have  opposed 
it;  one  step  at  a  time;  the  affair  does  not  deserve  it.  Simms  has  been 
relieved  from  his  orders.  I  don’t  know  who  takes  his  place. 

I  am  sorry  to  learn  such  accounts  from  Mobile.  The  admiral  reports 
his  inability  to  move  the  Tennessee ,  his  want  of  men,  officers,  etc.  The 
ship,  however,  must  be  gotten  over  the  bar  if  possible;  take  everything 
out  of  her  and  try  it. 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  801 


The  two  vessels  on  the  Roanoke  and  Neuse  are  coining  on  rapidly 
and  will  soon  be  ready  lor  work.  Cooke  commands  one,  Loyall  the 
other.  An  effort  should  now  be  made  to  g'et  possession  of  the  waters 
of  North  Carolina.  The  enemy  as  yet  have  no  ironclads  in  the  sounds. 

°n  this  river  we  have  three  vessels  ready,  or  nearly  so.  The  last, 
Graves’,  is  a  line  ship,  with  8  inches  of  iron  forward,  G  aft  and  on  broad¬ 
side.  Brooke  designs  giving  her  one  8-inch  rifle,  two  7-iuch,  and  one 
XI  inch  smoothbore.  She  has  an  engine  of  nearly  500  horses.  I  hope 
before  long  they  will  move  down  the  river. 

Wilkinson  is  going  out  to  bring  Carter’s  vessel  (Coquette).  Whether 
Carter  will  return  to  Europe  or  not  is  not  settled.  Mitchell,  Brooke, 
Porter,  Williamson,  Pegrara,  and  myself  are  on  a  board  to  report  upon 
the  best  form  of  construction,  shield,  battery,  etc.,  for  ironclads.  At 
your  leisure  (if  you  have  any)  let  me  know  your  views. 

Morris  has  taken  Barney’s  place  on  the  Florida, ;  the  latter  is  sick. 
The  prospect  of  getting  more  ships  out  is  not  encouraging.  The  cor¬ 
vettes  in  France  will  be  ready  in  the  spriug. 

Remember  me  kindly  to  Simms  and  wife. 

Yours,  truly, 


J.  Taylor  Wood.

Extract  from  the  report  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  regarding  the  loss 
of  the  steamer  Helen ,  March  10,  1864. 

Intelligence  has  reached  the  Department  of  the  loss  at  sea  in  a  gale 
of  wind,  on  the  10th  of  March  last,  of  the  steamer  Helen ,  from  Charles¬ 
ton  for  Nassau,  with  a  cargo  of  cotton.  She  was  commanded  and 
manned  by  naval  officers  and  men,  but  two  of  whom  are  known  to  have 
escaped.  Her  commander,  Lieutenant  Porcher,  was  one  of  the  most 
efficient  officers  of  the  service,  and  his  loss  is  deeply  deplored. 


Letter  from  the  Secretary,  of  the  Navy  to  the  Secretary  of  War  regarding 
the  delayed  transportation  of  iron  plates  for  vessels  under  construction 
at  Kinston  and  Halifax,  N.  C. 

Navy  Department,  C.  S.  A„ 

Richmond,  March  11,  1864. 

Sir  :  I  beg  leave  to  call  your  attention  to  the  enclosed  extracts  from 
letters  of  Flag-Officer  Lynch  and  Lieutenant  Loyall,  C.  S.  Navy,  dated 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  803 

the  8th  instant,  and  respectfully  request  that  instructions  may  be  given 
to  have  the  iron  plates  referred  to  transported  to  Kinston  and  Halifax 
at  the  earliest  moment.  The  gunboats  at  those  points  are  completed1 
with  the  exception  ot  the  iron  plating,  and  the  mechanics  are  delayed 
in  their  work  waiting  for  it.  The  work  upon  these  vessels  has  been 
delayed  for  months  by  the  want  of  transportation,  and  now  that  they 
are  very  near  completion  I  respectfully  urge  that  no  further  delay  on 
this  account  may  be  had,  for  unless  completed  at  an  early  day  the 
detention  of  the  boat  at  Kinston  by  the  fall  of  the  Neuse  River  will  be 
disastrous  and  may  cause  her  destruction.  The  subject  is  of  so  much 
importance  that  I  suggest  the  detail  by  the  Quartermaster-General  of 
an  officer  specially  charged  with  it. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Hon.  James  A.  Seddon, 

Secretary  of  War.

Extract  from  Flag-Officer  Lynch’s  letter  of  the  8th  instant  to  Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Fourteen  carloads  of  plate  iron  arrived  last  evening,  and  for  a  week 
past  we  have  had  two  carloads  waiting  transportation  to  Kinston  and 
Halifax.  The  whole  rolling  capacity  of  the  road,  except  passenger 
trains,  has  been  monopolized  by  the  Army,  and  I  fear  the  completion 
of  the  gunboats  at  those  places  will  be  delayed.  Besides  my  own  occa¬ 
sional  visits  to  the  depot,  a  reliable  officer  is  detailed  to  be  there  twice 
every  day  and  apply  for  and  report  the  prospects  of  obtaining  trans¬ 
portation.  The  rights  of  the  Navy  are  not  respected,  its  wants  are 
utterly  disregarded,  and  it  is  in  the  power  of  an  acting  assistant  quar¬ 
termaster  to  cause  our  transportation  to  be  set  aside  at  will.  The 
importance  of  speedily  completing  the  ironclad  on  the  Neuse  and  Roan¬ 
oke  does  not  seem  to  be  comprehended. 


Extract  from  Lieutenant  Loyall’s  letter  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  of  the  same  date. 

Flag-Officer  Lynch  telegraphs  me  to-day  that  he  can  not  procure 
transportation  for  me  from  Wilmington.  We  are  in  want  of  it  here.

Navy  Department,  0.  S.  A., 

Richmond,  March  11,  1864. 

Sir:  You  are  detailed  for  special  duty  under  the  immediate  orders  of 
this  Department  at  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  and  on  the  Cape  Fear  River  and 
its  entrances.  You  will  without  delay  establish  and  preserve  in  opera¬ 
tion  such  lights  at  Bald  Head,  the  Mound,  and  at  other  places  as,  in 
your  judgment,  will  best  aid  trading  vessels  to  enter  and  depart  from 
the  Cape  Fear  River.  In  connection  with  this  subject  you  will  estab¬ 
lish  day  and  night  signals  and  sailing  directions  for  all  such  vessels; 
determine  from  time  to  time  any  changes  in  the  depth  of  water  of  the 
entrances;  examine  the  qualifications  of  pilots  and  give  them  certili- 
cates  of  such  examinations.  You  will  also  exercise  such  a  general 
supervision  over  vessels  engaged  in  trade,  and  on  board  of  which  cotton 
is  being  shipped,  as  will  enable  you  to  determine  whether,  in  character 
and  condition,  as  well  of  the  vessel  as  of  the  officers  and  crews,  they 
justify  the  shipment  by  them  of  Government  cotton.  You  will  also 
establish  such  port  regulations  necessary  to  facilitate  and  exclusively 
connected  with  the  exportation  of  cotton  and  importation  of  Govern¬ 
ment  supplies,  and  not  inconsistent  with  the  rights  of  the  State  of 
North  Carolina,  as  you  may  deem  necessary.  Your  duties  are  very 
important,  and  you  will  on  all  proper  occasions  invite  the  cordial  coop¬ 
eration  of  the  military  authorities  in  command.  You  will  be  allowed  a 
writer  at  a  fair  per  diem  compensation,  and  will  keep  a  log  or  record 
of  your  proceedings,  embracing  all  arrivals  and  departures,  wrecks, 
movements  of  the  enemy,  and  other  matters  of  public  interest  immedi¬ 
ately  connected  with  your  duties,  reporting  to  and  corresponding  with 
this  Department. 

In  addition  to  the  duties  before  mentioned,  you  will  procure  boats 
and  will  render  such  aid  in  saving  life  and  Government  stores  from 
stranded  vessels  as  your  means  and  opportunities  may  admit.  To  aid 
in  the  execution  of  these  duties,  I  have  requested  the  Secretary  of  War 
to  order  a  transfer  of  such  men  as  you  may  require  from  the  military 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


805 


force  at  or  near  Wilmington ;  and  I  have  supposed  that  20  men  for 
your  lights  and  signals  and  50  for  other  duty  would  meet  your 
wants,  and  you  will  designate  the  men  you  require.  The  agent  of  this 
Department  at  Wilmington  will  import  for  you  oil  and  such  other 
necessary  articles  as  you  may  need  and  as  you  may  not  be  able  to  pro¬ 
cure  in  the  Confederacy,  and  you  are  requested  to  enter  upon  your 
duties  at  once,  prosecute  them  with  vigor,  and  promptly  to  call  upon 
the  Department  ior  all  necessary  aid.  Vessels  departing  from  Wil¬ 
mington  will  carryout  at  least  half  their  cargo  on  Government  account, 
and  hence  the  importance  of  facilitating  them  in  every  possible  manner, 
and  of  seeing  that  this  cargo  is  not  embarked  in  inefficient  carriers, 
whether  inefficient  from  the  character  of  the  vessel,  officers,  or  crew. 
You  will,  of  course,  confer  freely  with  the  military  authorities,  do  all  in 
your  power  to  secure  harmony  of  action,  especially  on  the  subject  of 
lights  and  signals,  and  guard  against  the  use  or  abuse  of  them  by  the 
enemy.  On  your  arrival  at  Wilmington  you  will  exhibit  your  instruc¬ 
tions  to  the  military  officers  in  command. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  E.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Lieutenant  John  Wilkinson,  C.  S.  Navy, 

Richmond ,  Va. 


Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  War  to  commanding  generals  regarding  the 
transfer  of  men  from  the  Army  to  the  Navy. 

Eichmond,  Va.,  March  22,  1864. 

General:  To  man  efficiently,  and  at  once,  the  vessels  of  the  Navy, 
it  has  become  necessary  to  transfer  1,200  men  from  the  armies.  To  this 
end  the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy  has  detailed  officers  with 
instructions  to  proceed  to  the  headquarters  of  each  army  for  the  pur¬ 
pose  of  selecting  and  designating  the  men  so  to  be  transferred.  From 
the  Army  of  Northern  Virginia,  not  including  General  Elzey’s  com¬ 
mand,  390  men  will  be  designated,  whom  you  are  requested  to  transfer 
to  the  Navy  upon  the  written  request  of  the  naval  officer  sent  to  your 
command,  and  under  his  direction  to  send  them  to  Eichmond. 

You  will  please  forward  a  list  of  the  men  so  transferred  to  this  office 
without  delay. 

By  command  of  the  Secretary  of  War: 

S.  Cooper, 

Adjutant  and  Inspector  General. 

General  E.  E.  Lee,

Unofficial  letter  from  Lieutenant  Minor ,  C.  S.  Navy ,  to  Commander  Jones 
C.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  various  officers  and  their  commands. 

Naval  Ordnance  Works, 

Richmond ,  Va.,  March  23,  1864. 

My  Dear  Sir:  *  *  *  There  is  but  little  navy  news  afloat.  Cap¬ 
tain  Page  was  selected,  I  hear,  by  the  President  to  command  all  the 
heavy  batteries  at  Mobile.  You  know  that  he  has  been  made  a  briga¬ 
dier-general,  1  suppose.  S.  S.  Lee  gives  up  Drewry’s  Bluff  to  Major 
Terrett,  of  the  Marines,  and  takes  Page’s  place  at  Charlotte.  I  hear 
he  does  not  fancy  it  much.  The  sailors  from  the  bluff  will  man  the 
ironclad  Fredericksburg,  commanded  by  Frank  Shepperd.  She  is  now 
fitting  out  at  Rocketts.  Wood  will  probably  see  service  in  her,  with 
other  vessels  under  his  command.  His  last  affair  at  New  Berne  was 
the  feature  in  the  attack,  and  though  not  attended  with  all  the  results 
he  had  cause  to  expect,  still  it  was  a  gallant  act,  well  planned  and 
boldly  executed.  He  is  surely  one  of  our  rising  men,  and  I  say  God¬ 
speed  to  him.  “Dave”  made  an  attempt  on  the  Minnesota  not  long 
since  with  his  torpedo,  but  it  failed,  though  it  was  not  his  fault.  Webb, 
Read,  Alexander,  Glassell,  and  some  of  our  other  fellows  are  looked  for 
by  the  next  flag  of  truce.  They  have  had  a  hard  time  of  it,  and  I  hear 
that  Glassed  was  at  first  rather  harshly  treated.  You  know  that  he  has 
been  made  a  commander,  and  deservedly  so,  I  say.  John  Wilkinson 
has  charge  of  the  blockade  runners  at  Wilmington.  Lyuch  and  Whiting, 
you  know,  had  a  blow  up  there,  and  I  hear  that  the  President  had  them 
both  here  for  a  while.  Bad  boys,  to  be  growling  in  school !  Ben  Loyall 
commands  the  ironclad  Neitse,  of  two  6.4s,  at  Kinston,  N.  C.  Cooke  has 
the  Albemarle,  a  similar  vessel,  at  Halifax,  N.  C.  No  one  has  yet  been 
ordered  to  the  Virginia  here.  She  will  soon  be  ready  for  her  officers  and 
is  perhaps  the  best  and  most  reliable  ironclad  in  the  service.  If  you 
were  not  on  more  important  duty,  I  am  inclined  to  believe  that  you 
would  have  command  of  her.  Captain  Matt.  Maury  writes  to  me,  under 
date  of  January  21,  that  we  have  nothiug  to  look  for  from  England  that 
money  can’t  buy.  His  letter  is  rather  gloomy  in  its  tone.  Charley 
Morris  has  the  Florida,  Barney  being  sick.  William  L.  Maury  had 
asked  to  be  relieved  from  the  Georgia  on  the  score  of  id  health.  Bul¬ 
loch  is  still  doing  good  service  in  England  and  France.  Bob  Carter 
lately  brought  the  navy  steamer  Coquette  into  Wilmington  with  a  cargo 
composed  of  two  fine  marine  engines,  etc.  He  goes  out  in  her  again  to- 
Bermuda.  Maffitt  commands  the  blockade  [runner]  Florrie ,  but  I  see 
by  a  late  Northern  paper  that  he  had  to  put  into  Halifax,  N.  S.,  for 
repairs.  Murdaugh  at  last  accounts  was  in  Paris. 

Speaking  of  Halifax  reminds  me  of  our  late  expedition,  which,  I  sup¬ 
pose  you  have  heard,  failed  through  the  treachery  of  a  Canadian  who 
was  in  our  secret.  We  worked  hard  and  had  victory,  and  such  a  vic¬ 
tory,  almost  in  our  grasp  when  the  chicken-hearted  fellow,  alarmed  at 


NORTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


807 


the  ultimate  bearing  which  our  success  would  have  on  his  individual 
fortunes  and  fearing  to  lose  his  high  position,  with  exile  and  perhaps 
a  long  imprisonment,  informed  on  us,  and  just  as  we  were  about  to 
embark  for  Johnson’s  Island  to  board  the  Michigan  and  under  her  guns 
to  compel  a  surrender  of  the  garrison,  with  afterthoughts  of  a  short 
but  very  brilliant  cruise  on  the  lake,  the  storm  burst  over  us,  and  with 
Yankees  and  John  Bull  both  on  the  lookout  for  us  our  raid  was  over, 
and  our  poor  fellows  still  hard  and  fast  in  the  bay  of  Sandusky! 
******* 

Van  Zandt  is  here,  en  route  for  Selma.  Where  we  are  to  get  officers 
for  the  ironclads  is  beyond  my  ken.  Tidball  says  we  will  have  to 
organize  the  Provisional  Navy,  but  this  will  hardly  officer  the  ships. 
There  is  no  talk  of  promotion,  and  very  few  officers  seem  either  to  think 
of  or  care  for  it.  All  hands  seem  to  look  forward  to  an  early  peace 
(though  I  can  hardly  see  a  glimmer  of  if)  for  the  creation  of  a  Navy, 
forgetting  that  war  is  the  time  to  create  a  love  for  the  service  which 
will  make  it  popular  in  peace,  and  I  begin  to  fear  that  our  opportunity 
has  passed  and  unimproved,  though  I  hope  not,  for  we  have  the  ele¬ 
ments  of  a  splendid  navy  in  the  Confederacy,  and  it  only  requires  zeal, 
pluck,  and  dash  to  bring  it  to  the  surface.

Very  truly,  yours, 

[Commander  Catesby  ap  It.  Jones.]

Report  of  the  Colonel  Commandant  C.  S.  Marine  Corps,  submitting  a 

return  of  his  command. 

Headquarters  C.  S.  Marine  Corps, 

Richmond ,  Va.,  April  28, 1864. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  herewith  a  return  of  the  Marine 
Corps,  showing  its  strength  and  disposition  on  the  31st  ultimo.  Since 
that  date  some  addition  lias  been  made  to  its  strength  by  recruits,  with 
a  fair  prospect  of  further  increase. 

The  marines  are  on  duty  with  the  naval  forces  at  Mobile,  Savannah, 
Charleston,  Richmond,  and  at  Drewry’s  Bluff,  on  the  James  River. 
There  is  also  a  marine  guard  at  sea  onboard  of  the  C.  S.  S.  Alabama. 

The  discipline  and  efficiency  of  the  corps  are  such  as  to  reflect  much 
credit  upon  the  captains  and  subordinate  officers.  In  this  connection, 
I  beg  leave  to  enclose  herewith  a  copy  of  a  letter*  addressed  to  me  by 
Colonel  J.  Taylor  Wood,  who  commanded  the  expedition  which  boarded 
and  captured  the  U.  S.  armed  steamer  Under  writer  off  New  Berne,  N. 
C.,  under  the  fire  of  the  enemy’s  shore  batteries.  Captain  [Thomas  S.] 
Wilson  therein  referred  to  commanded  a  detachment  of  marines,  and 
in  boarding  the  Underwriter  had  1  man  killed  and  3  wounded. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Lloyd  J.  Beall, 

Colonel,  Commanding  C.  8.  Marine  Corps. 

Hon.  S.  R.  Mallory, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Letter  of  General  Beauregard ,  G.  S.  Army,  to  Major-General  Hoke,  C.  8. 

Army,  regarding  proposed  movements  of  the  G.  8.  8.  Albemarle. 

Hdqrs.  op  North  Carolina  and  South  Virginia, 

Kinston,  N.  G.,  May  1,  1864. 

General:  *  *  *  There  are  three  methods  of  attacking  New 
Berne:  First,  by  surprise  and  assault;  second,  by  assault  without  sur¬ 
prise;  third,  by  regular  approaches.  The  first  and  last  methods  are 
impracticable  at  the  present,  for  the  enemy  must  be  aware  of  your 
intentions,  and  we  have  not  sufficient  time  to  execute  the  last;  the  sec¬ 
ond  plan  is,  therefore,  the  only  one  which  can  now  be  carried  into  effect. 
It  can,  however,  be  made  to  partake  more  or  less  of  a  surprise,  and 
with  the  assistance  of  the  ironclad  gunboat  Albemarle  from  Plymouth, 
the  attack  should  meet  with  complete  success.  I  regret  to  say  that  no 
hope  need  be  entertained  of  the  cooperation  of  the  ironclad  gunboat 
now  aground  in  the  Neuse  near  this  place,  for  it  is  not  probable  it  can 
be  got  afloat  again  or  be  made  to  pass  over  the  bars  and  sand  banks 
below  its  present  position  without  a  considerable  rise  in  the  river,  an 
event  which  is  not  likely  to  take  place  until  next  rainy  season.  The 
attack  on  New  Berne  should  be  so  made  as  to  capture  or  destroy  the 
separate  forces  of  the  enemy  before  they  could  be  concentrated.  For 
that  purpose  the  Albemarle,  immediately  after  having  sunk  the  two  or 
three  wooden  gunboats  aiding  in  the  defense  of  the  town,  should 
destroy  the  long  bridge  across  the  Trent,  so  as  to  isolate  the  troops 
now  stationed  on  its  south  side.  The  Albemarle  should  then  take  such 
a  position  in  the  Neuse  as  to  cut  off  from  New  Berne  the  communica¬ 
tion  of  the  forces  on  the  north  side  of  that  river,  and  it  should  also 
cooperate  with  General  Hoke’s  attack  by  taking  in  flank  and  rear  the 
works  and  lines  extending  from  the  Neuse  to  the  Trent,  defending  the 
direct  approach  to  the  city. 

*  *  *  #  #  #  * 
Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  T.  Beauregard, 
General,  Gommanding. 

Major-General  R.  F.  Hoke, 

Gommanding  Expedition  against  New  Berne.

Letter  from  Major-General  Hoke ,  G.  8.  Army ,  to  Lieutenant  Minor ,  G.  8. 
JSTavy,  proposing  cooperative  movement  to  Trent  River. 


May  3, 1864. 

Captain:  I  have  just  gotten  a  dispatch  from  Commodore  Pinkney. 
Cooke  found  the  boat  to  do  a  great  deal  better  than  he  had  expected, 
and  will  cooperate.  Will  be  around  on  Thursday.  I  think  you  and 
your  party  could  be  of  service  in  this  case,  and  suggest,  if  you  think 
the  time  can  be  taken  in  accordance  with  orders  from  the  Secretary  of 
the  Navy,  that  you  take  them  to  Free  Bridge,  on  Trent  River,  15  miles 
from  Kinston,  on  the  Upper  Trent  road,  whei  e  they  can  be  crossed,  and 
proceed  down  to  the  point  where  they  may  be  wanted.  Inform  me  of 
any  move  you  take  by  my  courier,  and  which  will  connect  with  me  from 
Kinston  on  the  Upper  Trent  road. 

Yours, 


R.  F.  Hoke, 
Major-  General. 


Captain  Minor, 

Commanding  Boat  Party.
